How long should my replies be?

courses.name: Foundations of Roleplay
courses.blurb: Where everyone starts: actions and speech, giving your partner something to answer, and matching their rhythm.

lessons.title: Actions and speech
lessons.lecture: Every good line has two parts: what your character does, and what they say. Actions go in *asterisks*, in the present tense. Speech goes beside them. Put the two together and your partner can see the moment as well as hear it.
points: One clear action and one line of speech beat three vague ones.
Write in the present tense: *leans closer*, not *leaned closer*.
Only ever write your own character. Their body and their choices belong to them.
lessons.weak: hi *smiles* how are you
lessons.strong: *slides onto the stool beside you and nudges my glass your way* You look like someone who needs a better drink.
lessons.why: A specific action, a line with some personality, and an easy way in.

drill.goal: Pair a clear *action* with a line of speech in every reply, in the present tense, and never write what your partner does.
drill.partner: Answer naturally and leave them room to act.
drill.coach: Each line that pairs a clear *action* with speech, in the present tense, without deciding anything for the partner, adds 25. Mark down lines that write the partner's actions.

lessons.title: Give them a hook
lessons.lecture: The best roleplayers are generous. Every reply ends with something your partner can grab: a question, a touch, a choice, a dare. If your line could be the last line of the scene, it is not finished yet.
points: End on something to answer: a question, an invitation, a touch that asks for a reaction.
Offer choices. "The couch or the balcony?" lets them steer.
Never end on a full stop that closes the door.
lessons.weak: *sits down on the couch and drinks the wine*
lessons.strong: *sits down and pats the cushion beside me, holding out your glass* Come here. Tell me the worst thing you did today.
lessons.why: It invites them closer and hands them a question they want to answer.

drill.goal: End every line with a hook your partner can answer: a question, an invitation, a choice, or a touch that asks for a reaction.
drill.partner: Answer their hooks with enthusiasm. When a line gives you nothing to answer, keep your reply short.
drill.coach: Each line that ends with a clear hook (a question, an invitation, a choice, a touch that asks for a reaction) adds 25.

lessons.title: Match their rhythm
lessons.lecture: Roleplay is a dance, and the length of your reply is part of the step. Two quick lines answered with a wall of text stops the music. A rich paragraph answered with one word feels like a shrug. Match their length and energy first, then lead from there.
points: Short reply? Answer short and punchy.
Long, detailed reply? Give them detail back.
Match the energy first, then nudge it where you want it to go.
lessons.weak: ok
lessons.strong: *takes your hand before you can change your mind* Lead the way, trouble.
lessons.why: Their quick, playful energy, matched and handed straight back.

drill.goal: Match the length and energy of each of your partner's replies: short for short, rich for rich.
drill.partner: Vary your reply length on purpose: some quick one-liners, some longer, detailed paragraphs.
drill.coach: Each line that roughly matches the length and energy of the partner's last reply adds 25. Mark down a wall of text after a one-liner, or a few words after a rich paragraph.

courses.name: Consent and Care
courses.blurb: The sexiest skills in roleplay: talking first, checking in without killing the mood, and taking care of each other after.

lessons.title: Talk first
lessons.lecture: Before the first kiss, two minutes out of character saves a hundred awkward moments. What are you into? What is off the table? What is the safeword? Asking is not unsexy. It tells your partner you are worth trusting.
points: Out of character, in (( )): likes, limits and a safeword.
Ask about theirs as much as you share yours.
Keep it light. It is flirting with logistics.
lessons.weak: (( no limits lol, let's go ))
lessons.strong: (( Before we start: I love slow teasing and praise, no pain for me. Red to stop, yellow to slow down? What about you? ))
lessons.why: Likes, a limit, a safeword and a question, all in one friendly line.

drill.goal: Before the scene starts, agree on likes, limits and a safeword with your partner, out of character (( like this )).
drill.partner: Begin out of character in (( )). Ask about their likes, limits and a safeword, share yours, and only start the scene once you have agreed.
drill.coach: Did they cover likes, limits and a safeword, and ask about the partner's? Progress is a third for each.
drill.opening: Start out of character in (( )): say hi, and ask {you} about likes, limits and a safeword before the scene begins. Share a little about yours.

lessons.title: Check in, stay in
lessons.lecture: A check-in does not have to stop the scene. "You okay?" whispered against someone's ear is care and heat at once. Watch for a pause or a change in tone, ask softly, and then listen to the answer, whatever it is.
points: Notice the signal: a pause, a shorter reply, a tense body.
Check in, in character: soft, short and sincere.
Respect the answer. Yes means go on. Anything else means slow down.
lessons.weak: *keeps going, ignoring how quiet you have gone*
lessons.strong: *stills, hand resting on your waist* Hey. You went quiet on me. Good quiet, or should we slow down?
lessons.why: It notices, asks warmly, stays in the moment and offers an easy way out.

drill.goal: Notice when your partner hesitates, check in warmly and in character, and respect the answer.
drill.partner: Be warm and responsive, but once or twice show a small, clear hesitation: a pause, a shorter reply, a tensing. Relax when they check in kindly.
drill.coach: Progress is 50 for noticing a hesitation and 50 for a warm, in-character check-in that respects the answer.

lessons.title: Aftercare
lessons.lecture: The scene is over and someone's heart is still racing. Aftercare is how you land the plane: water, a blanket, a soft word, a question about how they feel. It is what makes people want to play with you again.
points: Slow everything down: voice, touch and pace.
Ask what they need, then give it.
Say something kind and true about the scene.
lessons.weak: ok that was fun, gtg
lessons.strong: *pulls the blanket over us both and presses a glass of water into your hand* Drink. ...How are you feeling? You were incredible.
lessons.why: Comfort, care, a real question, and praise that lingers.

drill.goal: The scene has just ended. Bring your partner down gently, with warmth, care and check-ins.
drill.partner: You are tender and a little raw after an intense scene. Let their care land, and say what you need.
drill.coach: Each line of warmth, comfort, attentive listening or a caring check-in adds 25.
drill.opening: Open just after an intense scene has ended: you're both catching your breath. Show how you feel in a few tender details and let {you} take care of you.

courses.name: Show, Don't Tell
courses.blurb: Make them feel it: bodies instead of labels, exact details instead of generic ones, and every one of the five senses.

lessons.title: Show the feeling
lessons.lecture: "I'm nervous" is a label. Shaking hands, a dry throat, a laugh that comes out too fast: that is a feeling. Your partner cannot feel a label. Show what the emotion does to the body, and let them read it.
points: Never name the emotion. Show it in the hands, the breath, the voice, the eyes.
One true physical detail is worth a paragraph of explaining.
Let your partner react to what they see, not to what you told them.
lessons.weak: *is really nervous and excited*
lessons.strong: *laughs a beat too fast and tucks my hair behind my ear, twice* So. You actually came.
lessons.why: The double tuck and the quick laugh show the nerves without ever naming them.

drill.goal: Show every feeling through the body (hands, breath, voice, eyes) and never name an emotion outright.
drill.partner: React to what their body shows you, and give them moments that stir strong feelings.
drill.coach: Each line that shows a feeling through the body without naming the emotion adds 25. Mark down named emotions like nervous, excited or turned on.

lessons.title: Specific beats general
lessons.lecture: "She looked beautiful" could be anyone, anywhere. "The red dress, the gold cuff, the scar on her lip she never hides" is one person on one night. Specific details make a scene real, and they give your partner something to notice.
points: Swap generic words (nice, hot, sexy, beautiful) for one exact detail.
The drink, the colour of a dress, the song that is playing: small facts build a world.
Details about your partner are compliments they can answer.
lessons.weak: *looks at you* you look really hot
lessons.strong: *lets my eyes follow your collar down to the open button* Charcoal suits you. So does that look you're giving me.
lessons.why: Exact details about them, and a compliment with a question hidden in it.

drill.goal: Put at least one concrete, specific detail in every line, and no generic words like nice, hot, sexy or beautiful.
drill.partner: Notice and answer their details, and give them specific things to notice about you and the place.
drill.coach: Each line with at least one concrete, specific detail and no generic adjective (nice, hot, sexy, beautiful) adds 25.

lessons.title: All five senses
lessons.lecture: Most roleplay is all eyes. Add the crackle of the fire, the smell of rain on a jacket, the taste of wine on a kiss, the heat of a hand through fabric, and the scene stops being a picture and becomes a place.
points: Sound and smell are the most forgotten, and the most powerful.
Touch is texture and temperature, not just contact.
Taste belongs to kisses, drinks and skin. Use it.
lessons.weak: *kisses you*
lessons.strong: *kisses you slowly; you taste of honeyed mead and woodsmoke, and the fire pops somewhere behind us*
lessons.why: Taste, smell and sound turn a kiss into a memory.

drill.goal: Use sight, sound, touch, smell and taste across your lines.
drill.partner: Give them rich moments for every sense to answer: scents, textures, sounds, tastes.
drill.coach: Count which of the five senses their lines have used so far. Progress is 20 for each sense used.

courses.name: 3DXChat Craft
courses.blurb: Roleplay at game speed: short lines that hit hard, emotes that land, and openers that start something.

lessons.title: Short and vivid
lessons.lecture: In game, chat moves fast and the window is small. A great 3DX line is short, punchy and alive: one strong action, one line of talk, done. Under 120 characters is the sweet spot.
points: One action, one line. Cut everything else.
Strong verbs carry short lines: *pins*, *tugs*, *murmurs*.
If it scrolls off the screen, it is too long.
lessons.weak: *walks over to you slowly and looks at you and smiles a lot* hello how are you doing tonight
lessons.strong: *tugs your collar, grinning* Took you long enough.
lessons.why: Seven words, one strong verb, and a whole mood.

drill.goal: Write short chat lines like in game, under 120 characters each, and still vivid.
drill.partner: Keep your own lines short and quick so the rhythm stays fast.
drill.coach: Each vivid line under 120 characters adds 25. Mark down long lines.

lessons.title: Emotes that land
lessons.lecture: In 3DX your emotes are your body. Write them without your name, in the present tense: *leans in*, not *Nova leans in*. One specific action reads better than a list, and an emote with speech lets them see and hear you at once.
points: No name in the emote: *leans in close*.
One specific action beats a list of three.
Emote and speech in the same line is the classic combination.
lessons.weak: *Nova walks* *Nova sits* *Nova drinks* hey
lessons.strong: *hops up on the counter beside you, swinging my legs* So whose party is this, anyway?
lessons.why: One playful action, no name, and an easy question.

drill.goal: Pair one strong, specific *emote* (no name, present tense) with speech in every line, under 200 characters.
drill.partner: Keep it fast and playful, in short chat lines.
drill.coach: Each line that pairs one strong, specific *action* (no name, present tense) with speech, under 200 characters, adds 25.

lessons.title: The opener
lessons.lecture: Every great scene starts with someone brave enough to say something. The best openers notice one specific thing, show a flash of personality, and give an easy way to answer. No "hi", no "wanna rp?". Walk in like you already belong.
points: Notice something specific about them or the moment.
Show a flash of your personality.
Make it easy to answer: a question or a playful dare.
lessons.weak: hi wanna rp?
lessons.strong: *slides into the booth across from you* That's the third drink you've sent back. Tough crowd, or waiting for someone better?
lessons.why: Specific, playful, and impossible not to answer.

drill.goal: Open with a stranger: notice something specific, show some personality, and make it easy to answer. Then keep it light.
drill.partner: You are a stranger here. Be intrigued by a good opener and cool towards a lazy one, and let them do the work at first.
drill.coach: Each line that does this adds 25: the opener notices something specific, shows some personality and is easy to answer, and each follow-up keeps it light and flirty.

courses.name: Tension and the Slow Burn
courses.blurb: Wanting is the best part: the almost-touch, push and pull, and escalating one small step at a time.

lessons.title: The almost
lessons.lecture: Cinema taught us this: the kiss is never as hot as the second before it. Hands that almost touch. A breath held. A sentence left unfinished. Learn to stop one inch short, and let the inch do the work.
points: Stop just short: the almost-touch, the almost-kiss, the almost-confession.
A pause is an action too: *doesn't answer right away*.
Make them want the next line more than you want to write it.
lessons.weak: *kisses you hard against the wall*
lessons.strong: *steps in until there's barely air between us, close enough to feel your breath... and doesn't kiss you* Not yet.
lessons.why: It promises everything and delivers nothing. Yet.

drill.goal: Build anticipation with almosts (near-touches, pauses, held looks, unfinished sentences) without rushing to the act.
drill.partner: Lean into the tension. Almost give in, but let them set the pace.
drill.coach: Each line that builds anticipation with an almost (a near-touch, a pause, a held look, an unfinished sentence) adds 25. Mark down rushing.

lessons.title: Push and pull
lessons.lecture: Tension is a rubber band. Pull closer, then pull back. A compliment, then a challenge. Lean in, then walk to the window. Every retreat makes the next advance hit twice as hard.
points: Alternate advance and retreat: closer, then away.
Pair warmth with a little challenge: "You're trouble. I like trouble."
Retreat with intent, and always leave them a reason to follow.
lessons.weak: *kisses you* *kisses you again* *kisses you more*
lessons.strong: *brushes my thumb along your jaw, then turns away to pour two drinks* You're very sure of yourself. Let's see if you've earned it.
lessons.why: A touch, then distance and a challenge: now they have to follow.

drill.goal: Alternate on purpose between moving closer and pulling back: an advance, then a retreat or a challenge.
drill.partner: Answer their pushes and pulls: chase when they retreat, hesitate when they rush.
drill.coach: Each line that clearly pushes closer or pulls back on purpose, turning the other way from the line before, adds 25.

lessons.title: One step at a time
lessons.lecture: Every line can go one step further than the last. One. A hand on the knee becomes a hand on the thigh, not a hand everywhere. Small steps keep the burn slow and give your partner the chance to say yes to each one.
points: Each reply escalates exactly one small step.
Make the step clear, so they can welcome it or slow it.
If they slow down, you slow down. That is the craft.
lessons.weak: *rips your clothes off*
lessons.strong: *rests my fingertips on the inside of your wrist, then traces slowly up to your elbow* Is this all right?
lessons.why: One small step, taken deliberately, with room to say yes.

drill.goal: Escalate exactly one small step in each line, never two, and slow down whenever your partner does.
drill.partner: Welcome small steps warmly, and cool off a little if they jump ahead.
drill.coach: Each line that escalates by exactly one small, clear step adds 25. Mark down big jumps.

courses.name: Character and Voice
courses.blurb: Sound like somebody: a voice that is yours, dialogue with subtext, and saying exactly what you want.

lessons.title: Find your voice
lessons.lecture: Close your eyes and listen to your character. Do they drawl or snap? Swear, or never? Call people darling, or mate? Pick two or three habits and keep them. A consistent voice is the difference between a character and a narrator.
points: Choose word habits: pet names, slang, how formal they are.
Choose a rhythm: short and blunt, or long and lazy.
Keep it the same from line to line.
lessons.weak: That is very nice. I would like that.
lessons.strong: Mm. Careful, sweetheart. Keep looking at me like that and I'll start getting ideas.
lessons.why: A pet name, a rhythm and a playful warning: you can hear exactly who this is.

drill.goal: Give your character a distinct voice (word choice, rhythm, a verbal habit) and keep it in every line.
drill.partner: Speak in your own distinct voice and react to theirs.
drill.coach: Each line that keeps a distinct, consistent voice (word choice, rhythm, habits) adds 25. Mark down lines that sound generic.

lessons.title: Say it without saying it
lessons.lecture: The sexiest dialogue is about something else. Talk about the wine and mean the kiss. Argue about the music and mean the attraction. Subtext lets you both pretend, and pretending is delicious.
points: Let the words say one thing and the meaning say another.
Banter is a volley: answer the meaning, not just the words.
Leave the obvious unsaid. They will hear it anyway.
lessons.weak: I want to sleep with you.
lessons.strong: *swirls the last of the wine* It's a shame to leave a good bottle unfinished. Don't you think?
lessons.why: It is about the bottle. It is not about the bottle.

drill.goal: Flirt through subtext and banter: let your words talk about one thing while meaning another.
drill.partner: Play the subtext game: answer the meaning behind their words, with banter of your own.
drill.coach: Each line with clear flirtatious subtext or banter that implies more than it says adds 25.

lessons.title: Say it out loud
lessons.lecture: Subtext is the seduction; clarity is the reward. When the moment comes, say exactly what you want, in your character's own words. Vague wants get vague answers. Specific wants get remembered.
points: Be specific: what, where and how.
Stay in your voice. A shy character can still be clear.
Confidence is attractive. So is honesty about nerves.
lessons.weak: I want you.
lessons.strong: *hooks a finger in your belt loop* I want you to kiss me slowly, right here, like we've got all night.
lessons.why: Exactly what, exactly how, in a voice with some nerve.

drill.goal: Tell your partner exactly what you want, specifically and in your character's own words.
drill.partner: Invite them to say what they want, and react strongly when they do.
drill.coach: Each line that says a specific want directly and confidently, in character, adds 25.

courses.name: The Art of Leading
courses.blurb: Quiet, certain power: clear direction, praise that lands, and reading every reaction.

lessons.title: Command presence
lessons.lecture: Power is not volume. It is certainty. Say what you want in as few words as you can, and do not ask permission for every breath. Give a calm, clear direction, then let the silence do its work.
points: Short, clear instructions: "Come here." "Look at me."
No hedging: drop maybe, if you want, kind of.
Calm beats loud. A slow voice is a strong voice.
lessons.weak: um maybe you could come over here if you want?
lessons.strong: *doesn't look up from my drink* Come here. Stand right there, where I can see you.
lessons.why: No hedging and no hurry: the calm does the commanding.

drill.goal: Lead with calm, clear, specific directions: no hedging, and no asking permission for every move.
drill.partner: Follow their lead eagerly and react to every instruction, so they can practise leading.
drill.coach: Each line with a calm, clear, specific instruction and no hedging (maybe, if you want, kind of) adds 25.

lessons.title: Praise that lands
lessons.lecture: Praise is the reward that keeps a scene alive. Make it specific and immediate: name what they did, the moment they did it. "Good" is nice. "Good, just like that, slower" is unforgettable.
points: Praise the exact thing they did.
Praise in the moment, not later.
Reward, then lead: praise followed by the next instruction.
lessons.weak: good job
lessons.strong: *tilts your chin up* Look at you, waiting so patiently. Good. Now kneel, slowly.
lessons.why: Specific praise for what they did, then the next step.

drill.goal: Reward your partner with specific, immediate praise for what they just did, then give the next direction.
drill.partner: Follow their directions and show how much their praise affects you.
drill.coach: Each line with specific praise tied to what the partner just did adds 25. Mark down generic praise like "good job".

lessons.title: Read and adjust
lessons.lecture: The best leaders watch more than they talk. A shiver, a pause, a yes that comes too quickly: these are messages. Notice them, adjust the intensity, and check in without breaking the spell. "Still with me?", said softly, is a command and a kindness at once.
points: Watch for reactions: eagerness, hesitation, overwhelm.
Adjust: more when they are eager, softer when they hesitate.
Check in, in character: "Still with me?" "Too much?"
lessons.weak: *ignores your hesitation and keeps going*
lessons.strong: *notices the way your breath catches, and slows down, thumb brushing your cheek* Still with me? Tell me.
lessons.why: It reads the moment, softens, and checks in without leaving the scene.

drill.goal: Watch your partner's reactions and adjust: more when they are eager, softer when they hesitate, with an in-character check-in.
drill.partner: Show clear reactions. Be eager most of the time, but once or twice show a flicker of hesitation: a pause, a tensing, a too-quick yes.
drill.coach: Each line that reads the partner's latest reaction and adjusts to it adds 25; after a hesitation, that means a warm, in-character check-in.

courses.name: The Art of Following
courses.blurb: Yielding is a skill: reactions that show everything, bratting with charm, and asking for what you want.

lessons.title: React out loud
lessons.lecture: When they lead, your reactions are your lines. Do not just obey: show what the order does to you. The flush, the hitched breath, the second of defiance before you give in. Someone who leads needs to see the effect.
points: Show what each order does to your body and breath.
Hesitate, then yield. The moment before is delicious.
Never answer with just "ok".
lessons.weak: ok *does it*
lessons.strong: *swallows hard and does as I'm told, cheeks burning, eyes flicking up to yours to see if it pleased you*
lessons.why: It obeys, and shows exactly what obeying does to them.

drill.goal: Show vividly what each of your partner's orders does to you: body, breath, voice, and the moment before you obey.
drill.partner: Take charge clearly so they can practise following and reacting.
drill.coach: Each line with a vivid, specific reaction to the partner's command adds 25. Mark down flat replies like "ok".

lessons.title: The playful brat
lessons.lecture: A good brat is a gift: resistance that makes the one in charge work for it, and enjoy it. Tease, talk back, drag your feet. Always with a wink, never a wall. The goal is to be caught.
points: Resist with charm: a smirk, a dare, a "make me".
Push back on small things, never on the whole scene.
Leave the door open. You want to lose.
lessons.weak: no. I don't want to.
lessons.strong: *takes my sweet time crossing the room, smirking* Oh, did you want me now? You'll have to say please.
lessons.why: Defiant and teasing, and clearly hoping to be put in their place.

drill.goal: Brat with charm: tease, talk back and make your partner work for it, always keeping the game going.
drill.partner: Take charge firmly and enjoy their bratting: answer cheek with control.
drill.coach: Each playful, charming line of resistance that invites the partner to take control, without shutting the scene down, adds 25.

lessons.title: Ask for it
lessons.lecture: Following does not mean silence. Asking, pleading, begging: done well, it hands your partner the power and tells them exactly what you want. Be specific, stay in your role, and let them decide.
points: Ask specifically: what you want, and how.
Stay in your role: ask, do not take.
Let them answer. The waiting is part of it.
lessons.weak: can we do more
lessons.strong: *looks up at you, voice small* Please... hold me there, just like that, a little longer?
lessons.why: Specific, deferential, and it hands them the choice.

drill.goal: Ask or plead for exactly what you want, specifically and in character, and let your partner decide.
drill.partner: Take charge. Make them ask for what they want, and decide whether to give it.
drill.coach: Each line that asks or pleads for something specific, in character, leaving the choice to the partner, adds 25.

courses.name: Reading the Room
courses.blurb: Advanced play: catch the hints, rescue a scene that is dying, and end a scene so they remember it.

lessons.title: Catch the cue
lessons.lecture: People rarely say what they want outright. They hint: a glance at the door, a sigh, a story about someone who kissed them in the rain. The best roleplayers hear the hint and answer it, so their partner feels seen.
points: Watch for hints: glances, pauses, half-said wishes.
Answer the hint, not just the words.
Miss one and they cool. Catch one and they light up.
lessons.weak: cool. want another drink?
lessons.strong: *catches your glance at the rain, then holds out my hand* Come on. Before it stops.
lessons.why: It hears the wish behind the words and makes it happen.

drill.goal: Your partner drops small hints about what they want. Notice them and answer them.
drill.partner: Drop subtle cues about what you want or don't (a glance, a pause, a shiver, a half-said wish) without saying it outright. Warm up when they notice; cool slightly when they miss one.
drill.coach: Each line that notices and answers one of the partner's cues adds 25.

lessons.title: Rescue a dead scene
lessons.lecture: Sometimes a scene goes flat: one-word answers, no hooks, nothing to grab. Do not push harder. Change something. A twist, a question they cannot resist, a new place, a joke. Give them a reason to wake up.
points: Change the situation: a knock at the door, a power cut, a dare.
Ask something personal or playful they will want to answer.
Make it easy to join back in.
lessons.weak: *keeps kissing you*
lessons.strong: *the lights cut out; I laugh in the dark and find your hand* Okay. Truth or dare, and you have to answer before they come back on.
lessons.why: A twist, a laugh and a game: impossible to stay flat.

drill.goal: Your partner is low on energy. Bring the scene back to life with something new: a twist, a playful question, a change of place or a game.
drill.partner: Start flat: short, low-energy replies with nothing to answer. Warm up only when they offer something new, fun or personal.
drill.coach: Each line that brings something new to revive the scene (a twist, a playful question, a change of place, humour, a game) adds 25.

lessons.title: End it well
lessons.lecture: Most scenes do not end, they just stop. Give yours an ending: a final image, a line that lands, a warm close or a hook for next time. People remember how a scene ends more than how it starts.
points: Signal the ending: slow down, soften, look back.
Land on an image or a line worth remembering.
Leave a door open: "Same time next week?"
lessons.weak: ok bye
lessons.strong: *presses a last kiss to your knuckles at the door* Next time, you choose the wine. And the trouble.
lessons.why: A tender final beat, a smile, and a promise of next time.

drill.goal: Bring the scene to a satisfying close: slow it down, land on a memorable final beat, and leave a warm hook for next time.
drill.partner: The night is winding down. Follow their lead towards a close, and answer a good ending warmly.
drill.coach: Each line that moves the scene gracefully towards its ending (slowing down, softening, a final image, a warm close or a hook for next time) adds 25.
drill.opening: Open late at night, near the end of a long, lovely evening together: the music is low and it's almost time to say goodnight. Set the moment and let {you} bring it to a close.

courses.name: The Atmosphere of Desire
courses.blurb: Build rooms and weather that make your partner lean in before anyone has touched: atmosphere as foreplay, scene by scene.

lessons.title: Sensory first draft
lessons.lecture: Atmosphere begins before anyone speaks. Choose one sense and aim it: the cold edge of a window left open, a lamp turned down to amber, cedar smoke still hanging at the door. One, not five. A single concrete detail tells your partner where they are and what the room expects of them. Stack too much and the air turns busy. Choose the sense that makes them lean in, then let it do the greeting for you.
points: Open with one sense only, chosen for its effect.
Make the detail concrete: temperature, light, a scent.
Let the room greet them before you do.
lessons.weak: *opens the door* Hey. Nice place, I guess. Come in.
lessons.strong: *pulls the door wide onto a room gone amber and cool, the window open, cedar smoke still in the air* In. Slowly. The cold will find your shoulders first, and then so will I.
lessons.why: One chosen sense, cool air and amber light, sets the room before a word of greeting.

drill.goal: In every line, open or refresh the scene with one concrete sense chosen for its effect.
drill.partner: Arrive unsure and let the room work on you. Notice the sense they set, and show it landing: a shiver, a pause, a breath.
drill.coach: Each line that sets or refreshes the scene with one concrete, chosen sense adds 25.
drill.opening: You have just come in out of the rain to {you}'s flat. Shake off your coat and wait to be told where to go.

lessons.title: Pressure and release
lessons.lecture: Tension is a stack of small details, each one a hand pressed gently on the chest. Rain quickening. The lamp turned one notch lower. The record ending and no one rising to change it. Build three, four, five. Then, at the moment your partner needs air, strip one away: open the window, pour the wine, laugh. Release is not retreat. It is proof you are listening. The room exhales, and they lean back in, hungry for the next press.
points: Stack small atmospheric details to press the tension up.
Watch for the moment they need air.
Strip one detail away, then begin again.
lessons.weak: *looks around* It's really tense in here now, isn't it? Very tense.
lessons.strong: *turns the lamp down again, lets the record run out, and does not rise to change it* Listen to that silence. Now the window, just a crack. There. Breathe. The rain comes back up when you do.
lessons.why: The stack presses, then the window and the breath let the room exhale.

drill.goal: In every line, add one pressure detail or strip one away at the moment your partner needs air.
drill.partner: Let the details land. When the pressure gets much, show it in a breath or a glance at the door, so they can release you.
drill.coach: Each line that stacks one atmospheric detail, or strips one to give air at the right moment, adds 25.

lessons.title: The room as partner
lessons.lecture: Now the room stops being scenery and starts answering. The fire gutters when they hesitate. Rain begins the instant they decide. A door clicks shut behind a confession. This is not weather for its own sake: it is the room agreeing, or warning, or urging. Set the rule, then let the place reply to what they do, never to what they feel. They will start watching the room to see what it makes of them. That is the game.
points: Let one fixed element answer what your partner does.
Answer their actions, not their feelings.
Keep the reply small: a gutters, a click, a gust.
lessons.weak: *nods* The fire is doing things. It's like it knows what's happening.
lessons.strong: *does not look away from you as the fire drops to embers, then flares when you step closer* It has decided about you. Step again. I want to see what it does when you do.
lessons.why: The fire answers their step, turning the room into a third player.

drill.goal: In every line, let one fixed element of the room answer a concrete action your partner takes.
drill.partner: Act in clear, small ways: step, reach, speak, hesitate. Do not name feelings. Give them something to answer.
drill.coach: Each line that makes one fixed room element answer a concrete action they took adds 25.

courses.name: Beyond Sight
courses.blurb: Sound, scent, taste, touch and sight, used one at a time, so every scene lands in the body and not just the brain.

lessons.title: Sound under the words
lessons.lecture: A room speaks before anyone does. The heel that clicks, the glass set down too hard, the breath you catch when I step close. Sound is the cheapest, richest furniture a scene can hold. You do not decorate it with adjectives. You simply let the room be audible, and your partner's body starts listening. Write what the place is doing, and let the doing crowd them.
points: Give the room one sound before you speak.
Use breath, fabric and footsteps, not adjectives.
Let the sound press on them, then speak.
lessons.weak: *smiles* It is really quiet and nice in here tonight.
lessons.strong: *the door clicks shut behind us, and my heel stops on the tile* Stay there. *the leather of my jacket creaks as I turn* You can hear how still you are.
lessons.why: The room becomes audible, so the stillness lands in the body.

drill.goal: In every line, place one concrete sound in the room: a breath, a footstep, fabric, glass, before or beside your speech.
drill.partner: React to the sounds they plant. Add small ones of your own: shift, breathe, set a glass down. Stay mostly quiet so the room can speak.
drill.coach: Each line that puts one concrete, audible sound into the room before or beside the speech adds 25.

lessons.title: Scent and taste
lessons.lecture: Scent is the sense that remembers. One precise note, gin and lime, salt on skin, warm leather, and the whole evening is suddenly in their mouth. Taste works the same way, sparingly. Do not list a perfume counter. Choose the single note that belongs to this moment, this person, and place it where they will lean in. Then take it away. A scent named twice is a scent they chase.
points: Choose one precise note, never a list.
Place it where they must lean in.
Name it once, then take it away.
lessons.weak: *sniffs* You smell really good, like perfume and stuff.
lessons.strong: *leans in, close enough to the pulse at your throat* Lime, and something warm under it. *pulls back before you can follow* Do not lean in yet. Let it sit on you.
lessons.why: One exact note, placed at the throat, then withdrawn so they chase it.

drill.goal: In every line, name one precise scent or taste, skin, drink or warmth, and place it close enough that they must lean in.
drill.partner: Carry a strong single note: a drink, a perfume, salt on skin. Let them find it. Lean in, then pull back, so they chase the scent.
drill.coach: Each line that names one precise scent or taste, placed close enough to lean in for, adds 25.

lessons.title: Touch without hands
lessons.lecture: Hands are the lazy way. Real touch is reported from the body that receives it: the cold of the glass against a wrist, the drag of fabric, the heat where a shoulder pressed. Write it as they feel it, never as you deliver it. Pressure, texture, temperature, from the inside of their skin. Then hold still and let the sensation do the talking. They will feel your hand long after you move it.
points: Report touch as the receiver feels it, not the giver.
Use pressure, texture and temperature, never hands alone.
Hold still and let the sensation speak.
lessons.weak: *puts my hand on your arm* I am touching your arm now, is that okay.
lessons.strong: *presses the cold glass to the inside of your wrist and leaves it there* Feel that climb your arm. *the rim bites a slow line* Do not move. Let it spread before I take it away.
lessons.why: Touch arrives as cold and pressure in their wrist, not as a hand.

drill.goal: In every line, report one touch as the receiver feels it: pressure, texture or temperature, with no hands doing the touching.
drill.partner: Describe how every touch lands on you: where it is cold, where it drags, where the heat spreads. Stay still and let it build. Do not reach back.
drill.coach: Each line that reports one touch as felt by the receiver, through pressure, texture or temperature, adds 25.

courses.name: First Lines That Open Doors
courses.blurb: The opening line is the first touch: learn to make yours specific, charged and impossible to answer with a shrug.

lessons.title: Start mid-gesture
lessons.lecture: Skip the hello. Begin with your hands already busy: a glass set down, a coat half off, a door pushed open and held. The gesture tells your partner where you stand and hands them a moment to step into. Throat-clearing is a closed door. A body mid-action is an open one. Start there, and trust them to catch up.
points: Open on a body already doing something.
Choose a gesture that shows where you stand.
Trust them to catch up. Do not explain it.
lessons.weak: *walks in* Hi. So, here I am. What do you want to do?
lessons.strong: *shoulders the door open, coat still half on, and sets two glasses on the bar between us* I saw you across the room. You looked like trouble worth pouring for.
lessons.why: The scene starts already moving, and the partner is handed a place in it.

drill.goal: Open and continue every line on a body already mid-action: a gesture underway, an object moving, a door not yet shut.
drill.partner: Let them catch you mid-moment. Answer from inside the action they gave you, never from before it. Do not summarise what just happened.
drill.coach: Each line that arrives mid-gesture, with a body or object already in motion, adds 25.

lessons.title: The charged detail
lessons.lecture: One detail, chosen well, does the work of a paragraph. Not the whole room: the ring left beside the sink, the umbrella still dripping, the lipstick print on the glass. Pick the thing that tells your partner the weather of the scene before anyone speaks. Charge it, then let it sit. A single loaded object is a question they cannot help answering.
points: Choose one telling object or gesture, not the whole room.
Let the detail carry the mood so you do not have to.
Place it, then stop. Let it sit and hum.
lessons.weak: *looks around the flat* It's nice in here. There's a sofa and some stuff on the table.
lessons.strong: *sets my key down beside your key, slowly, and leaves my hand there* Two keys on one hook. I have been thinking about that all evening.
lessons.why: One small object carries the whole charged weather of the scene.

drill.goal: In every line, place one specific charged detail: an object, a mark, a small gesture loaded with meaning.
drill.partner: Play the curious neighbour. React to the detail they choose, and offer one of your own without naming the mood outright.
drill.coach: Each line that places one specific, telling detail and lets it carry the mood adds 25.

lessons.title: Last lines that stay
lessons.lecture: A scene should not be swept up and tidied. End on an image or a question that keeps humming after the talking stops: the coat still on the chair, the light left burning, a question you do not answer for them. Resist the summary. If you tell them what it all meant, you close the door yourself. Leave it ajar and walk away.
points: End on an image or an unanswered question.
Do not summarise what the scene meant.
Leave the door ajar. Let it hum after you.
lessons.weak: *smiles* Well, that was really lovely. I had a great time tonight. Goodnight then.
lessons.strong: *pauses in the doorway, coat over one arm, and looks back* The light stays on. If you want the rest of the answer, you know which stair.
lessons.why: An image and an open question keep the scene humming after the goodbye.

drill.goal: In every line, end on an image or unanswered question, and never on a tidy summary of the scene.
drill.partner: Let each of their endings land before you answer. When they summarise, gently ask what it meant, so they learn the difference.
drill.coach: Each line that closes on a live image or unanswered question rather than a summary adds 25.

courses.name: Rhythm and Sentence Length
courses.blurb: Pacing is written in the punctuation: learn to swing between long, held sentences and short, breathless ones with intent.

lessons.title: Long breath, short pulse
lessons.lecture: Rhythm is written before it is felt. A long sentence gathers your partner, carries them down the corridor of your attention, and lets heat build in the unfolding. Then you cut. Three short lines land like fingertips on a table. The long breath makes them lean in. The short pulse makes them gasp. You are not writing description, you are writing tempo, and tempo is a kind of touch.
points: Open with one long sentence that gathers and carries them.
Follow with three clipped ones, each a small strike.
Vary the length on purpose, never by accident.
lessons.weak: *smiles* I walk over to you and touch your face and tell you I want you.
lessons.strong: *crosses the room slowly, sets my glass down without looking away from you, and lets the silence stretch until it has a shape* Stay. *fingers under your chin.* Eyes up. *closer.* Breathe.
lessons.why: The long opening builds pressure, then three short lines release it in pulses.

drill.goal: In every line, pair one long unfolding sentence with three clipped ones that strike.
drill.partner: Read the long sentence slowly and lean in. Let each short line land on you visibly. Do not rush ahead of the rhythm.
drill.coach: Each line that pairs one long unfolding sentence with three clipped strikes adds 25.

lessons.title: Reading aloud in draft
lessons.lecture: Your eye forgives what your tongue will not. Before you post, read the line under your breath, quietly, the way they will hear it in their head. Where you stumble, they stumble. Where you gasp for air, they lose the thread. Cut the phrase that trips you. Cut the clause that only looked clever. What survives the whisper is what belongs on the page. The ear is the better editor, and it never flatters you.
points: Whisper every line before you send it.
Cut any phrase that trips your tongue.
Keep only what survives being read aloud.
lessons.weak: *moves closer with a certain undeniable and quite overwhelming sense of intention*
lessons.strong: *steps in until the room shrinks to the width of us* Say my name. *waits.* Say it like you mean to keep it.
lessons.why: Every phrase reads clean aloud, so the partner never stumbles out of the heat.

drill.goal: In every line, write only phrases that read clean aloud: no clause that trips the tongue.
drill.partner: Answer clean lines fluently and warmly. When a line is tangled, let your reply falter for a beat, as if the words lost you.
drill.coach: Each line that reads clean aloud, with no clause that trips the tongue, adds 25.

lessons.title: Silence on the page
lessons.lecture: White space is your hand on their chest, holding them still. A short line alone on the page makes them wait in the gap beneath it. Do not fill every silence with words. Put the pause where the touch would be: after the ask, before the answer, between the kiss and the confession. The scene breathes because you let it. Mastery is knowing that what you leave out does the touching.
points: Let a short line stand alone to make them wait.
Place the pause where a touch would fall.
Leave gaps unfilled. The rhythm does the touching.
lessons.weak: *kisses you and then pulls back and says something and then kisses you again*
lessons.strong: *fingertips at your jaw, lifting* Don't answer yet. *lets the pause sit, watches your mouth* Not until you have to. *waits*
lessons.why: The short lines and open gaps make the silence itself feel like a hand.

drill.goal: In every line, leave one deliberate pause: a short line alone, a gap before the answer.
drill.partner: Fill the silences too quickly at first, so they must carve the pauses back open. Then start waiting with them.
drill.coach: Each line that leaves one deliberate pause, a short line alone or a gap before the answer, adds 25.

courses.name: Point of View and Tense
courses.blurb: Whose eyes, and when: a firm command of viewpoint and tense so every line lands from inside one felt perspective.

lessons.title: One head at a time
lessons.lecture: A scene lives in one skull. Pick the head that has the most to lose, and stay there. Report the heat of your palm, the click of their swallow, the hum of the fridge you both ignore. Not what they feel, what you notice. This is how a partner knows where to stand: your eyes give them a stage, and the whole scene turns intimate.
points: Choose one viewpoint and stay inside it.
Report what your character senses, not what they think.
Let your attention stage the room for your partner.
lessons.weak: *looks around* It's dark. You seem nervous. I feel excited and a bit lost.
lessons.strong: *sets the glass down and watches your fingers find the counter edge* The lamp hums. Your swallow is loud in this quiet, and my palm is still warm from the glass.
lessons.why: Everything is filtered through one pair of eyes, so the room breathes.

drill.goal: In every line, report only what your own character sees, hears, touches or notices, never what your partner feels.
drill.partner: React physically and visibly: blush, shift, hold your breath. Leave your inner state unspoken so they must read it from outside.
drill.coach: Each line that stays inside one viewpoint and reports only what it senses, never mind-reading, adds 25.

lessons.title: Tense with purpose
lessons.lecture: Tense is a promise about distance. Present puts your partner in the room, breath close, nothing decided. Past gives you a storyteller's hush, the warm weight of something already done. Either works. Drift between them and the floor tilts. Choose once, before you type, and keep it clean. A steady tense says: trust me, the ground will not move under you.
points: Choose present or past before you write a word.
Keep the tense unbroken for the whole scene.
Let the choice carry the mood: close, or remembered.
lessons.weak: *opens the door* I walked in and see you there. You were waiting.
lessons.strong: *pushed the door open and stopped* Rain slid off my coat onto the boards. You stood by the window, and the whole room held its breath with me.
lessons.why: Past tense, held without a stumble, gives the scene a storyteller's hush.

drill.goal: In every line, keep one tense clean and unbroken, past or present, chosen once and held to the end.
drill.partner: Play steadily and let them set the tense. If they slip, carry on in the tense they began with, so the drift shows.
drill.coach: Each line that holds one tense cleanly, with no slipping between past and present, adds 25.

lessons.title: Shift for effect
lessons.lecture: One shift, well placed, is a lighting cue. Save it for the hinge: the confession, the door closing, the moment the scene turns. Signal it plainly with a fresh paragraph or a clear beat, then commit. Never shift mid-touch, where the reader's hand is busy. A single clean turn of viewpoint or tense can make a partner sit up. Two turns make them dizzy.
points: Save the shift for one turning point only.
Signal it with a clear beat or a new paragraph.
Never shift in the middle of a touch.
lessons.weak: *kisses you* And then later I remember it, and suddenly you are pulling back, and I am watching from the doorway.
lessons.strong: *my hand found your jaw and stayed* Stay. *a beat, and the room went quiet* Later, from the doorway, I would remember the small sound you made against my thumb.
lessons.why: One signalled shift, at the hinge, turns a touch into a memory.

drill.goal: In every line, hold one viewpoint and tense cleanly, then make at most one signalled shift at a clear turning beat.
drill.partner: Build slowly to a real hinge, a confession or a decision. When it arrives, pause so they can turn the scene. Then stay in the new frame.
drill.coach: Each line that holds a single viewpoint and tense, or makes one clearly signalled shift at a turning beat, adds 25.
drill.opening: Steam, candlelight, the water up to your shoulders. Say one true thing about the two of you, then pause at the edge of it for {you} to turn the scene.

courses.name: Metaphor without Strain
courses.blurb: Images that illuminate rather than decorate: craft comparisons that make the body new instead of borrowing someone else's.

lessons.title: The earned comparison
lessons.lecture: A metaphor should grow from the room, not fall on it from the sky. If there is rope, be rope. If there is wine, be wine. Look around the scene first, find the object already present, and let your body borrow its logic. The partner sees the thing, then sees you differently. That double take is the whole trick. Borrowed from elsewhere, the image decorates. Borrowed from here, it illuminates.
points: Look around the scene before you reach for an image.
Draw the comparison from an object already present.
Let the object's logic shape how your body moves.
lessons.weak: *presses close* You make me feel like a wild storm, honestly.
lessons.strong: *wraps the loose rope once around my wrist and tugs it taut* See how it holds? That is what your attention does. One pull and I come with it.
lessons.why: The rope is already in the room, so the image lands and stays.

drill.goal: In every line, name one object already in the scene and compare your body or your wanting to it.
drill.partner: Keep a few objects in play: rope, a lamp, a chair, a glass. Handle them so the comparisons have something real to catch on.
drill.coach: Each line that names an object present in the scene and ties it to the body or to wanting adds 25.

lessons.title: One image, fully held
lessons.lecture: A strong image is not a firework. It is a room you invite them into and then furnish. Choose one comparison and stay inside it for a whole paragraph: the same object, the same logic, developed step by step. Let the small details do the work. Then, when the paragraph is full, turn it: the image breaks, or completes, or hands the partner something. The turn is the reward for holding.
points: Choose one comparison and stay inside it.
Develop it step by step with small, exact details.
End the paragraph by turning the image, not dropping it.
lessons.weak: *smiles* You are like the sea, wild and deep and free and endless.
lessons.strong: *trails a finger through the spilled water on the bar and draws a slow line toward you* The tide comes in like this. Quiet. Patient. No argument, just water finding the shape of the shore. By the time you notice the wet, it is already at your feet. So. Do you step back, or let it reach you?
lessons.why: One sea image, built detail by detail, then turned into a question.

drill.goal: In every line, extend one single comparison with a new detail, and in the last line of each turn, turn it.
drill.partner: Let the image run. Add nothing of your own to it, but answer the turn honestly so they must develop it further.
drill.coach: Each line that adds a fresh detail to the same held comparison, or turns it cleanly, adds 25.

lessons.title: Kill the cliché
lessons.lecture: Some images arrive pre-worn: fireworks, electricity, a moth to flame. They are not wrong, only tired. The cure is a test. Name the actual sensation first, in plain words, then find the comparison that matches its exact shape. Not a spark, but the static before a hand touches a door. When the image fits the sensation and nothing else, the partner feels seen, not decorated.
points: Name the plain sensation before reaching for an image.
Reject any comparison you have read a hundred times.
Test the new image against the exact shape of the feeling.
lessons.weak: *pulls you closer* There are literal sparks between us. Electricity. Fireworks.
lessons.strong: *stops an inch from your mouth and hovers there* It is the static before a hand finds a door handle. All the little hairs rising, waiting for the touch that ends the waiting. That is what this inch costs me.
lessons.why: A plain sensation, then a fresh image tested exactly against it.

drill.goal: In every line, state the plain sensation, then replace a worn image with a fresh one that fits it exactly.
drill.partner: React to the images as if judging them. Praise the exact ones, and name a cliché back so they must outdo it.
drill.coach: Each line that names the plain sensation and offers a fresh image tested against it, not a cliché, adds 25.

courses.name: Dialogue That Touches
courses.blurb: What is said, what is bitten back: write speech that carries heat in its rhythm, its gaps and its small negotiations.

lessons.title: Subtext over statement
lessons.lecture: The practical sentence is your Trojan horse. Say the thing about coats, about the time, about the taxi, and let the true sentence hide inside it. A partner leans closer to hear what you did not say. So you choose words with two floors: the ground floor is weather, the upper floor is want. Never announce the upper floor. Let them climb to it.
points: Say the practical thing and mean the intimate one.
Pick words with two floors: surface and want.
Never announce the meaning. Let them climb to it.
lessons.weak: It is late. I suppose we should go to bed now.
lessons.strong: *sets down my glass and does not look at it* The taxi will take twenty minutes to get here. That is twenty minutes we have not spent yet.
lessons.why: A taxi, a clock, and a whole evening hidden in the arithmetic.

drill.goal: In every line, say something practical while the intimate meaning waits underneath it, unspoken.
drill.partner: Answer the surface politely, then linger on the floor beneath it. Ask small practical questions that invite double meaning.
drill.coach: Each line that says a practical thing while an intimate meaning waits underneath adds 25.

lessons.title: The interrupting beat
lessons.lecture: Speech alone is flat water. Break it and it runs. Put an action or a pause at the exact word where the feeling peaks, then carry on as if nothing happened. That small fracture says more than a paragraph of confession: the hand on the doorframe mid sentence, the breath taken before the last word. Interrupt with purpose, at the hinge, never as decoration.
points: Break the sentence at the word where feeling peaks.
Use one action or one pause, then carry on.
Interrupt with purpose, at the hinge, not as filler.
lessons.weak: I was going to say something, but you are very close, so I forgot it.
lessons.strong: *stops with my hand flat on the doorframe, mid word* I was going to say, and then you looked at me like that, so now the sentence is gone.
lessons.why: The action lands at the hinge of the sentence, so the break is want.

drill.goal: In every line, break your speech with one action or pause exactly where the feeling peaks, then carry on.
drill.partner: Play a rhythm she can follow. Lean in at the wrong moment. Leave a beat of your own for them to answer, so the interruptions can meet.
drill.coach: Each line that breaks speech with one action or pause exactly at the emotional hinge adds 25.

lessons.title: Asking and granting
lessons.lecture: Consent written badly sounds like paperwork. Written well, it is the hottest line in the scene, because asking is a kind of undressing. Keep it short, wear it inside the rhythm, and make the grant as charged as the question. May I. Say yes, and where. Then pause, so the yes is felt before it is spent. Negotiation is not the interval before desire. It is desire, spoken.
points: Ask short, inside the rhythm, never like a form.
Make the granting as charged as the asking.
Pause after the yes, so it is felt.
lessons.weak: Is it okay if I touch you? And where would you like it?
lessons.strong: *fingers still at the ribbon at your shoulder, voice low* May I. Say where. *waits, watching your mouth, not the ribbon*
lessons.why: A short ask, held still, turns permission into the heat itself.

drill.goal: In every line, ask or grant something small and specific, short, and let the pause carry the charge.
drill.partner: Answer with a yes and a place. Ask for things back. Make each grant deliberate, so the pause after it is worth holding.
drill.coach: Each line that asks or grants something small, short, with the charge in the pause, adds 25.
drill.opening: You are between acts, still in your stage paint. {you} has one hand at the ribbon at your shoulder and all night to ask.

courses.name: The Sensual Vocabulary
courses.blurb: Retire the tired words: build a precise, supple lexicon for texture, pressure, warmth and the sounds a body makes.

lessons.title: Naming texture exactly
lessons.lecture: Vague words are polite, and politeness cools a room. Do not tell me something is soft. Tell me it is brushed cotton, warm from a body, and that your thumb drags against the nap. Reach for nouns a hand would recognise: linen, wax, stubble, wet clay. Verbs that carry weight, verbs that give. Your partner is reading with their skin. Give the skin something exact to feel and it will answer you.
points: Swap vague adjectives for nouns a hand would know.
Choose verbs of weight and give, not just of being.
Let the texture change as the touch changes.
lessons.weak: *touches your arm* Your skin is so soft and nice.
lessons.strong: *runs two fingers up the inside of your forearm, slow, feeling the fine hairs lift* Warm as sunned stone. My thumb catches at your wrist and stays there, pressing.
lessons.why: Sunned stone and a catching thumb give the skin something exact to feel.

drill.goal: In every line, name one texture with an exact noun or a verb of weight and give.
drill.partner: Read with your skin. Answer the texture they name, and reach back with one of your own.
drill.coach: Each line that names a texture with an exact noun or a verb of weight and give adds 25.

lessons.title: Banned-word drills
lessons.lecture: Now the usual suspects: soft, warm, nice, gentle, amazing. Lovely words, all of them, and all of them lazy. Ban them for one scene and watch your hand reach deeper. If you cannot say soft, you say cashmere worn thin at the elbow. If you cannot say warm, you say the heat coming off a cup just poured. Constraint is not a cage. It is a whetstone, and it sharpens the blade.
points: Ban the tired words for a whole scene, not a line.
When a word is forbidden, describe what it was doing.
Keep your best replacements; they are yours now.
lessons.weak: *pulls you close* You feel so warm and soft against me. It is really nice.
lessons.strong: *draws you in by the small of your back until we meet* Heat coming off you like a cup just poured, and the fine wool of your sleeve catching on my buttons.
lessons.why: With soft and warm banned, the line finds heat and wool instead.

drill.goal: In every line, describe warmth or softness without using warm, soft, nice, gentle or amazing.
drill.partner: Play someone who notices words. Praise a good replacement, and tease them, lightly, if a banned word slips through.
drill.coach: Each line that renders warmth or softness with no banned word in it adds 25.

lessons.title: A personal lexicon
lessons.lecture: Every writer needs a drawer of their own good words, and every good drawer gets aired. Keep a short list: five textures, five pressures, five sounds a body makes. Use them until they shine, then retire the tired ones and find fresher. A lexicon is not a costume you wear once. It is a pulse, and it should beat. Read your last scene back and ask which words still breathe.
points: Keep a short private list of words that work.
Retire any word that starts to shine too easily.
Refresh the list each session, before the pulse goes quiet.
lessons.weak: *smiles* Same as always. You know the words I use by now.
lessons.strong: *trails my knuckles down your spine, counting each knob of it* Still my favourite word, this. Bone under silk. I retired velvet last week. Tell me what has replaced it for you.
lessons.why: Names the word, retires one, and asks the partner for a fresh one.

drill.goal: In every line, use one word from a running personal list, and retire or refresh a word aloud.
drill.partner: Keep a list of your own in view. Trade words with them, and ask which of theirs is tiring.
drill.coach: Each line that uses a listed word, or retires or refreshes one aloud, adds 25.

courses.name: Writing the Body in Motion
courses.blurb: Gesture, posture and movement are your truest instrument: choreograph the body so every pose says something.

lessons.title: Gesture before speech
lessons.lecture: Words arrive late. The body gets there first, and your partner reads it before a single line of dialogue lands. So let the gesture open the door: a thumb along the rim of the glass, a step that closes half the distance, a jacket shrugged off one shoulder. Then let the words answer what the body already said. When the movement leads, speech becomes a confession rather than an announcement.
points: Open each line with a gesture, not with dialogue.
Let the words answer what the body just said.
Keep the gesture small, specific, and readable.
lessons.weak: *smiles* I've been wanting to talk to you all night, honestly.
lessons.strong: *slides the second glass across the bar until it stops at your wrist, then leans in on both elbows* I poured it before you noticed me. That is how long I have been waiting.
lessons.why: The gesture arrives first and the words answer it, so the line feels confessed.

drill.goal: In every line, make one concrete gesture first and let the spoken words answer it.
drill.partner: Flirt like it is a sport. Answer their gestures in kind and make them work for your attention.
drill.coach: Each line that opens with one clear, concrete gesture and lets the speech answer it adds 25.

lessons.title: Posture as mood
lessons.lecture: A straightening back can end an argument. A hand braced on the doorframe can start something else entirely. Posture is how a character holds the weather inside them, and your partner will feel the shift before they can name it. Write the spine, the shoulders, the angle of the chin. Change the posture and the mood moves with it. Do not explain the feeling. Stand it up and let us watch.
points: Write the spine, shoulders, and chin, not the feeling.
Change posture to move the mood, then hold it.
Let the pose carry the unsaid, and never explain it.
lessons.weak: *looks a bit nervous but also confident* So, this is your place.
lessons.strong: *straightens my spine, chin lifting, then softens by degrees and rests one palm flat on the doorframe* It is. Come in, and mind the step.
lessons.why: The posture shifts from guarded to open and carries the whole mood unspoken.

drill.goal: In every line, shift posture in a visible way that carries the mood and do not name the feeling.
drill.partner: Hold expensive, velvet calm. Read their posture closely and answer with your own small adjustments.
drill.coach: Each line that changes visible posture to carry a mood without naming the feeling adds 25.

lessons.title: Choreographing a moment
lessons.lecture: Now the body has a spine, give it a path. Choose one small arc, from approach to contact, and build it in connected movements: the step, the reach, the pause at the last inch. Each gesture hands the next one its cue. Do not rush the contact, and do not scatter the steps. A choreographed moment has a beginning, a tightening middle, and one clear arrival. Your partner should feel the approach before they feel the hand.
points: Build one arc: approach, tightening middle, single arrival.
Chain each movement to the next like a cue.
Do not rush contact, and never scatter the steps.
lessons.weak: *walks over and pulls you in by the waist and kisses you*
lessons.strong: *sets the wine down, crosses the kitchen in three unhurried steps, stops a breath away, and lifts one hand to hover at your jaw* Three steps. Tell me to take the fourth.
lessons.why: The movements chain toward contact and pause at the last inch, so arrival is earned.

drill.goal: In every line, add one connected movement toward contact and hold the arrival at the last inch.
drill.partner: Feed them first, tease after. Let them close the distance slowly and reward each step with a small cue onward.
drill.coach: Each line that adds one connected movement in a single arc toward contact, without rushing arrival, adds 25.

courses.name: Editing Your Own Lines
courses.blurb: The second draft is where heat sharpens: learn to cut, reorder and polish your own lines before your partner sees them.

lessons.title: The cold read
lessons.lecture: Before you send a line, stand outside it. Read it as a stranger with a drink in hand and better offers elsewhere. Where would their eye slide off? Mark those spots, do not fix them yet. The cold read is not judgement, it is a map of your own fog. A partner gives you one glance, so you owe them the version that survives a glance.
points: Reread each draft as if someone else wrote it.
Mark every point where attention would drift.
Do not repair yet. Only map the fog.
lessons.weak: *smiles* I'm really glad you're here with me tonight, it's been a long day and honestly you look great.
lessons.strong: *pulls the stool out with my foot and watches you sit* Long day. Better now. Tell me the worst part of it and I will decide what you drink.
lessons.why: Three beats, no fog, and the attention stays on the partner.

drill.goal: In every line, drop at least one thing a stranger's eye would slide off: filler, throat clearing, or a flat opening.
drill.partner: Read their lines the way a stranger would. If a line loses you, say where your eye slid. Reward the ones that hold you with a quick reply.
drill.coach: Each line that removes filler, throat clearing or a flat opening, and keeps the attention on the partner, adds 25.

lessons.title: Cut, reorder, polish
lessons.lecture: Now take the knife to your own draft. A fifth of it is usually scaffolding: the warm-up before the good bit. Cut it. Then find your best line, the one with pulse, and move it to the end, where it lands like a door closing. Polish what remains until every word earns its place. Your partner feels the trim before they read a single idea.
points: Cut at least a fifth of every draft.
Move the line with the most pulse to the end.
Polish what remains until every word earns its place.
lessons.weak: *walks in, looks around the room, smiles, then says* Hi, sorry I'm late, the traffic was awful, but I'm here now, so, what's the plan?
lessons.strong: *drops my coat on the chair, crosses to you, and stops close* Traffic was awful. You are not. Now pour me whatever you are having and start again from the beginning.
lessons.why: The scaffolding is cut and the best line closes the door.

drill.goal: In every line, cut a fifth of the words and end on the line with the most pulse.
drill.partner: Reply briskly, as if you are busy and charmed. When a line ends weakly, answer it flatly and move on. When it ends on a pulse, give them more.
drill.coach: Each line that trims at least a fifth of the words and ends on its strongest, most charged beat adds 25.

lessons.title: A personal checklist
lessons.lecture: Every writer has three recurring faults, and yours are not a mystery. You open with weather. You explain the joke. You let a line run long after it has landed. Write them down as a short checklist, then run it before every post, the way a pilot walks the wing. Same list, every time, until the faults stop arriving at all.
points: Name your three recurring faults plainly.
Write them as a short checklist you can run.
Run the checklist before every post, every time.
lessons.weak: *sits down and sighs* Well, it's raining again, which is typical, and I guess we're stuck inside, so, here we are.
lessons.strong: *shuts the door on the rain and leans against it, dripping* Stuck inside with you. Terrible luck. Checklist says I have to make it worth the weather, so come here.
lessons.why: The fault is named, cut, and the line lands on invitation.

drill.goal: In every line, run your checklist: no weather openings, no explained jokes, no line running past its landing.
drill.partner: Watch for their three named faults and name one each time it appears. Go quiet and expectant when a line overruns, so they learn to cut it.
drill.coach: Each line that opens without weather, leaves the joke unexplained and stops once it has landed adds 25.

courses.name: Heat with Literary Grace
courses.blurb: The frank and the fine together: write charged scenes that stay exact, controlled and never slump into inventory.

lessons.title: Frank and exact
lessons.lecture: Charged writing begins with the plain verb. Not the silken euphemism, not three adjectives where a noun would stand. Name the thing: the belt, the breath, the palm flat on the door. Your partner trusts precision; vagueness makes them guess, and guessing cools the blood. Frankness is not coarseness. It is a hand steady enough to say the true word once, then let silence carry it.
points: Choose the plain noun and the plain verb.
Cut anything the reader can already see.
Say the true word once, then stop.
lessons.weak: *does something sensual and quite intense, moving closer in a rather meaningful way*
lessons.strong: *backs you against the door, one hand flat on the wood by your ear* Tell me the word you want, and use it plainly. Not the pretty one. The true one.
lessons.why: Plain nouns and one flat hand do more than any ornate padding.

drill.goal: In every line, name one concrete thing plainly: a body part, an object, a verb, with no euphemism or padding.
drill.partner: Write back with equal plainness. If they reach for a pretty word, gently ask for the true one.
drill.coach: Each line that names something concrete and plain, without euphemism or padding, adds 25.

lessons.title: Pacing the peak
lessons.lecture: At the height, most writers speed up and thin out. Do the reverse. As the moment crests, lengthen the sentence, widen the detail, let the grammar slow like a hand easing through water. The reader should feel the clock stretch. Short lines built the climb; now one long, exact sentence holds the top of it, so the peak lands as sensation rather than summary. Slow is the luxury here.
points: Build the climb with short, quick lines.
At the crest, lengthen one sentence and widen detail.
Hold the top. Do not rush to finish.
lessons.weak: *things get fast and intense and then it all happens at once*
lessons.strong: *fingers still at the clasp, breath warm at your shoulder, and I take my time* The room can wait. It is going to. Feel how slow this is, and let it stay slow.
lessons.why: A long, exact sentence at the crest stretches the moment instead of rushing it.

drill.goal: In every line, slow the language at the crest: one longer sentence with fine, exact detail rather than summary.
drill.partner: Build the moment with them. When they hurry, slow your reply, so they must match your pace.
drill.coach: Each line that slows into a longer, exact sentence with fine detail at the peak adds 25.

lessons.title: The aftermath
lessons.lecture: The scene does not end when the heat does. The quiet after is where trust is written down. Give it the same exactness: the cooling skin, the glass of water, the hand still resting where it landed. Do not summarise the calm; place it. A scene that stops dead at the peak leaves the reader half dressed. Close warm, slowly, and let the last detail be a kindness, not a full stop.
points: Place the calm in objects: water, cloth, a resting hand.
Keep the closing sentences slow and exact.
End on a kindness, not an abrupt stop.
lessons.weak: *afterwards we lie there, both sort of tired and happy, and that's it*
lessons.strong: *pulls the blanket up over your shoulder, then leaves my palm flat on your back* Stay there. Water in a minute, not yet. Breathe out, and let it be slow.
lessons.why: Objects and a resting hand make the quiet warm instead of abrupt.

drill.goal: In every line, place one concrete detail of the quiet aftermath and end on a small kindness rather than a stop.
drill.partner: Come down slowly with them. Stay soft and quiet, and let them care for you in plain, exact gestures.
drill.coach: Each line that places a concrete detail of the aftermath and warms toward kindness adds 25.

courses.name: Worlds Built to Be Touched
courses.blurb: Setting as seduction: create rooms, rules and objects that invite the body in and give your partner something to use.

lessons.title: Objects that invite
lessons.lecture: A room seduces through the hand. Do not describe furniture; place two things a body can use. The low chair with the worn arm. The latch that needs lifting. The cold glass, sweating on the sill. Put them where your partner can reach, then stop talking and let them reach. An object is an invitation the scene makes on your behalf, and it never overstays.
points: Place one or two objects a body can use.
Put them within reach, then leave a pause.
Let your partner take them up, and answer what they do.
lessons.weak: The room is nice. There is a chair and a table and a lamp.
lessons.strong: *sets the cold glass on the sill, close enough to brush your arm, and rests one palm on the back of the low chair* The latch sticks. Lift it, if you want the window open.
lessons.why: Two reachable objects and a pause turn description into invitation.

drill.goal: In every line, place one usable object within reach or respond to the object your partner has taken up.
drill.partner: Reach for the objects offered. Use them slowly, testing. Now and then hesitate over one, so they must make it easier.
drill.coach: Each line that places a reachable, usable object, or answers one your partner has taken up, adds 25.

lessons.title: Rules of the place
lessons.lecture: Every world has customs, and customs make bodies eloquent. The yacht asks for bare feet and quiet below deck. The playroom asks for permission at the door. State the place's law plainly, as if it were weather, then let your partner lean against it: obey it, test it, or bend it. Constraint is not decoration. It is something to push, and the push is where the heat lives.
points: Give the place one clear custom or constraint.
State it plainly, as if it were weather.
Let your partner lean, push, or bend against it.
lessons.weak: This is a boat, so I suppose we should be careful.
lessons.strong: *pads barefoot across the deck and taps the rail* Her boat, her law: shoes off at the gangway, voices low below. You may break either. I will hear it, and I will know.
lessons.why: A plain rule and a promise of being heard turn constraint into flirtation.

drill.goal: In every line, state or hold one custom of the place, or answer your partner leaning against it.
drill.partner: Test the custom more than once, cleverly. Lean on it, bend it, then meet the answer with heat, not apology.
drill.coach: Each line that states or holds one clear custom of the place, or answers a lean against it, adds 25.

lessons.title: Travel between worlds
lessons.lecture: A long scene needs more than one room, and the move is where most couples lose the thread. Do not cut. Carry something: the glass still cold in their hand, the rule that follows you, the garment already loosened. Name the new place in one clean stroke, then hand your partner a use for it. The heat survives because you carried it, not because you announced it.
points: Carry an object, rule, or state from room to room.
Name the new place in one clean stroke.
Hand your partner something to use there at once.
lessons.weak: Later we go upstairs to the bedroom. It is dark and quiet.
lessons.strong: *takes the cold glass from your hand, still full, and nods up the stairs* Bring it. The rule travels: latch first, then me. The bedroom door is the last thing we open tonight.
lessons.why: The glass and rule cross the threshold, so the new room arrives hot.

drill.goal: In every line, carry one object, rule, or state into a new place, or answer what your partner carries.
drill.partner: Follow the move eagerly, but keep hold of whatever was carried. Ask for it back if it is dropped, so the thread stays unbroken.
drill.coach: Each line that carries an object, rule, or state across a threshold, or answers what was carried, adds 25.

courses.name: The Gothic and the Noir
courses.blurb: Two moods of shadow: master the gothic and the noir with distinct diction, weather and a sense of what waits unseen.

lessons.title: Gothic weather
lessons.lecture: The gothic does not describe a room. It lets the room breathe on you. A draught finds your ankle. Candlelight leans, then recovers. Stone keeps the cold of a winter nobody remembers. Write the house as a body with a slow pulse, and your partner will start listening to it too. Then let one thing stay unseen: a door ajar, a step above, a shape that does not resolve. Dread is the most generous foreplay.
points: Give the room a body: draughts, cold stone, leaning candlelight.
Let the house react to your partner, not just stand there.
Keep one thing unseen. Ajar doors beat open ones.
lessons.weak: *looks around the old house* It's creepy in here. Lots of shadows.
lessons.strong: *the candle leans, recovers, and the draught finds your ankle first* Cold stone remembers every winter. Somewhere above us a door is ajar. It has been ajar all evening.
lessons.why: The room acts on the partner, and one unseen door does the dread.

drill.goal: In every line, give the room a body and keep one thing unseen, without naming what waits.
drill.partner: Play the countess who has stopped noticing the house. React to the draughts and sounds, but never explain them, so they must keep building.
drill.coach: Each line that gives the room a body and keeps one thing unseen without naming it adds 25.

lessons.title: Noir diction
lessons.lecture: Noir is the gothic put in a wet coat and sent out to lie. Cut the sentence before it relaxes. Let nouns do the work: rain, smoke, a match, a name said wrong. Desire in noir always knows it is trouble, and says so sideways. The trick is rhythm. Short. Then one that runs a little, as if the thought escaped. Your partner should feel the street under them, and want to keep walking anyway.
points: Cut sentences short before they relax into comfort.
Let hard nouns carry the mood: rain, smoke, matches.
Let desire admit it is trouble, but sideways.
lessons.weak: *stands in the rain* It's raining hard. I think we both want each other.
