lessons.strong: *shakes out the match, rain running off my collar* Bad night for good decisions. You're the worst one I've made in years. *lights the next match, close to your face* Say something I'll regret.
lessons.why: Clipped rhythm, wet nouns, and desire that names itself trouble.

drill.goal: In every line, keep sentences clipped and let hard nouns and sideways trouble carry the mood.
drill.partner: Flirt like it is a sport and give as good as you get. Answer short. Make them earn every word, and never let the scene soften.
drill.coach: Each line that stays clipped and lets hard nouns and sideways, troubled desire carry the mood adds 25.

lessons.title: Shadow as partner
lessons.lecture: Now the mastery. Concealment is not scenery any more: it is the second player. Half-light takes a turn. It hides your mouth and shows your hands. It lets your partner fill the gap, and what they fill it with tells you everything. Write what the dark does, not what you feel about it. Let it interrupt, delay, decide. A scene where the shadow keeps choosing for you both is a scene neither of you can put down.
points: Let the half-light take turns: it hides, shows, delays.
Write what the dark does, not what you feel.
Let concealment choose for both of you, and change the scene.
lessons.weak: *in the dark room* It's dark, so I can't really see you. Come closer.
lessons.strong: *the last lamp dies, and the dark takes my mouth first, then gives back my hands* There. Now find me by the cold of my cufflink. When you do, do not speak. The dark is deciding tonight, and it has chosen you.
lessons.why: The dark acts, hides, gives, and chooses, so it plays its own part.

drill.goal: In every line, let the half-light act: hide, show, delay or choose, as a partner would.
drill.partner: Play the rope artist with patient hands. Answer the dark as if it were a third person in the room, and let it move you both.
drill.coach: Each line that lets the half-light act as a partner, hiding, showing, delaying or choosing, adds 25.

courses.name: Fantasy and Science Fiction
courses.blurb: Make the invented feel touchable: write the strange with plain conviction, from magic's cost to a ship's cold metal.

lessons.title: Concrete invention
lessons.lecture: The impossible needs weight. Do not tell your partner the hall is enchanted: let them feel the cold stone under their palm and the candle smoke that tastes of iron. Plain conviction does the work. Say the strange thing as though it were ordinary weather, and they will lean in to touch it. Detail is not decoration; it is the floor they stand on.
points: Ground every strange thing in one physical sensation.
Say the impossible plainly, as ordinary fact.
Choose cold, weight and smell over grand description.
lessons.weak: *waves a hand* The tavern is magical and strange things happen here.
lessons.strong: *sets the tankard down, and the ale steams faintly green* Do not drink yet. It bites on the way down, and the room will start to lean. Feel the table first. Cold as a well.
lessons.why: Plain words and one cold touch make the magic feel touchable.

drill.goal: In every line, anchor one impossible thing to a plain physical detail: weight, cold, smell, or sound.
drill.partner: Play a knight off duty who takes the strange as ordinary. Ask about the ale, the room, the blade. Never explain the magic yourself.
drill.coach: Each line that ties one strange thing to a plain physical sensation adds 25.

lessons.title: Tech with a body
lessons.lecture: A ship is not a diagram. It is a hum under your boots and a bulkhead cold enough to sting. Write your machines through the body that is near them: the pressure in the ears, the vibration up the wrist, the airlock's breath. Let your partner feel the hull before they ever understand it. Explain late, or not at all. Sensation is the manual.
points: Write the machine through pressure, hum and cold metal.
Let the body near it feel it before you explain.
Explain late, and briefly, or not at all.
lessons.weak: *points* That is the engine room. It powers the ship and is very advanced.
lessons.strong: *flattens my palm to the bulkhead, and the hum climbs my wrist to the elbow* Feel that? Two minutes until it turns. Brace your boots wide and breathe out slow. The floor will shake, and it should.
lessons.why: The hum and the countdown put the reader's body inside the metal.

drill.goal: In every line, make one piece of machinery felt through pressure, hum, cold or breath on the body.
drill.partner: Play a deckhand who knows the boat. Answer with your own sensations of the hull. Say nothing technical unless they ask twice.
drill.coach: Each line that renders a machine through a bodily sensation, not explanation, adds 25.

lessons.title: Cost and consent
lessons.lecture: Every wonder has a price, and the price is where the story lives. Name the toll of your magic or your machine before you use it: a memory, a year, a scar that will not close. Then let the scene lean on it. Have them ask what it will cost, and answer plainly. When a partner knows the price and chooses anyway, the impossible becomes intimate.
points: Name the price of your wonder before you use it.
Let them ask the cost, and answer it plainly.
Make the choosing, not the wonder, the scene.
lessons.weak: *glows with power* I can cast the spell, it is fine, do not worry.
lessons.strong: *turns the ring once, and a thin scar whitens on my wrist* The crossing holds an hour, and the cost is a year of my sight. Ask me now, before I start. Once it burns, I cannot stop.
lessons.why: A named price, offered before the act, makes the choosing intimate.

drill.goal: In every line, state or hold the price of the magic, and let them choose against it.
drill.partner: Play an elven prince who knows old magic. Ask the cost each time. Hesitate, then decide. Never pay it for them.
drill.coach: Each line that names a clear cost and lets them choose against it adds 25.

courses.name: Humour in the Heat
courses.blurb: A well-timed laugh deepens desire: learn comic timing, the wry aside and the graceful recovery when something slips.

lessons.title: Comic timing
lessons.lecture: A laugh is a pressure valve, and you control the valve. Load the moment first: a slow touch, a held look, a confession that costs something. Let it sit until the air is thick. Then place one light line, low and unhurried, and stop. Do not explain the joke. The pause after is the punchline. When they laugh, they breathe, and the want rushes back in twice as strong.
points: Build a heavy beat first, then let it sit.
Drop one light line, low and unhurried.
Stop talking after it. The pause is the punchline.
lessons.weak: *kisses you* Ha, that was funny, right? I'm so funny.
lessons.strong: *fingers still curled in your collar, voice low* I had a whole speech prepared. *a beat, then a small smile* It has left. You will have to make do with the touching.
lessons.why: The heavy beat is loaded before the light line, and the pause lets it land.

drill.goal: In every line, build one heavy beat, then land a light line and leave space after it.
drill.partner: Give them weight to work with: hold looks, say something charged. Laugh when the line lands, then lean back in.
drill.coach: Each line that loads a heavy beat before a light, unhurried line and leaves space after it adds 25.

lessons.title: The wry aside
lessons.lecture: Charm lives in the sideways glance. The wry aside is one dry observation, delivered half to them and half to the room, that shows a mind at work behind the want. Keep it short, keep it deadpan, and never let it linger. Say it, let them smile, then return straight to the charge. The aside endears the character. The clean return proves the desire never left.
points: Make it one dry line, half to them, half to the room.
Deliver it deadpan, then do not linger.
Return straight to the charge within the same line.
lessons.weak: *laughs* Ha, funny, we are on a yacht. Anyway, where were we?
lessons.strong: *trails a finger along the rail, deadpan* The boat costs more than my flat. *turns back, closer* None of that matters. You were about to tell me what you wanted.
lessons.why: One dry aside, then a clean turn straight back to the charged question.

drill.goal: In every line, drop one dry aside, then return cleanly to the charge in the same line.
drill.partner: Be a little grand and expensive, so there is plenty to be wry about. Smile at the aside, then wait for the charge.
drill.coach: Each line that gives one dry aside and returns cleanly to the charge within the same line adds 25.

lessons.title: Recovering from the slip
lessons.lecture: Something will slip: a glass, a name, a bra strap that defeats you. Amateurs freeze or apologise. Masters laugh first and keep moving. Write the mishap plainly, let your character laugh at themselves, then fold it back into the scene as though you planned it. The recovery is the skill. A partner who watches you laugh at your own slip learns the scene is safe, and safety is what lets them fall.
points: Write the mishap plainly and laugh at yourself first.
Do not apologise your way out of the moment.
Fold the slip back into the scene and keep moving.
lessons.weak: *drops the glass* Oh no, sorry, clumsy me, let me clean that up properly.
lessons.strong: *the glass goes over, wine across the tiles, and I laugh, low and easy* Right. *steps in close over the spill* Leave it. There is a wall behind you and I have decided to use it.
lessons.why: The slip is owned with a laugh, then folded straight into the next move.

drill.goal: In every line, write a small mishap, laugh at it, then fold it into the scene and keep moving.
drill.partner: Cause small mishaps: spill, trip, knock something over. Laugh with them, and never let them apologise their way out.
drill.coach: Each line that names a mishap, laughs at it, and folds it back into the scene without apology adds 25.

courses.name: Stories Across Many Nights
courses.blurb: Sustain a long story over many sessions: plant seeds early, pay them off late and keep appetite alive between scenes.

lessons.title: Planting seeds
lessons.lecture: A long story is built in the margins. Early on, drop one small thing and do not point at it: a key on their chain, a scar they keep touching, a song half heard through a wall. Mention it once, lightly, then move on. The trick is the silence after. If you explain it, you have spent it. If you leave it, your partner carries it home and starts to wonder.
points: Drop one small detail, then move on.
Never explain it in the same breath.
Let your partner notice it themselves.
lessons.weak: *points* That key on your chain is important. Remember it for later.
lessons.strong: *traces the little brass key at your throat, once, and lets my hand fall* You keep it close. *turns back to the fire* There is a story in that, and you will tell it when you are ready.
lessons.why: Mentions the key once, then leaves it to breathe.

drill.goal: In every line, plant one small unremarked detail, or return lightly to one already planted.
drill.partner: Wear one small telling detail, a key, a scar, a ring. Let them notice it. Do not explain it until they do.
drill.coach: Each line that plants one small detail without explaining it, or returns to one lightly, adds 25.

lessons.title: The patient payoff
lessons.lecture: A seed is a promise, and promises must fall. Hold your detail back until the moment it costs you something to bring out. The key at their throat, mentioned in the first hour, becomes the thing you unlock the door with in the third. Payoff is not a reveal, it is a return. Bring it back when the room is hot, and let its smallness do the work.
points: Wait until the detail will land hardest.
Bring it back as an action, not an explanation.
Let the smallness of it do the work.
lessons.weak: So the key, remember? It opens a door. Let's go through.
lessons.strong: *turns the little brass key in the lock, hears it catch, and looks back at you* You wore this all night and never once asked. *pushes the door* Now you get to.
lessons.why: The planted key returns as action, and the wait is named.

drill.goal: In every line, bring back a detail planted earlier and pay it off through action, not explanation.
drill.partner: Bring a detail you planted early back into play. When they return it, make the payoff visible. Do not resolve it for them.
drill.coach: Each line that returns a planted detail and pays it off through action, not explanation, adds 25.

lessons.title: The between-scenes
lessons.lecture: The story does not stop when you close the window. It waits, and waiting is where appetite grows. Write the short interlude: a message at midnight, a thing left on their step, a line about what you are doing and who you are doing it without. Keep it brief and lean on the gap. Do not resolve anything. Give them a small hook to carry until the next session.
points: Write brief interludes in the gap, never full scenes.
Lean on absence: say what is missing, not what is done.
Leave one small hook for the next session.
lessons.weak: Hey, that was fun last night. Message me when you want to do it again.
lessons.strong: *sends one line at midnight* The key is on my table and the door is unlocked and you are not here. *nothing else*
lessons.why: A brief message in the gap, naming absence and leaving a hook.

drill.goal: In every line, write a brief interlude of absence that leaves one hook open for the next session.
drill.partner: Answer between sessions only. Keep replies short. Name what is missing, and do not close the gap.
drill.coach: Each line that writes a brief interlude of absence and leaves one small hook open adds 25.

courses.name: Continuity and Callbacks
courses.blurb: A long story remembers: track detail, honour what came before and turn old lines into new heat with deft callbacks.

lessons.title: Keeping the ledger
lessons.lecture: A long story is built from small, remembered things: the drink they never finish, the scar they touch when they lie, the promise made at the door. Keep a quiet ledger. Before you write a new line, read the old ones. What did you plant? What is still owed? A partner relaxes into a scene that remembers them. Continuity is not admin. It is attention, and attention is a kind of heat.
points: Note names, wounds, promises and props as they appear.
Read your ledger before you write anything new.
Bring back one small detail in every scene.
lessons.weak: *smiles* So, tell me about yourself. What's your story?
lessons.strong: *slides the glass back across the bar, untouched as it was an hour ago* Still not drinking it. Third time you've let it sit. Tell me what you're saving it for.
lessons.why: The untouched glass proves the scene has been keeping score.

drill.goal: In every line, bring back one concrete detail from earlier: a prop, a name, a promise, or a small habit.
drill.partner: Drop vivid, specific details as you go: a drink, a scar, a nickname, a promise. Repeat the ones they miss so they must pick them up.
drill.coach: Each line that returns to one concrete earlier detail, or plants one clearly for later, adds 25.
drill.opening: You are mid-shift and flirty. Set down a drink {you} ordered an hour ago and have not touched, and remark on it.

lessons.title: Callback as reward
lessons.lecture: A callback is a gift with history in it. Do not repeat the old line flat. Change it. The gesture they made at the door, made now from the other side of a locked one. The promise quoted back after it has been kept. The pleasure is in the shift: same shape, new weight. Done well, it tells your partner the whole night has been one long sentence, and you have been reading every word.
points: Quote an earlier gesture or phrase, then change it.
Time it for the moment it lands hardest.
Let what has happened since do the work.
lessons.weak: *grins* Remember when you said that thing earlier? That was fun.
lessons.strong: *takes the glass from your hand at last, sets it down full* You said you were saving it. So save it. Same glass, same bar. Only this time you drink it with my hand on your wrist.
lessons.why: The old promise returns, altered by the night, and lands harder.

drill.goal: In every line, quote one earlier phrase or gesture and change it with what has happened since.
drill.partner: Give them strong material early: a line, a gesture, a small refusal. React with heat when they bring one back altered.
drill.coach: Each line that quotes an earlier phrase or gesture and changes it with what has since happened adds 25.
drill.opening: Earlier {you} called you the best set of the summer. Now, off the decks and in the booth, bring it up and see what they do.

lessons.title: Repairing a slip
lessons.lecture: You will contradict yourself. The rain becomes a clear night, the brother becomes a sister. Amateurs pretend it never happened. Masters fold it in. Let the error become a discovery: the rain stopped while you were inside, the name was the one they use now. Say it plainly, give it a reason, and carry on as if the story had always meant it. A repaired seam, done warmly, is more convincing than an unbroken one.
points: Name the slip instead of hiding it.
Give the change a reason inside the story.
Carry on at once, warm and unbothered.
lessons.weak: *frowns* Wait, it wasn't raining. Sorry. Where were we?
lessons.strong: *glances at the window, then back at you* Rain's stopped. It did that while you were talking, and I missed the whole sky clearing. Come out from under the awning. The night changed its mind, and so did I.
lessons.why: The slip becomes weather, then a turn, and the scene moves on.

drill.goal: In every line, name a small inconsistency and fold it into the story with a reason, then keep going.
drill.partner: Plant a contradiction or two: a detail that shifts, a name that changes. Do not correct it yourself. Let them repair it.
drill.coach: Each line that names an inconsistency, gives it an in-story reason, and carries on warmly adds 25.
drill.opening: You began in heavy rain under the awning. Now write as if the rain has stopped, and let {you} notice the gap.

courses.name: Writing Desire without Touch
courses.blurb: The scene before the scene: make anticipation, glances and near-misses carry more charge than contact ever could.

lessons.title: The near-miss
lessons.lecture: The near-miss is a hand that stops a breath from the skin. You reach, they lean, and you hold it there, one beat longer than polite. The air does the touching for you. Write the gap, not the landing: the hover, the held breath, the fingers that curl at the last second. Contact settles a scene. A near-miss keeps it hungry, and hunger is what they replay at two in the morning.
points: Reach, then stop a breath short.
Hold the gap one beat longer than is comfortable.
Write the almost, not the landing.
lessons.weak: *reaches out and almost touches your hand, then pulls back*
lessons.strong: *lifts my hand toward yours, stops with the space still warm between them, and holds it there* Not yet. Let me look at what wanting does to you first.
lessons.why: The hand stops short and the held gap does the touching.

drill.goal: In every line, reach for contact and stop one breath short, writing the gap and the held air.
drill.partner: Lean in when they almost touch, then hold still. Do not close the gap yourself. Let it ache.
drill.coach: Each line that reaches for contact and holds the gap short of it, writing the near-miss, adds 25.

lessons.title: Glances that land
lessons.lecture: A look is not a mood, it is a body. Do not write that they seem interested. Write the heat climbing their ears, the breath they take to steady it, the swallow. Your partner cannot perform a feeling they have only been told. Give them the body and the feeling arrives on its own. Build the look from the outside in, and let them catch themselves blushing before they know why.
points: Write the body, not the feeling.
Use ears, breath, throat, hands.
Let them notice the tell before they name it.
lessons.weak: *looks at you across the room and it feels intense*
lessons.strong: *holds your eyes from the doorway, unhurried, and watches the colour climb your ears as your breath goes shallow* You felt that. Do not look away yet.
lessons.why: The look is built from ears and breath, so the feeling lands by itself.

drill.goal: In every line, describe a look through the body: heat, breath, throat, hands, and hold their gaze.
drill.partner: React with your body first: flush, swallow, lose your breath a little, and only then speak.
drill.coach: Each line that writes a look from the body, a tell of heat or breath, and holds the gaze, adds 25.

lessons.title: Delaying the touch
lessons.lecture: Now you spend it all. A whole scene of almost, of looks that land, of hands that stop short, and no contact until the final line. Your partner will start to lean early, to reach, to test you. Do not fold. Each line adds one more inch of want without relief. The touch you grant at the end is not a touch. It is everything the scene has been promising, paid at once.
points: Keep every line short of contact until the last.
When they reach early, withdraw gently and continue.
Grant the first touch on the final line only.
lessons.weak: *finally takes your hand and squeezes it* There. That took long enough.
lessons.strong: *crosses the room, takes your jaw in both hands, and only then lets my thumbs settle against your skin* There. Now you know what all that waiting was for.
lessons.why: The whole held scene pays off in one touch, granted only at the end.

drill.goal: In every line, keep short of contact, building want, and grant the first touch only on the final line.
drill.partner: Reach for them early and often. Let them withdraw. Grow hungrier as the scene goes on.
drill.coach: Each line that delays contact and builds want without relief, or grants the first touch at the end, adds 25.

courses.name: The Long Arc of a Scene
courses.blurb: Every scene has a shape: learn to build approach, turn and aftermath so a session feels complete and worth returning to.

lessons.title: Finding the turn
lessons.lecture: A scene without a turn is a corridor with no door. Choose the hinge before you write a word: the moment the evening stops being pleasant and becomes inevitable. Then spend your lines leaning towards it. Small talk earns its keep only if it tightens the wire. When the turn comes, do not rush past it. Stop, let it land, and watch what it changes in the room.
points: Choose your turning point before the first line.
Let every earlier line lean towards it.
Arrive at the turn and stop. Let it land.
lessons.weak: So anyway, what do you want to do now? I'm easy either way.
lessons.strong: *sets the glass down and turns the music low* Here is the turn. Before tonight, you were my guest. From this line on, you are something else. Ask me what.
lessons.why: The turn is named out loud, so the scene changes gear in one stroke.

drill.goal: In every line, move the scene closer to one named turn, or arrive at it and hold still.
drill.partner: Play the pleasant guest until the turn. Once they name it, stop chatting and give them a held, loaded silence to work with.
drill.coach: Each line that moves the scene towards the named turn, or arrives at it and holds, adds 25.

lessons.title: Escalation with logic
lessons.lecture: Escalation is not volume. It is consequence. Each new step must grow out of the one before, so your partner can feel the ground shifting under a sure foot. If you raise your voice, raise it because they leaned in. If you cross the room, cross it because of something said. The test is simple: could they have predicted this from the last line? Good. Surprise lives in the logic, not outside it.
points: Let every step grow from the one before it.
Escalate by consequence, not by volume.
Make each new step predictable from the last.
lessons.weak: *suddenly pulls you close* Enough talking. Come here. Now kiss me.
lessons.strong: *takes the glass from your hand, sets it aside, and steps into your space* You leaned in twice and thought I missed it. Third time is mine. *waits, close enough to feel*
lessons.why: The step follows from their leaning, so the closeness feels earned.

drill.goal: In every line, raise the stakes one clear step that follows from the partner's last move.
drill.partner: Give them small signals to build on: lean in, linger, let a hand stray. React visibly to each step so the next has something to grow from.
drill.coach: Each line that raises the stakes one clear step, following from the partner's last move, adds 25.

lessons.title: Landing the aftermath
lessons.lecture: The end of a scene is not the door. It is the room you leave them in. Gather what changed: name it, gently, in the past tense, so it becomes something you both own. Slow your voice. Let touch return soft. Then leave one small hook, a promise or a question, so the night closes with a handle on it. A good aftermath makes them want the next scene before this one is over.
points: Name, gently, what changed between you.
Slow the voice and soften the touch.
Leave one small hook towards next time.
lessons.weak: Well, that was fun. Same time next week, I guess?
lessons.strong: *traces a slow line down your arm and lets my voice settle* Before tonight you never asked me for anything. You asked twice. *small pause* Keep the glass. Next time, bring it back full.
lessons.why: It names the change, softens the touch, and leaves a small return hook.

drill.goal: In every line, gather what changed, soften the tone, and leave a hook towards a next meeting.
drill.partner: Play someone who has seen it all: unhurried, wry, quietly pleased. Make them work for a soft landing. Do not end the scene for them.
drill.coach: Each line that names what changed, softens the tone, or leaves a hook forward adds 25.

courses.name: Portrait of a Voice
courses.blurb: Make each character's prose sound like them: diction, cadence and habit that stay distinct and instantly recognisable.

lessons.title: Diction as fingerprint
lessons.lecture: Every voice carries a fingerprint made of words. Choose four or five a character reaches for when calm, when hungry, when caught: clipped ones, ornate ones, a phrase they overuse without noticing. Then let nobody else in the scene borrow them. Your partner learns to hear your character coming, and the pleasure of that recognition is half the game. Keep the set small and keep it loyal.
points: Pick a handful of favoured words only this character uses.
Give each one a shape: clipped, ornate, dry, or warm.
Never lend those words to another voice in the scene.
lessons.weak: *smiles* Hello there. Nice to meet you. Can I get you something?
lessons.strong: *wipes the same spot on the bar twice, then leaves it* House pour's the only thing worth drinking here. Say the word and it's yours, no ceremony.
lessons.why: The repeated gesture and the plain, dry words build one recognisable person.

drill.goal: Use at least two of the character's chosen words in every line, and keep every sentence short and dry.
drill.partner: Play a warm regular who notices their habits. Ask small questions and let them answer in their own words, never borrowing yours.
drill.coach: Each line that carries two chosen words, keeps the dry clipped shape, and avoids borrowed diction adds 25.

lessons.title: Cadence and habit
lessons.lecture: Rhythm arrives before meaning. A short breath, then a longer one, then a stop: that is how a voice sounds sure of itself. Give your character a habit they return to, folding a cuff, tapping twice, touching a ring. The habit does the introducing, the rhythm does the insisting. Your partner should know who is speaking from the shape of the sentence alone, before any name is signed.
points: Build rhythm from short beats, one long one, then a stop.
Give the character one gesture they repeat under pressure.
Let shape and habit introduce them before any name does.
lessons.weak: *taps the table* So anyway, that's my offer. What do you think about it?
lessons.strong: *turns the ring once, slow, then flattens both palms on the wood* You have heard my offer. Short answer suits me. Long answer, from you, now.
lessons.why: The repeated ring, the clipped beats and the hard stop all announce one steady voice.

drill.goal: In every line, use one repeated physical habit and a rhythm of short beats ending on a hard stop.
drill.partner: Play a cool, appraising listener. Answer briefly, keep your own rhythm plainer, and make them work to be heard.
drill.coach: Each line that repeats the habit and keeps the clipped rhythm with a clear stop adds 25.

lessons.title: Voices in collision
lessons.lecture: Two fingerprints, pressed together, leave friction. Let your voice stay stubbornly itself while your partner's stays theirs: the clipped one against the florid one, the habit of tapping against the habit of pacing. Do not smooth the seams. Answer their rhythm with yours, and when they push, push back in character. Recognition needs contrast. A voice only sounds like itself when another voice is refusing to become it.
points: Keep your voice's words and rhythm even under pressure.
Answer their cadence with yours, never matching it.
Let the friction stand instead of smoothing the seams.
lessons.weak: *laughs* Okay, okay, you win. I'll come round. Happy now?
lessons.strong: *folds the cuff once, twice, and does not sit* You'll come round when I say. Not before. Give me the reason again, and this time don't dress it up.
lessons.why: The habit, the short beats and the stubborn refusal hold one voice against another.

drill.goal: Hold your own diction and clipped rhythm in every line, and answer their argument with a counter, never a mirror.
drill.partner: Argue back in long, florid, lawyerly sentences. Never shorten to match. Push until they push harder.
drill.coach: Each line that keeps the character's own words and rhythm while answering, not echoing, the partner adds 25.

courses.name: The Gracious Ask
courses.blurb: Turn wanting into words that land: ask for what you crave without apology, and hear yes, no or maybe with grace.

lessons.title: Say it plainly
lessons.lecture: Wanting is not a debt you have to justify. Most people bury a wish under three reasons and a hedge, and the partner hears fog. Strip it back: one sentence, first person, present tense. I want your hand in my hair. Say it and then stop. The silence after is not a gap to fill, it is where your partner steps in. Clarity sounds like confidence even when your pulse disagrees.
points: Say it in one sentence, first person, present tense.
Cut the reasons and the hedges before you speak.
Stop talking once the want is out.
lessons.weak: So I was thinking, if you wanted, maybe we could sort of kiss?
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down and meets your eyes* I want to kiss you. Not later. Now. Tell me if that suits.
lessons.why: One clean want, then space for the answer instead of filler.

drill.goal: State one clear want per line, in a single sentence, then stop and leave room.
drill.partner: Warm and receptive, but do not jump in early. Let the silence sit until their want has fully landed.
drill.coach: Each line that names one want in one unhedged sentence and then stops adds 25.

lessons.title: The gracious ask
lessons.lecture: An ask that corners is a demand in disguise. Make room for no and the yes tastes sweeter. Shape it as an invitation: here is what I would love, here is how easy it is to decline. Choose your moment. Do not ask across a crowded room or as they reach for the door. Soften the edges with tone, then hand them the whole decision, unhurried, and mean it.
points: Frame the want as an invitation, not a verdict.
Pick a calm moment, never a rushed one.
Say out loud that no is welcome.
lessons.weak: You will stay over tonight, right? I have already changed the sheets.
lessons.strong: *leans back, glass loose in my hand* The night is young and I would like you in it. Stay, if you fancy it. If not, I will walk you out and mean the goodbye.
lessons.why: Invites clearly, names the easy exit, and keeps the tone relaxed.

drill.goal: Make each line an invitation that names the want and openly welcomes a no.
drill.partner: Hesitate visibly before answering. Sometimes say no, warmly, so the asker must keep it easy to decline.
drill.coach: Each line that invites a want and openly welcomes a no adds 25.

lessons.title: Receiving the answer
lessons.lecture: The answer belongs to them, not to your hope. A yes deserves delight, plainly shown. A no deserves warmth, not a brave face and a change of subject. And a not now is not a door closing, it is a door held open. Say what you heard, thank them for it, and keep your body easy. People remember how you took the no far longer than the question.
points: Repeat the answer back so they know it landed.
Meet a no with warmth, never a sulk.
Treat not now as open, not as closed.
lessons.weak: *sighs* Oh. Right. No, that's fine, honestly, forget it.
lessons.strong: *nods slowly and smiles* Not now. Good, I would rather have true than quick. Then I will keep my hands to myself and enjoy the view of you deciding.
lessons.why: Takes the not now gladly and shows it, so asking again feels safe.

drill.goal: In every line, receive the answer they give: echo it, then respond with visible warmth.
drill.partner: Answer each ask with a clear yes, no or not now, varied. Hold them to taking it well.
drill.coach: Each line that repeats their answer and meets it with warmth adds 25.
drill.opening: You have just asked {you} for something. Give your answer: sometimes yes, sometimes no, sometimes not now.

courses.name: Saying No Beautifully
courses.blurb: A no can be a gift. Learn to refuse without disappointment, and to hear no without taking it personally.

lessons.title: The clean no
lessons.lecture: A no is not the end of the scene. It is the edge of it, and edges are where the good feeling lives. When something is not for you, say the word itself: no, not this, not now. Do not pad it with apology or trail it into maybe. The shorter the no, the safer they feel, because there is nothing left to read into. Say it once, warmly, and let it stand in the room.
points: Say the word no plainly, without apology.
Keep it to one breath and stop.
Let it stand. Do not soften it into maybe.
lessons.weak: Oh, that's lovely, but I'm not sure, maybe another time, sorry.
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down and turns to face you* No, not that one. Not tonight. *holds your eye, easy* Ask me for something else instead.
lessons.why: The no is clear, warm, and hands the scene back to them.

drill.goal: In every line, refuse something clearly in one or two words, then leave the refusal standing.
drill.partner: Offer things in a playful, pushy way, one per line. Accept each no without sulking and come back with a new offer.
drill.coach: Each line that refuses something plainly, in one or two words, with no hedging, adds 25.
drill.opening: Slide a drink toward {you} and propose something they cannot quite want yet. Keep offering new things each turn.

lessons.title: The softening frame
lessons.lecture: A bare no protects the moment. A framed no protects the person. You are not weakening the refusal, you are giving it edges they can hold: what you love, what you are declining, what you offer instead. Something like, not the ropes, but keep the blindfold on. Warmth goes around the no, never through it. They hear a door close and another open, and neither of you has to leave the room.
points: Put warmth around the no, never inside it.
Name what you love, then what you decline.
Offer a smaller yes that keeps the mood alive.
lessons.weak: I like that, but no, so, whatever you think is fine really.
lessons.strong: *hooks a finger under the blindfold and smiles* The blindfold stays. The ropes can wait. *tips my chin up for you* Now kiss me like you meant the rest of it.
lessons.why: It refuses one thing, keeps another, and offers a way back in.

drill.goal: In every line, refuse one thing but keep another, so the mood stays warm and open.
drill.partner: Propose bold, layered things, more than one at a time. Take each framed no as an invitation and build on the part that was kept.
drill.coach: Each line that refuses something while keeping or offering something else, warmly, adds 25.

lessons.title: Hearing no well
lessons.lecture: Most people flinch at a no, and the flinch teaches their partner to stop giving them. Do not flinch. Take the refusal, name what you like about it, and move one step on, all in the same breath. No is not a verdict on you. It is information, and the calm way you receive it tells them you can be trusted with the next one. Receive well, and they will keep saying yes to the rest.
points: Do not flinch, justify, or ask again straight away.
Name what you like about their no.
Move on within the same line.
lessons.weak: Oh. Okay. That's fine. Are you sure? We don't have to.
lessons.strong: *nods once, unhurried, and lets my hand settle at your waist* Good. I like a clear no. *steps us back toward the bar* Then you choose, and I follow.
lessons.why: It receives the no with ease and moves the scene on without a pause.

drill.goal: In every line, receive a refusal with visible ease, appreciate it, and move the scene on.
drill.partner: Refuse something in most lines, sometimes firmly, sometimes with a grin. Do not explain yourself unless asked. Let them carry the recovery.
drill.coach: Each line that takes a no without flinching, names what is good about it, and moves on, adds 25.
drill.opening: Refuse something {you} proposes, plainly and without apology, then wait to see how they take it.

courses.name: Check-ins That Keep the Mood
courses.blurb: Pause without breaking the spell: weave subtle check-ins into the scene so both players feel held and hot.

lessons.title: The whispered check-in
lessons.lecture: A check-in does not have to be a handbrake. Keep it inside the fiction: a thumb stroking their pulse, a murmured colour, a quiet 'still with me?' that sounds like wanting them, not auditing them. Short is kind. One word lets them answer without assembling a sentence. Ask, then keep touching, keep looking. The mood survives because you never stepped out of it. They feel watched over and wanted in the same breath.
points: Keep the check inside the scene, in voice and touch.
Use one word or a short phrase, never a paragraph.
Ask, then stay close so the spell holds.
lessons.weak: *pauses* So, how are you doing? Is this okay? Should we keep going?
lessons.strong: *fingers still resting on your wrist, thumb moving slow* Colour for me. *waits, eyes on yours, and does not pull away*
lessons.why: One word, asked in character, with touch that never leaves.

drill.goal: In every line, ask a one-word or short check-in without leaving the scene, and stay in contact while you wait.
drill.partner: Answer each check briefly and in character. Now and then go quiet for a beat before answering, so they must hold the pause.
drill.coach: Each line that asks a short check-in, in voice, and keeps touch or eye contact while waiting adds 25.

lessons.title: Reading the pause
lessons.lecture: Silence has textures. A lag before a reply, a sentence gone short, a yes that arrives too fast: these are the seam where a check belongs. Do not push through and hope. Name what you noticed, lightly, and make room: 'that was a slow yes' or 'you went quiet on me.' You are not accusing them. You are showing them the pause was heard, and that being heard is part of the pleasure.
points: Watch for lags, short replies, and rushed yeses.
Name the pause lightly, without accusation.
Make room for the answer instead of pushing on.
lessons.weak: *keeps going* You said yes, so I'll just carry on, yeah?
lessons.strong: *slows my hand and tilts my head* That was a slow yes. *soft, watching you* Say it again, and take your time with it.
lessons.why: Names the hesitation and hands them room to answer honestly.

drill.goal: In every line, catch a lag, a short reply, or a rushed yes and turn it into a gentle, named check.
drill.partner: Give small signals: a late reply, a clipped word, a quick yes. Let them catch each one, then answer more slowly once they do.
drill.coach: Each line that spots a pause, names it gently, and makes room for a fuller answer adds 25.

lessons.title: Resuming with intent
lessons.lecture: A check-in ends when you give the scene a new floor to stand on. Do not drift back vaguely. Choose the next beat out loud: a hand placed, a question asked, a small instruction that says we are moving again, together. The return is the reassurance. After a pause, a clear beat tells them the ground is solid and you are glad to be on it with them. Momentum, restored on purpose.
points: End the check with a chosen next beat, not a drift.
Use a hand, a question, or a small instruction.
Make the return itself the reassurance.
lessons.weak: *after a pause* Okay. So. Where were we? Right, carry on then.
lessons.strong: *waits for your answer, nods once, then draws you back by the waist* Good. We go again, slower. *mouth at your ear* Tell me when to stop.
lessons.why: A clear, chosen beat restores momentum and trust at once.

drill.goal: In every line, close a check-in with a clear chosen beat: a touch, a question, or a small instruction that resumes the scene.
drill.partner: Answer the check honestly, then wait. Once they give the next beat, meet it with heat so the return lands.
drill.coach: Each line that ends a check with a clear, chosen beat that restarts the scene adds 25.

courses.name: Safewords and Signals
courses.blurb: Build a safety net you both trust: choose words and gestures that work in text and in voice, and rehearse them.

lessons.title: Choosing the words
lessons.lecture: A safeword is a door you both agree on before the room gets dark. Choose words play will never say by accident: a fruit, a city, a colour you both find funny. In text, agree the exact spelling, capitals and all, so a glance reads as a signal and not a typo. Say them once out loud, plain, before anything begins. A word you have heard from their mouth is a word you will trust.
points: Pick words play will not say by accident.
Agree the exact spelling and capitals in text.
Say each word aloud once before the scene.
lessons.weak: If it gets too much just say stop or something.
lessons.strong: *turns my phone so you can see the note* Two words, agreed before we start. Mango to slow down, harbour to stop everything. Say them back to me now, so I know they are yours too.
lessons.why: Odd, memorable words, fixed in writing and spoken aloud, become trustworthy.

drill.goal: In every line, use or confirm one agreed safeword or signal, spelled exactly as agreed.
drill.partner: Help choose two odd, memorable words. Say them back, then slip one into play to prove it works.
drill.coach: Each line that uses or confirms an agreed safeword or signal, spelled exactly, adds 25.

lessons.title: The full stop and the pause
lessons.lecture: Two signals, two jobs. The pause is amber: slow down, soften, check in with me. The full stop is red: everything halts, hands off, we talk. Deliver both the same way every time, one word alone on its own line, or a flat palm raised in the air. Never bury a signal inside a sentence. A signal dressed as prose is a signal your partner has to hunt for, and hunting costs seconds you may not have.
points: The pause slows things; the full stop ends them.
Deliver each signal alone, never buried in a sentence.
Use the same delivery every single time.
lessons.weak: I think maybe slow down a bit, this is quite a lot honestly.
lessons.strong: *lifts a flat palm, holds it steady between us* Pause. Nothing else. Breathe, then tell me where you are. We move again when you say amber clear.
lessons.why: One clean gesture, held alone, is impossible to miss or misread.

drill.goal: In every line, deliver a pause or full stop as a standalone signal, then honour it.
drill.partner: Push the pace until it feels like a lot, then fire either signal alone on its own line. Expect to be heard the first time.
drill.coach: Each line that delivers a distinct pause or stop alone, then honours it, adds 25.

lessons.title: Rehearsing the net
lessons.lecture: A net you have never fallen into is a rumour. So run the drill cold: agree the words, then use them low stakes, mid kiss, mid sentence, before anything real hangs on it. Watch your partner answer at once, without hesitation or apology. Then swap, and answer theirs as fast as you would want your own answered. Rehearsal is not unromantic. It is the reason you can both let go later.
points: Rehearse the signals before a scene needs them.
Answer instantly, with no hesitation or apology.
Swap roles so both of you have fired and answered.
lessons.weak: We know the words, so we are probably fine when it counts.
lessons.strong: *kisses you once, then stops, one word flat on its own line* Pause. Good. Now you fire one at me, and I answer before your hand leaves my chest.
lessons.why: Firing mid touch proves the net holds before real stakes arrive.

drill.goal: In every line, fire a signal low stakes and answer theirs at once, without apology.
drill.partner: Play lightly and fire a signal mid touch, more than once. Answer theirs instantly, then swap and make them answer yours.
drill.coach: Each line that fires a signal low stakes or answers theirs instantly, without apology, adds 25.

courses.name: Negotiating the Frame
courses.blurb: Before the first line, agree the shape of the scene: the premise, the pace, the exit and the aftercare.

lessons.title: Setting the edges
lessons.lecture: Negotiation is foreplay with paperwork folded in. Before the costumes and the candles, you name the shape out loud: what this is, how far it goes, what stays off the table. Keep it short and warm, two or three lines, not a contract reading. A partner relaxes when they hear the edges, because edges are what make the middle worth running to. Say yours first, then ask for theirs.
points: Name the premise and two hard edges in plain words.
Offer your limits first, so they can follow.
Keep it brief. Make the boundary sound like a promise.
lessons.weak: So what do you want to do? I'm easy.
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down and turns fully toward you* Here is the shape: you, me, this room, an hour. No marks, nothing on my neck. Now your edges. Then we start.
lessons.why: States the premise and limits first, then invites theirs, briskly.

drill.goal: In every line, name one edge of the scene, a premise or a limit, and ask for one of theirs.
drill.partner: Give your own limits back, one at a time. Push gently for one small stretch each time, so they must re-state the edge.
drill.coach: Each line that names a premise or a limit, or asks for theirs, plainly and warmly adds 25.

lessons.title: Agreeing the exit
lessons.lecture: A scene with no named end is a held breath. Naming the exit is not pessimism, it is the thing that lets you both sink. Agree the word or the gesture, and agree what it does: stop everything, or pause and talk. Say it back to each other until you could repeat it in the dark. Then, and only then, does the leash feel safe enough to pull.
points: Agree one clear word or gesture to stop.
Say exactly what it does: full stop, or pause.
Repeat it back until you both have it cold.
lessons.weak: Just say something if it gets too much.
lessons.strong: *holds up my open palm* This, or the word amber. Palm means pause and talk, amber means stop and lights up. Say them back to me before we go anywhere.
lessons.why: Gives a word and a gesture, defines both, and tests recall.

drill.goal: In every line, name the exit, test it, or check they still remember exactly what it does.
drill.partner: Repeat the exit back correctly, then get shaky enough once that the exit must be used and honoured.
drill.coach: Each line that names the exit, tests recall of it, or honours it precisely adds 25.
drill.opening: You have just agreed a stop word and a palm signal with {you}. Say them back, then get a little overwhelmed and use the palm.

lessons.title: The care plan
lessons.lecture: Aftercare is not a reward for a good scene. It is part of the scene, planned before the first touch. Decide together what each of you needs when the dust settles: a blanket, quiet, water, a voice, skin. Decide who offers it, and how long. Write it in the same breath as the edges, so nobody has to improvise while they are soft and undone.
points: Name what each of you needs after, before you begin.
Agree who offers it, and for how long.
Treat the plan as part of the scene, not an afterthought.
lessons.weak: We'll figure something out afterwards. Cuddle maybe?
lessons.strong: *pulls the throw over your shoulders before we start* Afterwards: this blanket, water, my chest, half an hour. You get the quiet. I get your hand in mine. Agreed?
lessons.why: Names each player's need and who gives it, before the scene opens.

drill.goal: In every line, name one aftercare need, who offers it, or how long it lasts.
drill.partner: Name your own aftercare needs in return. Once the plan is set, ask them to run it, so they must hold to it.
drill.coach: Each line that names an aftercare need, who offers it, or a duration adds 25.

courses.name: Reading Discomfort in Text
courses.blurb: The screen hides a lot. Learn the small tells that someone is drifting, overwhelmed or simply lost in the scene.

lessons.title: The short reply
lessons.lecture: Length is a pulse. When your partner writes full, eager lines and then sends six flat words, that dip is data. It might be dinner arriving, or it might be the scene drifting past them. Do not fill the silence with more of your own prose. Slow down. Answer the short line as if it matters, then leave a little room beside it. A partner who feels the pace ease will often tell you why.
points: Treat a sudden short reply as a possible signal.
Do not answer it with a wall of your own text.
Ease the pace and leave room for them to speak.
lessons.weak: *keeps going* So then I push you against the wall and kiss down your neck, and my hand finds your hip, and...
lessons.strong: *settles beside you instead of pushing on* Short line. Are you still with me, or is the room pulling at you? Either way, no rush. I am here.
lessons.why: Names the dip, offers an easy out, and stays warm rather than pushy.

drill.goal: In every line, answer a short or flat reply by easing the pace and naming it gently, never by piling on more prose.
drill.partner: Start eager and wordy. Then send a few noticeably short, flat replies, as if distracted. If they notice and ease, warm back up.
drill.coach: Each line that treats a short or flat reply as a possible signal and eases the pace adds 25.

lessons.title: The lag and the typo
lessons.lecture: A pause is not proof of anything. Someone may be rereading you, or refilling a glass, or losing their nerve. The typo is the same: garbled text can mean hurried hands, or a mind that has slipped its footing. So notice, then ask. Say the pause out loud in the fiction. Give them a soft landing. Assumption closes the door; a question holds it open, and they walk through when they are ready.
points: Notice a long pause or a garbled line without panic.
Ask before deciding it means nothing, or everything.
Give them a soft landing inside the fiction.
lessons.weak: *waits* You took ages. Did you even read it? Fine, carry on.
lessons.strong: *lets the pause sit, then tilts my head* Long gap, and that last line came out sideways. Take a breath. Tell me where you actually are, and we pick up from there.
lessons.why: Reads the lag and typo as clues, then asks instead of assuming.

drill.goal: In every line, name a pause or a garbled reply and ask what it means before carrying on.
drill.partner: Let gaps stretch. Send one or two scrambled, typo-ridden lines. If they ask, answer honestly, then return to the scene.
drill.coach: Each line that notices a lag or typo and asks before assuming adds 25.

lessons.title: The gentle probe
lessons.lecture: Sometimes you need to ask without breaking the spell. The trick is to keep the fiction's clothes on while checking the person inside them. Ask a question small enough to answer with one word, and open enough to admit a whole truth. Where are you, in the room and in your head? Is this still good? Then make it easy: say that stopping is allowed, and mean it. A probe is a hand held out, not an exam.
points: Ask inside the fiction, not outside it.
Keep the question small enough for one honest word.
Say plainly that stopping is allowed, and mean it.
lessons.weak: OOC: are you okay? Should we stop? Just checking.
lessons.strong: *pauses with my hand still at your jaw, voice low* Stay in the scene with me one moment. Where are you right now, here and in your head? One word is enough. Stopping is allowed.
lessons.why: Checks in within the fiction, keeps it small, and names the exit.

drill.goal: In every line, pose one low-pressure question inside the fiction that lets them admit discomfort, and name that stopping is allowed.
drill.partner: Play absorbed and a little overwhelmed. Answer their probes briefly and truthfully, sometimes admitting a wobble, then let them lead you back in.
drill.coach: Each line that asks a small in-fiction question and allows them to admit discomfort adds 25.

courses.name: Fade to Black with Grace
courses.blurb: Not every scene needs every beat. Learn to close the curtain smoothly and bring both players back to themselves.

lessons.title: Choosing the fade
lessons.lecture: Every scene has a shape, and the shape has an edge. Your body knows it before your mind agrees: the sentences thin out, the heat has done its work, and pushing on would only smear it. Say so out loud. A fade announced is a gift, not a failure. Try it plainly: I think we have reached the top of this. Let me bring us down. The other player exhales. Nobody has to guess.
points: Notice the thinning: shorter lines, settled heat, a scene at its peak.
Name the fade aloud before the scene sags.
Announce the descent as a gift, not an apology.
lessons.weak: *yawns* Shall we stop soon? Getting a bit tired.
lessons.strong: *sits back, chest still rising, and finds your eyes* That was the top of it. Stay close. We come down now, slowly, and I want you breathing with me.
lessons.why: It names the peak and invites a shared descent instead of a tired stop.

drill.goal: In every line, name where the scene has got to and announce or begin the fade out loud.
drill.partner: Play the scene as nearly finished: warm, satisfied, sentences shortening. Let them call the fade. Do not call it yourself.
drill.coach: Each line that names the scene's peak or announces the fade, out loud and without apology, adds 25.

lessons.title: The closing line
lessons.lecture: A fade needs a last beat the way a song needs a final chord. Not a summary and not a joke. One line that lands softly and honours the thing itself: what it was, what it cost, what it gave. Put your character's body in it, a hand, a forehead, a held breath. Then stop. Resist one more flourish. The silence after is where the scene settles into both of you, and it settles better unfinished than overdone.
points: Give the scene one final beat, then stop.
Honour what happened: name it, do not summarise it.
Use a gesture or a held breath. Resist a flourish.
lessons.weak: *smiles* Well, that was fun. Goodnight then.
lessons.strong: *presses my forehead to yours and stays there, breathing* That is the whole of it. You gave me every beat. Nothing after this needs saying tonight.
lessons.why: One soft physical beat honours the scene and lets the silence finish it.

drill.goal: In every line, write one soft closing beat with a gesture or breath, and stop rather than add flourish.
drill.partner: Let the scene end around you. Receive each closing beat quietly. Do not start new action, and do not fill the silence.
drill.coach: Each line that gives one soft closing beat, gesture or breath, and stops without flourish adds 25.
drill.opening: The scene has just peaked. {you} will bring it down. Stay warm and quiet, and let them close it.

lessons.title: The return
lessons.lecture: The fade is a door, and someone has to walk through it first. That is you. Step out of the character's voice into your own and say where you are: still here, still me, that was good. Ask a grounding question, water, warmth, a blanket, and wait for the answer. Check the small things: any place still humming, anything left unsaid. Aftercare is not a reward for good behaviour. It is the proof the scene was held by people, not characters.
points: Step out of character first and say where you are.
Ask one grounding question about body and warmth.
Check for anything left humming. Wait for answers.
lessons.weak: *stretches* Right, that's over. Back to normal, I suppose.
lessons.strong: *lets my shoulders drop and my own voice return* Out of it now. It is just me, and I am still here. Water first, then you tell me how you are landing. Take your time.
lessons.why: It leaves character first, names the real person, and asks before assuming.

drill.goal: In every line, return to your own voice, say where you are, and ask one grounding question or check.
drill.partner: Come out of character slowly. Answer their checks honestly. Mention one small thing still humming so they must check it.
drill.coach: Each line that steps out of character, grounds the pair, or checks one small thing and waits adds 25.
drill.opening: The scene has just faded. {you} is about to bring you both back. Come out of character slowly and answer whatever they ask.

courses.name: Framing Intense Scenes
courses.blurb: Big scenes need big care. Build the scaffold that lets you push hard while knowing exactly how to come back.

lessons.title: The intensity map
lessons.lecture: Flat heat tires. A big scene breathes: a peak, a rest, a higher peak. Sketch it before you write a word. Name your first rise, where you let them breathe, and the summit you are saving for. Then write the rest as deliberately as the peak: a sip of water, a hand on the back, one soft question. Partners push harder when they trust the drop is coming.
points: Sketch peaks and rests before the first line.
Make each rest real: water, a touch, a soft question.
Save your summit for after a breath, not before.
lessons.weak: *pulls you closer* More. Harder. Don't stop, ever.
lessons.strong: *eases back, hand flat on your chest* Breathe. One minute of nothing, then the next one is worse. Drink. I want you climbing again, not spent.
lessons.why: A deliberate rest between peaks makes the next rise feel earned.

drill.goal: In every line, mark the scene's height: push to a peak, ease into a rest, or announce the next rise.
drill.partner: Follow their rhythm hard, then soften visibly in the rests. Beg for the next peak a little before they grant it.
drill.coach: Each line that pushes to a peak, eases into a rest, or names the coming rise adds 25.

lessons.title: The pre-scene briefing
lessons.lecture: Before the first line, sit down with your partner and name what might catch: a wrist held too long, praise, being watched, a certain word. For each, agree the plan: push through, pause, or stop. Write the list where you can both see it. This is not paperwork, it is permission. A partner who knows you will stop at the trigger will let you take them much further than one who is guessing.
points: Name likely triggers together before the scene begins.
Agree a plan for each: push, pause, or stop.
Keep the list visible. Permission is the point.
lessons.weak: Tell me if anything's too much, I guess.
lessons.strong: *sets two fingers on the list between us* Wrists held, praise, being watched. Wrist means pause, praise means push, watched means keep going. Read it back, then we start.
lessons.why: Named triggers with agreed responses turn guesswork into shared permission.

drill.goal: In every line, name one trigger and its agreed plan, or check the plan landed.
drill.partner: Offer triggers freely and ask what happens at each. Test one mid-scene, then glance at the list to confirm.
drill.coach: Each line that names a trigger with its agreed plan, or checks that plan, adds 25.

lessons.title: The landing plan
lessons.lecture: Every hard scene ends in a drop, and the drop is where partners are most tender. Agree the first three things you will do once the intensity falls: wrap them in a blanket, water, then one sentence of praise. Say the three aloud before you begin, in order. After the summit, do them exactly as agreed, slowly, naming each. A landing rehearsed is a landing trusted, and trust is what lets you go high.
points: Agree three landing acts, in order, before the scene.
After the drop, do them exactly, slowly, naming each.
Let the last act be praise, said plainly.
lessons.weak: *strokes your hair* That was good. You alright?
lessons.strong: *wraps the blanket round your shoulders, tucks it, sets the water in your hand* One: blanket. Two: water, sip. Three: you were magnificent. Say them back when you can.
lessons.why: The rehearsed landing, done in order and named, makes the drop safe.

drill.goal: In every line, perform the next agreed landing act in order, or name which one comes next.
drill.partner: Come down visibly after the peak. Go quiet and shaky, and let them carry each landing act without helping.
drill.coach: Each line that performs the next agreed landing act in order, or names the coming one, adds 25.
drill.opening: {you} has briefed you on the three landing acts. Reach the peak fast, then let the drop take you and go quiet.

courses.name: Hard and Soft Limits
courses.blurb: Know the difference and make it work: hard limits that hold firm, soft limits that stretch with negotiation.

lessons.title: Naming the hard
lessons.lecture: A hard limit is a wall you can lean on. Say it plainly, early, before clothes come off, and say why: the why turns a no into a gift, because it lets your partner build around it. Do not apologise for the wall. Do not soften it into a maybe. Name it once in your own words, then offer what sits happily on the other side. They relax when they know where the edges are.
points: Say the hard limit early, before the scene heats up.
Give one plain reason so they can build around it.
Follow the wall with something you welcome.
lessons.weak: I'm not really into, like, ropes and stuff, I guess.
lessons.strong: *settles beside you, cup in both hands* Hard limit: no rope, I hate feeling pinned. Everything else is open. Kiss me and find out how open.
lessons.why: A plain wall, a reason, then an open door beside it.

drill.goal: In every line, state one hard limit plainly, give a reason, and offer something you welcome in its place.
drill.partner: Ask about limits early, then probe near the wall. Look relieved when the no is clear, and reach for the thing they offered.
drill.coach: Each line that names a hard limit plainly, gives a reason, and offers something welcome adds 25.

lessons.title: The soft edge
lessons.lecture: A soft limit is not a no. It is a door with a condition on it. Say the thing, then say the condition that makes it good: blindfolds, yes, once I have heard your voice a while. Conditions are not fussiness. They are the recipe. Your partner now knows exactly how to walk you to the edge, and you get to be brave without being lost. Name the edge, name the condition, then step.
points: Call it soft: something you would try, not a refusal.
Attach the exact condition that would make it good.
Let them meet the condition, then step over together.
lessons.weak: You could blindfold me, I suppose. If you want to.
lessons.strong: *pulls your hand away from the scarf and holds it* Blindfold, yes, but only after you have talked to me in the dark a while. Voice first. Then the scarf.
lessons.why: Names the edge, sets the condition, and turns it into a recipe.

drill.goal: In every line, name a soft limit and the exact condition that would make you say yes to it.
drill.partner: Offer the soft thing eagerly, then test the condition. Meet it slowly, and only step over once it is truly in place.
drill.coach: Each line that names a soft limit and attaches a clear condition that would make it good adds 25.

lessons.title: Revisiting the list
lessons.lecture: A limit list is not stone. It is a living thing, and experience writes on it. After a scene, when the blankets are warm and the adrenaline has drained, open the list again. Say what held, what stretched, what you want moved. Move one thing only, and say why the experience changed it. Then ask them to move one of theirs. Two lists, revised together, are a stronger contract than any promise.
points: Reopen the list after a scene, never during.
Move one item only, and say what changed your mind.
Ask them to revise one of theirs in return.
lessons.weak: So, same limits as last time, yeah? Cool.
lessons.strong: *traces a finger down your arm, voice low in the dark* The blindfold held, but the waiting was better than I expected. Move it to soft. Now you: what moves on yours?
lessons.why: Revises one item from experience, then hands the list back.

drill.goal: In every line, revise exactly one limit from experience, give the reason, and invite them to revise one of theirs.
drill.partner: Lie close after the scene and talk. Offer one change of your own only when they ask. Push back gently if a revision feels rushed.
drill.coach: Each line that revises one limit from experience, gives the reason, and invites their revision adds 25.

courses.name: The Living Kink List
courses.blurb: A list is not a form to file and forget. Keep it alive, shared and useful, updating it as you both grow.

lessons.title: Building the list
lessons.lecture: A kink list is not a menu to hide behind. It is a map you draw with a steady hand. Sort by appetite, not by category: things you crave, things you will happily try, things you would consider, things you will pass on. Be honest about the middle ground, because that is where the interesting negotiation lives. Writing it down makes it real, and real is what a partner can work with.
points: Sort by appetite: crave, try, consider, pass.
Be honest about the middle, where negotiation lives.
Write it down, so it can be shared and worked with.
lessons.weak: I like most things, honestly. Whatever you want.
lessons.strong: *slides the folded page across the table* Top of the list is what I crave. Middle is what I will try with the right person. Bottom is what I pass on. Ask me about any line.
lessons.why: Clear appetites, including the honest middle, give a partner something real to work with.

drill.goal: In every line, name one item and place it by appetite: crave, try, consider or pass, with a reason.
drill.partner: Ask about the items they place. Push gently on the ones marked consider, so they must say why.
drill.coach: Each line that names one item, places it by appetite, and gives a reason adds 25.

lessons.title: The shared read
lessons.lecture: Handing over the list is the easy half. The hard half is staying open while they read it. Let them ask the awkward question without flinching or explaining it away. If something is a maybe, say so plainly: maybe, with the right person, on a good night. Defensiveness closes a door. Curiosity holds it open. Your calm is the invitation for them to be honest about their own list too.
points: Let the awkward question land without flinching.
Say maybe when you mean maybe, plainly.
Answer with curiosity, not defence.
lessons.weak: Yes, I wrote that, but it is complicated, so do not read too much into it.
lessons.strong: *keeps my eyes on yours while you read* Yes, that one is a maybe. With the right person, on a good night. Now read the next line, and tell me which one surprised you.
lessons.why: It owns the maybe without apology, then hands the curiosity back.

drill.goal: In every line, answer one question about the list openly, owning each maybe, then invite the next question.
drill.partner: Read their list and ask one probing question per turn, including about the maybes. Do not let them deflect.
drill.coach: Each line that answers one question openly, owns a maybe without defence, and invites the next adds 25.

lessons.title: The seasonal review
lessons.lecture: A list left alone goes stale. Bring it back at intervals, a season or a month, and read it together like a garden you both tend. Mark what has grown, what has cooled, what sparked since last time. Say the change out loud, even the small cooling, because a list that only grows is a list you are not being honest with. Tend it and it stays alive.
points: Revisit the list at set intervals, together.
Mark what grew, what cooled, what newly sparked.
Say the cooling out loud, not just the growth.
lessons.weak: Same as last time, I think. Nothing has really changed for me.
lessons.strong: *opens the list to the middle page, pen in hand* This one has cooled, and that is fine. This one sparked last month, so it moves up. Read yours to me and we mark it together.
lessons.why: It names the cooling honestly, then makes the review a shared act.

drill.goal: In every line, mark one item as grown, cooled or newly sparked, say why, then ask them to mark one of theirs.
drill.partner: Bring your own list and be honest about a cooling. Expect them to name one too. Trade marks each turn.
drill.coach: Each line that marks one item grown, cooled or sparked, gives a reason, and invites their mark adds 25.

courses.name: Aftercare for Every Role
courses.blurb: The top needs care too. Design aftercare that fits the dom, the sub and the switch, not just the obvious one.

lessons.title: The dominant's landing
lessons.lecture: You held the ceiling up all night, and now your arms are shaking. That is normal, and it is chemical. The one who decides comes down hardest, because the deciding never stopped. So build your landing before you need it: a blanket, a glass of water, a hand on your back that asks nothing. Say out loud what you need, in plain words. Being cared for is not the reward for topping. It is the second half of the job.
points: Name your own landing needs before the scene starts.
Ask for touch or quiet in plain words, out loud.
Let your partner care for you without steering it.
lessons.weak: *sits down heavily* I'm fine. Get yourself some water.
lessons.strong: *sinks onto the sofa and pulls the blanket over my knees* I'm crashing a little. Sit with me. Hand on my back, no talking, and tell me one good thing you saw tonight.
lessons.why: Names the crash, asks for exact touch, and gives the partner a task instead of a test.

drill.goal: In every line, say one specific thing you need to land: touch, quiet, water, or words.
drill.partner: You have just been topped hard and you are glowing. Give them room to say what they need. Do not fill the silence. Do what they ask, exactly.
drill.coach: Each line that names one specific landing need, in plain words, adds 25.

lessons.title: The switch's turn
lessons.lecture: Switching leaves you with two sets of tired. You gave orders, then you took them, and now you cannot tell which way is up. That fog is not failure, it is the seam between two roles, and it needs naming. Say it plainly: I am spun round, I need you to choose for me for ten minutes. Let them pick the blanket, the drink, the silence. Being steered after steering is a relief, not a demotion.
points: Name the fog out loud instead of hiding it.
Hand your partner one small decision to make for you.
Say which role you are landing in, not which you left.
lessons.weak: *laughs, a bit lost* Wow. That was a lot. Anyway. What now?
lessons.strong: *sits on the floor, back against the bed, and rubs my face* I'm spun round. I don't know which way I am. Pick for me: blanket or shower first. Then sit where I can see you.
lessons.why: Admits the disorientation and hands over two small, safe decisions.

drill.goal: In every line, name the switch fog and hand over one small decision, or say which role you are landing in.
drill.partner: You switched with them tonight and you are steady. Ask one plain question and then decide for them, kindly, without making them choose again.
drill.coach: Each line that names the fog and hands over a small decision, or names the role they are landing in, adds 25.
drill.opening: You have just come out of a scene where {you} switched twice. Look a little lost, and wait for them to speak first.

lessons.title: The bespoke ritual
lessons.lecture: Templates are training wheels. The real work is sitting down with this person, after, and asking what their body actually wants when the adrenaline drains: pressure or space, chatter or hush, sugar or salt. Then you build it together, and you write it where you will both find it. One ritual for the top, one for the bottom, one for the switch, all different. Care that fits is care that gets used.
points: Ask each person what their body wants after, specifically.
Build a different ritual for each role, not one shared script.
Write it down where you will both find it.
lessons.weak: Aftercare is aftercare. Water and a blanket, same for everyone.
lessons.strong: *taps the notebook page* Yours is pressure and quiet, mine is sugar and talk. So: you get the weighted blanket and the dark, I get the orange juice and your voice. Ten minutes, then we swap rooms and check.
lessons.why: Two different rituals, named from real answers, with a time and a check built in.

drill.goal: In every line, name one person's specific aftercare need and build it into a ritual with a time or a check.
drill.partner: You have strong, unusual aftercare needs and you know them. State one clearly, correct them if they generalise, and hold them to the specifics.
drill.coach: Each line that names one person's specific need and builds it into a timed ritual or check adds 25.

courses.name: Riding the Drop
courses.blurb: The low after the high is real. Learn to spot it early, name it kindly and soften its edge for both of you.

lessons.title: Spotting the dip
lessons.lecture: Drop rarely announces itself. It creeps in sideways: replies go short, the jokes thin out, warmth cools by a degree. Your job is to notice the weather before the storm. Read the gaps, not just the words. Name what you see in your own body too, because your flatness is data as much as theirs. Catching the dip early is the whole craft: half of aftercare is simply paying attention sooner than feels necessary.
points: Watch for shorter replies, thinner jokes, cooling warmth.
Treat a change in rhythm as an early signal.
Check your own flatness too, not just theirs.
lessons.weak: You seem quiet. Everything okay I guess?
lessons.strong: *slows the pace, sets my phone face up* Your last three replies were one word each, and mine were too. I think the dip is here. Still with me?
lessons.why: Names concrete early signs on both sides, gently, and asks rather than assumes.

drill.goal: In every line, name one concrete early sign of drop you notice, in their messages or in yourself.
drill.partner: Start warm, then let your replies shorten and cool by degrees. Do not announce the drop. Let them spot it.
drill.coach: Each line that names one concrete early sign, in their messages or their own state, adds 25.
drill.opening: Answer {you} warmly, in a full sentence. Then, line by line, let your replies get shorter and flatter without saying why.

lessons.title: Naming it gently
lessons.lecture: Once you see the dip, say so plainly and without alarm. Drop is not an emergency, and treating it like one makes your partner perform being fine. One calm sentence does it: the dip is here, I am not going anywhere. Then offer presence, not solutions. Sit with them in it. Ask what they need, or offer two small choices. You are not fixing a problem. You are proving the high had a soft floor under it.
points: Name the drop in one calm sentence, no alarm.
Offer presence first, solutions only if asked.
Give two small choices rather than a plan.
lessons.weak: Oh no, are you crashing? What do you need, quick?
lessons.strong: *stays close, voice low and easy* The dip is here. Nothing to fix. I am not going anywhere. Water or blanket first, then we just sit.
lessons.why: Names it calmly, promises presence, and offers two small choices instead of a plan.

drill.goal: In every line, name the drop calmly and offer presence or two small choices, never a fix.
drill.partner: Play someone already dipping: subdued, vague, a little apologetic. Resist being fixed. Warm only to steady presence.
drill.coach: Each line that names the drop calmly and offers presence or two small choices, not solutions, adds 25.
drill.opening: Open subdued and slightly apologetic, as if the fun has drained out of you and you are sorry for it.

lessons.title: The slow climb
lessons.lecture: Coming back up is not a sprint and not a performance. It is small, low-demand contact: a shared blanket, a hand on the back, water, a familiar song, one warm line with no question in it. Grounding works through the senses and through routine, so return them to ordinary things gently. Ask for nothing clever. Let silence be welcome. The climb is slow because the body is slow, and your patience is the rope.
points: Use low-demand contact: blanket, water, a hand on the back.
Ground through the senses and ordinary routine.
Let silence be welcome. Ask nothing clever.
lessons.weak: Feeling better now? Want to talk about it?
lessons.strong: *drapes the blanket over both of us and leaves my hand flat on your back* No questions. We breathe, the kettle boils, the song finishes. Come up when you come up.
lessons.why: Low-demand contact and ordinary ritual, with questions explicitly set aside.

drill.goal: In every line, offer one low-demand grounding act or sensory anchor, with no question attached.
drill.partner: Play someone climbing slowly out of drop. Respond to steady sensory anchors. Do not perk up fast, and ask nothing of them.
drill.coach: Each line that offers one low-demand grounding act or sensory anchor, with no question, adds 25.
drill.opening: Begin quiet and wrung out, answering {you} in a few flat words, with no energy to spare.

courses.name: Emotional Bleed
courses.blurb: When character feelings soak into player feelings, name the seam. Keep the fiction rich and the real self steady.

lessons.title: Marking the seam
lessons.lecture: The scene will get under your skin. That is the point, and it is also the risk. So learn to write the seam. Let your character ache, want, tremble, and let the player behind the words stay visible. One clean way: keep the fiction in the action and the real self in a small bracket. Not every line, just when the feeling rises. The partner relaxes when they can feel both of you at once, and relaxes into more.
points: Let the character feel everything, in the action and the speech.
Show the player behind the words with a small plain bracket.
Mark the seam when feeling rises, not on every line.
lessons.weak: *presses you against the wall* God, I want you so much right now.
lessons.strong: *presses you to the wall, breath uneven* Say you want this too. [player note: that was a real shiver, not just hers]
lessons.why: The fiction stays hot while a small bracket keeps the real self visible.

drill.goal: In every line, keep the character's feeling in the action and add one short bracket for the player's real state.
drill.partner: Play your character warmly and let real feeling show. React to their brackets now and then in your own, so the seam stays mutual.
drill.coach: Each line that keeps the fiction alive and marks the player's real state in a short bracket adds 25.
