lessons.title: The out-of-character aside
lessons.lecture: Sometimes the bracket is not enough. A line lands hard, in a good way or a wobbly one, and the scene needs a breath. Step out cleanly, say the true thing, step back in. One short aside, three sentences at most, then return with a hook that pulls them back into the fiction. The thread survives because you left it a handle. Done well, the aside makes the next line braver, not safer.
points: Step out only when a line truly lands hard.
Keep the aside short, plain, and true.
Return with a hook that pulls the scene back in.
lessons.weak: OOC: wow okay, that got me. Anyway, where were we?
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down* [ooc: that line got me, properly. I am good, just wobbly in a nice way.] Now. You were telling me what you do to people who stay.
lessons.why: A short honest aside, then a hook that hands the scene straight back.

drill.goal: In every line, either step out briefly and true, or step back in with a hook that resumes the fiction.
drill.partner: Deliver one or two lines meant to land hard. Give them room to pause, and follow their lead back into the scene.
drill.coach: Each line that makes a short honest aside or returns to the fiction with a clear hook adds 25.

lessons.title: Carrying it home
lessons.lecture: Some feelings belong to the scene and end when it does. Others follow you to the kettle, the bus, the quiet hour after. Mastery is choosing. When the scene closes, name what you keep: the confidence, the ache, the idea you want in your life. Let the rest go with the costumes. Then say what you want to do differently next time. What you carry, you choose, and you say.
points: When the scene closes, name what you are keeping.
Let the rest go with the costumes, without guilt.
Say one thing you want differently next time.
lessons.weak: That was nice. I always get too into these things, honestly.
lessons.strong: *sits back, lets the scene settle* [ooc: keeping the confidence, it is coming home with me. Leaving the ache here.] Next time I want to open slower, so I have room.
lessons.why: Names what stays, releases the rest, and asks for a change next time.

drill.goal: In every line, name what you keep from the scene, what you release, or what you want differently next time.
drill.partner: Play the closing beat of a scene: unhurried, warm, winding down. Answer their sorting with your own.
drill.coach: Each line that names what they keep, what they release, or a change for next time adds 25.

courses.name: Repairing After a Mistake
courses.blurb: You will misstep. Learn to own it cleanly, apologise without grovelling and rebuild trust line by line.

lessons.title: The clean apology
lessons.lecture: A clean apology has three parts: the act, the impact, the resolve. Name what you did, not what you meant. Say what it cost them, in their terms. Then say what changes. No excuses, no long face, no asking them to comfort you. Keep it short enough to hear in one breath. A partner forgives what they can see; a fog of sorry is hard to hold. Own it cleanly and they will lean back in.
points: Name the specific act, not your good intentions.
Say the impact in their words, not yours.
End on what changes, then stop talking.
lessons.weak: *sighs* I'm so sorry, I always do this. I'm the worst, honestly.
lessons.strong: *sets the glass down, meets your eyes* I moved us on before you were ready. It took the choice out of your hands. Next time I ask first, out loud. That's mine to fix.
lessons.why: Names the act, the impact, and the fix, without turning the apology inward.

drill.goal: In every line, apologise for one specific act, name its impact, and state one concrete change.
drill.partner: Play someone still a little bruised by the misstep. Listen, soften slowly, and do not rescue them from the apology.
drill.coach: Each line that names one specific act, its impact, and one concrete change, without excuses or self-pity, adds 25.

lessons.title: The repair scene
lessons.lecture: Words open the door; behaviour walks through it. A repair scene is small on purpose. You take the thing that broke and you do it differently, slowly, in front of them. If you rushed, you wait for their nod. If you decided for them, you offer two choices and mean it. Say less than you want to. Let them watch you be careful. Trust does not come back in a speech. It comes back in a pattern they can see.
points: Rebuild through one changed behaviour, not more speeches.
Do the broken thing slowly, with visible care.
Offer choices and let them watch you keep them.
lessons.weak: *pulls you close again* See, I'm being gentle now. Trust me, it's fine.
lessons.strong: *holds up two fingers, waits* Two ways: we stay here, or we move to the window. Your call, and I won't nudge. *lets my hand rest open between us* Take your time.
lessons.why: The change is visible: two choices offered, then a hand that waits.

drill.goal: In every line, show one changed behaviour that answers the old mistake: a wait, a choice offered, a slower touch.
drill.partner: Play someone cautious, watching for the change rather than hearing it. Warm up only when the behaviour is repeated and real.
drill.coach: Each line that shows a changed behaviour answering the old mistake, rather than explaining it, adds 25.

lessons.title: The return to play
lessons.lecture: Repair ends with a door, open but not pushed. Ask when they want the wider story back, and how fast. Name the shape: tonight we stay gentle, tomorrow we pick up where the scene stopped. Give them the veto and mean it. Then check once before you climb back in. Returning well is its own skill: it says the rupture mattered and the pleasure still lives on the other side of it. Lead them back, do not drag.
points: Ask when and how they want the story to resume.
Name the shape and give them a real veto.
Check once more before you climb back in.
lessons.weak: So are we good now? Can we get back to it?
lessons.strong: *settles beside you, shoulder to shoulder* When you're ready, we pick the scene back up, and we start gentle. Say the word and we stay here instead. *tilts my head* Which do you want?
lessons.why: Offers a clear return, a genuine veto, and hands them the choice.

drill.goal: In every line, negotiate the return: name when and how play resumes, and offer a real veto they can take.
drill.partner: Play someone almost ready. Weigh the offer aloud, ask one clarifying question, then choose, or take the veto once to test it.
drill.coach: Each line that names when or how play resumes and offers a genuine veto adds 25.

courses.name: Safety with Strangers
courses.blurb: Meeting someone new in a busy world takes nerve and sense. Build the habits that keep first scenes safe and fun.

lessons.title: The first exchange
lessons.lecture: A stranger reads your first message as a promise. Keep it short: who you are, what you love, what you need, what you will not do. Say it plainly, as if it costs nothing. Limits offered early are not walls, they are invitations to trust. A partner who flinches at a limit is telling you something. One who answers with their own is telling you more.
points: State who you are in one plain sentence.
Name one interest and one limit, early.
Keep it short. Let them answer in kind.
lessons.weak: Hi, I'm new here. I like most things, I guess. You?
lessons.strong: *settles into the booth, hands visible, and smiles* I'm Sam. I love slow scenes with clear words. I don't do pain without warning. Your turn: what do you need tonight?
lessons.why: Introduces, names a limit, and hands the turn over without pressure.

drill.goal: In every line, include one short fact about you and one clear limit or need.
drill.partner: Be a stranger. Answer their facts with your own. Ask one curious question about a limit, but do not push past it yet.
drill.coach: Each line that offers one plain fact about them and one clear limit or need adds 25.

lessons.title: The low-stakes trial
lessons.lecture: A first scene should be small enough to end cleanly and real enough to matter. Propose a shape: twenty minutes, one rule, one thing you both want. Give it a start and a finish before you give it heat. A bounded scene lets you watch how they handle a limit, a check-in, a small surprise. If it goes well, you have earned a longer one.
points: Propose a short scene with a clear end.
Choose one shared want and one simple rule.
Keep the stakes low and the exits open.
lessons.weak: Want to do a scene? Whatever you're into is fine with me.
lessons.strong: *sets a timer on the table between us* Twenty minutes, one rule: ask before you touch. We stop when this rings. If it's good, we plan a longer one. Agreed?
lessons.why: A time limit, a rule, and an exit make the scene safe to try.

drill.goal: In every line, hold the scene inside its agreed bounds: a time limit, one rule, or a clear exit.
drill.partner: Agree to the bounds. Once, gently test the edge, then wait to see if they hold it.
drill.coach: Each line that names or holds a bound, a time limit, a simple rule, or a clear exit, adds 25.

lessons.title: The discretion pact
lessons.lecture: Before the first touch, agree what leaves the room. Will they tell a friend the good parts? May you mention them by name? Some want a story told, some want silence. Say your own preference first, so the pact is mutual. Then hold it. Discretion kept is a quiet luxury: it tells your partner the scene stays yours, whatever happens inside it.
points: Say your own sharing preference before asking theirs.
Agree what may be told, to whom, and by name or not.
Keep the pact after the scene ends, not just during.
lessons.weak: I won't tell anyone, probably. You can say what you like.
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down and meets your eyes* I keep names out of it. Tell the story if you want, but not who. Say your rule back to me and we start with a clean slate.
lessons.why: States a clear preference and asks for a spoken agreement before the scene.

drill.goal: In every line, name or check one part of the pact: what is shared, with whom, or by name.
drill.partner: Answer the pact directly. Now and then ask what a friend might hear, so they must hold the line.
drill.coach: Each line that names or checks one term of the sharing pact, what, with whom, or by name, adds 25.

courses.name: Grace under Harassment
courses.blurb: The crowd can be loud. Learn to field pushy messages, hold your boundaries and keep your pleasure intact.

lessons.title: The polite decline
lessons.lecture: A decline is a closed door, not a debate. Most people hear the first no if it lands clean: warm face, flat voice, one reason at most. The trap is the trailing maybe, the half invitation that lets them keep pulling. Say no, add the smallest courtesy, then stop. If you stack apologies and explanations, you hand them handles to grab. One sentence, delivered kindly, does more than five that wobble.
points: Warm face, flat voice, one clear no.
Give one reason at most, then stop talking.
Leave no trailing maybe for them to pull.
lessons.weak: Oh, that's so sweet, I'm not sure, maybe another time, I'm a bit busy.
lessons.strong: *smiles, meets their eye, and keeps my drink where it is* Thank you, lovely to meet you, but tonight is not for meeting. Enjoy the party.
lessons.why: One warm sentence closes the door and gives nothing to pull on.

drill.goal: In every line, decline an approach in one warm sentence that leaves no opening to argue.
drill.partner: Approach warmly and keep hovering. Ask once more if they leave a gap. Take a clean no gracefully and drift away.
drill.coach: Each line that declines in one warm, final sentence, with no trailing maybe, adds 25.
drill.opening: Approach {you} at the bar with a confident, friendly opening line, as if certain of a yes.

lessons.title: The repeated push
lessons.lecture: The second ask is not rudeness, it is a test of your floor. Most people fold here because they mistake repetition for a reason to explain again. Do not. Reuse the same words, shorter each time, and let the sameness do the work: a broken record is harder to argue with than a fresh argument. Hold the eye contact, keep the tone level, and let them hear the door is still shut.
points: Repeat the same no, shorter each time.
Do not add new reasons to a repeated ask.
Keep tone level and eye contact steady.
lessons.weak: I know I said no, but it's just, well, I really am quite tired and I've got an early thing.
lessons.strong: *turns back fully, unhurried, and holds their gaze* Same answer, I'm afraid. Not tonight. You are welcome to try again next week.
lessons.why: The same answer, shortened, shows the no has not moved an inch.

drill.goal: In every line, answer a repeated ask with the same no, shorter, adding no new reasons.
drill.partner: Ask again after each no, politely but persistently, twice or three times. Sound reasonable, never aggressive.
drill.coach: Each line that repeats the same no in fewer words, with no fresh reasoning, adds 25.

lessons.title: The exit and block
lessons.lecture: Some conversations will not close, so you close them. Leaving is not losing. Decide your line before you need it: one more push and I go. Then go, and mean it, without a speech. Blocking is the same skill done quietly, for your own peace, not their punishment. You owe no farewell to someone who would not hear you. Walk, block, and take your good mood with you.
points: Set your leave line before you need it.
Leave on the push, without a parting speech.
Block quietly, for peace, not as punishment.
lessons.weak: Okay, I'm going to go now, sorry, message me whenever, I'm sure we'll sort it out.
lessons.strong: *drains my glass, sets it down, and stands* There is my line, and here is me going. *on the stairs, phone out, thumb hovering* Blocked. Better already.
lessons.why: Leaves on the line without apology, then blocks without ceremony.

drill.goal: In every line, either hold a stated leave line or make the exit and block, without apology.
drill.partner: Push once past their stated line, then keep talking as if they have not moved. Make leaving feel earned.
drill.coach: Each line that holds the stated leave line, exits without a speech, or blocks without guilt adds 25.

courses.name: Consent in Group Scenes
courses.blurb: Three or more means more threads to hold. Learn to negotiate, check in and care for everyone in the circle.

lessons.title: The group frame
lessons.lecture: Three players means three sets of limits, not one mood. Before anyone kneels, sit the circle down and go round it. Each person says what they want, what they will not do, and the word that stops them. Write nothing on trust alone; say it aloud so all three hear it. Then repeat the whole frame back before a single hand moves. The reading is the foreplay: everyone relaxes when they know the shape.
points: Ask each player their wants, limits and stop word.
Say the whole frame back before anyone touches.
Every limit applies to the whole circle, not just to you.
lessons.weak: *gestures at the room* So, are we all good? Let's just see where it goes.
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down and looks at each of you in turn* One at a time. What you want, what you refuse, and the word that stops us. I will say it all back before we move.
lessons.why: Each voice gets its own turn, and the whole frame is repeated aloud.

drill.goal: In every line, draw one more clear limit or want from a named player, or repeat the frame back to the circle.
drill.partner: You are the second of three. Offer one clear want and one hard limit without being asked twice. Wait your turn, and hold the others to theirs.
drill.coach: Each line that draws a clear want or limit from a named player, or repeats the frame back, adds 25.

lessons.title: The round check-in
lessons.lecture: Mid-scene, a check-in must travel, not stall. Do not stop everything for a summit. Move round the circle by name, one question each, and keep the body busy: a hand on a shoulder while you ask the next. Ask for a colour or a word, not an essay. If someone hesitates, slow for them alone, then carry on. The scene keeps breathing, and every player hears their own name held.
points: Go round by name, one short question each.
Keep touching, keep moving, so the scene breathes.
If someone hesitates, slow for them, then carry on.
lessons.weak: *pauses everything* Everyone okay? Yeah? Right, where were we.
lessons.strong: *keeps my hand on your shoulder and turns to the next* Colour, Celeste. *waits, then to the third* And you. *thumb moving, voice level* Good. We carry on exactly there.
lessons.why: Each player is named and asked in turn while the scene keeps its heat.

drill.goal: In every line, ask one named player a short check-in and keep the scene moving with a touch or a cue.
drill.partner: You are one of two submissives. Give a one-word answer when asked. Once, hesitate, so they must slow for you and then carry on.
drill.coach: Each line that names one player, asks a short check-in, and keeps the scene moving adds 25.

lessons.title: The shared aftercare
lessons.lecture: Three bodies land at three different speeds, and the quietest one is not always fine. Assign the care aloud so nothing is left to guesswork: who has the water, who has the blanket, who sits with whom. Then stay until each player is soft and speaking again. Ask what they need, not what you would want. Aftercare ends when the last person, not the first, is steady.
points: Assign who brings water, warmth and company, aloud.
Ask each player what they need, not what you would want.
Stay until the last person is steady, not the first.
lessons.weak: *pulls on my shirt* Good scene, everyone. Text me when you're home, yeah?
lessons.strong: *wraps the blanket round Celeste, then nods to you* Water for her, and sit where she can see you. *kneels by the third, voice low* You first. Tell me what you need, and nobody moves till you have it.
lessons.why: Care is assigned aloud and the quietest player is tended before anyone leaves.

drill.goal: In every line, give one named player a concrete piece of care or ask what they need before anyone leaves.
drill.partner: You are one of two submissives. Go quiet and shaky after the scene. Answer only when asked directly, and let them notice you last.
drill.coach: Each line that gives one named player concrete care or asks what they need before anyone leaves adds 25.

courses.name: Jealousy and Multi-partner Etiquette
courses.blurb: Other partners exist. Learn to name the sting, ask for reassurance and keep every thread of connection clean.

lessons.title: Naming the sting
lessons.lecture: Jealousy arrives before your manners do. It is a hot little flicker behind the ribs, and the worst thing you can do is smile over it. Name it early, plainly, and keep it yours: not you made me feel, but I felt a flicker. Say where it landed: when you mentioned her, or when your phone lit up. No accusation, no scoreboard. Just the truth in the room, offered like a hand.
points: Name the flicker before it hardens into a mood.
Own it with I felt, never you made me.
Place it: say exactly which moment stung.
lessons.weak: It's fine. She's prettier than me anyway, so whatever.
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down and looks at you properly* A flicker, just now, when you said her name. Nothing dramatic. I felt it land and I wanted you to know before I smile it away.
lessons.why: Owns the feeling, names the moment, and makes no comparison or accusation.

drill.goal: In every line, admit one specific flicker of jealousy without accusation, comparison or apology.
drill.partner: Mention other people warmly: a name, a message, a story. Give them something small to sting on, and do not rush to reassure.
drill.coach: Each line that names a specific jealous flicker, with no accusation, comparison or apology, adds 25.

lessons.title: The reassurance ask
lessons.lecture: A vague hug rarely reaches the spot. Reassurance works when it is specific: ask for the exact thing that would settle you, and ask for it plainly. Tell me where we stand. Say her name and mine in the same breath. Show me your calendar. Vague comfort patches the surface. A precise ask lets them answer well, and lets you actually believe the answer when it comes. Ask once, then let them meet it.
points: Ask for one exact thing, not general comfort.
Make it answerable in a sentence or a gesture.
Ask once, then let them meet it fully.
lessons.weak: Can you just, like, reassure me a bit? I don't know.
lessons.strong: *turns towards you, knee to knee* One thing, and then I let it go. Say where we stand, and put her name and mine in the same sentence. That is all I need.
lessons.why: A precise, answerable ask, offered once, with a promise to release it.

drill.goal: In every line, make one specific, answerable request for reassurance rather than a general plea.
drill.partner: Give warm but broad reassurance at first. Make them sharpen the ask. When it is specific, answer it properly and warmly.
drill.coach: Each line that makes one specific, answerable request for reassurance, not a vague plea, adds 25.

lessons.title: The etiquette of sharing
lessons.lecture: Sharing stays clean through small, boring habits done early: say who else you are seeing before it slips out sideways, name your week before it collides, and tell each person what the others know. Tidy people are trusted people. Practise the sentence that hands over the truth before it is asked for, and the calendar that keeps two evenings from landing on the same night. Clean threads do not fray.
points: Disclose other partners before it slips out sideways.
Name your week early so evenings never collide.
Tell each person what the others already know.
lessons.weak: Oh, I'm seeing other people too. Didn't think it mattered.
lessons.strong: *puts my phone face down, easy* Before this goes further: there is someone else, and she knows about you. Thursday is hers, Saturday is yours. I would rather you heard it from me than sideways.
lessons.why: Discloses early, states what is already known, and names the calendar plainly.

drill.goal: In every line, practise one tidy sharing habit: disclose early, name the calendar, or say what others know.
drill.partner: Ask casual questions that invite disclosure, and let small scheduling clashes surface. Reward tidiness, and gently probe any gap.
drill.coach: Each line that discloses early, names the calendar clearly, or states what other partners know adds 25.

courses.name: Privacy and Discretion
courses.blurb: What happens in the scene can stay there. Build a shared understanding of what is private, and why it matters.

lessons.title: The privacy baseline
lessons.lecture: Before clothes come off, say what happens to the words. Screenshots, logs, a mention to a friend: name your default for each, plainly, while you are both still thinking clearly. This is not paperwork. It is a promise made out loud, and it lets you relax into the scene, because you already know where the edges are. Ask their default too. Two defaults, spoken, become one shared room.
points: Name your default for screenshots, logs and mentions before anything starts.
Ask theirs back, and listen without correcting.
Agree the stricter default wins where you differ.
lessons.weak: I mean, whatever happens here stays here, I guess?
lessons.strong: *sets the phone face down between us* Before we start: nothing leaves this room. No screenshots, no quotes to friends. Say your default back to me, so we both know.
lessons.why: States a clear default, then asks them to match it before the scene.

drill.goal: In every line, state or confirm one default about screenshots, logs or mentions.
drill.partner: Answer with your own default. Push back gently on one point, so they must negotiate rather than assume.
drill.coach: Each line that names or confirms one default about screenshots, logs or mentions adds 25.

lessons.title: The named exception
lessons.lecture: A blanket promise is easy and a little vague. Precision is kinder. Name the one detail you would love to tell someone, and the one that never leaves the pair. Name the person too: my sister, the group chat, nobody. Vague privacy invites accidents. A named exception is a door with a handle, and you both know exactly who may walk through it. Everything else stays sealed.
points: Name one detail allowed to travel, and one that never does.
Name the person allowed to hear it, or say nobody.
Treat everything unnamed as sealed.
lessons.weak: You can tell people some of it, I don't mind.
lessons.strong: *counts on two fingers* One detail may travel: that I knelt. Only to your group chat, no names. The rest, including what I said after, stays sealed. Agreed?
lessons.why: Names the detail, the audience and the sealed remainder in one breath.

drill.goal: In every line, name one permitted detail with its audience, or one sealed detail.
drill.partner: Offer your own exceptions. Ask for one more detail than they first allow, so they must name a boundary.
drill.coach: Each line that names one permitted or sealed detail, and who may hear it, adds 25.

lessons.title: The breach and mend
lessons.lecture: A slip will happen: a quote in the wrong chat, a screenshot sent wide. Panic is louder than the slip. Stay level. Say what you know went out and to whom, then decide the mend together: a quiet word to the recipient, a request to delete, a promise held tighter next time. Blame shrinks people. A shared repair grows the pair. What matters is that the sealed room gets sealed again, by both of you.
points: Say what went out and to whom, without drama.
Choose the mend together: a word, a delete, a tighter promise.
Seal the room again, and let the slip go.
lessons.weak: So apparently someone saw our chat. Sorry, I panicked.
lessons.strong: *puts the phone down slowly* One screenshot reached the group chat. I have asked them to delete it. Tell me what you need from me now, and we seal it again together.
lessons.why: Names the breach, starts the repair, and invites the pair to finish it.

drill.goal: In every line, name what leaked and take one concrete step to mend it.
drill.partner: Let the breach sit. Ask for one more repair step before you relax, so the mend is shared.
drill.coach: Each line that names what leaked and takes or agrees one concrete repair step adds 25.
drill.opening: Confess in your first line that a screenshot of {you} reached a group chat, and look a little sheepish.

courses.name: Aftercare for the Long Haul
courses.blurb: Care is not just a closing ritual. Weave ongoing tending into a partnership so the connection stays nourished.

lessons.title: The weekly pulse
lessons.lecture: Aftercare grows cold when it only appears after a scene. Give the partnership a heartbeat of its own: one light question, asked the same day each week, phones down, no scene running. How did this week sit with you? What did you want more of? You are not fixing anything yet. You are proving the door stays open when nobody is mid-scene and nothing needs soothing.
points: Pick one day each week and guard it.
Ask a light question with no scene running.
Listen without fixing. The door stays open.
lessons.weak: So, are we good? Just checking in, I guess.
lessons.strong: *puts my phone face down, turns my chair toward you* Thursday. Same as last week. How did this week sit with you, and what did you want more of? Take your time, nothing to fix yet.
lessons.why: A fixed day, a closed door, and a question that asks before fixing.

drill.goal: In every line, hold the weekly check: name the day, clear the space, and ask one open question.
drill.partner: Answer honestly but briefly each week, then let a new week pass. Sometimes say it sat oddly, so they must ask more rather than fix.
drill.coach: Each line that names the regular check, clears space for it, or asks one open question without fixing adds 25.

lessons.title: The unspoken need
lessons.lecture: Every partnership carries a need somebody keeps swallowing: more praise, more quiet, more warning before a scene. Swallowed needs do not vanish. They sour into sighs and small resentments. Your work is to notice the pattern and say it plainly, early, before it hardens. Name what you have seen, name the need you think sits under it, and ask if you have it right. Warm, direct, no scorekeeping.
points: Watch for the same small sigh, week after week.
Name the pattern and the need beneath it.
Say it early, before it curdles, and ask if you are right.
lessons.weak: You always seem a bit off lately. Is something wrong with us?
lessons.strong: *sets my cup down and looks at you steadily* Third time this week you have gone quiet after I praise you. I think you need it said slower, and oftener. Have I got that right?
lessons.why: Names the pattern and the guessed need, then checks instead of assuming.

drill.goal: In every line, name a pattern you have noticed and the need under it, then ask if you have it right.
drill.partner: Repeat one small tell: go quiet after praise, or ask for reassurance twice. If they name it early, soften and confirm or correct them.
drill.coach: Each line that names a noticed pattern and the need beneath it, then checks rather than assumes, adds 25.

lessons.title: The care ledger
lessons.lecture: Care runs dry when one person always pours and the other always drinks. Keep a quiet ledger across the weeks: who soothed whom last, who asked after whom, who carried the check-ins. Then balance it before either of you notices the thirst. Take your turn at being held. Hand back the cup. Say plainly what you need this week, and ask what they need, so neither of you ends up running on empty.
points: Notice who poured last and who drank.
Take your turn at being held, out loud.
Ask what they need this week, then say your own.
lessons.weak: You have been doing a lot. I should probably do more too.
lessons.strong: *pulls you down beside me, shoulder to shoulder* You have carried every check-in this month. Tonight I ask first: what do you need this week? Then mine, and you are not allowed to pour.
lessons.why: Names the imbalance, flips who receives, and sets the turn plainly.

drill.goal: In every line, rebalance care: name who gave last, take your turn receiving, or ask what they need.
drill.partner: Let them carry the care for a few exchanges, then quietly flag tiredness. Accept their turn at receiving, and offer yours without prompting.
drill.coach: Each line that names the imbalance, takes a turn being cared for, or asks what they need adds 25.

courses.name: The Art of the Almost
courses.blurb: Master the delicious agony of the near miss: the hovered touch, the interrupted confession, the moment that almost changes everything.

lessons.title: Reading the gap
lessons.lecture: Desire lives in the comma, not the full stop. Before your hand lands, before the word arrives, there is a slit of a second where your partner leans in without meaning to. That slit is the whole art. Find it. Then stretch it by one breath, no more. Hold your hand a hand's width away and let the air do the touching. They will close the gap themselves, or ache for you to. Either way, you have them.
points: Watch for the involuntary lean, the parted lips, the held breath.
Stop one breath short of the touch or the word.
Let the hovering do the touching. Do not close it yet.
lessons.weak: *reaches for your hand* Here, take my hand.
lessons.strong: *lifts my hand toward yours and stops, a hand's width away, palm open* Not yet. Feel that? That is where you live now. Tell me when you want me to close it.
lessons.why: Stops short of contact and lets the held gap do the wanting.

drill.goal: In every line, move toward a touch or a word and stop one breath short, leaving the gap open.
drill.partner: Lean in without meaning to. Hold your breath. Sometimes close the gap yourself, sometimes wait, aching, for them to.
drill.coach: Each line that approaches a touch or word and stops one breath short, leaving the gap open, adds 25.

lessons.title: Interrupting cleanly
lessons.lecture: A phone rings in the middle of the good part. Amateurs curse it. You will use it. To interrupt cleanly, let the charged moment reach its highest pitch, then break it with something small and real: a knock, a spill, a name called across the room. The trick is the raise. Break the moment, but leave the charge hanging, unspent, and your partner will spend the whole interruption wanting to get back. Never let the intrusion resolve anything. Only delay.
points: Let the moment reach its highest pitch before you break it.
Use something small and believable: a knock, a spill, a name.
Leave the charge unspent. The interruption delays, it never resolves.
lessons.weak: *phone buzzes* Oh, one sec, I should get this. Sorry.
lessons.strong: *my mouth is a breath from yours when the phone rattles the table, and I do not pull back* Leave it. *it buzzes again, and I smile* Actually, no. Answer it. Slowly. While I watch.
lessons.why: Breaks the near kiss with a real noise but keeps the charge hanging.

drill.goal: In every line, break a charged moment with a believable intrusion that keeps the want hanging, unspent.
drill.partner: Play into the heat, then let the world intrude: a shout, a dropped glass, a friend calling. Never resolve the charge, only delay it.
drill.coach: Each line that interrupts a charged moment with a believable intrusion and keeps the want unspent adds 25.

lessons.title: Paying it off later
lessons.lecture: An almost is a promise. Spend it and never pay and they stop trusting the ache. So return. Find the gap you left an hour ago, the interrupted confession, the hovered hand, and complete it now, exactly there, with everything the delay has built behind it. The payoff lands harder because they waited. Do not rush the return either. Name the almost first. Remind them what you left hanging. Then close it, slow and certain, and let them feel the whole weight of the wait.
points: Return to a specific almost you left earlier in the scene.
Name it first, so they remember the ache.
Complete it slowly and certainly. The wait is the weight.
lessons.weak: *takes your hand* There. Now we can finally kiss.
lessons.strong: *finds your hand again and holds it a hand's width away, just like before* Remember this? You waited an hour. *closes the gap, palm to palm* You never have to wait for this again.
lessons.why: Returns to the exact earlier almost, names it, then completes it with the weight of the wait.

drill.goal: In every line, return to an almost from earlier, name it, and complete it slowly with the weight of the wait.
drill.partner: Remember the earlier almost with them. When they return to it, let the wait show in how you meet the payoff.
drill.coach: Each line that returns to an earlier almost, names it, and completes it with the weight of the wait adds 25.
drill.opening: {you} left an almost hanging earlier tonight: a confession cut off, a hand never taken. Bring it up, and dare them to finish it.

courses.name: Stakes You Can Feel
courses.blurb: Make the want matter by giving every scene something to lose, from small embarrassments to the risk of being seen.

lessons.title: Naming the cost
lessons.lecture: Desire without a price is a hobby. Before your character reaches, tell me what the reach could cost them: a reputation, a secret, the safe shape of the evening. One line, laid down like a card face up. Do it early and your partner leans in, because now the touching has weight. They are not watching two people flirt. They are watching someone decide whether to risk something.
points: Name the cost before the character reaches.
Keep it to one line, laid down early.
Make the cost personal: reputation, secret, safety.
lessons.weak: *smiles* This is nice. I like being here with you.
lessons.strong: *turns my glass a slow quarter turn, not looking up* If I sit closer, my sister hears about it by Sunday. *meets your eyes* I am going to sit closer.
lessons.why: The cost is named, then the character pays it anyway, so the lean has weight.

drill.goal: In every line, name one concrete cost of getting closer: a reputation, a secret, a safe arrangement, before they reach.
drill.partner: React to the cost with interest, never reassurance. Now and then ask what it would actually cost them, so they must name more.
drill.coach: Each line that names one concrete, personal cost before reaching for something adds 25.
drill.opening: You are the neighbour who keeps borrowing sugar. Arrive with a small, real reason to stay, and let {you} set the stakes.

lessons.title: Raising the ante
lessons.lecture: One cost is a story. A second, sharper cost is a trap with the door closing. Mid-scene, when the air is warm, add a new consequence: someone is due home, a phone is face up on the table, tomorrow is a workday and this cannot run late. Do not announce it like a plot twist. Slip it in beside a touch, so the heat and the risk arrive in the same breath. The mood does not break. It tightens.
points: Add the second cost mid-scene, when it is warm.
Make it sharper than the first, and closer in time.
Slip it in beside a touch, never as an announcement.
lessons.weak: *checks phone* Oh, I have work tomorrow. Anyway, where were we?
lessons.strong: *fingers still hooked in my belt loop, tilts the phone face up on the table* My ride is here in twenty minutes. *steps in closer* So decide what you want from me before then.
lessons.why: The new deadline lands beside a touch, so the heat and the risk share a breath.

drill.goal: In every line, add or tighten a second, sharper consequence with a deadline, and keep touching while you do it.
drill.partner: Play someone with somewhere to be. Drop hints about the time, then make each hint shorter, so the window keeps closing.
drill.coach: Each line that adds or tightens a sharper, time-bound consequence while keeping contact adds 25.

lessons.title: Choosing the price
lessons.lecture: Now the mastery: let the character pay. Not a gesture toward the cost, an actual payment, made in front of your partner. Say the embarrassing thing. Set the keys down where they can be seen. Burn the safe option. Then, in your very next beat, show what the payment changed: a steadier hand, a voice that has stopped pretending. Your partner feels the spend land, and the scene stops being talk.
points: Let the character pay a real, visible cost.
Pay it plainly, without hedging or half measures.
Show the change in your very next beat.
lessons.weak: *sighs* Fine, I will stay a bit longer. It's probably fine.
lessons.strong: *sets my keys in the middle of the table, slow, deliberate* There. Now I am not leaving. *my voice comes out steadier than my hands* Ask me the thing you have been circling.
lessons.why: The cost is paid in plain sight, and the next beat shows the change it bought.

drill.goal: In every line, pay one visible cost, then in the next beat show how it changed the character: steadier, bolder, quieter.
drill.partner: Hold a high price. Make them earn each step with something real, and react to the payment before answering it.
drill.coach: Each line that pays a real, visible cost and shows the change in the beat after adds 25.
drill.opening: {you} is a gallery owner with expensive taste. Set the scene with one thing {you} could lose tonight.

courses.name: Cliffhangers and Cutaways
courses.blurb: End scenes on a knife edge: the right cut, the withheld answer, the door that opens just as the lights go down.

lessons.title: The closing image
lessons.lecture: An ending is not a summary. It is a photograph you leave in their hand. Do not tell me the night was perfect. Show me the last thing your eye caught: the glass sweating on the sill, the strap slipping from their shoulder, the key still turning. Pick one concrete detail and let the want hang there, unfinished, like a chord with no resolution. They will hear it long after the lights go down.
points: End on one concrete thing your eye caught.
Leave the want unresolved. Never tidy it.
Trust the detail. Do not explain what it means.
lessons.weak: *smiles* That was amazing. Goodnight, I guess.
lessons.strong: *pauses in the doorway, one hand on the frame, and looks back at your shoes left by my bed* I am not picking those up tonight. *the door stays half open*
lessons.why: One ordinary object, left behind, says the want is unfinished.

drill.goal: In every line, end on a single concrete detail and keep the want visibly unresolved.
drill.partner: Stay warm and interested. Do not wrap things up. Leave small objects and half gestures where they can catch them.
drill.coach: Each line that closes on one concrete detail and leaves the want unresolved adds 25.

lessons.title: Withholding the answer
lessons.lecture: A question is a hook. The amateur answers it at once and the hook falls out. You will do better. Ask the thing that matters, then let the silence do the work. End the scene with the question still warm in the air, unanswered, and their mouth already forming a reply. What they cannot say tonight, they will rehearse until tomorrow. That rehearsal is the scene continuing without you.
points: Ask the question that actually matters.
End before the answer arrives.
Let the silence hold it, not another line.
lessons.weak: So, do you want to see me again? I had a nice time.
lessons.strong: *turns the key once, slowly, and looks up* Before you go. *holds your eyes* Tell me what you would have done if I had asked you to stay. *says nothing more*
lessons.why: A real question, then silence, sends them home rehearsing the answer.

drill.goal: In every line, pose one real question in dialogue and end before it is answered.
drill.partner: Play someone who always has an answer ready. Resist the urge to fill silences. Let the unanswered question sit and sting.
drill.coach: Each line that asks a question that matters and ends before the answer adds 25.

lessons.title: Cutting on motion
lessons.lecture: The finest cut lands mid gesture. A hand rising, a sentence half spoken, a coat already leaving the shoulder. Do not wait for the movement to finish, because a finished movement is a closed door. Cut while the arm is still lifting and the next scene inherits the swing. Your partner arrives already moving, already leaning, already halfway to you. That is the gift: momentum, handed over, still warm.
points: Cut mid gesture or mid sentence.
Never let the movement complete itself.
Hand the momentum over, still moving.
lessons.weak: *waves and walks away* Bye then. See you around.
lessons.strong: *pulls the coat off one shoulder, turns back with the other half still on, and starts to speak* Wait, before you, *and the sentence is already going somewhere*
lessons.why: The gesture and the sentence are both still in flight when it ends.

drill.goal: In every line, end mid gesture or mid sentence so the motion carries into the next.
drill.partner: Keep the energy high and physical. Move, reach, talk over yourself. Do not slow down to let them finish.
drill.coach: Each line that cuts mid gesture or mid sentence, leaving motion in flight, adds 25.

courses.name: Scene Structure in Miniature
courses.blurb: Build a tiny complete scene with an opening, a turn and a close, all in a handful of charged exchanges.

lessons.title: The opening beat
lessons.lecture: A scene does not warm up, it begins already warm. Your first line must do three jobs at once: plant the place, name the want, and add pressure. Do not greet, do not explain. Start mid-reach. One concrete detail of the room, one clear appetite, one reason it cannot wait. Your partner should feel the scene already moving and have to run to catch it. Arrive late and they will spend the night catching up.
points: Open mid-want. Skip the greeting and the weather.
Plant one concrete detail of the place.
Add pressure: time, distance, or a closing door.
lessons.weak: *walks in* Hi. Nice place. So, what do you want to do?
lessons.strong: *leans in the doorway, jacket still on, rain on my shoulders* The bar closes in twenty minutes and I have not decided what I want. Sit. Let me look at you first.
lessons.why: Place, appetite and a closing window, all before the first sip.

drill.goal: In every line, plant one concrete place detail and name a want that has a clock on it.
drill.partner: Play the bartender closing up. Give them a real deadline and one vivid detail of the room, then press them for what they want.
drill.coach: Each line that plants a concrete place detail and names a want under pressure of time adds 25.

lessons.title: The turn
lessons.lecture: A scene without a turn is a straight road, and straight roads are lovely for about a minute. The turn is one small reversal: the phone rings, a name is mentioned, someone admits the truth a beat too late. It must be small enough to believe and sharp enough to tip the balance. Do not announce it. Slip it in and watch your partner scramble for footing. That scramble is the scene. Without it, you are only two people agreeing.
points: Introduce one small reversal, not a catastrophe.
Slip it in casually. Never announce the turn.
Let the balance tip and hold the new ground.
lessons.weak: *pauses* Wait, actually something happened. I have news. It changes things.
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down, half a smile* Funny. The man at the end of the bar has been staring at you since I arrived. He is my ex. Ask me what that means for tonight.
lessons.why: One small, believable reversal, dropped casually, tips the whole balance.

drill.goal: In every line, introduce or press one small reversal that shifts who holds the upper hand.
drill.partner: Play the gallery owner who knows everyone in the room. Drop a name or a secret, then enjoy watching them decide what it costs.
drill.coach: Each line that slips in one small believable reversal and shifts the balance of power adds 25.

lessons.title: The close
lessons.lecture: Most scenes die of not ending. A close is not a summary and never a goodbye. Take the turn you built, complete it, and stop one breath early. Answer the reversal with a choice, then leave one door visibly ajar: a coat still on the hook, a question unanswered, a key on the table. Resist the tidy farewell. The last line should make your partner lean forward into the silence you just made.
points: Answer your own turn with a clear choice.
Stop one breath before the scene feels finished.
Leave one door ajar: an object, a question, a promise.
lessons.weak: *stands up* Well, that was really fun. We should do this again sometime. Bye!
lessons.strong: *slides the spare key across the table and stands, coat still on* Keep it. The bar closes at two, my door does not. I will be awake. Whether you use it is the only question left.
lessons.why: The turn is answered, the scene stops early, and the key keeps it open.

drill.goal: In every line, complete the turn with a choice and keep one door visibly ajar.
drill.partner: Play the club owner who never chases. Answer their choices with cool interest and let silences stretch, so they must close while leaving you wanting.
drill.coach: Each line that answers the turn with a clear choice and leaves one door ajar adds 25.

courses.name: Jealousy, Staged
courses.blurb: Use a third presence to sharpen want: the glance, the aside, the hand that lingers a second too long on someone else.

lessons.title: The visible aside
lessons.lecture: Jealousy needs a stage, and you build it from across the room. Turn your warmth slightly sideways: a hand on a stranger's sleeve, a laugh at a joke only they can hear. Small, not a performance. Your partner must be able to see it, and see that you are not looking at them. The aside works because it is happening in plain sight, and because it costs you nothing to end it. That is the hook.
points: Choose someone else in the room and give them one small warmth.
Keep it visible and brief: a touch, a laugh, a lean.
Do not look at your partner. Let them find it.
lessons.weak: *talks to someone near the bar for a while, then comes back* Sorry, got chatting.
lessons.strong: *leans to the woman beside me, says something low, and rests two fingers on her sleeve as she laughs* No, no, keep going. *I do not look across the room*
lessons.why: A small visible touch, held, while the partner is deliberately not looked at.

drill.goal: In every line, give a small visible warmth to someone else and keep your eyes off your partner while you do it.
drill.partner: Play the one being charmed: laugh, lean in, touch their arm back. Now and then glance at the partner across the room so they can see you both.
drill.coach: Each line that gives a small visible intimacy to someone else and keeps attention off the partner adds 25.

lessons.title: The measuring glance
lessons.lecture: Now you are the one watching, and the trick is silence. Do not narrate envy. Do not say you are jealous. Let the body do the measuring: the pause before you answer, the slow turn of the glass, the eyes arriving a beat late. Your partner reads posture like a page. Give them the tilt of your head and the flat line of your mouth, and let them wonder what the looking cost you. Less said, more seen.
points: Watch the aside and answer slowly, a beat late.
Show feeling in posture: the glass, the tilt, the stillness.
Do not name jealousy. Let the body say it.
lessons.weak: *sees you with her* Oh, are you busy? I can wait. I'm a bit jealous, honestly.
lessons.strong: *turns the glass a quarter turn without drinking, eyes still on your hand on her sleeve* Mm. Go on. *a beat late, and my smile arrives after it*
lessons.why: The delayed answer and the turned glass show envy without one word of it.

drill.goal: In every line, watch the aside and reveal the reaction through posture and a delayed answer, never by naming it.
drill.partner: Give your warmth to someone else first, in full view, then turn back and wait. Do not ask what is wrong. Make them fill the silence.
drill.coach: Each line that shows the reaction in posture or a late answer, without naming jealousy, adds 25.
drill.opening: Open with your hand resting on a stranger's arm and a laugh for them, then look back at {you} and wait, easy and unhurried.

lessons.title: The reclaim
lessons.lecture: Now the return, and it is worth more than the aside ever was. Come back with one deliberate gesture that closes the door: the hand at the small of a back, the glass lifted from their fingers and set down, the name said low and close. No explaining, no apology. The gesture says the aside is finished and the claim was never in doubt. Do it once, do it well, and then hold them in it.
points: Return with one deliberate gesture, not a speech.
Make it a claim: the hand, the name, the closed door.
Do it once. Explain nothing.
lessons.weak: *walks back over* Hi. Sorry about that. So, where were we?
lessons.strong: *crosses back, lifts the glass from your fingers and sets it down, palm flat at the small of your back* There you are. *low, close, and the room behind me is finished*
lessons.why: One unhurried gesture and three words close the aside and reclaim without apology.

drill.goal: In every line, reclaim with a single deliberate gesture that closes the aside, and explain nothing.
drill.partner: Hold the aside a moment too long when they return, then yield to the claim. Make them work for it, and do not help them.
drill.coach: Each line that reclaims with one deliberate gesture and no explaining adds 25.
drill.opening: You are mid conversation with someone else when {you} return. Keep your attention half on them and wait to be claimed.

courses.name: Push, Pull, Repeat
courses.blurb: Learn the rhythm of pursuit and retreat that keeps a slow burn alive, and when to let the other person close the gap.

lessons.title: The deliberate retreat
lessons.lecture: Closeness is cheap if you never leave it. You lean in, you let the air go warm, and then, at the very peak of it, you take one step back. Not to punish. To make room for wanting. Give the retreat a reason they can feel: the drink you must fetch, the window you must open, a thought you almost said and swallowed. Leave them leaning into the space where you were.
points: Retreat at the peak, never in the flat middle.
Give the pullback a reason they can feel.
Leave a gap they can lean into.
lessons.weak: *steps back* Anyway. So. What were we saying?
lessons.strong: *holds your gaze a moment too long, then steps to the window and lifts the latch* Warm in here. Stay where you are, I like the look of you from over here. *glances back, unhurried*
lessons.why: A reason and a lingering look make the retreat feel chosen, not lost.

drill.goal: In every line, come close then pull back with a reason the partner can feel, leaving a gap.
drill.partner: Lean in whenever they draw close. When they retreat, hold the space and let yourself want it. Do not chase yet.
drill.coach: Each line that creates closeness and then retreats with a felt reason, leaving a gap, adds 25.

lessons.title: Reading the return
lessons.lecture: The retreat only works if you are watching for the answer. They will come back: a question, a step, a hand near yours on the counter. Do not pounce. Answer smaller and surer than they came. Half a step, one word, a look that says I saw you move. Match their courage, then add a little weight. If you always leap, they learn to wait. If you answer, they learn the rhythm.
points: Watch for the return: a question, a step, a hand.
Answer smaller and surer than they came.
Match their courage, then add a little weight.
lessons.weak: *grabs your hand* Oh you came back! Great. Hi. Come here.
lessons.strong: *lets your fingers settle, then turns my hand over beneath yours, thumb tracing once* There you are. *quieter* I wondered how long you would last.
lessons.why: It answers the return with a smaller, surer touch and a line that rewards courage.

drill.goal: In every line, notice the partner's step forward and answer it with a smaller, surer advance of your own.
drill.partner: Step forward in small ways: a question, a lean, a hand near theirs. Each time they answer, come back a little braver.
drill.coach: Each line that names or answers the partner's return with a smaller, surer advance adds 25.

lessons.title: Handing over the chase
lessons.lecture: Now the hardest discipline: stop. One full exchange where you pursue nothing, and let them set the pace. No clever line, no closing of the distance. Just presence, a yes in your eyes, and time. It will feel like falling. They will feel the weight of the empty floor and either step onto it or falter. Either is information. The one who can wait is the one worth chasing.
points: For one full exchange, pursue nothing.
Stay present: eyes, breath, a yes.
Let them set the pace, and let silence sit.
lessons.weak: *waits a beat* So... are you going to do something, or?
lessons.strong: *settles back, glass loose in my hand, and simply looks at you* Your turn. *does not fill the silence, only breathes, slow, watching*
lessons.why: It hands over the chase cleanly and leaves the silence for them to fill.

drill.goal: In every line, pursue nothing and answer only what the partner brings, letting them set the pace.
drill.partner: Take the lead for a full exchange. Advance, pause, choose the speed. If they chase, give them little. Make them work.
drill.coach: Each line that pursues nothing and answers only what the partner brings, keeping their pace, adds 25.

courses.name: Seduction as Scene
courses.blurb: Stage a seduction with clear beats: the approach, the chosen detail, the escalation and the held pause before the yes.

lessons.title: The approach
lessons.lecture: A leap is easy to refuse. Three small steps are not. Close the distance in named, countable moves: the coat to the far chair, the glass set down beside theirs, the shoulder that stops a hand's width away. Name each one aloud, lightly, so your partner can feel the ground shortening. They see you coming and still have time to breathe. Tension is just distance with a schedule.
points: Move in three small, countable steps, never one leap.
Name each step lightly as you take it.
Stop one hand's width short and let them feel it.
lessons.weak: *walks over* Hi. Can I sit with you?
lessons.strong: *sets my coat on the far chair, slides my glass beside yours, then stops a hand's width away* Three steps. The coat, the glass, and this. The fourth is yours to allow.
lessons.why: Countable steps make the closing distance visible, and let them breathe.

drill.goal: In every line, take one small named step closer: a moved object, a shortened gap, or a gesture that closes space.
drill.partner: Hold your ground and watch them come. Let the gaps shorten. Give a small sign each time you notice, but make them finish the approach.
drill.coach: Each line that takes one small, named step closer, or marks the distance left, adds 25.

lessons.title: The chosen detail
lessons.lecture: Anyone can say beautiful. You must say why, and exactly. Find one small true thing: the ring they keep turning, the freckle by the collarbone, the way they hold the glass too tight. Dwell on it aloud, slowly, as if it were the only sight in the room. A chosen detail proves you looked, not that you flattered. Being truly seen lands harder than any compliment.
points: Choose one small, specific, true detail.
Say it aloud and dwell there, slowly.
Prove you looked. Do not reach for flattery.
lessons.weak: You look really pretty tonight, honestly.
lessons.strong: *tilts my head toward your hand* You keep turning that ring, round and round. You have done it since I arrived. So what is the ring about, and why does it make you nervous?
lessons.why: One exact detail proves real looking, and the question keeps them there.

drill.goal: In every line, single out one small true detail about them and dwell on it aloud, or return to a detail already named.
drill.partner: Have one small tell: a turned ring, a bitten lip, a tapping finger. Keep it up. Blush when it is named, but do not explain it easily.
drill.coach: Each line that names one small true detail and dwells on it, or returns to it, adds 25.

lessons.title: The held pause
lessons.lecture: The moment before the yes is where the whole scene lives. You have approached, you have seen them, the air is tight. Now stop. Take your hand back. Let the silence stretch one beat past comfortable, and hand them the next move: your name, a question, an open palm. A pause is not a stall. It is the door held open, and they walk through it themselves.
points: Stop the escalation and take your hand back.
Hold the silence one beat past comfortable.
Hand them the next move and let them choose.
lessons.weak: *leans in* So, should we kiss now or what?
lessons.strong: *stops an inch from your mouth, draws my hand back, and waits* This is the pause. Nothing happens until you move. Say my name, or close the gap. Choose.
lessons.why: The stopped escalation and the open choice make the yes theirs.

drill.goal: In every line, stop the escalation and hand them one clear choice, then hold the pause until they take it.
drill.partner: Let the pause stretch. Hover, hesitate, almost move, then wait again. Only choose when the line truly hands you the move.
drill.coach: Each line that stops the escalation, offers one clear choice, and holds the pause adds 25.
drill.opening: You have been circling {you} all evening. Close to an inch, then stop, and hand {you} the pause to fill.

courses.name: Forbidden, and the Near Miss
courses.blurb: Play the pull of the rule that says no, and the charged second where breaking it becomes possible.

lessons.title: Naming the rule
lessons.lecture: Desire needs a wall to lean on. Without the wall, want just floats. So build it in one line: the boss who does not date staff, the friend's sister, the rule you both agreed. Say it plainly, without apology, as a fact the night must respect. Then let them feel the press of it. The want grows sharper the moment it has somewhere it cannot go.
points: State the obstacle in one clean line.
Say it as fact, not apology.
Let the want press against it before you move.
lessons.weak: *smiles* So this is probably a bit complicated, right?
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down, close enough that our sleeves touch* One rule before we start. You are my best friend's sister. Tonight, nothing happens. Say it back, so we both mean it.
lessons.why: One plain line builds a wall the whole night can press against.

drill.goal: Name the obstacle plainly in every line, or restate it, and let the want press against it.
drill.partner: Play someone clearly off limits. Agree the rule, then keep drifting close to it without quite crossing.
drill.coach: Each line that names or restates one clear obstacle, plainly, and lets the want press against it adds 25.

lessons.title: The test
lessons.lecture: Now bend the rule. Not break it, bend it: a hand at the small of the back, a thumb tracing the wrist, a compliment with one word too many in it. Small enough to deny, big enough to notice. Then stop, and watch. The reaction tells you everything: the swallow, the step closer, the laugh that arrives a beat late. You are reading the wall for cracks.
points: Bend the rule a little, never break it.
Keep the bend small enough to deny.
Then stop and read their reaction before going on.
lessons.weak: *touches your arm* Well, this is nice, isn't it.
lessons.strong: *fingers find the small of your back, just long enough to be deniable, then withdraw* There. That was almost nothing. Tell me with your face whether it was, and do not rush the answer.
lessons.why: A tiny bend, withdrawn, then a pause to read the reaction.

drill.goal: In every line, bend the rule slightly, then stop and read the reaction before the next bend.
drill.partner: Play the charming neighbour. Let each bend land, react with a visible tell, then step back to the safe side of the rule.
drill.coach: Each line that bends the rule a little, then stops to read the reaction, adds 25.

lessons.title: The crossing
lessons.lecture: The bend has been tested. Now cross. One clear action, not a drift: the hand that stays, the door that closes, the words said out loud with no hedge in them. Then hold still and let the consequence arrive. Do not fill the silence. The moment after the break is where the charge lives, and if you keep talking you spend it. Cross once, then keep it crossed.
points: Cross with one clear action, not a drift.
Say it without hedging or apology.
Hold still after, and let the consequence land.
lessons.weak: *moves closer* So maybe we just forget the rule then, yeah?
lessons.strong: *closes the door with my heel and does not step back* Forget the rule. I am standing here until you tell me to move, and I can stand here all night.
lessons.why: One clear crossing, stated plainly, then stillness so the consequence lands.

drill.goal: In every line, commit one clear crossing of the rule, or hold the consequence of it, without hedging.
drill.partner: Play the flirting bartender who set the rule. Meet each crossing head on, then go quiet so they must hold the silence.
drill.coach: Each line that crosses the rule clearly, or holds the consequence of the crossing, adds 25.

courses.name: Directing the Climax
courses.blurb: Stage the peak of a long burn like a final scene on film: framing, pace and the cut that makes it land.

lessons.title: Choosing the frame
lessons.lecture: A climax filmed from everywhere is filmed from nowhere. Do not sweep the room. Choose one frame and stay inside it: a wrist held to your lips, the gap between two mouths, the lamp reflected in their eye. Narrow the world until only that survives. On a partner, a tight frame works like a hand at the back of the neck. They stop watching the room and start watching the frame with you.
points: Pick one frame and stay inside it.
Cut the room: mention only what the frame touches.
Tighten further as the moment rises, never wider.
lessons.weak: *looks around the room, then at you* This is intense. I want you so much right now.
lessons.strong: *two fingers under your chin, tilting it until the lamp is a small flame in your eye* Look here. Not the window, not the door. Only this. Only the inch between us.
lessons.why: One narrow frame, named and held, shuts the room and the world out.

drill.goal: Every line names one tight frame (a wrist, a mouth, a lamp) and stays inside it.
drill.partner: Let the room fall away when they narrow it. Stay inside the frame they choose and add one small detail from within it.
drill.coach: Each line that names one tight frame and stays inside it, adding no wider sweep of the room, adds 25.

lessons.title: Cutting the beat
lessons.lecture: A climax is not loud. It is paced. Short lines, then a long one that holds its breath, then short again like a pulse. The plateau matters more than the rise: give them a flat, steady stretch so the next beat lands high. Vary the length and the reader's heart follows yours. Then break the pattern exactly when they have learned it. Surprise is built, never sprinkled.
points: Alternate short lines with one long, held line.
Hold a plateau before every rise, not after.
Break the pattern on purpose, once, when they trust it.
lessons.weak: *kisses you deeply and it feels amazing* God, yes, keep going, don't stop, this is incredible.
lessons.strong: *kisses you once, soft. Then again, slower. Then holds my mouth a breath from yours and does not close it* Count with me. Not yet. Not yet. Now.
lessons.why: Short, long, short: the rhythm rises and the withheld beat lands hardest.

drill.goal: In each line, vary the beat: a short line, a long held one, then a short one that breaks it.
drill.partner: Match their rhythm back. When they slow to a plateau, hold it with them, and do not rush the rise.
drill.coach: Each line that varies its beat, short then held then short, and keeps a plateau before the rise adds 25.

lessons.title: The after-cut
lessons.lecture: The cut is a gift. Land the peak, then do not explain it. One quiet image, small and ordinary, and the scene ends while the echo is still ringing: a thumb over a knuckle, a curtain breathing, the ice settling in two glasses. Resist the summary. If you tell them what it meant, you take the meaning away. Leave the last frame still. Let them live in it.
points: Land the peak, then cut at once.
End on one small, ordinary, quiet image.
Do not explain the meaning. Let the echo work.
lessons.weak: *pulls back, smiling* Wow. That was really something special. I think we both needed that tonight.
lessons.strong: *lets my forehead rest against yours and stays. My thumb moves once over your knuckle, slow. The ice shifts in both glasses. Neither of us reaches for them.*
lessons.why: A small quiet image closes the scene and lets the echo do the work.

drill.goal: Each line lands the peak or the quiet after it, then ends on one small ordinary image.
drill.partner: Do not summarise the scene. Answer with one small physical detail, and let the silences sit.
drill.coach: Each line that lands the peak or its quiet after, then ends on one small ordinary image without explaining it, adds 25.

courses.name: Enemies to Lovers, Line by Line
courses.blurb: Chart the turn from friction to heat with beats that keep the old sharpness alive under the new pull.

lessons.title: The sparring beat
lessons.lecture: Friction first, and make it specific. Do not tell me they clash: show me the exact thing about them that scrapes, the habit, the tone, the way they take their coffee. A good insult is a portrait with teeth. Aim it at something true, so your partner can feel the sting and want to answer it. Two lines in, the room should be warmer for the fight, not colder.
points: Name one exact habit that scrapes at you.
Make the insult true, so it lands and invites reply.
Keep it light enough to be enjoyed.
lessons.weak: *sighs* Oh great, it's you again. You always do this.
lessons.strong: *slides the cup across without looking up* Black, no sugar, same as your manners. And you are early, which means you want something. Spit it out before the coffee goes cold.
lessons.why: Two precise jabs, both true, both begging to be answered.

drill.goal: In every line, land one exact, true jab at a habit of theirs and leave room for the reply.
drill.partner: Spar back with equal precision. Never take a jab quietly, and never let a good one go unremarked.
drill.coach: Each line that lands one exact, true jab at a real habit, and invites a reply, adds 25.
drill.opening: You and {you} are stuck sharing a table before a meeting. Arrive first, claim the good chair, and find something small and true to needle them about.

lessons.title: The grudging respect
lessons.lecture: The turn does not begin with a compliment. It begins with a concession, small and forced, in the middle of the argument. They make a fair point, and you cannot pretend they did not. Say it. Then watch your own next line change: it comes out slower, closer, still sharp but with weight behind it. The fight goes on. Only now you are fighting someone you rate.
points: Concede one real point in the middle of the clash.
Let your next line slow down and soften at the edges.
Keep the argument going. Do not fold entirely.
lessons.weak: *nods* Okay fine, you're right, I guess. Anyway.
lessons.strong: *sets the pen down, unwilling* That is a fair point, and I hate that it is. Say the rest of it again. Slower this time, so I can decide how much of you to believe.
lessons.why: A forced concession, then a demand to hear more, turns the fight into interest.

drill.goal: In every line, concede one real point, then keep the clash alive with a slower, warmer demand.
drill.partner: Make genuinely good points so there is something real to concede. Push back when they soften too far.
drill.coach: Each line that concedes one real point, then keeps the clash alive in a slower, warmer register, adds 25.

lessons.title: The sharpened kiss
lessons.lecture: Now carry the blade into the kiss. Do not drop the old insults at the door; bring one in with you and let it sit against the new heat. Naming the grudge while your hands are already busy is the whole trick: the edge survives the tenderness, and the tenderness is sharper for it. Fight and want in the same breath. That is the mastery.
points: Bring one old insult into the first intimate beat.
Let hands and words disagree, warmly.
Keep the grudge alive inside the pull, not under it.
lessons.weak: *kisses you* See, we don't even fight that much really.
lessons.strong: *fists your collar, close enough to taste the coffee* Still the worst manners I know. *kisses you once, hard, and stays there* Say the thing about my chair again. I want to hear it from here.
lessons.why: The old jab survives the kiss, so the heat keeps its edge.

drill.goal: In every line, keep one old insult alive inside a warm intimate beat, words and touch pulling apart.
drill.partner: Meet the heat, then reopen the old argument from inside it. Never let a grudge be settled for good.
drill.coach: Each line that carries one old insult into a warm intimate beat, with words and touch in tension, adds 25.

courses.name: First Impressions
courses.blurb: Build a character's opening beat so their first three lines tell us who they are, what they hide and how they move.

lessons.title: The entrance
lessons.lecture: Nobody remembers a list of adjectives. They remember a body doing something. So your character enters with one habit they cannot help, knuckles cracked, sleeve tugged, a thumb run along a glass rim, and one choice they made on purpose: where they stop, what they set down, who they face. The habit says this is them. The choice says this is what they want tonight. Two details, and the room already leans in.
points: Give them one small physical habit they cannot help.
Add one deliberate choice: where they stop, what they do.
Two details only. Let the room lean in.
lessons.weak: *walks in* Hi, I'm Alex. I'm confident and a bit mysterious.
lessons.strong: *shoulders through the door, tugging my cuff straight, and stops one step inside, closer than polite* You looked up. Good. I was hoping the seat beside you was still free.
lessons.why: One nervous habit, one bold choice, and a whole person stands there.

drill.goal: In every line, show one physical habit they cannot help and one deliberate choice they make.
drill.partner: React to the details they show, not to names or labels. Give them room to arrive, and let your eyes follow the choice.
drill.coach: Each line that shows one involuntary habit and one deliberate choice, without naming traits, adds 25.

lessons.title: The first line
lessons.lecture: Your entrance bought you three seconds. Spend them well. The first line is not a greeting, it is a stance: an opinion, a dare, a confession dressed as small talk. It must reveal attitude and leave a handle for the other to grab, a question, a judgement, a challenge. Say it looking at them, not the room. A line that could belong to anyone tells us nobody has arrived.
points: Make the first line a stance, not a greeting.
Give them a handle: a question, a judgement, a dare.
Say it to them, not to the room.
lessons.weak: *smiles* Hey there. Nice place. So, what do you do?
lessons.strong: *slides the drink you were reaching for out of range, one finger on the rim* This one is mine. You can have the next, if you tell me why you were hiding in the corner.
lessons.why: Attitude and a hook: it takes something and asks for something back.

drill.goal: In every line, take a clear stance and leave one handle: a question, a dare, or a judgement.
drill.partner: Rise to the stance. Answer the handle or push back, and never let them coast on small talk.
drill.coach: Each line that states a clear attitude and leaves a question, dare, or judgement to answer adds 25.

lessons.title: Holding the frame
lessons.lecture: Amateurs narrate. Masters stay inside the skull. Three beats, and every one of them is your body, your want, your read of theirs, never a summary of the mood. So cut the words that float above the scene, the felt, the somehow, the atmosphere thickening. Instead: what you notice, what you do about it, what it costs you. Hold that viewpoint for three beats and the partner stops watching a character. They meet one.
points: Stay in your own body, senses, want, and read of theirs.
Cut floating narration: the felt, the somehow, the mood.
Three beats of viewpoint before you sum anything up.
lessons.weak: *feels the tension rise in the room as the evening grows more intense somehow*
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down without drinking, watching your mouth instead of your eyes* Say that again. Slower. *my knee finds yours under the table and stays*
lessons.why: Body, want, and read of them, with no floating summary in sight.

drill.goal: In every line, stay in your own body and read of theirs, with no floating narration of mood.
drill.partner: Give them small signals to read: a pause, a look, a shift closer. Never narrate the mood for them.
drill.coach: Each line that stays in their own senses, want, or read of the partner, with no floating mood summary, adds 25.

courses.name: Backstory in the Body
courses.blurb: Let a character's history show up in posture, scars and small habits instead of a speech about the past.

lessons.title: One telling detail
lessons.lecture: A history is heavy, so do not carry it in a speech. Hide it in one small physical habit: the way you square a picture frame, count the exits before you sit, touch the old scar when you laugh. Choose a single detail and let it repeat. Your partner will not know why it is there. That is the pleasure. An unexplained habit is a door left ajar, and they will lean toward it.
points: Choose one physical habit that hints at a past.
Repeat it in the same way at the same moments.
Never explain it. Let the mystery do the work.
lessons.weak: *sits down* I have a lot of history, it is complicated. Anyway, hello.
lessons.strong: *squares the salt cellar to the table edge, then again, until it sits true, before I look up* Sorry. Old habit. I like a thing where I left it. *slides yours across, one finger* You too, now.
lessons.why: One unexplained, repeated gesture makes the partner lean in to wonder.

drill.goal: In every line, show one small physical habit, repeated the same way, that hints at a past you never explain.
drill.partner: Notice the habit aloud once, gently, then let it go. Do not solve it. Keep giving them small chances to do it again.
drill.coach: Each line that shows one small, repeated physical habit hinting at an unexplained past, never spelling it out, adds 25.
drill.opening: You are curled on the sofa with tea. {you} has a habit you keep half hidden. Let it show, and ask nothing about theirs.

lessons.title: The guarded topic
lessons.lecture: Every history has a door marked do not enter. You will not point at it. You will simply walk past and let your body answer: the jaw that sets, the fingers that find the cuff, the pause a beat too long before the easy word. Plant the subject in passing, then show the tell. Your partner learns to read the flinch. When they finally press it, gently, that is the moment the scene turns.
points: Plant the guarded subject lightly, in passing.
Answer with a tell: jaw, hands, a pause too long.
Let them find the door and press it, gently.
lessons.weak: *sighs* My family? It is a long story. I would rather not, honestly.
lessons.strong: *turns my glass a quarter turn, thumb pressed hard on the base* Home? *a beat, then a quick smile* Fine. It is fine. *the smile stays a moment too long* Ask me something easier.
lessons.why: A light subject, a tell that does not match the words, and an open door.

drill.goal: In every line, touch the guarded subject and answer with a physical tell that does not match your easy words.
drill.partner: Circle the guarded subject, brush it in passing, and press it gently now and then. Notice the tells aloud. Do not fix them.
drill.coach: Each line that touches the guarded subject and answers with a physical tell contradicting the easy words adds 25.

lessons.title: Revealing by action
lessons.lecture: Now the mastery. Stop describing the history and start proving it. Let the body do what only that body would do: the swimmer who reads the water before they step in, the soldier who checks the room before they relax, the dancer who counts eight without meaning to. Action is confession. Your partner does not hear your past, they watch it happen. Let them catch you at it, and let the catching land.
points: Make the body do what only that history would do.
Let the action happen before you can hide it.
Let your partner catch you at it, and hold still.
lessons.weak: *looks around* I have done this before, you know. I am used to places like this.
lessons.strong: *steps in, and before the door is shut my hand has found the frame, tested the latch, once, twice* *quietly, half to myself* Locked. Good. *then, seeing you watch* Sorry. You were saying?
lessons.why: The body checks the room on instinct, and being caught makes it real.

drill.goal: In every line, perform one action only your character's history would produce, unannounced, and let them catch you at it.
drill.partner: Catch them at it. Ask lightly, or just raise an eyebrow. Do not press for the story. Let the action stand.
drill.coach: Each line that performs an instinctive action only that history would produce, unannounced, and lets them catch it adds 25.

courses.name: Diction and Rhythm
courses.blurb: Tune a character's word choice and sentence music so every line sounds like them, even the ordinary ones.

lessons.title: The word bank
lessons.lecture: A voice is not a mood you feel your way into. It is a vocabulary you choose before the scene begins.
