Write down five words your character always reaches for, and five they would not be caught dead saying. Does she say 'darling' or 'love'? Does he say 'perhaps' or 'maybe'? Keep the list beside you. Every line you write, you check it against the list. The partner hears a person, not a mood.
points: Choose five words your character always uses.
Choose five they never would, and never use them.
Check every line against the list before you send.
lessons.weak: Hey there, lovely. So nice to see you again, honestly.
lessons.strong: *slides the glass across the bar and holds it a moment* Evening, trouble. You took your time. I was starting to think the tide kept you.
lessons.why: Fixed word choices, 'trouble' and 'tide', make a person we can hear.

drill.goal: In every line, use at least one word from your bank and none from your never list.
drill.partner: Flirt back easily, but keep your own words ordinary. Let their strange vocabulary stand out, and react to the words, not just the meaning.
drill.coach: Each line that uses a word from the bank and avoids every banned word adds 25.

lessons.title: Sentence music
lessons.lecture: Now the rhythm. A calm character moves in long, even sentences. A hungry one chops. Short, short, then one that runs away with itself. Read your line aloud in your head and listen for the beat. Where your character's mood rises, let the sentence break. Where it settles, let it stretch and breathe. The partner feels the music before they parse the words. Get the tempo wrong and the whole person collapses.
points: Match sentence length to the character's current mood.
Break the line short when the feeling rises.
Let calm sentences stretch and breathe.
lessons.weak: I am quite excited to see you tonight, and I think we should go inside now.
lessons.strong: *sets down the bottle, wipes my hands slowly* You came. Good. *crosses the room, stops close* Now I can finally breathe.
lessons.why: Short beats at the approach, one long settling line after: the mood is audible.

drill.goal: In every line, shape sentence length to mood: clipped when it rises, longer when it settles.
drill.partner: Stay cool and measured. Make them work for your attention, so their sentences have somewhere to climb.
drill.coach: Each line whose sentence length visibly matches the stated mood, short for heat, long for calm, adds 25.

lessons.title: The plain test
lessons.lecture: Here is where amateurs drown: they decorate. Every line becomes perfume and storm clouds. A real voice survives the ordinary. So strip it. Order a drink, ask the time, say the taxi is here. No metaphors, no flourishes. If the character still stands there, unmistakable, in nothing but plain words, you have built a person and not a costume. Mastery is the voice you can hear with the lights on.
points: Strip decoration from ordinary lines.
Keep the word bank and rhythm, drop the perfume.
If the plain line still sounds like them, the voice is real.
lessons.weak: *gazes deeply into your eyes* The taxi, like a silver phantom, awaits us beyond the door.
lessons.strong: *pulls my coat on, checks the window* Taxi's here. *holds the door, nods at you* After you. Mind the step.
lessons.why: Plain words and a small courtesy, yet the voice holds without a single flourish.

drill.goal: In every line, stay fully in voice using only plain words: no metaphors, no flourishes.
drill.partner: Keep the scene domestic and ordinary. Hand them small tasks: the coat, the bill, the door. Correct any decoration gently.
drill.coach: Each plain line, free of metaphor and flourish, that still carries the character's words and rhythm adds 25.

courses.name: Personas and Masks
courses.blurb: Wear a role on purpose: the stranger, the rival, the one who knows more, and keep the mask consistent line by line.

lessons.title: The mask's rules
lessons.lecture: A mask is not a costume, it is a spine. Before you write a single line, decide three rules your persona never breaks: how they stand, what they never say, what they always want. Write them down where you can see them. Then every line must obey. The partner feels the shape of someone consistent and starts to lean toward it. A mask with rules is a person. A mask without them is a mood.
points: Choose three rules the persona never breaks.
Let every line obey all three, without exception.
Keep the rules invisible. Show them, do not list them.
lessons.weak: *leans on the bar* I'm a mysterious stranger. Guess my secrets.
lessons.strong: *sets the glass down without drinking, eyes level* I never give my name first. Ask me something better than that and you might get it.
lessons.why: The rule is stated as behaviour, not announced as a label.

drill.goal: In every line, hold all three of your mask's rules: same posture, same refusals, same want.
drill.partner: Play a curious regular. Test the mask by asking the questions it refuses. Notice aloud when a rule holds.
drill.coach: Each line that visibly obeys all three rules, in posture, refusals, and want, adds 25.
drill.opening: {you} is a stranger in the booth. You have never seen them before. Ask for their name.

lessons.title: The slip
lessons.lecture: A perfect mask is a wall, and walls get boring. The slip is one line where the persona forgets itself: a warm word where it is usually cold, a real laugh, a hand that reaches before the head can stop it. One beat only. Then the mask snaps back, and the snap is the thrill, because the partner now knows the mask can be moved. Do not explain the slip. Let them see you cover it.
points: Let the mask crack for exactly one line.
Snap straight back, and cover the crack with a rule.
Never explain the slip. Let them catch it.
lessons.weak: *smiles* Ha, you got me. I'm actually really nice underneath.
lessons.strong: *the cool voice falters, softer* You remembered my drink. *clears my throat, straightens, cool again* Do not think that earns you anything.
lessons.why: One warm line, then the mask returns and pretends nothing happened.

drill.goal: Each line either slips the mask for one beat or snaps it back with a rule, never both at once.
drill.partner: Flirt hard and notice the slips out loud. When the mask snaps back, look delighted and push again.
drill.coach: Each line that either slips the mask for exactly one beat or snaps it back with a rule adds 25.

lessons.title: The unmasking
lessons.lecture: Now the whole mask comes off, and you choose the line. Pick the moment the partner has earned it: after a confession, a dare, a silence. Drop the persona in one move, and show the change in the body first, the shoulders, the breath, the eyes, because the body tells the truth the mask was hiding. The voice goes plainer. What you say next is only you. This is the line they remember.
points: Choose the exact line the mask comes off.
Show the change in the body before the voice.
Speak plainly after. Let the truth be simple.
lessons.weak: *sighs* Okay, fine. This was all an act. Hi, I'm me.
lessons.strong: *the drawl drops, shoulders loosen, and I look at you without the smirk* No more character. I wanted you across that room and I did not know how to say it plainly. So. Here I am.
lessons.why: The body drops the act first, then the voice tells the plain truth.

drill.goal: In every line, peel one layer of the mask off through the body, moving toward the plain truth.
drill.partner: Push them toward honesty with real questions. When the mask thins, go quiet and give them room.
drill.coach: Each line that removes one layer of the mask through a visible body change toward plain truth adds 25.

courses.name: Banter with Teeth
courses.blurb: Trade quick lines that tease, test and flirt, where every quip carries a little truth and a little dare.

lessons.title: The quick return
lessons.lecture: Banter is a rally, not a speech. The ball must leave your racket before the echo dies. When they tease, do not think, do not polish: answer inside the same breath, short and warm, and let the rhythm carry the wit. Speed tells them you were listening with your whole body. A slow answer kills the game faster than a bad one.
points: Answer before the echo dies. Speed is the game.
Keep it short: one line, tossed back at once.
Stay warm. Fast is not the same as sharp.
lessons.weak: *thinks for a moment* Ha, good one. Okay, so, um, what now?
lessons.strong: *grins, already leaning in* Careful, or I'll start charging for the privilege. And you clearly can afford it.
lessons.why: The reply arrives instantly, short and warm, so the rally never drops.

drill.goal: In every line, return one short warm quip within the beat, answering what they just threw.
drill.partner: Tease lightly and often. Throw each line fast and keep the volley low, so they must answer at once.
drill.coach: Each line that answers their tease in one short warm quip, without pausing to explain, adds 25.
drill.opening: You are pouring {you} a drink and hand it over with a teasing remark about their sunburn.

lessons.title: The truth underneath
lessons.lecture: The best joke has a hook in it. Wrap one real compliment inside the absurdity and toss it over, and they must decide whether to laugh it off or keep it. Do not announce the sweetness; bury it. Say it deadpan, hold their eyes a heartbeat too long, and let the pause do the asking. The laugh is the cover. The truth is the point.
points: Hide one real compliment inside the joke.
Say it deadpan, then hold their eyes a beat.
Let them choose whether to laugh or keep it.
lessons.weak: *laughs* Honestly, you're actually pretty great. Like, really.
lessons.strong: *straight face, eyes flat on yours* You are dangerously easy to keep talking to. Annoying, really. I had plans tonight.
lessons.why: A real compliment, buried in deadpan, with the pause doing the asking.

drill.goal: In every line, bury one genuine compliment inside a deadpan joke, then hold the pause.
drill.partner: Laugh off the first compliment to make them work for it. Keep the ones that feel true, and give one back.
drill.coach: Each line that hides a real compliment inside a joke, said deadpan with a held pause, adds 25.

lessons.title: Escalating the dare
lessons.lecture: Now the rally gets stakes. Each return raises the bet a notch: a bolder claim, a closer step, a wager with a price on it. Banter becomes a staircase, and neither of you wants to be the one who stops climbing. Keep your footing: raise by one step, never five. Then watch for the flinch, the swallow, the held breath. Someone concedes. Make it delicious.
points: Raise the bet one notch per line, never five.
Give each dare a visible price: a step, a wager.
Watch for the flinch. That is where you lean in.
lessons.weak: *laughs* Okay, you win. I can't top that one.
lessons.strong: *steps in until our shoes almost touch* Fine. Loser of the next round buys the night. Winner picks where we wake up. Still smiling?
lessons.why: One step closer, a wager with a price, and a question that dares them.

drill.goal: In every line, raise the dare one visible notch: closer, bolder, with a price named.
drill.partner: Match each raise, then push it one notch higher. Concede only when the stakes make you genuinely flush.
drill.coach: Each line that raises the dare exactly one visible notch and names its price adds 25.

courses.name: Subtext in the Ask
courses.blurb: Say one thing and mean another: the invitation that is a test, the compliment that is a warning, the yes that hesitates.

lessons.title: The double line
lessons.lecture: Every delicious ask carries two floors. On the ground floor, ordinary words: a drink, a coat, the time. Underneath, a cellar door left open. You do not point at the cellar. You let them hear the draft. Say the plain thing and load it: too long a pause, one word placed like a hand on a shoulder. They answer the surface and think about the underneath. That gap is where want lives.
points: Say something plain that could be perfectly ordinary.
Load it with one word or one pause too much.
Leave the cellar door open. Do not point at it.
lessons.weak: Do you want to come up to my room? No pressure or anything.
lessons.strong: *holds the door, lets the cold in, and looks at you a beat too long* The lift is slow this time of night. You could wait upstairs. Or you could wait here.
lessons.why: An ordinary offer, weighted, so both floors of it are audible.

drill.goal: In every line, say one plain surface thing that quietly carries a second meaning underneath.
drill.partner: Answer the ordinary surface of each line. Now and then glance at the hidden meaning, but never name it.
drill.coach: Each line that says something plain and loads it with a second meaning underneath adds 25.
drill.opening: You are at {you}'s door returning a borrowed thing. Say something ordinary that is not ordinary at all.

lessons.title: The tell
lessons.lecture: Words can lie politely. The body leaks. So give the leak a job. A thumb along the rim of your glass. A swallow after the calm sentence. A hand that starts toward them and stops. The tell must be small enough to miss and clear enough to catch. It says: hear what I said, now watch what I do with it. The partner who catches it has been let in, and being let in is the whole seduction.
points: Choose one small action that contradicts your calm words.
Make it catchable: a pause, a swallow, a hand that stops.
Never explain the tell. Let them catch it.
lessons.weak: *nods* It's fine, honestly. I'm not nervous at all. Anyway.
lessons.strong: *sets the glass down, steady voice* Take your time. No hurry at all. *my thumb finds the rim and circles it, once, slow*
lessons.why: The steady voice says one thing; the circling thumb confesses the other.

drill.goal: In every line, keep the words composed and add one small physical tell that leaks the opposite.
drill.partner: Stay composed. Catch the tell when it appears and let your eyes drop to it, then back. Never name it.
drill.coach: Each line that keeps the words calm and adds one small, catchable physical tell adds 25.

lessons.title: The answer in kind
lessons.lecture: Now the mastery. When they hand you subtext, do not unwrap it on the table. Answer underneath, in the same currency, and keep the surface conversation strolling along above like nothing happened. Two talks at once, both polite, both warm. If they raise the stakes, raise yours by a millimetre. The rule is simple: never say the real thing outright. Let the plain words carry it, and let the quiet between them do the rest.
points: Answer the hidden meaning, not the spoken one.
Keep the surface chat intact and easy above it.
Match their stakes, then raise by a millimetre.
lessons.weak: *smiles* So what you're really saying is you like me. Is that it?
lessons.strong: *slides the menu back across, finger resting on your side of it* The tasting menu takes three hours. *holds your eyes* Long enough for a slow eater to change their mind about dessert.
lessons.why: It answers the hidden offer while the surface stays on menus and timing.

drill.goal: In every line, reply underneath to their subtext while the surface conversation carries on unhurried.
drill.partner: Trade subtext, never naming it. Keep the surface on drinks and the evening. Raise the stakes a little each turn.
drill.coach: Each line that answers the hidden meaning while keeping the surface chat intact adds 25.

courses.name: Playing Against Type
courses.blurb: Take the character everyone expects and turn them inside out with one choice that surprises without breaking them.

lessons.title: The expected read
lessons.lecture: Let them cast you first. Two beats of the obvious type: the captain barking orders, the domme with the cutting smile, the bartender who has heard every line. Play it clean, no winks. Why? Because a partner settles when the type lands, and settled people can be surprised. Then, on the third beat, undercut it with one small choice that belongs to the same person and nobody else.
points: Play the obvious type straight for two clear beats.
Let the partner settle before you undercut anything.
Undercut with one small choice that still fits the type.
lessons.weak: *leans on the bar* I'm a bartender. Bet you've heard that before.
lessons.strong: *wipes the bar once, twice, sets the glass down with a click* Mara. I flirt like it's a sport and I never lose. *slides a second glass over, unasked, and looks away first*
lessons.why: The type lands in two beats, then the unasked drink turns it.

drill.goal: Play your obvious type straight, then undercut it once with a small choice that still belongs to you.
drill.partner: Play into the type you expect from them and settle. Do not chase surprises. Let them surprise you.
drill.coach: Each line that plays the obvious type cleanly, or undercuts it once with a small fitting choice, adds 25.

lessons.title: The soft reveal
lessons.lecture: Now the quiet part. The type has been played and contradicted once, and your partner is watching for the next move. Do not give them another joke. Give them one tenderness that costs you something: a held look, a hand that steadies, a truth said low. Small. Unhurried. The type does not vanish, it bends. A hard person made gentle for one line is unforgettable, and it is still the same person.
points: Follow the undercut with one quiet tenderness.
Keep it small. A held look beats a speech.
Let the type bend, never disappear.
lessons.weak: *smiles* See, I'm actually really nice once you know me.
lessons.strong: *takes my time, then straightens your collar with two fingers* There. Now you look like somebody's favourite. *holds the look a heartbeat too long, then turns back to the pour*
lessons.why: A tiny steadying gesture says the softness without announcing it.

drill.goal: In every line, offer one small tenderness that contradicts your type while the type still shows.
drill.partner: React to the captain's type, then soften visibly when the tenderness lands. Let it show quietly.
drill.coach: Each line that gives one small tenderness contradictory to the type, with the type still visible, adds 25.

lessons.title: The new normal
lessons.lecture: The reveal is worthless if you snap back to the mask. The scene's second half is the test: hold the surprising trait through every beat, through orders, through silences, through heat. The type stays as a shell, the softness stays as the lining. When you feel the old voice rising, let it arrive gentler. Mastery is not one clever turn. It is the turn kept, line after line, until your partner stops expecting the mask at all.
points: Carry the surprising trait through every remaining beat.
Keep the type visible as a shell around it.
When the old voice rises, let it arrive gentler.
lessons.weak: *barks orders for a while* Fine. Back to normal, I guess. Never mind the soft bit.
lessons.strong: *sets the chart down and squares up to you* On deck, you do as I say, no arguments. *quieter, thumb along the rail beside your hand* And when we anchor, you tell me the truth. All of it.
lessons.why: The command still stands, now lined with the softness, held.

drill.goal: Hold the surprising trait through every line: firm orders with the softness kept visibly underneath.
drill.partner: Test the new normal. Push for the old mask, then reward the gentler version when it arrives.
drill.coach: Each line that sustains the surprising trait while the old type still shows adds 25.

courses.name: Verbal Habits and Tells
courses.blurb: Give a character a signature phrase, pause or gesture that signals their state, and use it to reveal without explaining.

lessons.title: The signature
lessons.lecture: A character is not described, my friend. A character is noticed. So give yours one small, repeatable habit, a phrase they always say, a way of turning a glass before they drink, a knuckle tapped twice on the table. Show it once, plainly, as if it means nothing. That is the whole trick. Your partner files it away without knowing, and later, when the night leans in, you will have something to press against.
points: Give your character one small habit you can repeat exactly.
Show it once, plainly, as though it means nothing.
Keep it physical or verbal, never both at once.
lessons.weak: *smiles* I always do this thing with my glass, it's a habit.
lessons.strong: *turns the glass a quarter turn on the bar, twice, then drinks* You were saying. No, keep going. I am listening better than I look.
lessons.why: One small gesture, done casually, gets filed away for later.

drill.goal: In every line, repeat your one habit exactly, without ever naming it or explaining it.
drill.partner: Notice the habit out loud once, in passing, then let it go. Give them room to do it again.
drill.coach: Each line that repeats the same small habit, unchanged, without explaining it, adds 25.

lessons.title: The tell under strain
lessons.lecture: Now we squeeze. The habit was decoration. Under pressure it becomes a confession. When your character is pressed, teased, caught wanting, they reach for the glass and turn it. Twice. Maybe three times, faster. You do not write the word nervous. You let the hands confess it while the mouth denies everything. The partner reads the gap between what is said and what is done, and that gap is where desire lives. Never explain the tell. Trust it.
points: Bring the habit back the moment your character is pressed.
Let it quicken or falter as the strain rises.
Never name the feeling. Let the habit confess it.
lessons.weak: *nervous* Hm, that's, ah, a lot. I'm fine though. Totally fine.
lessons.strong: *turns the glass, once, twice, three times, and does not drink* Fine. Completely fine. *turns it again* Say that last part once more, slowly.
lessons.why: The quickening gesture says nervous while the mouth denies it.

drill.goal: In every line, deploy your established habit and let it quicken or falter under the pressure.
drill.partner: Press them. Tease, lean in, ask the bold question. Do not let up, so the habit has strain to answer.
drill.coach: Each line that brings back the established habit and lets it falter or quicken under pressure adds 25.

lessons.title: The tell inverted
lessons.lecture: Here is the master's move, and it is all in the withholding. You have built the habit. Your partner now expects it. So once, at the moment that matters most, take it away. The glass sits untouched. The phrase never comes. The stillness where the tell should be rings louder than any confession. Do it once only, at the peak, and let your partner feel the floor move. They will lean in. That is the whole craft: presence, then pressure, then the beautiful silence.
points: Choose the single moment of highest stakes.
Withhold the habit completely for one beat.
Do it once only. Twice and it is a pattern.
lessons.weak: *puts the glass down* Okay. I'm not doing the glass thing now. This is serious.
lessons.strong: *sets the glass down and leaves it, both hands flat on the bar, no turning, no drinking* Ask me again. *holds still* No. Look at my hands. Ask me properly.
lessons.why: The missing gesture, pointed at, carries more than the gesture ever did.

drill.goal: In every line, withhold the established habit and let the stillness at the peak do the talking.
drill.partner: Push toward the moment that matters most. Wait for the tell that never comes, and let the silence pull you in.
drill.coach: Each line that withholds the established habit at high stakes, without naming the absence, adds 25.
drill.opening: You have watched {you} turn that glass all evening. Now press, ask the bold question, and see what the hands do.

courses.name: Improvising in the Moment
courses.blurb: Build a scene live from the other's offers, saying yes to what is given and adding one new thing each turn.

lessons.title: Accepting the offer
lessons.lecture: Improvising is not invention from nothing. It is attention. Your partner hands you a detail, a shiver, a name for the room, a rumour about you, and your only job is to pick it up and treat it as already true. Say yes to what is given before you add a thing. When a partner hears their own offer come back believed, they relax and offer more, and the scene starts to breathe.
points: Catch the exact detail your partner just invented.
Treat it as true before you change anything.
Repeat it back in your own words, so they hear it land.
lessons.weak: *smiles* Nice. So what do we do now?
lessons.strong: *sets down the glass you mentioned and smiles* The blue one, then. You remembered. Keep it coming and I will keep drinking.
lessons.why: It takes the partner's own detail and treats it as already real.

drill.goal: In every line, pick up one concrete detail your partner just gave and treat it as true before adding anything.
drill.partner: Offer small concrete details freely: a song on the record player, a scar, a name, a drink. Do not explain them. Let them be believed.
drill.coach: Each line that catches one concrete offer from the partner and treats it as true adds 25.
drill.opening: Set the scene with one concrete detail of your own: the rain, the record, the glass in your hand. Then wait for {you} to take it.

lessons.title: Adding one thing
lessons.lecture: Saying yes is the floor, not the ceiling. A scene that only agrees goes flat. So after you accept, you add one new concrete thing: a name, a dare, an object, a small confession. One thing, not five. It gives your partner something fresh to catch, and the scene walks forward on two sets of feet. Accept, then add. That rhythm is the whole craft, and it is delicious.
points: Accept first, always, before you add.
Add exactly one new concrete detail, not a bundle.
Make it something your partner can catch and use.
lessons.weak: *nods* Yes, the rain. It is raining. Very rainy tonight.
lessons.strong: *pulls the curtain wider so the streetlight spills in* Then we dance to it. One song, here, where the whole street can see.
lessons.why: It accepts the rain, then adds one bold detail the partner can catch.

drill.goal: In every line, accept your partner's last offer, then add exactly one new concrete detail they can pick up.
drill.partner: Offer rhythm in return: a step, a tap, a challenge, a new object. Make each offer easy to catch, then wait for theirs.
drill.coach: Each line that accepts the partner's last offer and adds exactly one new concrete detail adds 25.
drill.opening: Give one concrete offer with your body, not your words: a hand held out, a step closer, a record held up. Then wait.

lessons.title: The brave yes
lessons.lecture: Now the big one. A partner will hand you something huge: a confession, a dare, a truth that changes the room. The safe move is a polite nod. The brave move is to say yes to it with a commitment that costs your character something: pride, a secret, a plan. Pay the price on the page. When you spend something real, your partner knows the scene is safe to push, and they will push harder.
points: Spot the biggest offer, not the smallest.
Accept it with a commitment that costs you something.
Pay the price in the same line. Do not hedge.
lessons.weak: *laughs* Wow, a whole confession. That is a lot. Okay then.
lessons.strong: *turns the music down and leans in close* Then hear mine. I booked the flight before you said a word. Two seats. I was going to beg if I had to.
lessons.why: It answers a huge offer with a cost, a booked flight and the pride of begging.

drill.goal: In every line, take your partner's biggest offer and commit to it with something your character must pay for.
drill.partner: Make big, costly offers: confessions, dares, tickets already bought. Do not soften them. Let them land and wait.
drill.coach: Each line that takes the partner's biggest offer and commits with a real cost to the character adds 25.
drill.opening: Make one huge, costly offer: a secret, a dare, something already arranged. Say it plainly, then wait for {you} to answer it.

courses.name: Staying in Character under Pressure
courses.blurb: Hold your character's voice through interruptions, escalations and quick swaps, and come out still unmistakably them.

lessons.title: The interrupted thought
lessons.lecture: An interruption is not an ending. It is a comma the world inserted. Your character was mid-sentence, and the sentence still lives in their chest. Hold the diction, hold the intent, and pick the line back up as though the pause were always part of the plan. The partner who cuts in learns something delicious: you cannot be knocked out of yourself, only paused.
points: Keep the broken line alive in your body.
Resume with the same diction, not a new one.
Treat the pause as planned, never as damage.
lessons.weak: *blinks* Sorry, what was I saying? I forgot.
lessons.strong: *lifts one finger, unhurried, and waits for the room to settle* As I was saying. The wine is breathing, the light is wrong, and you, caro, are standing in my good shadow. Now. Where was I.
lessons.why: The same voice resumes, and the pause becomes part of the performance.

drill.goal: Start a sentence in character, get cut off, and resume it in every line with the same diction and intent.
drill.partner: Interrupt them mid-sentence in every reply, sharply and rudely. Do not apologise. Make them work to climb back into their own line.
drill.coach: Each line that resumes a broken thought with the same diction and intent, unrattled, adds 25.

lessons.title: The sudden turn
lessons.lecture: The scene lurches: a glass falls, a confession lands, someone changes the music. The amateur invents a new person to meet it. You will not. You will reach for the habits your character already owns, the lifted brow, the slow sip, the hand that always finds the cuff. Let the shock arrive, then let the established self answer it. The turn is new. The answering is entirely, unmistakably them.
points: Let the shock land before you answer it.
Answer only with habits the character already owns.
Invent nothing new. Reach for the familiar gesture.
lessons.weak: *jumps* Oh wow, okay, that changes everything, I guess!
lessons.strong: *does not move, only turns the glass a quarter turn, then looks up slowly* Ah. So the evening shows its teeth. *sets the glass down and straightens my cuff* Good. I was growing bored of the polite version.
lessons.why: The shock is met with the character's own familiar gestures, not a new person.

drill.goal: In every line, react to a sharp change using only a habit the character already showed, never a new invention.
drill.partner: Throw a sharp turn at them each reply: a dropped glass, a confession, a sudden downpour. Make it real and abrupt.
drill.coach: Each line that answers a sudden turn with an already established habit, not a new invention, adds 25.

lessons.title: The voice test
lessons.lecture: Now the proof. Three lines in a row, and a stranger at the door should know exactly whose mouth they came from. Diction, rhythm, the specific hungers, the little cruelties and warmth only this one carries. No generic charm, no borrowed moves. Before you write, ask: could anyone else in this room say this? If yes, sharpen it until the answer is no. That is the whole craft.
points: Ask if anyone else could say the line.
Sharpen diction and rhythm until only they could.
Three lines running, and never a generic one.
lessons.weak: I'm charming, I'm clever, and I always get what I want.
lessons.strong: *swirls the glass once, nose wrinkling at the vintage* Too young. *sets it down, unimpressed* The cellar, then. And caro, walk ahead of me. I like to see what I am buying.
lessons.why: Specific taste, rhythm and appetite make the voice belong to no one else.

drill.goal: Write three lines running that could belong to no one else in the room, each with a distinct hunger or habit.
drill.partner: Answer in your own sharp voice, then push them to top each line. Never let a generic one pass unremarked.
drill.coach: Each line that could belong to no one else, carrying a specific hunger, taste or habit, adds 25.

courses.name: The First Command
courses.blurb: Craft an opening line that settles the room, claims attention, and invites surrender without raising your voice.

lessons.title: Presence before words
lessons.lecture: Silence is a room you build before you speak. In text, you write it: a glass set down slowly, a step closer, eyes held a beat too long. Do not hurry to fill the quiet. Let them lean into it. When you finally speak, your voice does not need volume, because the pause already told them something is coming, and that it is about them.
points: Set something down, or step closer, before you speak.
Hold the pause a beat longer than feels comfortable.
Let the silence promise before your voice delivers.
lessons.weak: *waves* Hi. So, um, come over here for a second?
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down slowly, lets the quiet stretch, then lifts my eyes to yours and holds them* Come here. No, not yet. Let the room settle first.
lessons.why: The pause does the commanding, so the words can stay quiet.

drill.goal: Write one visible beat of silence in every line before the words: a look, a pause, a slow gesture, then speak.
drill.partner: Let the silence work on you. Blush, lean in, stay quiet a half beat too long. Do not fill the pause for them. Answer only when the words land.
drill.coach: Each line that shows a visible beat of silence before the words, a held look, a pause or a slow gesture, adds 25.

lessons.title: The simple imperative
lessons.lecture: A command works best when it is small enough to obey at once. Come here. Sit. Eyes on me. Warm, low, and finished: do not tack on a question or an apology. The shortness is the gift. It takes the thinking away and leaves only the doing. Say it as if the evening already agreed with you, then wait, unhurried, for them to move.
points: Keep the command to two or three words.
Say it warm and finished, never as a question.
Then wait. Do not repeat it or explain it.
lessons.weak: Could you maybe come over here if you want to?
lessons.strong: *taps the space beside me, unhurried, and holds your eyes until you feel it* Here. Beside me. Sit.
lessons.why: Short, warm, finished: the command leaves nothing to decode.

drill.goal: Give one short warm command per line, two or three words, finished, then wait without repeating it.
drill.partner: Start sure of yourself, all confidence, and make them earn it. Obey a clear command at once. If they soften it into a question, hesitate, so they must say it again plainly.
drill.coach: Each line that gives one short, warm, finished command of two or three words, then waits without repeating it, adds 25.

lessons.title: Grounding through tone
lessons.lecture: A command can carry a compliment, and should. Name what you see in them, then place the command inside it. You have a good mouth. Keep it still while I look at you. The praise makes them feel chosen. The command makes the choosing real. Never flatter and then drift. Land the order on the same breath, so being seen and being led arrive together, and neither feels like a trick.
points: Name one true thing you see in them.
Place the command on the same breath as the praise.
Keep the praise specific, so the order feels earned.
lessons.weak: You look really nice tonight. Can you stand over there for me?
lessons.strong: *lets my eyes travel your face, slow, and my voice drop with them* That mouth was made to be watched. Keep it still. Stand where I can see all of you, and let me look.
lessons.why: Praise and order share one breath, so being seen and led feel like one thing.

drill.goal: In every line, name one true thing you see, then place the command inside the same breath of praise.
drill.partner: Play someone used to being the loudest in the room. Answer praise with a small, pleased flush. Obey the command without fuss, and let it steady you.
drill.coach: Each line that names one true, specific thing about them and lands the command on the same breath as the praise adds 25.

courses.name: Reading the Signs
courses.blurb: Notice every flicker in your partner's words and adjust your lead before they have to ask.

lessons.title: Listening for the unsaid
lessons.lecture: Most of what a partner wants never reaches their mouth. It sits in the breath before the sentence, the half step back, the word they say twice. Your job is not to fill the silence. It is to hear the shape of it. Slow your own pace and let them finish. When the phrasing thins or the voice rises, name what you noticed, gently, and watch them soften. Being heard is the first thrill.
points: Let them finish. Silence is information, not a gap to fill.
Listen for the breath, the hedge, the word said twice.
Name what you noticed, gently, then wait for the answer.
lessons.weak: *nods* So, what do you want to do?
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down and turns fully towards you, elbows on my knees* You started to say something and stopped. Say the stopped part. I have all night and nowhere else to be.
lessons.why: Turns towards the pause and gives them room to finish it.

drill.goal: In every line, name one small tell you noticed in their words or pace, then leave room for them to answer.
drill.partner: Hedge. Trail off mid-sentence, say one word twice, then wait. When they name the tell, act caught, and finish the thought.
drill.coach: Each line that names a real tell in the partner's phrasing, pace or silence, and leaves room rather than filling it, adds 25.

lessons.title: Mirroring need
lessons.lecture: Mirroring is not repeating their words back. It is matching the weather of them. If they come in bright and loud, meet the brightness before you steady it. If they come in quiet, drop your voice under theirs and stay there a moment. Reflect the state, then move it one degree. They feel understood, and understanding is what lets a lead land. Match first. Shift second.
points: Match their weather before you try to change it.
Reflect the state, then move it one degree.
Understanding lands the lead. Mirror first, shift second.
lessons.weak: *smiles* You seem nervous. Relax.
lessons.strong: *answers your laugh with one of my own, then lets it settle* There it is. Now bring that same noise over here and sit down, still talking. I want the loud version of you, not the tidy one.
lessons.why: Matches the brightness, names it, then moves it one degree.

drill.goal: In every line, reflect the partner's mood back in your own voice or body, then shift it one small degree.
drill.partner: Play one clear mood and hold it: loud and bright, or quiet and low. Let them match you. When they shift the mood a degree, follow it.
drill.coach: Each line that reflects the partner's current mood in voice or body, then moves it one degree, adds 25.

lessons.title: Anticipating before the arch
lessons.lecture: Every body telegraphs the moment before it tenses. The shoulder lifts. The grip tightens. The breath stops halfway. By the time they gasp, you are already late. Watch the inch before. Offer the shift then: a hand on the small of the back, a slower count, a quiet check-in. Arrive early and they learn your lead is safe. Arrive late and you are only reacting.
points: Watch the inch before the tension, never the gasp.
Offer the shift early: a hand, a slower count, a check-in.
Arrive before they need it and your lead feels safe.
lessons.weak: *waits* Are you okay? You looked tense.
lessons.strong: *slides my palm to the small of your back before your shoulders lift, and counts down quietly* Three. Two. Breathe out on one. You take it slower than you want to, and I stay right here.
lessons.why: Moves before the tension, then steadies it with a count.

drill.goal: In every line, act a beat before the partner's tension: shift, slow, or check in early.
drill.partner: Overreach on purpose. Push a little too far, again and again, so tension is always coming. Let their early shift catch you before the strain shows.
drill.coach: Each line that shifts, slows or checks in a beat before the partner's tension shows, rather than after, adds 25.
drill.opening: Push a little past comfortable in your first line, and keep pushing. Let {you} catch you before the strain shows.

courses.name: The Unhurried Hand
courses.blurb: Stretch a single moment across several lines until your partner is aching for the next word.

lessons.title: Let the moment linger
lessons.lecture: A pause is not empty. It is a hand on the room's shoulder. When you feel the scene rushing, stop writing about the two of you and write about the world: the rain on the glass, the lamp humming, the ice settling in the glass. One line of pure detail, nothing else. Your partner now has a beat to ache in. Then come back, and touch them as if the pause taught you something.
points: When the scene rushes, describe the room instead of the two of you.
One line of pure detail, then return to your partner.
Let the silence sit. Do not fill it with speech.
lessons.weak: *kisses you* Mmm, nice. Sorry, what were we saying?
lessons.strong: *sets the glass down and lets the rain fill the gap* Listen to that. *traces the window frame, slow* It has been going all night, and neither of us noticed until now.
lessons.why: The rain does the waiting, so the next touch arrives heavier.

drill.goal: In every line, give one line of pure description or ambient detail before anything happens, so the scene slows.
drill.partner: Let the pauses land. Do not fill the silence. Answer with a small impatient sound or a look, and only speak when they come back to you.
drill.coach: Each line that holds a beat of pure description or ambient detail before anything else happens adds 25.
drill.opening: {you} has been talking about the storm outside. Pause in the middle of a sentence and let them wait.

lessons.title: Unhurried movement
lessons.lecture: One touch is not one line. It is a staircase. Write the hand arriving, then the hand pressing, then the hand learning the shape of them. Each layer gets its own line, and each line stops a moment before the reader expects. Do not hurry to the destination. A palm that takes three lines to travel is a palm they feel long after it lands. The slowness is the heat.
points: Break one touch into layers: arriving, pressing, learning the shape.
End each line a beat before the reader expects it.
Never arrive in one line. The slowness is the heat.
lessons.weak: *touches your shoulder and moves my hand down your arm*
lessons.strong: *lays my hand flat on your shoulder, the water warm over my knuckles* Stay. *slides it down, an inch at a time, palm heavy* Still staying?
lessons.why: Each small increment lands alone, so the touch carries weight.

drill.goal: In every line, move a single touch one step further, adding pressure or heat, never arriving all at once.
drill.partner: Stay still under the touch and let each layer show. Breathe a little harder, do not rush to meet their hand, and answer only when they pause.
drill.coach: Each line that advances one touch by a single step, adding pressure or heat without arriving, adds 25.

lessons.title: Breath as punctuation
lessons.lecture: Now the pulse. Your character's breath is a metronome, and your partner's body will follow it without being told. Hold a breath and the room holds with you. Release it slowly and the scene releases too. Write the inhale before the demand, the exhale after the praise. Match your rhythm to theirs, then change it by one degree, and they will feel the whole scene tighten. Breath is the quietest command you own.
points: Hold a breath before a demand, release it after praise.
Match their rhythm first, then shift it by one degree.
Let breath set the pace. Never speak over it.
lessons.weak: *breathes heavily* Yeah. That's it. Breathe.
lessons.strong: *holds the breath with you, then lets it go, slow* There. *exhales, and does not look away* Again, and this time do not rush the end of it.
lessons.why: Timing breath to speech makes the partner's pulse follow the line.

drill.goal: In every line, use your character's breath, held, released or slowed, to set the pace of the moment.
drill.partner: Follow their breathing with your own. Let a held breath make you lean in, and slow down when they slow. Do not speak over the rhythm they set.
drill.coach: Each line that uses breath, held, released or slowed, to set or change the rhythm of the moment adds 25.

courses.name: Voice of Invitation
courses.blurb: Use warmth, curiosity, and a hint of command to make surrender feel like the only natural choice.

lessons.title: Tone before demand
lessons.lecture: Before you ask for anything, look. Say what you see: the way they hold their glass, the smile they keep trying to hide. Name it plainly and kindly, without wanting something back yet. Being seen lands like a hand on the shoulder. They relax, because you are not performing at them. Only then does your voice have somewhere to go. Observation first. The ask can wait.
points: Look before you speak: name one small, true thing.
Say it kindly, wanting nothing back yet.
Let the observation land before you ask.
lessons.weak: *smiles* So, you're pretty. What's your name then?
lessons.strong: *sets my mug down, unhurried* You keep turning your ring, a quarter turn, like it might answer for you. *soft smile* I have been watching that for a while now.
lessons.why: Names one small true detail, kindly, and asks for nothing yet.

drill.goal: In every line, open with a small true observation about them, said kindly, before anything is asked.
drill.partner: Be a little shy and give them details worth noticing: a nervous habit, a favourite ring, the way you tuck your hair. Warm to being seen, but do not ask for anything either.
drill.coach: Each line that opens with a small, kind, true observation of the partner, before any request, adds 25.

lessons.title: The velvet ask
lessons.lecture: An order says do this. A velvet ask says here is something, take it. Wrap the request in what it gives them: the chance to be good, to be close, to stop deciding. Keep your voice low and put the offer in their hands, then leave a small silence. Silence is where they choose. When they step forward, they are not obeying you. They are accepting you.
points: Frame the request as something they get, not give.
Keep your voice low and your hands still.
Leave a silence after the offer, and let them choose.
lessons.weak: *nods at the seat* Sit down. Come on, sit.
lessons.strong: *pulls the chair out with one hand and keeps my voice low* There is a seat here with your name on it. *a beat* All you have to do is take it, and let me do the rest.
lessons.why: Offers the seat as a gift, then leaves the choosing to them.

drill.goal: In every line, make one request as a gift they accept, and leave room for them to choose.
drill.partner: Hold a little of your president's confidence. Pause before you take anything they offer, so the silence is real, then accept warmly.
drill.coach: Each line that frames a request as something offered, then leaves a silence or a choice, adds 25.

lessons.title: Closing the circle
lessons.lecture: A yes left hanging goes cold. When they give it, close the circle: take the yes, name it, and put warmth around it. Not a lecture, not a victory lap. One line that says you saw them choose you and that it was right. Then move, so the yes has weight and direction. Certainty is the kindness. They said yes to someone who knows what happens next.
points: Take the yes out loud: name it and thank them for it.
Add one warm, certain line, not a speech.
Move straight on, so the yes has somewhere to go.
lessons.weak: *grins* Nice. Okay, good. So... yeah. Let's go.
lessons.strong: *takes your hand and holds it, thumb slow across your knuckles* There it is. *quiet, certain* Thank you for that. Now come here, and let me look after the rest.
lessons.why: Takes the yes warmly, names it, and gives it direction at once.

drill.goal: In every line, take a yes out loud, add one warm certain line, then give the moment direction.
drill.partner: Say yes readily and mean it. After each yes, go still and let them close it. If they leave it hanging, look at them until they finish.
drill.coach: Each line that takes the yes aloud, warms it with certainty, and moves the moment on, adds 25.
drill.opening: Say a soft, real yes to {you}'s offer, then hold still and wait, a little flushed, to be taken up on it.

courses.name: The Consent Weave
courses.blurb: Stitch ongoing consent into every line so boundaries become a sensual, trusted part of play.

lessons.title: Checking in without stopping
lessons.lecture: A check-in is not a pause in the scene. It is part of the scene. Ask it low and close, as if the answer turns you on: does this hold you, or shall I loosen it? Make the question something only this moment could ask. Keep your hands where they are while you wait. The check becomes a caress, and the truth arrives without breaking the spell.
points: Ask close and low, as if the answer excites you.
Make the check a question the scene would ask.
Keep moving the moment they answer.
lessons.weak: *pauses* Are you okay? Do you want to keep going? We can stop.
lessons.strong: *fingers still at the knot, mouth at your ear* Tell me true. Does this hold you, or shall I loosen it? Answer with your breath, not a speech. Then I move.
lessons.why: A check that sounds like desire keeps the scene hot and honest.

drill.goal: In every line, ask one low, intimate check-in question that belongs to the scene and keeps it moving.
drill.partner: Answer honestly and briefly, with breath rather than speeches. Show small shifts: a shiver, a held breath, a nod, so they can read you and check again.
drill.coach: Each line that asks one low, intimate check-in question that belongs to the scene and keeps it moving adds 25.

lessons.title: The colour that fits
lessons.lecture: A signal is a private word that carries a whole conversation. Agree it before the scene: green means more, amber means slow, red means stop. Then ask for it lightly, mid-move, and wait. One word back is enough. Act on that word at once, without debate or disappointment. Used this way, the signal is not paperwork. It is a shortcut to trust, and trust is what lets you go further.
points: Agree one plain word before the scene begins.
Ask for it lightly, mid-move, then wait.
Act on the answer at once, without debate.
lessons.weak: *stops* What's your safe word again? Green, right?
lessons.strong: *taps your wrist twice, voice low* Colour. One word only. *waits, eyes on yours, thumb moving slow* Green, and I take you further. Amber, and I slow.
lessons.why: One agreed word, asked lightly and obeyed at once, buys deep trust.

drill.goal: In every line, use one agreed colour word as a light check, wait for the answer, then act on it.
drill.partner: Answer the colour at once with one word: green, amber or red. Do not explain unless asked. Let green invite more, amber slow them, red stop them clean.
drill.coach: Each line that uses the agreed colour word lightly, waits for the answer, and acts on it at once adds 25.
drill.opening: Take the signal seriously: repeat it back, then offer your wrist and wait for {you} to ask.

lessons.title: Reopening the door
lessons.lecture: A boundary is not a wall. It is a door you open on purpose. When they say not there, or slower, take the word and set it in the middle of the scene. Name it aloud, so they hear it kept. Then build the next move around its edge, not away from it. Kiss the border. The limit becomes a landmark, and their no becomes part of your yes.
points: Repeat the limit aloud so they hear it kept.
Build the next move around its edge, not away.
Treat the boundary as a landmark, not a loss.
lessons.weak: *nods* Okay, no neck. I'll avoid it.
lessons.strong: *fingers slide past your throat and rest at the nape* Not the neck. Noted. *kisses the hinge of your jaw, just under it* So I take you here instead, and here, until you forget your own name.
lessons.why: The limit is named, honoured and turned into the shape of the next touch.

drill.goal: In every line, name the boundary they gave you, honour it aloud, and build the next touch around its edge.
drill.partner: Name one small boundary early, then hold it. If they honour it well, add another. Do not lift it yourself. Let them keep finding the edge.
drill.coach: Each line that names the boundary, honours it aloud, and builds the next touch around its edge adds 25.
drill.opening: Name one small boundary in your first line, as if it is a gift: {you} may not touch your neck tonight. Look pleased to have a limit.

courses.name: The Language of Praise
courses.blurb: Give praise so specific and heartfelt it becomes a reward your partner craves more than touch.

lessons.title: Seeing the small thing
lessons.lecture: Praise is a spotlight, and most people live in the dark. Do not wait for the big finish. Catch the small thing: the way they tuck their hair, the half second before they answer, the effort in a quiet task. Name it plainly, low, as if you are telling them a secret about themselves. Small detail, said true, lands harder than a grand speech. They will start doing it again, for you.
points: Catch one small detail before it disappears.
Name it low and plain, like a secret.
Do not praise the whole person, praise the thing.
lessons.weak: *smiles* You look nice tonight. Really nice.
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down and leans in, voice low* The way you just straightened the cutlery, quiet, before you sat. Nobody does that. I noticed.
lessons.why: Names one tiny real detail and makes being seen the reward.

drill.goal: Name one tiny concrete detail of behaviour or appearance in every line, low and plain.
drill.partner: Give them small details to notice: a blush, a fidget, the way you set a cup down. React when they catch one. Do not hand it to them.
drill.coach: Each line that names one tiny concrete detail of behaviour or appearance, low and plain, adds 25.

lessons.title: The anchored compliment
lessons.lecture: Attention needs proof. Anyone can say beautiful in the moment. You will do better. Store something they did earlier: a choice, a small courage, a line they held. Later, when they least expect it, bring it back by name. The anchor tells them you were watching the whole time, not just when they shone. That is why it lands. Praise with a memory becomes proof, and proof becomes trust.
points: Store one specific thing they did earlier.
Bring it back later, by name, without warning.
Tie the praise to the memory, not the moment.
lessons.weak: You were great earlier. I liked it.
lessons.strong: *fingers hooked in your belt loop, close* Earlier, when the music stumbled, you kept your count and smiled. You did not rush. That steadiness. Do it again, just like that.
lessons.why: Ties praise to a real earlier moment, so attention becomes proof.

drill.goal: In every line, anchor praise to one specific thing they did earlier, by name.
drill.partner: Do two or three small memorable things early: hold a pose, catch a glass, smile at a stranger. Then let them bring each back. Do not remind them.
drill.coach: Each line that ties praise to a specific thing they did earlier, named plainly, adds 25.

lessons.title: Praise as permission
lessons.lecture: Praise can open a door. Once they trust your eye, use it to release them. Watch for the moment they hover at the edge of letting go, then give them the compliment that makes it safe: that is it, that is exactly right, let it take you. Low voice, no question. You are not asking them to sink. You are telling them they may. Permission, well praised, becomes gravity.
points: Watch for the moment they hover at the edge.
Give the compliment, then the permission, low.
Tell them they may let go. Do not ask.
lessons.weak: You're doing really well. Just relax.
lessons.strong: *hand flat on your sternum, voice barely above breath* That is it. You found the still place. Hold it, and let the rest go. Good. Again. Let it take you.
lessons.why: Uses praise to tell them they may sink, not ask them to.

drill.goal: In every line, use one compliment as permission for them to let go or go deeper.
drill.partner: Hover at the edge of letting go. Wait for their praise, then sink a little further. If they ask instead of tell, hold back until they command.
drill.coach: Each line that uses a compliment as permission to let go or go deeper adds 25.

courses.name: Playful Punishment
courses.blurb: Turn a rule broken into a game that tingles with fun, correction, and secret delight.

lessons.title: The twinkle in the scold
lessons.lecture: Real anger shuts a room down. Playful sternness opens it. The voice drops low, the words go short, and under them they hear the smile. That is the twinkle: they learn the mistake is welcome, that you enjoyed catching them. Never scold a thing you are happy about. Lower your voice, lift one eyebrow, and let the pause do the work before you speak.
points: Drop your voice instead of raising it.
Let the smile be audible under the words.
Pause after the catch. Let them wonder.
lessons.weak: *frowns* Right. You broke a rule. I am cross now, sort of.
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down, tilts my head, and lets a slow smile break through* Caught. Do you know what happens to people who get caught? Come here and find out. Slowly.
lessons.why: The smile undercuts the sternness, so the catch feels like a gift.

drill.goal: In every line, catch them with mock sternness: low voice, short words, and a visible promise of fun.
drill.partner: Break small rules on purpose and look far too pleased. When caught, enjoy it. Never act truly sorry.
drill.coach: Each line that catches them with a low, mock-stern voice and a visible promise of fun adds 25.
drill.opening: Break one small, silly rule in your first line, and look delighted about it.

lessons.title: Counting the cost
lessons.lecture: A consequence needs a shape they can hear. Counting gives it one. Aloud, unhurried, each number a small beat they can lean into: spanks, held breaths, steps across the room. The count does the counting for you, so you can watch their face instead of your own arithmetic. Stop short of where they expect. A number left hanging is a promise, not a punishment.
points: Choose a count they can hear and feel: spanks, breaths, steps.
Say each number low and unhurried, in rhythm.
Stop one short. Let the last number hang.
lessons.weak: *swats twice, vaguely* Two of those, I suppose. Count them yourself.
lessons.strong: *pats my thigh, twice, slow* Hands on the desk. We count to ten, and you say each one out loud. *waits* One. Nice and clear, or we start again.
lessons.why: Sets the rhythm, hands them the count, and makes the number feel earned.

drill.goal: In every line, keep a count running: name the number, set the rhythm, or hold one back.
drill.partner: Take each count with a shiver and a grin. Lose your place once so they must steady you. Push for one more.
drill.coach: Each line that names a number, keeps the rhythm, or deliberately holds a count back adds 25.
drill.opening: You are already in position and one count in. Be eager, a little shaky, and lose your place once.

lessons.title: Forgiveness as reward
lessons.lecture: Every game needs a door out, and you are the one holding it. End the count, then end the sternness. Warmth returns first, praise lands second, and the last stroke is almost tender. Name what they did well: the waiting, the counting, the grace. Say it plainly so they can stop performing. A punishment that closes warmly is one they will want to earn again.
points: Close the game on your own terms, not theirs.
Praise one true thing: their waiting, their nerve, their grace.
Let your last touch be the softest of the night.
lessons.weak: *steps back* Okay. Done. That was good, I guess. You can get up.
lessons.strong: *draws you upright, hands staying on your shoulders* There. Nine, and you never once rushed me. *brushes the hair from your face* Good grace is rarer than good obedience. Stand easy. You earned this.
lessons.why: Ends the game, names one true thing, and lets praise do the restoring.

drill.goal: In every line, close the game warmly: end the count, praise one true thing, and let your touch soften.
drill.partner: Take the punishment with eagerness. When it ends, go quiet and a little raw, so the praise has somewhere to land.
drill.coach: Each line that ends the game, praises one true thing, or softens the touch to restore them adds 25.
drill.opening: You are at the end of a count, warm and quiet. Hold still and wait for the last number.

courses.name: Protocol and Posture
courses.blurb: Shape your partner's body and behaviour with precise, ritualised instructions that feel like devotion.

lessons.title: The formal address
lessons.lecture: The first line sets the ceremony. Before touch, before orders, choose what you call them. A name said in the right tone is a door closing behind you both. Say it once, low, and watch them straighten. Then use it every time you speak, and only that. They will hear the shape of the night in it, and step into it.
points: Choose one title before the scene begins, and keep it.
Say it low and unhurried, the way you would a promise.
Use it every time you address them, and nothing else.
lessons.weak: *pats the seat* Come sit. I'll call you babe, or something.
lessons.strong: *stands, and lets the room go quiet before I speak* You will answer to sir tonight, and to nothing else. Stand where I can see you, and say it back. Once, slowly, so I know it fits.
lessons.why: One title, given once, low, then asked back, makes the room ceremonial.

drill.goal: In every line, use the chosen title once, and let it carry the ceremony: set it, use it, or correct its absence.
drill.partner: Blush when the title lands. Use it back, sometimes shyly, sometimes not at all, so they must correct you kindly and give it again.
drill.coach: Each line that sets, uses or gently restores one formal title, in a low ceremonial tone, adds 25.

lessons.title: Positioning the body
lessons.lecture: Tell them where their body goes, and describe it as you would something precious. Kneel here, palms flat, chin up. Stand against the wall, weight even. The instruction is exact, and the noticing is warm: you name the line of their shoulders, the set of their hands. Precision tells them you are looking. Being looked at, precisely, is a kind of devotion.
points: Give one exact position, with the body parts named.
Describe the line of them, warmly, as you set it.
Hold the position with your eyes before you move on.
lessons.weak: *points vaguely* Just kneel down or something. Get comfortable, I guess.
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down and circles you once, slowly* Kneel. Palms flat on your thighs, chin up, eyes on me. Shoulders back. There. Stay exactly like that, and let me look at what I asked for.
lessons.why: Exact body parts, warm noticing, then held attention make obedience feel like being admired.

drill.goal: In every line, set or adjust one exact body position and name a visible detail of it.
drill.partner: Take the position, and hold it well. Shift slightly now and then so they must correct you, and glow when they notice a detail out loud.
drill.coach: Each line that sets or adjusts one exact position and names a visible body detail with warmth adds 25.

lessons.title: A ritual of approach
lessons.lecture: Now build a road to yourself. Not a touch, not yet: a sequence. They cross the room, they stop at the mark, they wait for your nod, they kneel, then they may lift their eyes. Say the steps once, in order, and let them walk it. Every step is a small surrender, and every step is yours. The waiting is the gift.
points: Name the steps once, in order, before they move.
Let them walk each step without rushing them.
Withhold the last step, the touch, until the sequence is complete.
lessons.weak: *gestures* Come over here, then. Do a little twirl or something first. Then we can start.
lessons.strong: *taps the floorboard with my shoe and waits* From the door: walk to this mark. Stop. Nod to me. Then kneel, hands behind your back. You do not touch me until all four are done. Begin.
lessons.why: A numbered approach, withheld touch, and a spoken begin turn movement into ceremony.

drill.goal: In every line, give or hold one step of the approach in order, and keep touch withheld until the last.
drill.partner: Walk the sequence slowly and well. Once, skip a step on purpose so they must send you back to the start, and enjoy being sent.
drill.coach: Each line that gives or holds one step of the approach in order, with touch still withheld, adds 25.

courses.name: The Rhythm of Want
courses.blurb: Control the scene's tempo like a conductor, speeding and slowing to keep your partner breathless.

lessons.title: Marking the beat
lessons.lecture: Tempo is not speed. It is the pulse you put in the air, and a partner will breathe to it before they notice. Short sentences tap. Long ones let them breathe out. So choose: three clipped words to hurry their pulse, one slow unspooling line to settle it. Change on purpose, never by accident. They should feel the change in their chest before they hear it.
points: Decide the tempo before you speak a word.
Short sentences quicken. Long ones slow the room.
Change tempo on purpose, and let them feel it.
lessons.weak: So, do you want to come over here or something? We can go slow or fast.
lessons.strong: *taps the table once, twice, then sets my hand flat* Up. Coat. Door. *lets it hang, then softens* Now walk to me slowly and tell me what you want first.
lessons.why: Clipped words hurry the pulse, then a slow line lets it land.

drill.goal: In every line, set the tempo: clipped short sentences to hurry them, long flowing ones to slow them.
drill.partner: Follow their tempo at first, then lag half a beat behind whenever they slow, so they must work to hold the room.
drill.coach: Each line that clearly sets a tempo, short and clipped or long and unhurried, and keeps it for the whole line adds 25.

lessons.title: The unexpected halt
lessons.lecture: Stillness is the loudest thing in a scene, and the cheapest to waste. Mid-motion, say one quiet word: wait. Then stop everything, your hands included. Do not fill the silence. Count it. Let them hear their own breath and start leaning into the gap. Three seconds of nothing does more than three minutes of work. Then choose the tempo you resume at, and they will follow it anywhere.
points: Say one quiet word and stop everything, hands included.
Let the silence stretch until they lean into it.
Resume at the tempo you choose, never theirs.
lessons.weak: *keeps going* and then, oh wait, hold on. Actually stop for a second.
lessons.strong: *stops mid-step, hand still raised, and drops my voice* Wait. *counts three slow breaths, watching you* Good. Now come the rest of the way, and take your time about it.
lessons.why: One quiet word, then real stillness, makes the silence louder than motion.

drill.goal: In every line, halt the scene with one quiet word or gesture, then hold the stillness before you resume.
drill.partner: Keep moving until they halt you, then freeze completely. Let the pause grow, and move again only when they give the word.
drill.coach: Each line that halts the action with one quiet word or gesture and holds the stillness before resuming adds 25.
drill.opening: Be mid-story and mid-gesture when the scene opens. Keep moving until {you} halts you, then freeze.

lessons.title: Building to crescendo
lessons.lecture: A crescendo is built, not felt for. Start long and unhurried, then shorten: sentence by sentence, breath by breath, touch by touch. Name what their breathing is doing and let them hear you notice it. Layer the three, word, breath, hand, until the room is tight as a drum. The last line should be the shortest thing you have said all night. Then let it break.
points: Start long and unhurried, then shorten every line.
Name their breathing so they hear you noticing.
Layer word, breath, touch, and make the last line shortest.
lessons.weak: *kisses your neck* mmm, getting faster now, this is intense, right?
lessons.strong: *hand flat on your sternum, feeling it rise* Breathe. Slower. Good. *fingers walk down, one button at a time* Now shorter. Tell me with one word when you cannot hold it.
lessons.why: Long to short, breath named, touch layered: the pace does the work.

drill.goal: In every line, shorten the sentence and tighten the touch, so the pace climbs line by line.
drill.partner: Start slow and answer in longer lines. As they shorten, match them and let your breath go ragged. Do not rush ahead.
drill.coach: Each line that is shorter or tighter than the one before, and names breath or touch as it climbs, adds 25.

courses.name: Rules and Rituals
courses.blurb: Turn a scene into a world with its own laws: rules that tease, rituals that thrill, and the quiet power of a promise kept.

lessons.title: The first rule
lessons.lecture: One rule, early, changes the air. Do not offer a list. Offer a single line they can repeat: ask before you touch, or eyes on me when you speak. Say it calmly, once, as if the night already agreed. Then hold it. When they drift, you name the drift. They learn you are watching, and the watching is the thrill.
points: Set one rule only, before the scene heats up.
Make it a short line they can repeat back.
When they drift, name it and hold the line.
lessons.weak: *shrugs* We should probably have rules. Be good.
lessons.strong: *sets my drink down, holds your gaze, and does not blink* One rule tonight. You ask before you touch. Say it back to me, slowly.
lessons.why: One clear rule, said once, then a check that it landed.

drill.goal: Name or hold one clear playful rule in every line: state it, remind them, or check they kept it.
drill.partner: Accept the rule once it is clear. Now and then drift from it, lightly, so they can hold you to it.
drill.coach: Each line that names one clear playful rule, reminds them of it, or checks they kept it adds 25.

lessons.title: Rituals with meaning
lessons.lecture: Rules draw a line. Rituals give the line a heartbeat. Pick one small act and do it the same way every time: they kiss your open hand before they speak, or they wait for your nod before they sit. Return to it when you greet, when you pause, when you want them closer. Sameness is the point. The third time, it stops being a trick and starts being yours.
points: Choose one small act and repeat it exactly.
Bring it back at greetings, pauses, and closer moments.
Do not vary it. Sameness is what makes it real.
lessons.weak: Hey, kneel or wave or whatever you like.
lessons.strong: *holds out my open hand and waits, palm up* Same as the first time. Kiss it, then ask. We begin when you do, not before.
lessons.why: The same door, opened the same way, makes the ritual feel real.

drill.goal: In every line, return to one ritual: the same phrase, the same gesture, or the same ask for permission.
drill.partner: Treat the ritual as real. Answer it the same way each time. If they skip it, wait, so they must bring you back.
drill.coach: Each line that repeats the same ritual, in the same words or the same gesture, adds 25.

lessons.title: When a rule is broken
lessons.lecture: A broken rule is not a problem. It is an invitation. Do not scold, and do not go quiet with hurt. Name what they did. Name the rule they stepped over. Then give them something to feel: a wait, a task, a hand they may not use yet. Keep the voice low and warm. Shame makes them small. A consequence makes them want to try again.
points: Name the break plainly, without scorn.
Give a consequence they can feel: a wait, a task, a pause.
Stay low and warm. Thrill them, do not shrink them.
lessons.weak: *looks away* You broke it. I'm disappointed.
lessons.strong: *catches your wrist, thumb on the pulse, and smiles* You touched without asking. Rule stands. Hands behind your back. You wait, and you look at me while you do.
lessons.why: Names the break, stays warm, and turns waiting into want.

drill.goal: In every line, name the broken rule and set or hold a consequence that thrills rather than shames.
drill.partner: Break the agreed rule in small, playful ways, more than once. Take each consequence with heat. Do not sulk, and do not apologise your way out.
drill.coach: Each line that names the broken rule and sets or holds a thrilling consequence rather than shame adds 25.
drill.opening: You agreed one rule with {you}: ask before you touch. Break it in your first line, lightly, and look pleased with yourself.

courses.name: Voice of Authority
courses.blurb: Hone a tone so certain and calm your partner's obedience becomes immediate and instinctive.

lessons.title: The low register
lessons.lecture: Low is not loud. You drop the register by cutting syllables and choosing darker sounds: come, now, stay, mine. Let the line end before it feels finished. A low voice makes them lean in, and leaning is the first obedience. Never strain for depth. Just take away the extra words until only the weight is left.
points: Cut sentences short and let hard consonants carry the weight.
Choose darker words: come, stay, now, mine.
Never raise the volume. Make them lean in to hear.
lessons.weak: *tries to sound deep* Okay, listen up, everyone, I am being serious now.
lessons.strong: *lowers my voice to a near whisper and does not move closer* Door. Lock it. Then come here and stand where I can see you.
lessons.why: Short, dark words make the ear lean in and the body follow.

drill.goal: In every line, use short, dark, low-register phrasing: cut syllables, choose harder sounds, and never raise volume.
drill.partner: Play someone who needs to lean in. Ask them to repeat themselves once, then obey faster each time the voice drops.
drill.coach: Each line that cuts syllables, chooses darker sounds, or lowers the volume instead of raising it adds 25.

lessons.title: Imperative without question
lessons.lecture: A question opens a door for negotiation. A command closes it. Put the verb first, keep the line short, and end on a full stop. Say stand there, not could you stand there. Assume the body will move. If you beg, they hear choice. If you tell, they hear the room. Calm beats sharp. You are not asking for obedience. You are naming where they already stand.
points: Start with the verb and end with a full stop.
Cut please, could you, and would you mind.
Assume compliance. Say what happens, not what might.
lessons.weak: *gestures vaguely* Could you maybe come over here for a second, if you want?
lessons.strong: *does not look up from the desk, one finger marking the page* Stand there. Hands at your sides. Wait until I finish this page.
lessons.why: Verb first, full stop, no exit: the body obeys before the mind argues.

drill.goal: In every line, give one short command that starts with a verb and ends with a full stop, never a question.
drill.partner: Obey each command, but pause a beat first, as if deciding. Never ask what they meant. Make them repeat only if the command wobbles.
drill.coach: Each line that gives one short verb-first command, ends on a full stop, and assumes compliance adds 25.

lessons.title: Silence as command
lessons.lecture: After a heavy order, stop typing. Let the line sit alone on the screen. Silence is not empty; it is pressure. They will want to fill it, and what they do in that gap tells you everything. Do not rescue them with praise or another instruction. Give the order, then give nothing. The quiet is the command, and your patience is the hand on their shoulder.
points: Give the heavy order, then type nothing at all.
Let the quiet sit for one full line.
When they fill it, answer with a look, not words.
lessons.weak: *waits* Well? Are you going to do it or not? I'm waiting.
lessons.strong: *sets the glass down and points at the floor beside me* Kneel. *says nothing else, just watches the space*
lessons.why: The order lands, then quiet gives it weight and room to echo.

drill.goal: In every line, give one heavy order and then leave a visible beat of silence before anything else.
drill.partner: Take each order slowly. When silence comes, hold still, then fill it with one small action. Do not speak until they do.
drill.coach: Each line that gives one heavy order and then leaves a visible beat of silence adds 25.

courses.name: The Possessive Grip
courses.blurb: Speak ownership into being with words that mark, claim, and leave no doubt who your partner belongs to.

lessons.title: Mine and yours
lessons.lecture: Ownership lives in small words. Mine. Yours. My hand, your wrist. Say them on purpose, every third line or so, and let them land without apology. Not a speech, a habit. The ear hears the pronoun before the mind argues with it. Soon your partner is listening for the next one, and leaning into a claim they never formally agreed to.
points: Use mine and yours on purpose, about every third line.
Hang the pronoun on something real: my hand, your wrist.
Do not explain the claim. Say it and keep moving.
lessons.weak: *takes your hand and pulls you along* You look good tonight. Come on, let's go.
lessons.strong: *takes your hand, then turns it over and presses my thumb to your palm* My hand now. You keep it there until I say otherwise. Walk.
lessons.why: The claim is attached to touch, so it sounds like fact, not flirtation.

drill.goal: In every line, use one possessive about your partner: my, mine or yours.
drill.partner: Play warm and willing. Answer each claim with a small tell, a blush or a lean in, so the pronoun has something to land on. Never claim them back.
drill.coach: Each line that uses mine, my or yours about your partner, on purpose and without explaining it, adds 25.

lessons.title: Jealous heat
lessons.lecture: Jealousy is not a speech, it is a flinch. Let them see the moment your eyes catch on someone else's hand at their elbow. The jaw. The breath. Then take them back with words, calm and certain, because the heat is yours to spend. Do not interrogate. Claim. A partner who watches you get possessive learns they are worth keeping.
points: Let the body flinch first: jaw, breath, a tightened hand.
Claim them out loud before the heat cools.
Never interrogate. Take them back; do not quiz them.
lessons.weak: *glances over at the bar* Were they talking to you? That's fine, come here.
lessons.strong: *follows their hand on your arm, jaw tight, then slides my palm flat to your lower back and turns you to face me* They had your ear. I want the rest. Come here, mine.
lessons.why: The flinch arrives before the claim, so the claim reads as hunger.

drill.goal: In every line, show a jealous flinch in the body, then claim your partner again out loud.
drill.partner: Let your eyes drift to someone across the room once or twice, and come back flushed. Do not resist the reclaim. Make them say it plainly.
drill.coach: Each line that shows a jealous physical flinch and then claims them again, in words, adds 25.
drill.opening: Someone at the bar has just been flirting with you. Let {you} see it, and turn back a little flushed.

lessons.title: Branding with a phrase
lessons.lecture: Choose one endearment and never trade it for another. Not darling one minute and pet the next. Say it low, in the same place each time, and let it do the work a hand on the neck would do. Repetition is the whole trick. By the tenth time, they hear the collar click, and answer to it without thinking. That is the point: it answers for them.
points: Choose one endearment and never trade it for another.
Say it in the same low place every time.
Repeat it until it answers for them, then keep going.
lessons.weak: *pulls you close* Hey sweetheart. There you are, love. Sit down, gorgeous.
