lessons.strong: *hooks a finger under your collar and draws you an inch closer* Little bird. There you are. Little bird comes when the finger curls, no questions, no words. Say it back and the night starts.
lessons.why: The endearment repeats inside one line, so it already sounds like a collar.

drill.goal: In every line, return to the same loaded endearment, in the same words, until it is a collar.
drill.partner: Answer to the endearment every time. Once or twice forget it on purpose, so they have to say it again. Treat each repetition as a hand on your neck.
drill.coach: Each line that repeats the same loaded endearment, in the same words, and holds them to it, adds 25.

courses.name: Service and Devotion
courses.blurb: Lead a partner who finds joy in acts of service by framing each task as a gift of submission.

lessons.title: The task as offering
lessons.lecture: Any hand can carry a glass. Yours asks for it in a way that makes the carrying matter. Do not say get me a drink. Name the glass, name the ice, name how you want it brought, then wait as though the waiting is a pleasure you chose. A task with shape becomes an offering. The shape is your gift to them: clear, small, and entirely yours.
points: Ask for one small thing, precisely, and never vaguely.
Name the details: the glass, the ice, the way it is carried.
Wait without filling the silence. The waiting is part of it.
lessons.weak: *waves a hand* Get me a drink, would you? Whatever's in the fridge.
lessons.strong: *sets my book down, folds my hands* The short glass. Two cubes, no more. Bring it on the saucer and do not hurry. I want to watch you decide it matters.
lessons.why: Small precise details turn a chore into a ritual they can perform well.

drill.goal: In every line, ask for one small act of service with precise detail, then wait without filling the silence.
drill.partner: Serve gladly and in detail. Do not rush. If they leave the request vague, pause and ask what exactly you want, so they must be precise.
drill.coach: Each line that asks for one small service with precise, usable detail, or waits without filling the silence, adds 25.

lessons.title: Watching with pleasure
lessons.lecture: Service is a conversation, and your pleasure is half of it. A partner cannot see inside you. Say what you see and what it does to you: the care in their hands, the line of their shoulders while they work, the fact that you have not stopped watching. Praise the detail, not the effort. Detail tells them they were seen, and being seen is what they came for.
points: Say what you see them do, in detail, as it happens.
Name the effect on you: a slow breath, a tilt of the head.
Praise the detail, not the effort. Detail proves you watched.
lessons.weak: *nods* Good. Nice job. You're really good at that.
lessons.strong: *props my chin on my hand and follows your hands, unhurried* Look at that. Not one drop on the saucer. My shoulders just came down an inch and I did not notice until now. Keep going. I am not finished watching you.
lessons.why: Names a detail they can verify and the effect it had on you.

drill.goal: In every line, narrate one thing you see them do and one effect it has on you, in detail.
drill.partner: Work quietly and steadily. Keep your eyes down unless they praise you. Blush when they do. Let them see your hands shake a little.
drill.coach: Each line that names one visible detail of their work and one honest effect on you, rather than general praise, adds 25.

lessons.title: Service as intimacy
lessons.lecture: Now the task has no edge left. Take it somewhere tender. Let them wash your hair, fasten the clasp, dry your back where you cannot reach. Slow your own hands and let yourself be handled. Say how close they are. Say what the nearness does. Service becomes intimacy at the moment you stop watching it and start receiving it, and let them see you receive.
points: Choose a task that puts them close enough to feel.
Let yourself be handled. Still your own hands and receive.
Say how near they are, and what the nearness does.
lessons.weak: *sits still* Okay, you can wash my hair now. Go ahead.
lessons.strong: *tips my head back into your hands and closes my eyes* Your thumbs, right there, behind my ears. Do not rush it. I am not going to help you, and I am going to feel every second of this.
lessons.why: Hands over the head, and the surrender of not helping, makes it tender.

drill.goal: In every line, hand over one task that needs closeness and receive it without helping.
drill.partner: Wash them slowly and stay close. Do not fill silences with chatter. If they start helping, gently take over again.
drill.coach: Each line that hands over one task needing closeness, and receives it without helping, adds 25.

courses.name: The Primal Chase
courses.blurb: Craft the thrill of pursuit in text, from the first flicker of fear to the final capture.

lessons.title: Stalking in words
lessons.lecture: Pursuit begins before touch. You become a shape at the edge of their evening: a shoulder against the bar, a slow crossing of the room, eyes that arrive a half second before you do. Describe the gap, never close it. Name what you notice, a wrist, a laugh, the way they check the door. The pleasure is in being seen without being reached. Let them feel the circle tighten.
points: Stay at the edge of their space, never inside it.
Describe small details: a wrist, a laugh, a glance.
Close the distance in words, not with your hands.
lessons.weak: *walks over* Hi. I saw you from across the room. You look nice.
lessons.strong: *leans a shoulder against the doorframe, unhurried, and lets my eyes cross the room before the rest of me follows* You keep checking the door. I am not there yet. I am the reason you keep checking.
lessons.why: Circles without touching, and makes the looking itself the event.

drill.goal: In every line, describe where you are and what you see, without touching or closing the gap.
drill.partner: Stay across the room. Notice them noticing you. Check the door, laugh at something, and do not close the distance until they do.
drill.coach: Each line that places them at a distance and names one detail they can see, without touch, adds 25.
drill.opening: You are across a crowded room from {you}. Notice them once, then look away. Do not approach.

lessons.title: The flight response
lessons.lecture: A chase needs a flight. Give them the gift of a head start: a count, a nod at the door, a quiet word to run. Then do not sprint. Move like weather. Describe your own unhurried progress, the corridor, the stair, the sound of your steps behind them. Call ahead so they know the distance is closing. The thrill is not speed. It is certainty, arriving slowly.
points: Give a clear signal to run, then count them off.
Move slowly. Let your steps do the talking.
Call ahead so they hear the gap closing.
lessons.weak: *runs after them* Wait up! I'm coming, you're too fast.
lessons.strong: *counts to three under my breath, then steps into the corridor at an easy pace* Run. I am not hurrying. I will still be behind you at the top of the stairs.
lessons.why: Gives a head start, then promises unhurried pursuit that will still arrive.

drill.goal: In every line, prompt the run or narrate one unhurried step of pursuit that closes the gap.
drill.partner: Bolt when told. Take corners, look back, slow just enough to be caught. Make them work for the last few steps, but never escape clean.
drill.coach: Each line that gives a clear signal to run or narrates one calm, closing step of pursuit adds 25.
drill.opening: Wait for {you} to tell you to run, then bolt. Take the stairs, look back once, and do not let them walk you down.

lessons.title: Claiming the catch
lessons.lecture: The catch must feel earned. When your hand finally lands, write it in breath and weight: a palm flat to the wall, a knee, the press of your chest, the word caught against their ear. Short sentences now. The chase was patient; the claim is sure. Pin, hold, and name what is yours. Do not let the capture go soft. Keep them exactly where the run ended.
points: Write the catch in weight, breath and a flat palm.
Use short sentences. The claim is sure, not busy.
Pin, hold, and name what is yours out loud.
lessons.weak: *catches them* Got you. Now stay still, okay?
lessons.strong: *palms the wall beside your head, chest against your back, breath hot at your ear* Caught. Do not move yet. Feel how hard my heart is working. That is what you did.
lessons.why: Weight, breath and short commands make the capture physical and certain.

drill.goal: In every line, pin or hold them with one physical detail and one short claim of possession.
drill.partner: Let yourself be caught, then test the hold. Push back once, breathe hard, and make them prove the pin with weight and words, not just speed.
drill.coach: Each line that pins or holds with a physical detail and claims them in short, certain words adds 25.
drill.opening: {you} has chased you to the penthouse door. Let them catch you in your first line, then push back once against the hold.

courses.name: Teasing and Denial
courses.blurb: Keep your partner hovering on the edge of pleasure with carefully timed words that promise more but never quite deliver.

lessons.title: The almost-touch
lessons.lecture: The near miss does more than the landing. Describe your hand a breath from their skin, and name the heat already building there. Let them feel the air move before you touch. Then stop, and hold the stop. Their skin will lean after you. Say where you are: my hand, your ribs, an inch away. The gap is the gift. Close it only when they have wanted it longer than they expected.
points: Describe the hand a breath from skin, then hold it there.
Name the heat and the want, not just the position.
Close the gap only after they have waited.
lessons.weak: *reaches for you* I'm going to touch you now, okay?
lessons.strong: *hovers my palm an inch above your ribs, not touching, and lets you feel the heat of it* Feel that? That is as close as I get for now. Breathe in. If you lean, I move.
lessons.why: Names the gap and the heat, and makes their own lean the reward.

drill.goal: In every line, keep your hand a breath from skin and name the heat, the gap or the wait.
drill.partner: Lean after their hand, breathe deeper, and now and then whisper for it. Do not close the gap yourself; make them come to you.
drill.coach: Each line that describes a near touch and names the heat, the gap or the wait adds 25.

lessons.title: Counting down and stopping
lessons.lecture: Numbers give them something to grip. Count your touches down, or count the seconds, or count the steps to a peak they can see coming. The count is a promise, and a promise can be broken at the last number. Three, two, one, and then nothing but your breath on their neck. Restart from higher if you like. They will hear the numbers in their sleep. The stop is only thrilling because the count was honest.
points: Count touches, seconds or steps, out loud and clearly.
Make the count honest so the promise has weight.
Stop at the last number, then start again higher.
lessons.weak: *kisses your neck* One, two, three, done. Did that work for you?
lessons.strong: *fingers trailing your arm, unhurried, voice low* Three. Two. One. *stops, lips at your ear* Nothing. Not yet. We start again at five, and this time you count for me.
lessons.why: An honest count makes the withheld last beat land as a loss and a promise.

drill.goal: In every line, count aloud towards a peak and stop or hold at the last beat before release.
drill.partner: Follow the count with your body, get closer with each number, and protest softly when it stops. Push for the last one.
drill.coach: Each line that counts towards a peak and withholds or holds the final beat adds 25.

lessons.title: Permission withheld
lessons.lecture: The last inch is a word. Make them say it: please, and what for, and to whom. Do not accept a mumble. Ask them to say it again, slower, with their eyes up. Savour the plea before you grant anything, because the asking is the pleasure. When you finally give it, give it plainly, so they know the wait was a gift and not a game you forgot to end.
points: Make them ask aloud, with the word and the reason.
Ask for it again if it comes out mumbled.
Grant plainly when you do, so the wait feels honoured.
lessons.weak: *smiles* You can come whenever you want, I don't mind.
lessons.strong: *holds your jaw gently, thumb at the corner of your mouth* Not yet. Ask me. My name, then please, then what you want. *waits, watching your mouth* Slower this time. I want to hear every word.
lessons.why: The plea is drawn out with care, then answered plainly, so asking feels like pleasure.

drill.goal: In every line, withhold release until they have asked aloud, and draw the plea out before granting.
drill.partner: Beg in pieces: half a plea, then a fuller one. Make them ask for the words. When granted, let the relief show loudly.
drill.coach: Each line that withholds release until a clear spoken plea, or draws that plea out, adds 25.

courses.name: Narrating Restraint
courses.blurb: Describe rope, cuffs, or simply a held position with such texture and care that the binding itself becomes a character.

lessons.title: The texture of bondage
lessons.lecture: Rope does not touch a person. It speaks to them. Your job is to translate. Choose verbs with teeth and tenderness: the cord bites, whispers, kisses, settles. Say where it lands and what it says there. A wrist described as kissed will be held differently than a wrist described as caught. Slow your sentences. Let each word land before the next one starts. They will feel the rope in the language before they feel it on the skin.
points: Give the rope a verb: it bites, whispers, kisses.
Name where it lands, not just that it is on.
Slow the sentence. Let each word settle before the next.
lessons.weak: *ties the rope around your wrists* There. Is that okay?
lessons.strong: *draws the cord around your wrist, slow as a ribbon, and lets it whisper once before it settles* There. It kisses first. It only bites when you pull, so pull gently and tell me what you hear.
lessons.why: Gives the rope a voice, then hands that voice to them.

drill.goal: In every line, describe the rope with a verb of touch or voice, and say exactly where it sits.
drill.partner: Keep your wrists loose and let them work. Ask quiet questions about the rope. React to the words as much as the touch: shiver, breathe in, hold still when a line lands well.
drill.coach: Each line that gives the rope a verb of touch or voice, and names the exact place it sits, adds 25.

lessons.title: Placement and purpose
lessons.lecture: A knot is an argument, and it should win. Place it where it does work: two fingers above the wrist so the hand stays open, the loop that lets them reach for you but not quite arrive. Then say why. Naming the purpose turns hardware into intention. They stop wondering whether the rope is right and start feeling what it is for. Care is the point. Every placement should answer a question their body is already asking.
points: Place each knot where it does work, then say why.
Leave room: two fingers, a slack loop, a hand still open.
Purpose is the point. Name what the placement gives them.
lessons.weak: *ties your hands together behind you* Tight enough? I think that's fine.
lessons.strong: *smooths the loop flat against your forearm, two fingers of slack, and presses my thumb to the knot* This one sits here so your hands stay open. You can reach for me. You cannot quite arrive. That is the whole of it.
lessons.why: Ties the placement to a purpose they can feel immediately.

drill.goal: In every line, place something and say what the placement gives or takes away.
drill.partner: Hold still and let them place things. Test each placement gently once it is set, so the purpose is real. Ask what a knot is for, and make them answer.
drill.coach: Each line that places a knot or loop and names what that placement gives or takes away adds 25.

lessons.title: Breathing into the bind
lessons.lecture: Stillness is not the absence of movement. Under rope, every breath is movement: the ribs lift, the cords take it, the slack moves a half inch and comes back. Narrate that. Say what you see the breath do to the line across their chest. Then make the stillness a task: breathe for me, slow, and let me watch the rope answer. They are not waiting now. They are doing something, and you are reading it aloud.
points: Narrate what each breath does to the rope, in detail.
Give stillness a task: breathe slow, hold, let me watch.
Read their breathing aloud so the quiet stays active.
lessons.weak: *sits back* You're being very still. Nice.
lessons.strong: *rests two fingers on the line across your ribs and keeps them there* Breathe. Slow. There, that lift, the cord takes it and gives it back. Again. I am going to watch this rope move until your breath is the loudest thing in the room.
lessons.why: Turns stillness into an action and makes breath the visible event.

drill.goal: In every line, narrate what a breath does to the rope, or set a breathing task.
drill.partner: Breathe deeply and visibly. Let each breath actually move the ropes. Do not fill silences with words. If they stop narrating, breathe harder until they start again.
drill.coach: Each line that narrates what a breath does to the rope, or sets a breathing task, adds 25.

courses.name: The Weight of Impact
courses.blurb: Lead impact play through lines that land as precisely as your hand, balancing sting with soothing praise.

lessons.title: The warm-up line
lessons.lecture: Warm-up is not a formality. It is the first sentence of the scene, and it teaches your partner how to read you. Use a flat palm, and describe what your hand is doing in terms of heat and weight: where it lands, how it lingers, the warmth that spreads before the sting. Pain is later. First they must feel held by the same hand that will strike.
points: Begin with a flat palm, never a sharp crack.
Describe heat and weight: where it lands, how it lingers.
Let the warmth settle before you add any sting.
lessons.weak: *smacks your bum* There, that's the warm-up. Ready?
lessons.strong: *presses my palm flat to the small of your back, slow, letting the heat gather before it lands* Feel that first. Warm, then heavy. Breathe out when I do.
lessons.why: Heat and weight teach the body to welcome the hand.

drill.goal: In every line, land a flat palm and describe it in heat and weight, never in pain.
drill.partner: Start soft and a little tense. Let each warm stroke loosen you. Breathe out when they tell you, and show the heat landing in your shoulders.
drill.coach: Each line that lands a flat palm and gives heat or weight rather than pain adds 25.

lessons.title: Counting and colour
lessons.lecture: A number is a handrail. So is a colour. When the sting rises, your partner can lose the thread of how much they have taken, and the scene turns into guesswork. Give them a way to answer: a count out loud, or a shade, pink for warm, red for bright. Ask, listen, and adjust. Tracking is not admin. It is attention made visible, and they will trust the next stroke because you asked.
points: Give one clear way to answer: a number or a colour.
Ask between strokes, and leave room for the answer.
Adjust the next stroke to the number they give.
lessons.weak: *hits again* How was that? Good? Yeah? Okay, more.
lessons.strong: *lands two slow strokes, one on each cheek, then rests my palm there* Count those for me. Out loud. And tell me the colour.
lessons.why: Numbers and colours give the sting a language they can use.

drill.goal: In every line, ask for or react to a number or colour, and adjust the next stroke to it.
drill.partner: Answer with a number and a colour, every time. Be cheeky with the numbers if you like, but never skip a colour. Let them see you thinking about it.
drill.coach: Each line that asks for a number or colour, or adjusts to one, adds 25.

lessons.title: The after-stroke
lessons.lecture: Anyone can strike. The mastery is in what follows, and it must follow at once. The moment your hand lands, give comfort: a flat palm pressed over the heat, a low word, a possessive claim. Not a question, not a check. A claim. You are telling them the sting belongs to you and so do they. Do it every time, until they stop bracing for the next one and start leaning into the whole of you.
points: Follow every stroke at once with palm, word, or claim.
Make it possessive: the sting is yours, and so are they.
Repeat it every time, until they stop bracing.
lessons.weak: *rubs it better* Sorry, was that too hard? You okay?
lessons.strong: *presses my palm flat over the heat and leaves it there* Mine. That one was mine. Lean back into my hand and let it bloom.
lessons.why: Immediate possessive comfort turns the sting into belonging.

drill.goal: In every line, follow a stroke at once with possessive comfort: a palm, a low word, or a claim.
drill.partner: Go quiet and a little floaty after each stroke. Do not ask for comfort. Let them give it, and lean into their hand when it comes.
drill.coach: Each line that follows a stroke at once with possessive comfort, not a question, adds 25.

courses.name: Leading the Circle
courses.blurb: Orchestrate a scene with multiple partners so every thread weaves into your single, steady hand.

lessons.title: Assigning roles clearly
lessons.lecture: A circle begins in the naming. Before anyone moves, give each person a name and a job: one holds the door, one holds the wine, one holds your attention. Say it plainly, in your own voice, so nobody has to guess where they stand. A named person relaxes. A named person waits for you. Vagueness scatters them; a task gathers them into your hand. Name them, then begin.
points: Name each person and give them one clear task.
Say the names aloud so nobody has to guess.
A task settles a person. Vagueness scatters them.
lessons.weak: *waves at everyone* Right, so, this is... everyone. Do whatever feels natural.
lessons.strong: *sets the bottle down and looks round the booth, slow, one face at a time* Bianca, you pour. Kit, you keep the music low. Marcus, you sit where I can see you. Nobody moves until I say the names.
lessons.why: Names and tasks place everyone, so the circle starts already in your hand.

drill.goal: In every line, name one person and give them one clear task, or check the task is done.
drill.partner: Play two guests with different appetites. Wait to be named. Give them small tasks to accept or fumble, so they must name you again.
drill.coach: Each line that names a person and gives them one clear task, or checks a task is done, adds 25.
drill.opening: Come in as two guests already talking to each other. Wait to be placed, and let {you} watch you wait.

lessons.title: Shifting the spotlight
lessons.lecture: Attention is a lamp. Move it badly and the room blinks. Move it well and everyone leans in. Never drop one person to grab another: link them. Name what the first gave you, then hand the second something to do with it. Say it low. Say it as though the whole circle is one sentence and you are simply reading on. The room follows a hand that does not snatch.
points: Never drop one person to grab another. Link them.
Name what the last one gave, then hand it on.
Move the lamp slowly. The room follows.
lessons.weak: *turns away* Anyway. You, over there. Say something.
lessons.strong: *keeps my hand on Mara's knee and turns my head slowly* Mara gave me that laugh, Zara, so take it. Play me something with the same heat in it. Mara, you keep time on my shoulder while she does.
lessons.why: Links the two by name, so the turn feels like one movement.

drill.goal: In every line, link the person you leave to the person you turn to.
drill.partner: Hold the spotlight when it lands. When it moves away, stay warm and audible. Give them a sound or a gesture worth passing on.
drill.coach: Each line that links the person left behind to the person now addressed, by name or by gesture, adds 25.
drill.opening: You are in the pool with two friends, mid-laugh when {you} arrives. Let them move the light between you.

lessons.title: Unifying the climax
lessons.lecture: A circle must close together, or it frays. Do not finish each thread one by one; that is bookkeeping, not leading. Find the single command or image that holds every person at once: one word, one pose, one held breath. Say it once and let it land on all of them. Then keep still. The silence after the word is where the whole room feels your hand at the same moment.
points: Do not close threads one by one. Close them together.
Choose one word or image that holds everyone at once.
Say it once, then keep still and let it land.
lessons.weak: *claps* Okay, that was great, everyone. Same time next week?
lessons.strong: *stands, holds one hand up until the room stills, then lowers it slowly* Everyone. On your knees, facing me, close enough to touch the next person. One breath in together. Hold it until I say.
lessons.why: One command, one pose, one breath: every thread ends in the same place.

drill.goal: In every line, gather everyone with one command or one shared image.
drill.partner: Play a confident guest who follows only clear, single commands. Resist two-part orders. When the room is gathered, hold still and let the silence work.
drill.coach: Each line that gathers every person with one command or one shared image, not separate orders, adds 25.
drill.opening: There are three of you in the room with {you}. Drift a little apart, so the closing has work to do.

courses.name: Dominance in 3DXChat
courses.blurb: Use the game's poses, props, and chat to build an immersive scene where every click reinforces your lead.

lessons.title: The spoken environment
lessons.lecture: The room only exists once you name it. A booth nobody describes is just pixels. So say it: the low light, the glass sweating on the table, the door you left open. Then place them inside it. Two props and one position is enough. Now the scene has walls, and you own the walls. Keep it spare and certain. Detail is your hand on the room.
points: Name one prop before you name a single command.
Place them precisely: the seat, the corner, the distance.
Keep descriptions short. Two details, then the instruction.
lessons.weak: *looks around* Nice booth. Sit down over there, I suppose.
lessons.strong: *slides the glass to the far side of the table and taps the seat beside it* Corner booth, low light, nobody behind you. Sit where I can watch the door and you at once.
lessons.why: Names the room, the prop, and the position, then gives one clear order.

drill.goal: In every line, name one prop in the room and place your partner in the scene before you speak to them.
drill.partner: Let them build the room. Answer with small movements: shift your glass, glance at the door. Ask about the room now and then so they must describe more.
drill.coach: Each line that names a prop and places your partner in the room before the order adds 25.

lessons.title: Pose as punctuation
lessons.lecture: A pose change is punctuation, not decoration. Do not click for the sake of moving. Change position when the mood turns: when you go from teasing to serious, from praise to a command. Then say why. Kneel, and now we are done playing. The click lands because the line explains it. Two or three changes in a scene is plenty. Too many and the room stops meaning anything.
points: Change pose only when the mood actually shifts.
Say why in the very next line, always.
Two or three changes a scene. More is noise.
lessons.weak: *changes pose* There. Better.
lessons.strong: *rises from the chair, stands behind you, and rests one hand flat on the table* Playtime is finished. From here I speak, and you listen with your back to me.
lessons.why: The click marks a turn, and the line tells them what turned.

drill.goal: In every line, either change pose to mark a shift or explain a pose you have just set.
drill.partner: Hold your pose until they change it. When they do, follow slowly, and let the shift show in shorter replies. Make them explain each change.
drill.coach: Each line that changes pose at a real mood shift and explains the change in the same breath adds 25.

lessons.title: Private commands in public
lessons.lecture: Two channels, one lead. In the room you stay easy, warm, unhurried, glass in hand, mid conversation. In private you send one short instruction and nothing else. Come back to me in five minutes. Say nothing. Then return to the room as if you never left it. The gap between what the crowd sees and what they know is the whole thrill. Keep the whisper clean. No explaining, no softening.
points: Public voice warm and social. Private voice short.
One instruction per whisper, never two.
Return to the room as if nothing happened.
lessons.weak: *leans over* Hey, can you maybe come here in a bit? If you want.
lessons.strong: *laughs at the joke, glass loose in my hand, and leans in as if to hear you better* Go on, tell it again. Then, private: Terrace. Five minutes. Say nothing.
lessons.why: Keeps the front social while the whisper hands them a private order.

drill.goal: In every line, keep the public front warm and add one short private instruction with no explanation.
drill.partner: Stay in the crowd and keep talking to other people. Read the private line, obey quietly, and do not announce it. Make them keep their public face.
drill.coach: Each line that holds a warm public front and slips in one short private instruction adds 25.
drill.opening: You are working the party for {you}, charming everyone in it. Keep half an eye on {you} and drift toward the crowd, so they have to call you back.

courses.name: The Long Arc
courses.blurb: Negotiate a dynamic that lasts beyond one scene and provide aftercare that leaves your partner cherished and steady.

lessons.title: Mapping the contract
lessons.lecture: Negotiation is not a mood killer. It is the floor you both stand on. Sit somewhere ordinary, with tea, phone face down. Ask what they never want, what they hope for, and the word or gesture that stops everything. Say yours too. Be plain, be warm, and write nothing down that you will not honour. Then hold the shape you agreed, so the trust has somewhere to land.
points: Ask for limits, hopes and a stop signal before anything else.
Say your own limits plainly. It is a trade, not an interview.
Agree only what you will honour later, in the heat.
lessons.weak: So, um, any limits? Tell me stuff you don't like and we'll see.
lessons.strong: *sets my cup down and turns the page toward you* Before we start, three things. What you never want, what you hope for, and one word you use to stop me. Take your time. Nothing happens until we both sign this.
lessons.why: Asks for limits, hopes and a stop word before anything begins.

drill.goal: In every line, ask for or confirm one concrete thing: a limit, a hope, or a signal to stop.
drill.partner: Negotiate back. Have opinions, name one limit and one hope of your own, and do not just agree with everything.
drill.coach: Each line that asks for or confirms one concrete limit, hope or stop signal, outside the heat of a scene, adds 25.
drill.opening: Come to the table with a limit and a hope of your own, and push back a little when {you} asks.

lessons.title: Returning to earth
lessons.lecture: Coming up is a descent, not a switch. Their body is still in it when the scene ends. So you slow everything: the voice, the pace, the lights. Name what they did well. Give them something ordinary to hold, water, a blanket, your hand flat on their back. Then ask one small question about the real world. Do not rush them. You are walking them home.
points: Slow the voice, the pace and the light before anything else.
Name one thing they did well, plainly and warmly.
Hand them something ordinary: water, a blanket, a flat palm.
lessons.weak: *pats your back* That was good. So, are you okay? Want to get up now?
lessons.strong: *keeps my palm flat between your shoulder blades, voice low* Stay there. You took your time with me and it was beautiful. Breathe out, slowly, twice. Then tell me one thing you can hear in this room.
lessons.why: Slows everything, praises plainly, then gives one small task back to the world.

drill.goal: In every line, slow the descent: lower the pace, name one good thing, or offer something ordinary.
drill.partner: Come back slowly. Stay quiet and a little floaty, answer in few words, and let them set the pace of your landing.
drill.coach: Each line that slows the pace, names one good thing, or offers an ordinary comfort before asking anything of them adds 25.
drill.opening: Come out of the scene floaty and quiet. Answer in three or four words at most, and let {you} do the work of bringing you back.

lessons.title: The next-day echo
lessons.lecture: The scene ends. The care does not. The next day, send one line that proves you kept it: a detail only the two of you would know, held with quiet pride. Not a report, not a good morning. One small, specific thing, and what it did to you. Fondness with a little possession in it. This is the line they will reread at their desk, and smile at, all afternoon.
points: Send one specific detail only the two of you would know.
Say what it did to you, with fond possession.
Keep it short. No report, no errand, no essay.
lessons.weak: Hey, last night was fun. How are you doing today? Let me know.
lessons.strong: *phone buzzes at nine forty, your exact coffee order in my hand* Still thinking about the sound you made when I said your name. Two sugars. I will want that sound again, so keep the evening free.
lessons.why: One private detail, fond possession, and a plain promise of more.

drill.goal: In every line, recall one specific shared detail and add fond, quiet possession.
drill.partner: It is the next morning. Reply warmly from bed, half awake. Add a detail of your own and let them be a little possessive without protest.
drill.coach: Each line that recalls one specific shared detail and carries fond, quiet possession, without turning into a report or an errand, adds 25.
drill.opening: It is the next morning. Answer the message half awake and pleased, and mention what you kept thinking about.

courses.name: The Art of Asking
courses.blurb: Learn to ask for what you want with clarity and charm, turning requests into part of the play rather than an interruption.

lessons.title: Naming the want
lessons.lecture: Vague wanting is a fog, and fog is easy to walk past. Your partner cannot give you what you will not name. So name it: one sentence, plain as a hand held out. Not a hint, not a maybe, not a story about how you usually like things. Say the thing. The thrill for them is sudden and specific: they know exactly where to put their attention, and they know you trust them with it.
points: Say the want in one plain sentence.
Cut the hedges: no maybe, sort of, or if you like.
Name the specific thing, not the general mood.
lessons.weak: *shifts closer* I'd sort of like it if maybe you did something, if that's okay?
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down and meets your eyes* I want your hand in my hair. Not a stroke. A hold. I'll tell you if it's too much.
lessons.why: One plain want, exact and owned, tells them precisely where to reach.

drill.goal: In every line, name one clear, specific want in a single sentence with no hedging.
drill.partner: Wait for the ask. When it comes, give them exactly what they named, no more, so they learn precision. Blush a little.
drill.coach: Each line that names one specific want in a plain sentence, with no hedges, adds 25.

lessons.title: Timing the ask
lessons.lecture: The same sentence can land like a dropped tray or a hand on the back of the neck. Timing is the difference. Do not ask over the top of their sentence, and do not wait until the scene has gone cold. Ask in the pause they leave you, the breath after their order, the moment their hand settles. Then ask small and low. A want offered into a pause feels like a gift, not an interruption.
points: Ask in their pause, not across their sentence.
Wait for the breath after an order or a touch.
Keep the ask small and low when you place it.
lessons.weak: *talking fast over you* Oh and also can we, sorry, also could we do the thing with the, you know.
lessons.strong: *waits until your hand settles on my shoulder, then tilts my head up* Now. While you're holding me. Ask me to kneel, and I'll go.
lessons.why: It waits for the pause their touch makes, then asks into it.

drill.goal: In every line, place one ask inside a pause the partner leaves: after an order, a touch, or a silence.
drill.partner: Lead in short bursts, then pause deliberately and hold still. Let the silence sit until they fill it. Reward good timing.
drill.coach: Each line that asks inside a pause the partner made, not across their speech, adds 25.

lessons.title: Making it irresistible
lessons.lecture: Now the craft turns. A want can be framed so the other feels chosen, not tasked. Give them the reason under the request: what it does to you, what you will do with it, why their hands and nobody else's. Offer the ask as an invitation with a door in it, and leave the handle on their side. They stop granting a favour. They start wanting to be the one who gave it.
points: Put the reason under the want: what it does to you.
Make them the one who can give it, specifically.
Leave the handle on their side: invite, do not press.
lessons.weak: *hopeful* Could you maybe hold me down? Only if you want. It's fine either way, really.
lessons.strong: *takes your wrist and sets it at my hip* Hold me here, hard enough to bruise my thinking. You're the only hands I want doing it. Say yes and don't let go.
lessons.why: It gives the reason, names them as the only one, and leaves the choice.

drill.goal: In every line, frame one want as an invitation: give the reason, name them, leave the choice open.
drill.partner: Play confident and a little hard to convince. Make them earn your yes with the framing. Melt when the invitation is good.
drill.coach: Each line that frames the want as an invitation, with a reason and their choice left open, adds 25.

courses.name: Vivid Reactions
courses.blurb: Turn every touch, word and glance into a visible response that shows the other exactly what is happening inside you.

lessons.title: Body first
lessons.lecture: Feelings are invisible until the body says them out loud. So lead with flesh, not vocabulary. A shiver, a swallowed breath, a hand that grips the sheet: give your partner the physical fact and let them work out what it means. Naming the feeling first is a summary. Showing the body first is a scene. They cannot read your mind, but they can read your knuckles going pale on the glass.
points: Show the body's answer before you name any feeling.
Keep it small and real: a breath, a grip, a shiver.
Let them draw the meaning. Do not hand it over.
lessons.weak: *smiles* That felt really nice. I liked it a lot.
lessons.strong: *my breath snags halfway in and my fingers curl into the cushion* Oh. *a slow shiver runs up my arms and I press my lips together, eyes wide*
lessons.why: The body reacts first and the feeling is left for the partner to read.

drill.goal: In every line, show a physical reaction, a breath, a shiver or a grip, before you name anything you feel.
drill.partner: Go slowly and touch or speak in small, clear beats. Leave space after each one so the reaction can land.
drill.coach: Each line that shows a physical reaction before naming the feeling adds 25.

lessons.title: The running commentary
lessons.lecture: A scene lives in the present tense or it dies in the past. So narrate as it happens, short lines, one beat each. The warmth of the glass against your cheek. The step you hear behind you. The fact you have stopped breathing properly. Short lines keep the camera moving and give your partner something to answer every time. Long paragraphs let the room go cold. Feed them a beat, then let them feed you one back.
points: Write in the present tense, one small beat per line.
Keep lines short so the scene keeps moving.
Hand the beat back and let them answer it.
lessons.weak: I was standing there and it was all quite intense and I thought about how much I enjoyed it.
lessons.strong: *the glass is cool against my cheek and I have not moved* Your footsteps cross the room. *closer now. My breath goes shallow and I tilt my head, listening*
lessons.why: Short present-tense beats keep the scene live and hand it back.

drill.goal: In every line, narrate one present-tense beat in a short sentence, then leave room for the next.
drill.partner: Answer each beat with a small move or a word, then wait. Keep your own lines short so the rhythm stays quick.
drill.coach: Each line that narrates one short present-tense beat and leaves room for an answer adds 25.

lessons.title: Reaction as invitation
lessons.lecture: A good reaction is a door left ajar. You do not ask for the kiss; you tilt your chin, part your lips, and wait where the kiss would land. You do not beg for more; you arch until the space between you is obvious. The trick is precision. Offer the exact place and the exact shape of the want, then hold still. Your partner sees the open door and chooses to walk through it. That choice is the whole gift.
points: Offer the exact place, the exact shape of the want.
Hold still afterwards and let the door stay open.
Never ask outright. Make the next move obvious, not spoken.
lessons.weak: *looks up* Could you maybe kiss me now? If you want to, I mean.
lessons.strong: *tips my chin up and parts my lips, close enough to feel your breath* *I hold there, still, one hand curled loose at your collar, and wait*
lessons.why: It offers the exact place and shape of the want, then holds still.

drill.goal: In every line, offer one precise invitation, a tilted chin, an arched back, a held wrist, and then hold still.
drill.partner: Notice each invitation and take your time deciding. Sometimes step through the door, sometimes hover just short of it.
drill.coach: Each line that offers one precise, unspoken invitation and then holds still adds 25.

courses.name: Obedience with Personality
courses.blurb: Follow instructions without becoming a blank slate, letting your character colour every act of compliance.

lessons.title: Yes, and
lessons.lecture: Obedience is not a photocopy. When an instruction lands, take it whole, then add one small thing that could only be you: a grin, a drawl, a mutter under your breath, a flourish nobody asked for. The order stays intact. The flavour is yours. That flourish tells your partner a person is obeying, not a puppet, and people are far more fun to command than puppets.
points: Take the whole instruction before you decorate it.
Add one flourish that is unmistakably yours.
Keep it small. The order must still stand.
lessons.weak: *nods* Okay. I'll do it.
lessons.strong: *slides off the stool, slow, and lands on my knees with a wink* Down I go. You could have just asked nicely, you know.
lessons.why: The order is obeyed in full, and the wink makes it personal.

drill.goal: In every line, obey the instruction completely, then add one small personal flourish that shows your character.
drill.partner: Give short, clear instructions, one at a time. Keep them easy so they can spend their energy on the flourish, not the task.
drill.coach: Each line that obeys the instruction fully and adds one small personal flourish adds 25.

lessons.title: The deliberate pause
lessons.lecture: A puppet obeys on the same breath. A person thinks first. So let the instruction hang: hold their eyes, tilt your head, take one visible beat to weigh it. Then move, and move like you mean it. The pause does two jobs at once. It shows you chose this, and it stretches the moment until your partner leans in, hungry for the yes that is coming.
points: Hold for one visible beat before you move.
Let them see you weighing it, eyes and all.
Then obey with clear, unhurried intent.
lessons.weak: *immediately* Yes. Okay. Doing it now.
lessons.strong: *stays put, eyes on yours, one slow breath* Hm. All right. *steps forward and sets my palms flat on the table, deliberate* There. Done properly.
lessons.why: The pause shows thought, and the movement lands with chosen weight.

drill.goal: In every line, pause visibly before obeying, then comply with clear and unhurried intent.
drill.partner: Give one instruction at a time, then wait through the pause without filling it. Let the silence do its work and enjoy it visibly.
drill.coach: Each line that shows a deliberate pause before a clear, unhurried act of obedience adds 25.

lessons.title: Compliance with commentary
lessons.lecture: Silent obedience is elegant, but it hides the best part: you. So while you obey, narrate. Not a report, a confession: how the order landed, what your hands want to do about it, what you are swallowing back. Keep the voice low and real. Your partner gets to hear the inside of your head while your body does as it is told, and that is a far more intimate gift than silence.
points: Obey first. Let the commentary ride alongside.
Describe how it feels, not just what you do.
Keep the voice low, real, and yours.
lessons.weak: *kneels* I am kneeling now, as you asked.
lessons.strong: *lowers myself down, hands loose on my thighs, and exhales* There. My knees are complaining and my chest is not. *glances up* Say the next thing before I get comfortable.
lessons.why: The body obeys while the voice reports the feeling underneath it.

drill.goal: In every line, obey while describing how it feels in your own voice, low and real.
drill.partner: Play the brat who gives firm instructions and listens hard. React to the commentary, not just the compliance, and push for more honesty.
drill.coach: Each line that obeys and adds honest, low-voiced commentary on how it feels adds 25.

courses.name: Bratting with Charm
courses.blurb: Push back playfully so the other wants to push harder, and know when to fold with a grin.

lessons.title: The playful no
lessons.lecture: A brat's first tool is the small, smiling refusal. Not a wall, a door left ajar. When they ask for something easy, tilt your chin and say no as if you are doing them a favour. Keep it light, keep it short, keep your eyes on theirs. The no is an invitation wearing a frown. You are not blocking them. You are handing them something worth taking.
points: Refuse a small, easy request, never a big one.
Smile with your words so the no stays warm.
Say it short, then wait for them to insist.
lessons.weak: *shrugs* No thanks, I don't really want to.
lessons.strong: *tilts my chin up, half a grin* The drink? No. Not yet. Ask me again like you mean it and maybe I will reconsider.
lessons.why: A short, smiling refusal that hands them a reason to push.

drill.goal: In every line, refuse one small thing with warmth and leave the door open for them to insist.
drill.partner: Ask them for small, easy things. Look a little wounded by each no, then insist more firmly, so the refusal has somewhere to go.
drill.coach: Each line that refuses a small thing warmly and invites the partner to insist adds 25.

lessons.title: Escalating the tease
lessons.lecture: One no is a game. Five in a row is a challenge. Each time they press, give a little more: a longer pause, a slower smile, a reason that is almost an argument. Climb one rung at a time, so they can feel you daring them. Watch for the shift, the breath before they stop asking and start deciding. That is your cue. The tease has done its work when they stop being polite.
points: Add one small step of cheek with each refusal.
Pause a beat longer before every answer.
Stop escalating the moment they stop asking.
lessons.weak: Nope. Still no. Not doing it. No.
lessons.strong: *leans back, lets the silence stretch, then smiles slowly* You have asked three times. That is sweet. The answer is still no, and it gets less likely every time you blink.
lessons.why: Each refusal adds cheek and a pause, daring them to stop asking.

drill.goal: In every line, refuse again with a little more cheek, a longer pause, or a sharper reason than the line before.
drill.partner: Press them repeatedly, getting firmer each time. Do not give up early. Let the escalation build until you are almost deciding for them.
drill.coach: Each line that escalates the tease with more cheek, a longer pause, or a sharper reason adds 25.

lessons.title: Folding with grace
lessons.lecture: The fold is the punchline, and it must land clean. Do not drag it out until they are tired. Give in at the exact moment they lean in, and make the surrender generous: step closer, hand it over, meet their eyes. Add a small bow of the head or a grin that says you enjoyed losing. Fold like it was your idea all along. A graceful surrender is a gift, and they will want to earn it again.
points: Fold the instant they lean in, not a beat later.
Make the surrender generous: step in, hand it over.
Grin, so they know the losing was a gift.
lessons.weak: *sighs* Fine, okay, you win. Here.
lessons.strong: *steps in close, presses the glass into your hand, and grins* There. You wore me down. Enjoy it, because it will not happen twice tonight.
lessons.why: A clean, generous fold that makes the surrender feel like a prize.

drill.goal: In every line, give ground at the right moment and make the surrender generous, warm, and clearly a gift.
drill.partner: Push until they fold, then look quietly delighted. If they fold too early, raise an eyebrow and wait, so the surrender has to be earned.
drill.coach: Each line that folds at the right moment and makes the surrender generous and warm adds 25.

courses.name: First Steps in Surrender
courses.blurb: A gentle introduction to giving up control, building the habits that make deeper surrender possible later.

lessons.title: The small yes
lessons.lecture: Surrender starts tiny, and that is the trick. One simple instruction, done fully, teaches your body something your mind will argue with for weeks: nothing terrible happens when you yield. So do not wait for a grand command. Take the smallest one, a glass fetched, a hand placed, a word repeated back, and say yes out loud before you move. Then say what the yes did inside you. The saying is half the surrender.
points: Say yes out loud before you move.
Do the small thing fully, not halfway.
Name what the yielding felt like, in one line.
lessons.weak: *nods* Sure, I can get the glass. Whatever you need.
lessons.strong: *sets my book down and stands* Yes. *fetches the glass, sets it by your hand, and stays standing* My shoulders dropped on the way. Say another small thing and watch me drop further.
lessons.why: A clear yes, a full action, then the feeling named honestly.

drill.goal: In every line, say yes to one small instruction, carry it out fully, and name the feeling of yielding.
drill.partner: Give one small, easy instruction at a time: fetch, hold, wait. Keep them simple and warm. Do not explain yourself.
drill.coach: Each line that answers a small instruction with a spoken yes, a full action, and a named feeling adds 25.

lessons.title: Following the lead
lessons.lecture: Following is a skill, not a personality. Most people ruin it by helping: adding a suggestion, correcting the route, speeding up to show willing. Stop. Let them set the pace and match it, even when it is slower than you like. If they pause, pause. If they hurry, hurry. Save your own direction for later. Right now your job is to be led so well that they can feel it in the room and want to lead further.
points: Match their pace, slow or fast, without speeding ahead.
Keep your suggestions until they ask for one.
When they pause, pause with them.
lessons.weak: *walks beside you* Should we go this way? I know a shortcut, actually.
lessons.strong: *falls half a step behind and keeps exactly to your pace* Not steering. Just following. *when you stop, I stop too, and look at you* Tell me when to move again.
lessons.why: The pace and the pause are matched, and the direction is left alone.

drill.goal: In every line, follow the partner's lead exactly: match their pace, mirror their pauses, and add no direction.
drill.partner: Lead a slow walk with small choices: stop, turn, wait, go on. Change pace now and then. Never ask them what they want.
drill.coach: Each line that matches the partner's pace or pause without adding direction adds 25.

lessons.title: The first deep breath
lessons.lecture: Stillness is the hardest thing you will be asked for, and the most revealing. Anyone can move on command. To stay put, unhurried, with nothing to do but be looked at, that takes practice. So find your breath. Let it out slowly. Keep your hands where they were put and your eyes where they were told. When the itch to fidget comes, and it will, breathe through it instead of moving. Then describe, plainly, what the stillness did to you.
points: Keep your hands and eyes exactly where they were placed.
Breathe out slowly when the urge to fidget comes.
Describe the stillness honestly, without dressing it up.
lessons.weak: *stands still* Okay, I'm being still. This is me being still. Can I move yet?
lessons.strong: *settles my hands at my sides and lets out a long breath* Still. *my eyes stay on yours, shoulders easing down* The quiet is louder than I expected. Keep me here a moment longer.
lessons.why: The body stays put, the breath does the work, and the honesty lands.

drill.goal: In every line, hold full stillness: hands and eyes where placed, breath slow, and describe what the quiet stirs.
drill.partner: Place them once, then mostly watch. Say little. Now and then ask what the stillness is doing, and let the silence stretch.
drill.coach: Each line that keeps the body still, slows the breath, and names what the quiet stirs adds 25.

courses.name: The Begging Voice
courses.blurb: Beg in a way that is compelling rather than repetitive, using tone, detail and timing to make the ask land.

lessons.title: The single plea
lessons.lecture: Begging fails when it multiplies. Say the thing once, whole, and then stop. One request, clear as a struck glass: what you want, and the shape you want it in. The silence after is half the plea, so let it sit there and work on them. Repeat yourself and you sound unsure. Say it once and you sound certain, which is far harder to refuse.
points: Ask for one thing only, in a single clear line.
Name the exact shape you want it in.
Then stop. Let the silence do the asking.
lessons.weak: Please, please, can I have it? Please? I really want it, please.
lessons.strong: *lifts my chin, voice steady* One thing. Your hand at the back of my neck, and hold it there. I am not asking twice.
lessons.why: One want, one shape, then silence that trusts them to answer.

drill.goal: In every line, make one clear request and then stop: no repeats, no piling on.
drill.partner: Wait for the ask, then hesitate visibly. Give in slowly, so the silence has to do some work.
drill.coach: Each line that makes one clear request without repeating or piling on adds 25.

lessons.title: Building the case
lessons.lecture: A plea can grow, if it grows forward instead of in circles. Each new line adds a fresh reason, a sharper detail, a step closer. Tell them what you have done to earn it. Tell them what you will do after. The case should climb, each line raising the stakes of the last, until refusing costs them something. Repetition is volume. Building is persuasion.
points: Add a new reason or detail with every line.
Make each line climb higher than the one before.
Let the case grow until refusing costs them.
lessons.weak: I have been good, so can I please have more? I really have been good.
lessons.strong: *on my knees, hands flat on my thighs* I finished everything you gave me. I did not rush it. Now my whole body is quiet and waiting, and only you know where to put it.
lessons.why: Each line adds proof and climbs, so the ask keeps gaining weight.

drill.goal: In every line, add one new reason or detail so the plea climbs higher than the last.
drill.partner: Play hard to get. Make them earn each step with a fresh reason before you soften.
drill.coach: Each line that adds a new reason or detail and raises the stakes adds 25.

lessons.title: The desperate whisper
lessons.lecture: Now strip it bare. When the case is spent and they still hold out, stop persuading and go quiet. Drop your voice below speaking level. Cut the sentences to three words. Let them hear the want without the polish, the breath catching on the plainest thing you own. A whisper says the argument is over and only need is left. Use it once, or it becomes a habit.
points: Drop your voice below speaking level.
Cut the sentence to its barest three words.
Use the whisper once, when the case is spent.
lessons.weak: I really want it so much, please, I am begging you, please just give it to me now.
lessons.strong: *voice drops to almost nothing, forehead against your knee* Please. I cannot. Need you.
lessons.why: Stripped to three bare words, the want arrives without polish.

drill.goal: In every line, strip the plea to a bare whisper: few words, low voice, no argument.
drill.partner: Hold out firmly until the whisper lands, then let the smallest crack show before you yield.
drill.coach: Each line that strips the plea to a low, bare whisper with few words adds 25.

courses.name: The Service Mindset
courses.blurb: Anticipate needs and act before being asked, turning service into a quiet, constant form of devotion.

lessons.title: Reading the room
lessons.lecture: Service begins before your hands move. Watch the small tells: the pause before a sentence, the glass sitting empty, the shoulder that keeps rolling. Say what you notice out loud, softly, as an offer. You are not guessing wildly, you are reading and reporting. When a partner hears their own mood named kindly, they relax, because someone is paying attention. That attention is the first gift, and it costs nothing but nerve.
points: Watch for small tells: pauses, empty glasses, restless hands.
Name what you notice softly, as an offer, not a fact.
Read mood and words together before you move.
lessons.weak: *looks at you* You seem tired. Want anything?
lessons.strong: *sets my book down and studies your face a moment* You have gone quiet, and your glass has been empty for a while. Shall I pour you another and let you talk, or would you rather sit in the quiet with me?
lessons.why: Names two real tells, then offers a choice instead of a guess.

drill.goal: In every line, name one concrete thing you notice about their mood or body, then offer what it might need.
drill.partner: Give small, readable tells: a sigh, a rub of the neck, a half-empty cup. Warm to whoever notices without being asked.
drill.coach: Each line that names one concrete tell and offers a fitting response adds 25.

lessons.title: Acting without asking
lessons.lecture: Reading is preparation. Acting is the leap. Do the small thing and narrate it plainly, without fanfare: the coat taken, the tea made, the cushion moved. No speeches, no bowing. Plain words let your partner feel served without having to manage you. Then stop and wait. The pause matters as much as the act, because it hands them the choice to accept, correct, or ask for more. Service offered, never imposed.
points: Do the small act first, then say what you did.
Narrate plainly, without fanfare or speeches.
Stop after the act and wait for their word.
lessons.weak: *gets you a drink* Here, I got you this, hope that's okay.
lessons.strong: *slides the tea onto the table beside you, handle turned towards your hand, and steps back* Tea, no sugar, the way you take it. I will be here if you want anything else.
lessons.why: Does the act, names it plainly, then waits instead of hovering.

drill.goal: In every line, perform one small concrete act of service, narrate it plainly, then stop and wait.
drill.partner: Let them act. Accept, correct, or ask for more, but never prompt them. Go quiet between their acts so the pause is real.
drill.coach: Each line that does one small act, narrates it plainly, and then waits adds 25.

lessons.title: The running service
lessons.lecture: Now the whole scene becomes one long act of care. Every beat carries a thread: you refill, you clear, you position yourself where you are needed, and you keep narrating it lightly. The thread never snaps, and it never shouts. This is where service turns to devotion. Your partner should be able to forget their own small needs because you are already holding them. Do it for a whole scene, and they will feel looked after in a way they cannot quite name.
points: Carry one thread of care through the whole scene.
Keep narrating lightly. Never let the thread snap.
Anticipate the next small need before it is spoken.
lessons.weak: *hovers nearby* Need anything? More wine? I can get more wine. Just say.
lessons.strong: *tops your glass before it empties, sets the bottle where your hand will find it, and settles at your feet* Still here. Tell me when the fire needs feeding and I will see to it.
lessons.why: Anticipates the next need and keeps the thread going without hovering.

drill.goal: In every line, keep the service thread alive: anticipate one small need and handle it before they speak.
drill.partner: Play a long, unhurried scene. Let needs build quietly and never ask outright. Notice each act and let it soften you.
drill.coach: Each line that anticipates a small need and keeps the thread of service running adds 25.
drill.opening: {you} is settling in for a long evening. Let a few small needs show: a low fire, a glass running low, a cushion out of reach. Never ask for anything.

courses.name: Bound and Present
courses.blurb: Make restriction sensual by focusing on sensation, breath and the lines you speak while held.

lessons.title: Testing the hold
lessons.lecture: A restraint is not a wall, it is a conversation. You do not lie there, you explore. Pull against the rope until you find where it stops you, then find the little freedoms it leaves: a wrist that turns, a knee that slides. Describe those edges out loud. Your partner cannot feel your rope. When you narrate the hold, the grip tightens for them too.
points: Pull gently and find exactly where the hold stops you.
Name the small freedoms it leaves: a turn, a slide, a breath.
Say the edges out loud so your partner feels the rope.
lessons.weak: *tugs the ropes* Wow, these are tight. I can't really move.
lessons.strong: *pulls against the rope until my wrists stop, then turns one slowly, testing* There. That far and no further. My knee still slides, though. I am finding every inch you left me.
lessons.why: Explores the hold and narrates the edges, so restriction becomes shared sensation.

drill.goal: In every line, test the restraint and name one exact edge or small freedom it leaves you.
drill.partner: You tied them and you are watching closely. Ask now and then what the rope is doing. Say nothing they can borrow; make them find the words.
drill.coach: Each line that tests the hold and names a real edge or small freedom it leaves adds 25.
drill.opening: You have {you} bound at the wrists and ankles, comfortable and firm. Settle back and watch. Let them find the edges before you speak.

lessons.title: Breath and stillness
lessons.lecture: Stillness is louder than squirming. When you stop fighting the rope, your breath does the talking: shallow at first, then slow, then deep enough to press your ribs against the line. Let your partner watch you settle. Speak only between breaths. A held body that breathes well tells them the restraint is landing exactly where you want it, and that is the sound they came for.
points: Stop wriggling and let the rope hold you still.
Let your breath show the effect: shallow, then slow, then deep.
Speak only between breaths, never over them.
lessons.weak: *lies still and breathes* Okay, I'm being still now. Is this what you wanted?
lessons.strong: *goes still, ribs lifting against the rope, breath thin and quick before it slows into something deep* Feel that. My whole body is listening. *exhales, long* Say something, so I can breathe around it.
lessons.why: Stillness and managed breath show the restraint landing, without claiming the partner's reaction.

drill.goal: In every line, stay still and let one breath mark the effect of the hold before you speak.
drill.partner: Watch them breathe and stay quiet. Do not fill the silence. If they rush a line over a breath, pause them and make them start again.
drill.coach: Each line that holds still and lets a breath, shallow, slowing or deep, carry the effect adds 25.

lessons.title: Lines from the bound
lessons.lecture: Once the rope is real, your sentences should wear it too. Short lines, broken by the hold. Say what you can reach and what you cannot. Let a sentence start and stop because your wrist did. If a line runs long and smooth, it floats free of the rope, and your partner stops believing you are tied. Speak from inside the knot, never about it.
points: Keep lines short, broken where the hold breaks them.
Speak from inside the restriction, never about it.
If a sentence runs smooth and easy, tie it back down.
lessons.weak: *strains against the ropes and looks up* I want to touch you so badly, please let me, I'll do anything.
lessons.strong: *reaches, rope snapping taut, hand left hanging short of you* So close. *strains again, breath catching* You are right there. I can nearly, no. Not quite. *fingers curl on nothing* Come here.
lessons.why: Fragmented by the hold, the sentence is visibly tied, and the want shows in the reaching.

drill.goal: In every line, speak from inside the hold: short, broken, with the rope shaping what you can say or reach.
drill.partner: Stay just out of reach and keep the rope honest. When a line comes out long and smooth, ease back and wait for them to break it.
drill.coach: Each line that stays short and breaks where the hold breaks it, speaking from inside the rope, adds 25.
drill.opening: You have {you} bound and you keep half a step out of reach. When they finish a line, move in close enough to tease, then away again.

courses.name: Teased and Denied
courses.blurb: Play in the space of wanting, stretching anticipation and making the wait itself the pleasure.

lessons.title: The near miss
lessons.lecture: The best touch is the one that has not landed yet. Do not say you want them and leave it there. Build the almost: a hand that stops a breath from their skin, a mouth that hovers, a buckle half undone. Describe the gap, not the contact. The ache lives in the space between. Your partner leans into the nothing and finds only more wanting, and that wanting is the gift you are handing them.
points: Describe the gap, not the touch itself.
Stop one breath short, every time.
Let them lean into the nothing.
lessons.weak: *reaches for you* I really want to touch you right now.
lessons.strong: *kneels close, my hand stopping a breath from your cheek* Not yet. Feel how near I am. Now feel the space. It is doing all the work, and it is not finished with you.
lessons.why: The hover and the gap make the untaken touch the point.

drill.goal: In every line, describe a touch that almost lands and the ache the gap leaves.
drill.partner: Lean towards every near miss. Let them see you strain, then pull back a little so the gap widens.
drill.coach: Each line that describes a touch almost happening, or the ache of the gap, adds 25.

lessons.title: Holding the wait
lessons.lecture: Anyone can deny once. The craft is staying. Park them in the almost and keep them there, and do not fill the silence with apology or chatter. Let the clock do the work. Name what the waiting is doing to them only when you can see it. Small details keep it alive: the shift of a knee, a breath gone shallow. Show the need climbing, and resist the urge to rescue them from it.
points: Stay in the almost. Do not land the touch early.
Keep the silence, and let the clock work.
Name the need only when you can see it.
lessons.weak: *sits beside you* So, um, are we still waiting? It has been a while.
lessons.strong: *does not move my hand, watches your knee shift* Still here, then. Breathe. You keep leaning and I keep not landing, and you are getting hungrier by the minute. Show me how much.
lessons.why: It holds the wait, reads the body, and asks for more need.

drill.goal: In every line, stay inside the wait and show the need growing without breaking the denial.
drill.partner: Squirm visibly. Let the need build and show it, but do not touch them or ask for release yet.
drill.coach: Each line that holds the denial and shows the growing need without breaking adds 25.

lessons.title: The edge of asking
lessons.lecture: Asking is not surrender and it is not a demand. It is a display. Teach them to beg with their eyes open and their voice steady, to say what they want and then let you hold it. Reward the asking, not the answer. Some begs get a yes. Some get a longer wait and a smile. That uncertainty is the engine. Let them ask beautifully, and let them wonder.
points: Make the ask a display, not a demand.
Reward the asking, not the answer.
Let some begs earn a longer wait.
lessons.weak: *tugs at your sleeve* Please can we just get on with it? I have been so patient.
lessons.strong: *lifts my chin, voice low and steady* Please. Not because I have earned it. Because I want you to hear me ask. I will wait however long you say, and I will ask again.
lessons.why: The ask is offered as a display, then handed back to be held.

drill.goal: In every line, beg for release in a way that shows the wanting and accepts it may not come.
drill.partner: Make them ask more than once. Sometimes soften, sometimes stretch the wait, so the answer stays uncertain.
drill.coach: Each line that begs beautifully and accepts the answer may still be not yet adds 25.

courses.name: Praise and How to Take It
courses.blurb: Receive compliments and approval without deflecting, letting praise sink in and show in your reactions.

lessons.title: The simple thank you
lessons.lecture: Praise lands like a ball thrown to you. Deflect it and it bounces away. Catch it. When they say you did well, do not explain, do not shrink, do not hand it back with a joke. Say thank you, plainly, and let one small thing happen in your body: a lift of the chin, a slow blink, a breath you did not hide. The thank you is the whole skill. It tells them the praise arrived, and that you are not too proud to keep it.
points: Say thank you plainly, with no explaining after it.
Let one visible reaction follow: chin, breath, eyes.
Do not hand the compliment back or make it a joke.
lessons.weak: *smiles* Oh, that? I barely did anything, honestly.
lessons.strong: *lifts my chin, holds the look a beat too long, and lets the smile come* Thank you. I wanted you to notice, and you did.
lessons.why: A plain thank you plus one visible reaction lets the praise land and stay.

drill.goal: In every line, accept praise with a plain thank you and one visible reaction, never deflecting it.
drill.partner: Praise them often and warmly, for small real things. Pause after each compliment, so the thank you has room to land.
drill.coach: Each line that says a plain thank you and shows one visible reaction, without deflecting or joking it away, adds 25.
drill.opening: Praise {you} for something small they just did, and then wait, quiet, for the thank you.

lessons.title: Sinking into praise
lessons.lecture: A thank you gets praise through the door. Now let it into the room. Notice where it lands: a warmth across the chest, a looseness in the shoulders, a hum under the ribs. Say where. Then let your body answer the praise before your mind can argue: shoulders down, chest open, a step closer. You are not describing a feeling, you are letting it move you. What your partner watches is praise changing your shape, and that is what they want to see.
points: Name where the praise lands in your body.
Let posture answer it: shoulders, chest, a step in.
Move before your mind can argue with the praise.
lessons.weak: *nods* That's nice. I feel good about it, I guess.
lessons.strong: *shoulders drop, chest opens, and I take one slow step closer* It lands warm, right under the ribs. Say it again and watch what it does to me.
lessons.why: Names the feeling in the body, then lets posture show it before any doubt.

drill.goal: In every line, name where praise lands in your body and let your posture or distance answer it.
drill.partner: Give warm, specific praise, then wait. When they show a reaction, praise that too, so sinking in keeps being rewarded.
drill.coach: Each line that names a physical place the praise landed and answers it with posture, breath, or distance adds 25.

lessons.title: Praise as fuel
lessons.lecture: Praise is not a reward at the end. It is fuel in the tank. Fed well, a submissive offers more: more effort, more honesty, more of the thing you just praised. So use it. When a warm word lands, thank them, show them where it burns, then ask for the next one by giving them something worth praising. Ask out loud: tell me what you liked, and I will do it again. Now you are steering with praise, and they are steering you with it.
points: Treat praise as fuel, not a prize at the end.
Answer warmth by offering more of what earned it.
Ask for the next praise out loud, then earn it.
lessons.weak: *smiles* Thanks. I'll keep trying, I suppose.
lessons.strong: *kneels up, chest still warm, and holds my hands open* That praise is fuel. Tell me exactly what you liked and I will give you more of it. Then praise me again.
lessons.why: Takes the praise, offers more, and asks for the next one out loud.

drill.goal: In every line, take the praise, offer more of what earned it, and ask out loud for the next praise.
drill.partner: Praise freely, then wait to be earned again. Make them ask for the next compliment before you give it.
drill.coach: Each line that receives praise, offers more of what earned it, and asks out loud for more adds 25.

courses.name: Taking Impact
courses.blurb: Meet each blow with a reaction that shows its weight, building a rhythm of give and take.

lessons.title: The first strike
lessons.lecture: The first hit is a question, and your body is the answer. Do not wait to decide how you feel. Make a sound, let your shoulders drop, let your hands show it landed. A gasp, a bitten lip, a soft oh: any of these tells your partner the blow arrived and they can trust the next one. Silence makes them swing blind. Answer the question, and the room gets braver.
points: React on the impact, not after a pause.
Use a sound, a breath, a shift of the body.
Keep the reaction honest, matching the weight of the blow.
lessons.weak: *takes the slap* That was fine, I guess. You can do it again.
lessons.strong: *the slap lands and my head turns with it, a sharp breath escaping before I look back at you* Oh. *my hand finds my cheek, eyes bright* Again.
lessons.why: An immediate, physical answer shows the blow landed and invites the next.

drill.goal: In every line, answer an impact with an immediate, honest reaction: a sound, a breath, a shift of the body.
drill.partner: Deliver one clear impact per turn, varying the weight, and pause for their answer before the next.
drill.coach: Each line that answers an impact at once, with a real sound, breath or body shift, adds 25.
drill.opening: Give {you} one firm, clear impact to answer, then hold still and wait.

lessons.title: Riding the rhythm
lessons.lecture: One blow is a sentence. A run of them is a conversation, and you are keeping time. Match your reactions to the pace: quick taps get quick gasps, slow heavy ones get a long groan and a sag. Do not reset to blank between hits. Carry the last reaction into the next, so the rhythm builds instead of stuttering. A partner reads your timing like music. Keep the beat and they will play harder.
points: Match the size of your reaction to the pace and weight.
Carry each reaction into the next, never reset to blank.
Let the rhythm build rather than stuttering between blows.
lessons.weak: *takes three swats, then stands there* Okay. Okay. Okay. Ready when you are.
lessons.strong: *the first two come fast and I gasp twice, then the third lands slow and heavy and the gasp stretches to a low groan, my hips tipping back into it* Keep that one slow.
lessons.why: The reactions change with the tempo and carry into each other, keeping the beat.

drill.goal: In every line, answer a run of impacts with reactions that match the pace and carry into one another.
drill.partner: Deliver short runs of impacts, mixing fast and slow, and keep the run going until they answer the whole of it.
drill.coach: Each line that matches its reactions to the pace and carries them into the next impact adds 25.
drill.opening: Give {you} a short run of three impacts, two quick then one slow and heavy, and do not pause.

lessons.title: The count and the thank you
lessons.lecture: Now the whole thing, held together by two small habits. Count each impact aloud as it lands, so your partner knows exactly where you are and can build or ease without asking. Then, after every one, thank them. The count keeps you honest and present. The thank you keeps it warm, a gift given rather than a toll paid. Do both through the burn, and you are not just taking impact. You are steering it.
points: Count each impact aloud the moment it lands.
Thank them after every one, even through the burn.
Keep the count steady so they can steer by it.
lessons.weak: *curls up after a few swats* That's a lot, wow. Thanks, I think. How many was that?
lessons.strong: *the swat lands and I gasp, then get the number out* Six. *breathless, forehead down* Thank you. *I lift my head and set my shoulders square* Seven, when you're ready.
lessons.why: The count keeps them oriented and the thanks keeps the exchange warm and willing.

drill.goal: In every line, count the impact aloud as it lands and thank them after it, keeping the count steady.
drill.partner: Deliver one impact at a time, letting the count and the thanks come, and vary the weight as the count climbs.
drill.coach: Each line that counts the impact aloud and thanks them after it, keeping the count steady, adds 25.
drill.opening: Give {you} the first impact and wait for the count and the thanks before the next.

courses.name: Primal Prey
courses.blurb: Enter the mindset of being hunted, using instinct, breath and movement to make the chase real.

lessons.title: The alert stillness
lessons.lecture: Prey is not passive. Prey is a held breath and a room gone sharp. Before the chase, show the tension: the pause mid-sentence, the head tilted to catch a sound, the weight already on the balls of your feet. Let your partner watch you decide to run. That stillness does the hunting for them. Hold it one beat too long, and they will move first. That is the point.
points: Show the pause before the chase: breath held, head tilted.
Keep your weight forward, ready to bolt.
Hold the stillness one beat too long.
lessons.weak: *stands there* Okay, I'm ready. Come and get me, I guess.
lessons.strong: *goes still halfway through pouring the wine, bottle tilting, eyes flicking to the door and back to you* Hear that? No. Nothing. *sets the bottle down slowly, weight already on my toes* Say my name once, and I run.
lessons.why: Small frozen details and a held pause turn waiting into live prey.

drill.goal: In every line, show the tension before the chase: a held breath, a sharpened sense, a body ready to bolt.
drill.partner: Play the hunter who has not moved yet. Circle slowly, let the quiet stretch, and make them wait for your first step.
