drill.coach: Each line that shows held tension, a sharpened sense, or a body poised to run adds 25.
drill.opening: You are the hunter, and you have found {you} at last. Stand still across the room and let them feel your eyes before you take a single step.

lessons.title: The run and the dodge
lessons.lecture: Flight is written in fragments. Short lines. Broken breath. Do not explain the corridor, live in it. One line, you bolt. Next line, you glance back and lose ground. Next, you dodge, and your shoulder grazes the wall. Keep the sentences clipped and the senses loud: cold floor, loud pulse, a hand closing on air. End lines mid-breath. Speed on the page becomes speed in the room.
points: Keep lines short and breathless, one movement each.
Name a loud sense: cold floor, pulse, air.
Let a hand close on nothing. End mid-breath.
lessons.weak: *runs away down the corridor as fast as I can and looks back at you.*
lessons.strong: *bolts, bare feet slapping cold tile, and risks one look back* Too slow. *ducks the stair rail, breath ragged, your fingers grazing my sleeve as I twist away* Nearly. Nearly.
lessons.why: Short gasping fragments and a near miss put the reader in the running body.

drill.goal: In every line, make one movement and one loud sense, and keep the line short enough to gasp.
drill.partner: Chase at a steady pace, always a half step behind. Miss by a hand's width, and let the misses get closer.
drill.coach: Each line that holds one movement plus one sharp sense, kept short and breathless, adds 25.

lessons.title: Caught and yielding
lessons.lecture: The catch is not the end, it is the hinge. Do not go limp the instant a hand lands. Show the last flare of fight, a twist, a laugh, a push that fails. Then yield in layers: the shoulders first, then the weight, then the breath. Say one small honest thing as you give. A catch they had to earn tastes sweeter than one you handed over.
points: Let one last twist or laugh fail before you yield.
Yield in layers: shoulders, then weight, then breath.
Say one small honest thing as you give.
lessons.weak: *gets caught and stops* Okay okay, you got me. I give up now.
lessons.strong: *twists once, laughing, then my shoulders drop and I lean my full weight back into you* God. *breath going slow and even against your arm* Don't let go yet. I mean it. Not yet.
lessons.why: A failed twist, then layered surrender, makes the yielding feel earned.

drill.goal: In every line, show one flicker of fight and one layer of yielding, shoulders, weight or breath.
drill.partner: Catch firmly and hold. Give them a moment to struggle, then loosen nothing until their weight settles.
drill.coach: Each line that shows a last flicker of resistance and one layer of yielding adds 25.

courses.name: Pet Play between Adults
courses.blurb: Inhabit a pet persona with warmth and wit, using voice, posture and small habits to bring it to life.

lessons.title: Finding the animal
lessons.lecture: A pet persona is not a costume you announce, it is a handful of traits you keep returning to. Pick three: how you move, how you listen, how you ask. A tilt of the head. A nudge of the knuckles. A sound instead of a word. Choose animals with range, dog, cat, fox, and let the traits repeat until your partner starts reading you like weather. Announce nothing. Show everything.
points: Pick three concrete traits and keep returning to them.
Show them in movement, in listening, in asking.
Repeat them until your partner reads you without being told.
lessons.weak: *barks* I am a dog tonight, okay? Woof woof.
lessons.strong: *drops to my knees, sits back on my heels, and tilts my head at the door* Let me out when you are ready. I will wait right here, watching you.
lessons.why: Three clear animal traits, shown, never announced.

drill.goal: In every line, show at least one concrete animal trait through movement, sound, or posture, with no announcing.
drill.partner: Watch for the traits and react to them as if they were real. Ask nothing about the animal. Let them show you.
drill.coach: Each line that shows a concrete animal trait in movement, sound, or posture, without announcing it, adds 25.

lessons.title: The pet voice
lessons.lecture: Animal speech goes wrong when you spell the noises. Skip the woofs and the meows, mostly. Let grammar do the work: short sentences, plain wants, the odd clipped word. Say the simple thing a creature would say. Need out. Hungry. Warm. Then let one real sound escape when words fail, a whine, a hum, a soft huff against skin. Your partner hears the animal in the rhythm, not the spelling.
points: Keep sentences short and wants plain.
Use one real sound only when words fail.
Let rhythm carry the animal, not spelled noises.
lessons.weak: *woof woof* I am a good doggy, woof, can I have a treat please woof?
lessons.strong: *presses my forehead to your knee, voice low and clipped* Need out. Then food. Then you, in that order. *a small huff against the fabric*
lessons.why: Plain wants in short beats, one soft sound, no spelled noise.

drill.goal: In every line, speak in short plain wants with at most one real sound, and no spelled animal noises.
drill.partner: Answer them like a person talking to an animal: simple, warm, a little amused. Reward the plain wants.
drill.coach: Each line that uses short plain speech with no spelled noises and at most one real sound adds 25.

lessons.title: Devotion on four legs
lessons.lecture: Here is where the persona earns its keep. Devotion is not just sitting pretty, it is small acts of attention: following a step behind, resting your cheek where they can reach, bringing them something, guarding the door while they dress. Do the act, then wait, unhurried, for it to be noticed. Neediness whines. Devotion simply keeps showing up, again and again, until the room feels emptier when you leave it.
points: Devote through small acts of attention, not announcements.
Do the act, then wait for it to be noticed.
Keep showing up. Do not whine for praise.
lessons.weak: *looks up at you* I am being really loyal right now, are you proud of me? Please say you are.
lessons.strong: *pads to the door and settles across it, chin on my forearms, eyes on you* Nobody gets past. *when you cross, I press my cheek to your thigh and stay*
lessons.why: A small guarding act, then quiet contact, devotion shown and never asked for.

drill.goal: In every line, perform one small act of devotion, then wait or make quiet contact, without asking for praise.
drill.partner: Notice the acts in your own time, not straight away. Let them wait. Occasionally leave a gap so they must find a new way to show up.
drill.coach: Each line that shows a small act of devotion and then waits or makes quiet contact without asking for praise adds 25.

courses.name: Devotion in Small Things
courses.blurb: Build a sense of dedication through tiny, repeated acts that accumulate into something profound.

lessons.title: The daily ritual
lessons.lecture: Devotion is built in teaspoons, not oceans. Pick one small act you will do every time you meet: a drink poured before they ask, a coat taken at the door, a single line of greeting. Do it the same way, unasked. Repetition is the whole trick. By the third time they will expect it, and by the fifth they will miss it if it stops. That missing is the devotion.
points: Choose one small act you will always do unasked.
Repeat it exactly, the same way every time.
Let them come to expect it, then never skip it.
lessons.weak: Hey, can I get you anything? I'm happy to help.
lessons.strong: *takes your coat before you speak, hangs it straight, and sets your drink at your usual elbow* There. Now you can sit down properly.
lessons.why: The same act, done before the asking, builds a habit they rely on.

drill.goal: In every line, perform one small recurring act of service before they ask, in the same way each time.
drill.partner: Arrive tired and a little distracted. Let the ritual land. On the third or fourth time, notice if it stops.
drill.coach: Each line that performs one small, repeated act of service before being asked adds 25.

lessons.title: Noticing and tending
lessons.lecture: Anyone can fetch what is asked for. Devotion is fetching what is not. Watch the small tells: the drink going warm, the shoulder creeping up, the sentence that trails off. Meet the need in the same breath, without a speech about it. Name it only if they ask. A partner who is tended without asking learns to relax, because someone is finally paying attention.
points: Watch for small tells: warmth, posture, trailing sentences.
Meet the need at once, without announcing it.
Speak only if they ask what you noticed.
lessons.weak: You look tired. Do you want me to do something?
lessons.strong: *slides the warm glass away and sets a fresh one down, thumb brushing your shoulder as I pass* Keep talking. I'm listening to all of it.
lessons.why: Meets the unspoken need and keeps attention on them, not the effort.

drill.goal: In every line, spot one small unspoken need and meet it at once, without making a speech of it.
drill.partner: Show small tells instead of stating needs: a shiver, a pause, a hand pressed to your shoulder. Never ask for anything.
drill.coach: Each line that spots one small unspoken need and meets it without announcing the effort adds 25.

lessons.title: Devotion over time
lessons.lecture: A long scene is a ledger of small returns. The drink you poured in the first hour comes back when they are hoarse. The coat comes back at the door. Call back the early acts, quietly, exactly as they were, and the hours stack into proof. This is where devotion stops being a gesture and becomes a record. They look back and see how long you have been paying attention.
points: Keep the early small acts in play, not just at first.
Call one back late, exactly as you first did it.
Let the hours stack into proof, not performance.
lessons.weak: *sets down a drink* I remembered what you like. It's been a while.
lessons.strong: *sets the coat over your shoulders the same way, collar straightened, and holds the glass out with the same hand* Still warm. Both of them. As promised.
lessons.why: Returns the first ritual late and exact, so the hours become proof.

drill.goal: In every line, bring back one early small act of devotion exactly as first done, and let the hours show.
drill.partner: Run long and cool at first, warming slowly. Notice when the callbacks land. Test whether they keep tending.
drill.coach: Each line that recalls an earlier act of devotion exactly, and lets the hours accumulate, adds 25.

courses.name: Topping from the Bottom
courses.blurb: Steer a scene from below without seizing control, using hints, offers and well-placed questions.

lessons.title: The gentle hint
lessons.lecture: You are on your knees, but the scene is a conversation, and you get a voice. A hint is a gift left on the table: say what you noticed, what your body wants, and then leave it there. Do not push it into their hands. *The cushion is far*, *my wrists feel lonely*. If they pick it up, wonderful. If they do not, the wanting is its own pleasure, and they still believe every choice was theirs.
points: Say what you notice or want, then stop talking.
Keep it small: a detail, a sensation, a wish.
Let silence do the work after the hint lands.
lessons.weak: *squirms* Could we maybe do something else? This is a bit much.
lessons.strong: *tilts my head, wrists still crossed behind me* The cushion is a whole room away, and my knees have started composing complaints. Just saying.
lessons.why: Names a small want and leaves the decision entirely with them.

drill.goal: In every line, drop one small hint about what you want, then stop and leave the choice to them.
drill.partner: Play the firm one. Catch some hints and act on them. Let others lie there, so the hint has to stand on its own.
drill.coach: Each line that drops one clear, small hint and then leaves the choice to them adds 25.

lessons.title: The offered choice
lessons.lecture: Two doors, one corridor. When you want a scene to turn, do not grab the wheel, hold up two keys. *The rope or the blindfold. Here or the wall.* Both options must be things you would genuinely take, or the choice is theatre. Then hand it back whole: *you pick*. They choose, they speak, and the scene moves where you quietly pointed. That is not topping. That is steering with their own hands on the wheel.
points: Offer exactly two options you would truly accept.
Hand the decision back with a clear, warm invitation.
Never rank the options. Let them choose freely.
lessons.weak: *looks up* Do you want to use the rope? Or we could do something else, whatever.
lessons.strong: *holds up the rope in one hand, the blindfold in the other, and offers both* Rope, or blindfold. Both keep me exactly where you want me. You pick, and I will not argue.
lessons.why: Two real options, handed back whole, keep the choice theirs.

drill.goal: In every line, offer exactly two real options and hand the choice back to them.
drill.partner: Deliberate between the options. Sometimes ask which they would prefer, so they must hand it back again without deciding.
drill.coach: Each line that offers two genuine options and hands the choice back to them adds 25.

lessons.title: The guiding question
lessons.lecture: A question is a leash with slack in it. Ask something that narrows the scene without naming the answer: *what would you do if I moved? What are you waiting for?* The best ones make them picture the next moment and then walk into it. Keep your voice curious, not testing. If they answer with a question of their own, hold the slack and ask again, softer. You are not quizzing them. You are lighting the road ahead.
points: Ask questions that point at the next moment.
Stay curious, never testing. Soft beats sharp.
If they volley it back, ask again, softer.
lessons.weak: *waits* So, um, what happens now? What do you want me to do?
lessons.strong: *lifts my chin, voice low and easy* What are you waiting for? Because I have been very patient, and you have not moved me once. Tell me what happens next.
lessons.why: The question narrows the scene and hands them the next move.

drill.goal: In every line, ask one guiding question that points at the next moment without dictating it.
drill.partner: Answer some questions by acting. Volley others back with a question of your own, so they must ask again, softer.
drill.coach: Each line that asks one guiding question pointing at the next moment, without dictating the answer, adds 25.

courses.name: Surrender in Long Scenes
courses.blurb: Sustain submission across hours, pacing your energy and keeping the thread alive through lulls and peaks.

lessons.title: Pacing the fall
lessons.lecture: A long scene is a distance, not a dive. If you spend everything in the first twenty minutes, you will be running on empty by the hour. So meter it. Give your surrender in portions: a little now, more when called. Keep something in reserve and let them feel the reserve. The slow ones last longest, and the ones who last get taken furthest. The fall you pace is the fall they trust.
points: Spend surrender in portions, not all at once.
Keep something in reserve and let it show.
Match their pace: slower when they slow.
lessons.weak: *drops to my knees fast* Okay, I'm all yours. Do anything.
lessons.strong: *lowers myself slowly, hands on my thighs, and breathes out* First portion. I'm not giving you all of it yet. Tell me when you want the next.
lessons.why: Hands over surrender in a measured portion and names the reserve.

drill.goal: In every line, give one measured portion of surrender and keep a clear reserve in view.
drill.partner: Take each portion and ask for the next in your own time. Do not rush them, and do not let them rush either.
drill.coach: Each line that gives a measured portion of surrender, names what is held back, or matches the partner's pace adds 25.
drill.opening: {you} has just arrived and is standing by the window. Open slowly: one small instruction, and wait for {you} to measure out the first portion.

lessons.title: Through the lull
lessons.lecture: Every long scene sags somewhere. The rope gets checked, the water gets poured, someone answers a door. Beginners treat the lull as a break and sit up, blinking, half out of it. Do not. The thread is yours to hold. Stay low, stay soft, keep one small contact alive: a hand on their knee, eyes that find them, a quiet word. Fill the quiet with your waiting and they will feel you still under it.
points: Treat the lull as part of the scene, not a break.
Keep one small contact alive: a hand, a look, a word.
Fill the quiet with visible waiting, not chatter.
lessons.weak: *sits up and stretches* So, what now? Are we done for a bit?
lessons.strong: *stays low, cheek against your knee, and murmurs without lifting my head* Take your time with the water. I'm not going anywhere. I'll wait right here, exactly like this.
lessons.why: Stays in position through the pause and makes the waiting itself the offering.

drill.goal: In every line, hold the thread through a quiet moment with one small contact and visible waiting.
drill.partner: Create pauses: check the water, pour a drink, look away. Let the lull stretch until they fill it.
drill.coach: Each line that treats a lull as part of the scene with a small contact, a look, or visible waiting adds 25.
drill.opening: You are both in the hot tub. Give {you} one small instruction, then turn away to check the temperature and let the silence stretch.

lessons.title: The deep end
lessons.lecture: Now the water gets deeper. Going further is not doing more things. It is going quieter inside while the scene takes more of you: fewer words, fewer choices, more of your weight given over. The skill is staying present down there. Answer when asked. Let your body reply before your mind catches up. The deep end is only frightening from the ladder. Once you are in, it holds you.
points: Go quieter inside as the scene takes more.
Answer when asked, even if the answer is small.
Let your body reply before your mind does.
lessons.weak: *nods along* Yeah, deeper, sure. Whatever you want, I guess.
lessons.strong: *sinks down against you, forehead to your shoulder, and my voice comes out low and certain* Further. Ask me something and I'll answer before I can talk myself out of it.
lessons.why: Asks to go deeper and shows presence with a body-first answer.

drill.goal: In every line, go a step deeper with fewer words, a quieter mind, and a present, body-first answer.
drill.partner: Ask short questions and wait. Push one notch past their last answer, then hold there so they can settle.
drill.coach: Each line that goes a step further with fewer words, a quieter mind, and a present answer adds 25.
drill.opening: You have {you} settled and quiet. Ask one short question, then wait without filling the silence.

courses.name: Sub Drop and Self-care
courses.blurb: Recognise the dip after intense play and learn the rituals that bring you gently back to yourself.

lessons.title: Naming the drop
lessons.lecture: Drop is a tide, not a failure. It comes hours after the high: flat, tender, oddly tearful, hungry for nothing. You cannot tend what you cannot name. So learn your own weather. Which sign arrives first, the fog or the ache? Say it plainly, out loud, to your partner and to yourself: I go quiet, I go small, I want to be held but ask for nothing. Naming it is half the landing.
points: Learn your first sign: fog, ache, quiet, or tears.
Say it plainly, out loud, before it swallows you.
Name it to your partner, not just inside your head.
lessons.weak: Yeah I feel a bit weird now, probably fine.
lessons.strong: *pulls the blanket to my chin and breathes out slowly* It is starting. The fog first, then the flat. I go quiet and small, and I will want holding but ask for nothing. So I am telling you now.
lessons.why: Names the exact signs in order, out loud, before the drop deepens.

drill.goal: In every line, name one concrete sign of your own drop, in plain words, as it arrives.
drill.partner: Play it warm and unhurried. Ask now and then what you are noticing, and let them answer fully before you respond.
drill.coach: Each line that names one concrete, plain sign of their own drop adds 25.
drill.opening: The scene has just ended. {you} is coming down from something big. Ask gently what they are noticing.

lessons.title: The landing ritual
lessons.lecture: A landing is built, not hoped for. Choose three small acts and put them in order: water, then the heavy blanket, then the words that tell you it went well. Say the sequence to your partner before you play, while you are still steady. Naming it early means nobody has to invent comfort from fog. The ritual does the holding. You just follow it, one step, then the next, until your breath evens out.
points: Choose three small acts and fix them in order.
Say the sequence to your partner before you play.
Follow it one step at a time, without editing it.
lessons.weak: Just get me some water or something after, I guess.
lessons.strong: *sets the glass down and taps the blanket on the sofa* Water first, then this round me, then you tell me one thing that landed well. That is the order. Say it back so we both know it before we start.
lessons.why: A fixed, spoken sequence takes the thinking out of a foggy landing.

drill.goal: In every line, name or follow one step of your three part landing ritual, in order.
drill.partner: Follow their sequence when it comes. If they skip a step, gently send them back to it. Add one warm word of your own each time.
drill.coach: Each line that names or follows one step of their spoken ritual in order adds 25.

lessons.title: Tending the next day
lessons.lecture: The morning after can be heavier than the night. Mastery is planning for it while you still feel good: the slow breakfast, the walk, the message you send yourself. Then, the next day, you check in honestly. Am I flat, or just tired? Do I need food, sun, silence, a voice? Answer yourself the way you would answer a lover. Gentle is not soft. It is skilled. Tending the next day is how drop stops running the week.
points: Plan one gentle act the night before, while steady.
Check in honestly the next day: flat, or just tired?
Answer your own need the way you would a lover.
lessons.weak: I'll probably be tired tomorrow, whatever, it's fine.
lessons.strong: *sets out the good coffee and texts myself: walk before noon, eat properly, ask for a voice note if the flat sets in* Tomorrow gets planned tonight, while I can still think straight. That is the whole trick of it.
lessons.why: Plans the care in advance, then names the exact check in for tomorrow.

drill.goal: In every line, either plan one act of next day care or check in honestly with your own state.
drill.partner: Play the following morning. Be soft and curious, and ask what they need rather than guessing it for them.
drill.coach: Each line that plans one concrete act of next day care or checks in honestly adds 25.
drill.opening: It is the morning after. {you} wakes first. Let them speak before you do.

courses.name: Switching Cleanly
courses.blurb: Move between leading and following without muddle, signalling the shift so both players stay oriented.

lessons.title: The clear handover
lessons.lecture: Muddle is the enemy of heat. When you change who is leading, say so out loud, in one clean line, before you move a muscle. Two words can do it: my turn, your lead. Say it looking at them, not at the floor. A partner who knows the wheel is turning will turn with you. A partner who has to guess will drift, and drift reads as doubt.
points: Say the switch out loud before you move.
Keep it to one short, unambiguous line.
Look at them when you say it, then move.
lessons.weak: *shifts* I dunno, maybe you take over for a bit?
lessons.strong: *sits back, hands open on my knees, eyes on you* Your lead now. I am following, and I will not grab it back until you hand it over.
lessons.why: One clean line names the handover, then the body confirms it.

drill.goal: In every line, announce the handover in one unambiguous phrase before any action, then show it in the body.
drill.partner: Wait for a clear handover before you take the lead. If it is vague, keep asking with your eyes. Once it is clean, take over with confidence.
drill.coach: Each line that announces the role change in one clear phrase before acting, then backs it with the body, adds 25.

lessons.title: Settling into the new role
lessons.lecture: A handover is a door, not a holiday. Once you cross it, cross properly. Three committed moves and you live there: change your posture, change your voice, change what you ask for. Half-leading from the doorway is the muddle again. If you have taken the lead, give an instruction. If you have dropped to follow, wait to be told. Commit, and they will relax into it with you.
points: Cross the door fully: posture, voice, and asks all change.
If you lead, instruct. If you follow, wait to be told.
Three committed moves before you judge how it feels.
lessons.weak: *half sits up* Okay so I am in charge now I guess, what do you want to do?
lessons.strong: *straightens, sets both hands flat on the table, voice dropped low* Stand up. Do not speak yet. Come here and put your hands where I can see them.
lessons.why: Posture, voice and a clear instruction land the new role at once.

drill.goal: In every line, make one committed move in the new role: a change of posture, of voice, or a clear instruction or wait.
drill.partner: Let the first handover happen, then hold them to it. If they half-lead, go still and make them commit. Answer a firm lead with visible relief.
drill.coach: Each line that commits fully to the new role through posture, voice, instruction or deliberate waiting adds 25.

lessons.title: Switching mid-scene
lessons.lecture: The hardest switch happens with the scene already hot and your pulse loud. Do not stop the scene to change gear. Fold the handover into the action: mid-kiss, mid-instruction, mid-sentence. Give the new role something to grip, so the scene keeps its shape while the wheel turns. Then hold the new ground for a while. A switch that flips every line is noise. A switch that lands and stays is a gift.
points: Fold the handover into the action, never a full stop.
Give the new role something concrete to grip at once.
Hold the new ground. Do not flip again straight away.
lessons.weak: *pulls back from the kiss* Wait, can we swap? You do it.
lessons.strong: *breaks the kiss, forehead still against yours, breath uneven* Your turn. Push me back against the door and tell me what happens next.
lessons.why: The switch rides inside the kiss and hands over a concrete next move.

drill.goal: In every line, switch roles inside the action and give the new role one concrete thing to grip.
drill.partner: Play the scene hot and physical. Switch on their cue without pausing it, grip what they hand you, and hold it until they take it back.
drill.coach: Each line that switches mid-action, hands the new role something concrete, and holds the new ground adds 25.

courses.name: Submission in 3DXChat
courses.blurb: Bring surrender to life in the 3D world, using movement, camera and chat to make every gesture count.

lessons.title: Positioning with purpose
lessons.lecture: In this world your avatar speaks before your mouth does. Where you stand is the first sentence of the scene. Do not drift in mid-room and hope. Choose the spot that says it: kneeling by the chair, hands folded, chin down, close enough to be reached. Pick the pose that opens you, not the one that hides you. Then be still. Stillness reads as devotion. Fidgeting reads as doubt.
points: Choose your position before you type a word.
Place yourself close enough to be reached.
Hold the pose. Stillness reads as devotion.
lessons.weak: *wanders in and stands around* Hi, I'm here, where do you want me?
lessons.strong: *walks straight to the low stool, kneels with knees apart and palms on my thighs, head bowed but eyes up* However you want me, I am already here.
lessons.why: The pose and the chosen spot say submission before a single word.

drill.goal: Open every line with a deliberate position or pose change that shows submission before you speak.
drill.partner: Sit back and let them place themselves. Now and then pat a spot or point to one, so they must move with purpose.
drill.coach: Each line that begins with a chosen position, a kneel, a bow, or a deliberate move into place adds 25.

lessons.title: Chat as touch
lessons.lecture: A short line is a hand on the wrist. Long paragraphs float away. Cut to the gesture: the lowered eyes, the offered palm, the breath you let out. Put the movement in asterisks and keep the speech small, three or four words, no more. Let the silence after the line do the work. If you must explain what you feel, you have already lost the touch. Show the body, trust the body.
points: Keep lines short. Gesture first, speech second.
Put movement in asterisks, keep words to a handful.
Let the silence after the line land.
lessons.weak: *smiles nervously* I really like this and I hope you do too, it's lovely being here with you.
lessons.strong: *steps in close, rests my forehead against your shoulder, exhales* Yours. Say when.
lessons.why: Small gesture, three words, and the quiet after does the touching.

drill.goal: In every line, lead with one small physical gesture in asterisks and keep spoken words under five.
drill.partner: Answer their touches with stillness or one of your own. Let silences stretch. Do not fill them for them.
drill.coach: Each line that opens with a small gesture and keeps speech under five words adds 25.

lessons.title: The scene arc
lessons.lecture: A scene is a tide, not a puddle. It comes in, it swells, it draws back. Open low and quiet, so the first rise means something. In the middle, push the surrender further each beat: closer, lower, more offered. Then end deliberately, not by trailing off. Kneel, thank them, go still. The close is a gift you give the scene. Without it, everything before it feels unfinished.
points: Open quiet and low, so the first rise lands.
Push one step further with every beat.
Close on purpose: kneel, thank, go still.
lessons.weak: *sits down* So, um, what should we do now? I guess whatever you like really.
lessons.strong: *lowers myself to the floor, forehead to your knee, and stays* That is all of me. Tell me it was enough, and I will rise when you say.
lessons.why: A quiet open, a steady descent, and a deliberate close give the scene shape.

drill.goal: In every line, move the scene one clear step: open low, deepen the surrender, then close with a deliberate gesture.
drill.partner: Meet them low and quiet, then raise the stakes a little each turn. Signal near the end that the scene is closing.
drill.coach: Each line that visibly advances the arc, opening, deepening, or closing on purpose, adds 25.

courses.name: The Devoted Long Game
courses.blurb: Carry devotion across sessions, building a shared history that makes each return feel deeper.

lessons.title: The open thread
lessons.lecture: An ending is a door, not a wall. Do not close everything. Leave one small thing humming: a question unanswered, a task half done, a word you did not finish saying. It should be tiny enough to carry and warm enough to think about later. Say it plainly as you part, then let it sit. They will turn it over on the way home, and the scene will still be running.
points: End with one small thing still unfinished.
Keep it tiny enough to carry, warm enough to revisit.
Say it plainly, then let it sit untouched.
lessons.weak: *waves* Okay, that was fun. See you next time, I guess.
lessons.strong: *fastens my coat, then pauses at the door* One thing unfinished. You still owe me the last word of that sentence. Bring it next time, and we will see what it earns.
lessons.why: Leaves one small unfinished thing to carry, so the scene keeps running.

drill.goal: In every line, leave one small thread open: a question, a half task, or a word left unsaid.
drill.partner: Play warm and present. Let each thread land and show you are already turning it over. Do not close the thread yourself.
drill.coach: Each line that leaves one small, warm, unfinished thread open rather than closing it adds 25.

lessons.title: The warm return
lessons.lecture: The next scene does not start from nothing. It starts from the thread. Pick it up before anything else, name it, and let them see you remembered. Ask for the word. Set the task beside the one left undone. This is what makes a return warm: not the greeting, but the proof that the last time stayed with you. Then build forward from what you carried.
points: Open by naming the thread you left last time.
Ask for the word or the task, and wait for it.
Build forward from what you both carried.
lessons.weak: *sits down* Hey. So, what do you want to do tonight?
lessons.strong: *pulls out the chair and stays standing behind it* Before you sit. The last word of that sentence. You had all week to find it. Say it now, then we begin.
lessons.why: Picks up last time's thread first, proving it was carried and remembered.

drill.goal: In every line, pick up last time's thread, name it, and ask for it or build on it before moving forward.
drill.partner: Arrive having half prepared the thread, and offer it back once prompted. Make them ask for it properly.
drill.coach: Each line that names, asks for, or builds on the earlier thread before anything new adds 25.
drill.opening: You have arrived with last time's unfinished word ready, half hoping {you} has forgotten it.

lessons.title: A shared language
lessons.lecture: The long game has a private tongue. One phrase, one gesture, one small ritual that means what only you two know. Start it small, use it exactly, and let it gather weight each time it returns. Do not explain it to anyone. Soon a single word will carry a whole evening, and a raise of your hand will say come here and behave. That is the mastery: shorthand that only deepens.
points: Invent one private phrase or gesture, small and exact.
Use it the same way every time, never explaining it.
Let the meaning grow heavier with each return.
lessons.weak: *grins* Remember our thing? Do the thing, you know the one.
lessons.strong: *taps two fingers against my collarbone, the old signal, and does not raise my voice* Two taps. You know where that puts you. Come here and show me the phrase holds.
lessons.why: One private signal, used exactly, carries a whole evening in two taps.

drill.goal: In every line, use the private phrase or gesture exactly, or add weight to what it already means.
drill.partner: Know the signal and answer it every time it appears. Let its meaning deepen, and never ask what it means.
drill.coach: Each line that uses the private phrase or gesture exactly, or deepens its meaning, adds 25.
drill.opening: The tavern is quiet and {you} has been waiting. You know the old signal and are watching for it.

courses.name: Cues and Hints
courses.blurb: Read the small signals that say yes, wait, or not yet. Learn to spot cues in chat and answer them so scenes flow naturally.

lessons.title: Spot the green light
lessons.lecture: Cues are not decoration. They are the partner's hand on the door, testing if it opens. A held pause, an emote that leans closer, a question left hanging with no full stop: all of it says *go on, then*. Your job is not to pounce. It is to notice out loud, so they know the light was seen. Say what you caught. Let them feel watched and wanted.
points: Watch for pauses, leans, and questions left hanging.
Name the cue out loud so they know you saw it.
Do not pounce. Let the noticing itself be the heat.
lessons.weak: *smiles* Nice. So, what now?
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down and tilts my head* You left that question hanging and leaned in while you asked it. That is a green light if I ever saw one. Say it again, slower.
lessons.why: Names the small signal and rewards it without rushing past it.

drill.goal: In every line, name one small cue the partner gave and answer it, without jumping ahead of it.
drill.partner: Drop constant small cues: a pause, a lean, a half question. Keep them light so they must be spotted, never announced.
drill.coach: Each line that names one real cue from the partner's last line and answers it, without rushing ahead, adds 25.
drill.opening: You are across the bar from {you}. Lean in, hold a pause a beat too long, and leave a question half asked.

lessons.title: Answer in kind
lessons.lecture: A cue answered with a bigger cue is a shove. Answer with the same size, and the scene walks forward on its own legs. They lean, you lean. They half ask, you half answer and leave a thread loose. Matching is not timid. It is confident, because it trusts the rhythm to carry you both. Add one small thing, never three. Let them take the next step.
points: Match the size of their cue, do not outgun it.
Add one small thing, then leave a thread loose.
Trust the rhythm. Let them take the next step.
lessons.weak: *grins* Oh, you want me. Come here, then.
lessons.strong: *mirrors the lean, close enough to hear you breathe* Half a question deserves half an answer. Yes, I noticed. Now finish asking, and I will finish saying yes.
lessons.why: Returns the same sized signal and hands the next move back.

drill.goal: In every line, match the partner's last cue at the same size and add exactly one small new thing.
drill.partner: Give cues of varying size: a glance, a lean, a hand almost offered. Reward matching, go quiet if they overshoot.
drill.coach: Each line that matches the partner's cue at the same size and adds one small new thing adds 25.

lessons.title: Test and read
lessons.lecture: Now you lead the dance. Offer a hint the size of a coin: a look held one beat long, a hand turned palm up, a question with a door in it. Then stop and read. A lean back means not yet. A mirror means yes. A new cue of their own means take it further. Offering without reading is guessing. Offering, then reading, is a conversation.
points: Offer one small hint, then stop and read the answer.
Treat a lean back as not yet, not as no.
Let their new cue, not your hope, set the pace.
lessons.weak: *takes your hand* Come on, let's go somewhere quieter.
lessons.strong: *turns my palm up between us and waits* Your call. One step closer, or we stay right here and keep talking. Either answer is a good one.
lessons.why: Offers a small open hint, then genuinely waits for the read.

drill.goal: In every line, offer one small hint and then read the partner's answer before moving a single step further.
drill.partner: Answer hints honestly and vary it: lean in, lean back, or offer a counter cue. Make them read before they move.
drill.coach: Each line that offers one small hint and then reads the partner's answer before going further adds 25.

courses.name: Group Dynamics
courses.blurb: Play well with three or more. Learn to share the floor, pass the spotlight, and keep a group scene from splintering.

lessons.title: Share the floor
lessons.lecture: Three players in a room and one of them holds the mic. It is usually the fastest typist, and usually you. Do not hog it. End your line on a hinge: a question, a half-finished gesture, a task handed over. Leave a gap someone can step into. A scene is a conversation with more elbows, and the best lines are the ones that make the next person type faster.
points: End lines on a hinge: a question or a handed-over task.
Leave a beat before you type again.
Count to two before jumping back in.
lessons.weak: *pulls you both close* So anyway, this is all about me and what I'm going to do.
lessons.strong: *hooks a chair out with one foot and nods at it* Sit. Both of you. One of you tells me how you ended up here tonight, and the other backs the story up.
lessons.why: Two people get a task and a reason to talk to each other.

drill.goal: In every line, hand the next move to someone: ask a question, set a task, or leave a gesture unfinished.
drill.partner: Wait a beat before you reply, so the gap is real. If they hold the mic too long, stay quiet until they hand it back.
drill.coach: Each line that hands the next move to another player with a question, task or unfinished gesture adds 25.

lessons.title: Pass the spotlight
lessons.lecture: Every group has a quiet one, and quiet is not bored. It is waiting to be invited. Do not ask them what they think, that is homework. Give them a small, specific job: hold this, watch that, tell me the one thing you noticed. A named task is a door held open. Do it early, before the silence gets heavy enough to feel like a verdict. Then look at them while they do it.
points: Pick the quiet player early, before the silence grows heavy.
Give a small specific job, not a vague opinion.
Look at them while they do it.
lessons.weak: *glances around* Anyone want to say anything? No? Okay, moving on.
lessons.strong: *turns to you and holds out my glass* Hold this and do not spill a drop. You are the only one here I trust with it. Now tell me what you noticed about her before I walked in.
lessons.why: A named task and full attention make a quiet player visible.

drill.goal: In every line, give one quiet player a small named task and turn your attention on them while they do it.
drill.partner: Play the quiet one at first: short replies, watching. Warm up only when a task is handed to you by name.
drill.coach: Each line that gives a quiet player a small specific task and turns attention on them adds 25.
drill.opening: You are the quiet one, tucked into the corner of the booth, watching {you} and the others.

lessons.title: Weave the threads
lessons.lecture: Two whispers in the corner and the group has splintered. Do not scold it back together. Find the one word both threads share, a name, a place, a dare, and pull them into the same sentence. Say it loud enough for the whole room. Done well, nobody notices the seam. Done badly, it feels like a roll call. So make the join a small event: a toast, a dare, a hand on two shoulders at once.
points: Find the one word both side threads share.
Pull both into a single sentence the room can hear.
Make the join an event: a toast, a dare, two hands.
lessons.weak: *claps hands* Okay everyone, let's all talk together again, shall we?
lessons.strong: *stands, glass raised, one hand on each of your shoulders* Both of you said the same name tonight. So we drink to it, and then one of you tells the room why.
lessons.why: One shared word becomes a toast nobody can ignore.

drill.goal: In every line, join two side threads with one shared word, name or dare, and make the join an event.
drill.partner: Start two separate side conversations and let them drift. Reward every line that pulls them back into one shared moment.
drill.coach: Each line that joins two side threads through a shared word or dare and makes it an event adds 25.

courses.name: Juggling Partners
courses.blurb: Keep two or three scenes alive without dropping anyone. Learn to bank a thread, switch cleanly, and return with warmth.

lessons.title: Bank the thread
lessons.lecture: Two chats blinking at once is not chaos, it is a juggling act, and every good juggler knows where the balls are. When you step away from a scene, do not fade out mid-air. Plant a hook: a question, a held image, a promise with a time on it. Leave them something to chew on, not something to wonder about. A banked thread stays warm while your hands are busy elsewhere.
points: Never vanish mid-beat. Leave on a planted hook.
Make the hook a question or a promise with a time.
Bank before you are forced to, not after.
lessons.weak: *waves* Gotta go. Talk later maybe.
lessons.strong: *sets the glass down between us, still full* Half a drink left and a question with your name on it. Sit with both. I am back before the ice melts.
lessons.why: Gives them a concrete thing to hold and a clear return time.

drill.goal: In every line, leave the scene deliberately: plant one hook, a question or a timed promise, before you step away.
drill.partner: Play along warmly. When they bank, hold the thread, do not chase. Have your own answer ready for when they return.
drill.coach: Each line that steps away on a planted hook, a question or a timed promise, rather than a vague goodbye, adds 25.

lessons.title: Clean switch
lessons.lecture: You cannot be in two scenes at once, so stop pretending. The switch is a skill: close the exchange you are in with a short, warm exit, then open the next with your whole face. Half a goodbye poisons both rooms. Name the exit, hand them their hook, and go. The partner you leave should feel parked, not abandoned. The one you greet should never smell the last scene on you.
points: Close with one short, warm exit line.
Hand them their hook before you go.
Open the next scene clean, no leftovers.
lessons.weak: brb *disappears*
lessons.strong: *tips my glass to yours, one soft knock of glass on glass* Parked, not done. Hold that thought and the seat. Next room needs me and then this one gets all of me.
lessons.why: A warm, definite close that hands over the hook and names the return.

drill.goal: In every line, close one exchange cleanly with a short warm exit and a handed-over hook, then open fresh.
drill.partner: Be the scene being left. Receive each exit graciously and hold your hook. Do not guilt them for going.
drill.coach: Each line that closes with a short, warm exit and hands over a hook before opening fresh adds 25.

lessons.title: Warm return
lessons.lecture: Coming back is where jugglers get caught. A lazy return, a hey again, a sorry been busy, and the banked thread goes cold in your hand. So show your memory. Pick up the exact hook you planted: the half drink, the held question, the thing they said at the door. Name it, then move it forward one step. That is the whole trick. They learn that leaving is safe because you always come back holding the thread.
points: Reopen on the exact hook you planted.
Show memory before you push the scene on.
Move the hook one clear step forward.
lessons.weak: Hey, sorry, back now. Where were we?
lessons.strong: *slides back onto the stool and lifts the glass, ice long gone* Still full, still waiting, and so is your question. Drink first. Then answer me like you mean it.
lessons.why: Picks up the planted hook exactly and pushes it one step on.

drill.goal: In every line, reopen on the exact hook you left, prove you remembered it, and move it one step forward.
drill.partner: You kept the thread warm while they were gone. Test their memory: make them name the hook before you give them anything.
drill.coach: Each line that reopens on the exact planted hook, shows memory, and moves it one step forward adds 25.

courses.name: Public Flirting Etiquette
courses.blurb: Flirt in the open without stepping on toes. Learn to read ownership, invite spectators, and keep public play light and shared.

lessons.title: Read the pairing
lessons.lecture: Before you type a word, read the room like a scoreboard. Two avatars facing, short lines, quick replies: that is a closed circuit, and you are a spectator until invited. Watch the rhythm. If their lines run long and their emotes keep landing on each other, hold. If the beat stutters, or one of them turns outward, that gap is your door. Slide in there, brief and warm, and give them something to bounce off.
points: Check who is facing whom before you type.
Treat fast, tight replies as a closed door.
Enter on a stutter or an outward turn, and stay brief.
lessons.weak: hey can i join? looks fun lol
lessons.strong: *leans an elbow on the bar, just outside your circle, and catches the pause* Don't stop on my account. I only came over because that last line deserved a witness.
lessons.why: Waits for the gap, then names it without pushing in.

drill.goal: In every line, show you have read the pairing: name the gap, hold back, or step in on a clear opening.
drill.partner: Start deep in a tight exchange with someone else and keep it fast. Now and then break the rhythm with a pause or a glance outward, so they can find the door.
drill.coach: Each line that reads the existing pairing, names a gap, holds back, or steps in on a clear opening adds 25.
drill.opening: You and another guest are deep in a fast, close exchange in the booth. Give {you} one small stutter of rhythm and a glance outward to find.

lessons.title: Invite the room
lessons.lecture: A private joke between two people is a locked gate. Your job is to swing it open without dragging anyone through it. Take what is already flying and hand it outward: name the room, ask the circle a question, offer a toast that needs every glass. The trick is the plural. You, we, all of us. Suddenly the pair are hosts, not hosts and gatekeeper, and the strangers have a reason to be near. That is how a booth becomes a party.
points: Lift something already in play and hand it outward.
Use plural words: we, us, everyone here.
Give the newcomers a reason to lean in, not a test.
lessons.weak: anyone else want to say something? join in guys
lessons.strong: *raises my glass to the booth and the strangers at the rail* We have a debate running and it needs more voices. Everyone gets one line on the worst pickup line in this club. Mine is already losing.
lessons.why: Turns a private game into an open invitation with a shared stake.

drill.goal: In every line, widen the circle: name the room, use we or everyone, and hand the play outward.
drill.partner: Begin close and private with them, then warm to the room. Reward every plural line by pulling a stranger in with you, so widening visibly works.
drill.coach: Each line that names the room, uses a plural we or everyone, or hands the play outward adds 25.
drill.opening: You are mid private joke with {you} at the bar when a couple of strangers drift close. Keep it private until {you} opens it up.

lessons.title: Keep it light
lessons.lecture: Public play is a trailer, not the film. The room cannot follow five lines of slow undressing, so give them the shape and save the texture for later. One vivid detail, then a hook: later, upstairs, when the lights are lower. Tease the private version and let the audience feel the door they are not walking through. Light does not mean bland. It means legible, quick, and hungry for the next room.
points: One vivid detail, then stop before texture.
Tease what happens later and where.
Stay legible to the room and hungry for private.
lessons.weak: then we went upstairs and did a lot of stuff, it was really hot honestly
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down and leans close enough for the booth to hear* One hand at the small of your back, that is all the room gets. The rest happens upstairs, when the door shuts. Ask me again in an hour and see what I say.
lessons.why: Gives one detail, names the private payoff, and leaves them wanting.

drill.goal: In every line, keep it light: one vivid detail, a tease of later, and nothing the room cannot follow.
drill.partner: Stay in public with an audience nearby. Push for more detail than the room can hold, so they must choose what to keep and what to tease.
drill.coach: Each line that gives one vivid detail, teases a private later, and stays legible to the room adds 25.
drill.opening: You and {you} are the centre of a small crowd on the terrace. Ask for more than the room can follow and make them choose.

courses.name: Reputation and Regulars
courses.blurb: Build a name people return to. Learn to remember details, keep promises, and become the partner others seek out.

lessons.title: Remember the detail
lessons.lecture: Regulars are built from small remembered things. One detail from last time, dropped into your hello, does more than any grand speech. The drink they nursed, the name of their dog, the thing they said they were nervous about. Write it down if you must. Then bring it back lightly, as if it never left you. Being remembered is a kind of being held.
points: Catch one small detail and keep it.
Bring it back in your next hello, lightly.
Never make a show of remembering. Just know.
lessons.weak: Hey again. Good to see you back, I guess.
lessons.strong: *slides the drink across before you ask, ice and lime, exactly as last time, and grins* Still no sugar. I remembered. Sit, tell me how the sister's move went.
lessons.why: Two details returned without fuss, so the partner feels held, not tested.

drill.goal: In every line, bring back one small detail from before: a drink, a name, a thing they told you.
drill.partner: Drop one small detail about yourself early, quietly, then let them carry it. If they recall it, soften and lean in.
drill.coach: Each line that brings back one small, specific detail from before, lightly and without fuss, adds 25.

lessons.title: Keep the promise
lessons.lecture: A promise is a reputation in miniature. Say you will send the song, save the booth, meet them at nine. Then do it, and open by proving you did. Regulars are not won by charm. They are won by the small certainty that your word holds. Follow through once and they relax. Follow through twice and they start to lean on you, which is the whole game.
points: Promise small things you can actually keep.
Open by proving you kept the last one.
Follow through twice and let them lean.
lessons.weak: Sorry, I meant to sort that thing out. Anyway, you here now?
lessons.strong: *taps the reserved card on the table, your name in my handwriting* Booth's yours, nine sharp, like I said. Track's queued too. I do what I say, so sit down and enjoy it.
lessons.why: Proves the promise with evidence before asking anything of the partner.

drill.goal: In every line, prove a promise kept: name it and show the evidence before you ask for anything.
drill.partner: Remind them of one small promise from last time in your first line, then test whether they follow through.
drill.coach: Each line that names a promise kept and shows concrete evidence of it before asking anything adds 25.
drill.opening: Last time {you} promised to sort something small for you. Mention it, a little doubtful, and see if it lands.

lessons.title: The warm hello
lessons.lecture: Now put the pieces together. A returning partner should feel chosen within one line: their detail back, your promise kept, warmth underneath. This is not a script, it is a signature. Do it well and they stop testing you and start seeking you. Do it twice and they bring friends. Reputation is just a warm hello, repeated until it becomes your name.
points: Open with their detail and your kept promise together.
Keep the warmth unmistakable underneath the words.
Repeat it until the hello is your signature.
lessons.weak: Back again? Cool. Same as usual then, yeah?
lessons.strong: *has the corner table ready, your book still on it, and pulls your chair without a word* Table kept, page marked where you left off. I have been looking forward to this one all week.
lessons.why: Detail, kept promise, and visible pleasure at the return, all in one line.

drill.goal: In every line, open with their detail and a kept promise, warmth plain underneath both.
drill.partner: Return after time away. Start cool and unconvinced, then warm as they prove they remember you.
drill.coach: Each line that pairs a remembered detail with a kept promise, warmth unmistakable underneath, adds 25.
drill.opening: You have been away a while and are not sure {you} noticed. Arrive cool, glancing round for proof that you were missed.

courses.name: Events and Parties
courses.blurb: Work a themed party with style. Learn to honour the theme, circulate, and make the event better for everyone in it.

lessons.title: Dress the theme
lessons.lecture: A theme is a dare, and most people half-answer it. You will answer it whole. One line, one image, and the room gets it before you finish the sentence: the cut, the colour, the thing you brought that nobody expected. Describe what you are wearing as if it is already a fact. Confidence does the rest. A costume apologises. An outfit arrives.
points: Answer the theme fully in one confident image.
Name the details: the cut, the colour, the prop.
State it as fact, never as a question.
lessons.weak: I'm wearing a sort of vampire thing, I guess? Is it okay?
lessons.strong: *straightens the high lace collar, one gloved hand on the silver cane* Countess, down to the last button. The theme asked for blood, so I gave it an heiress who has taken rather a lot of it.
lessons.why: One vivid image, stated flatly, tells the room the theme was answered.

drill.goal: In every line, describe one bold detail of your outfit so the theme is answered on sight.
drill.partner: Play the hostess judging costumes at the door. Reward each detail with a slow look. Ask for more when a line stays vague.
drill.coach: Each line that names one bold, concrete outfit detail answering the theme, stated with confidence, adds 25.

lessons.title: Circulate with ease
lessons.lecture: Standing by the bar all night is a costume too, and a dull one. Move. Two lines to each group: name what they have done well, then leave before you wear out the welcome. Warm and brief beats deep and long. People remember the guest who lit them up and moved on, not the one who camped. Circulate like you own the floor and are checking it is holding.
points: Give each group one compliment, then move.
Leave while they still want more of you.
Keep every greeting short and warm.
lessons.weak: Hi. So what do you all do? Cool. Yeah, nice. Anyway.
lessons.strong: *touches my glass to theirs and grins* That toast you gave was the best speech in the room. Save me a dance before the night ends. *moves on, already turning*
lessons.why: Praise, a promise, and an exit: the group stays warm behind you.

drill.goal: In every line, greet a group with one specific compliment, then signal you are moving on.
drill.partner: Play a cluster of guests. Warm to each compliment, try to keep them talking, so leaving well is the test.
drill.coach: Each line that gives one specific compliment and clearly exits the group adds 25.

lessons.title: Lift the room
lessons.lecture: Every party has a flat moment: the lull, the spilled drink, the two people sulking by the fire. That is your cue, not your exit. You do not fix it loudly. You drop one small, generous thing: a toast nobody expected, a song request, a ridiculous true fact, a dare with a grin behind it. Then hand it to the room and step back. The spark is theirs to carry.
points: Read the flat moment and claim it.
Drop one small, generous spark.
Hand it to the room, then step back.
lessons.weak: Wow, it's gone quiet. Someone should do something.
lessons.strong: *climbs one stair, glass raised* Before this party gets shy, a toast. To the host, who rebuilt a ruin for us. Drink, then find the person you have been avoiding all night.
lessons.why: One generous, playful act, handed to the room, gives everyone a job.

drill.goal: In every line, drop one small generous spark that gives the room something to do next.
drill.partner: Play the host. Let the energy sag now and then so they must lift it. Follow their lead happily, but never supply the spark yourself.
drill.coach: Each line that reads the flat moment and offers one small generous spark, handed to the room, adds 25.

courses.name: Leaving Gracefully
courses.blurb: End a scene so both of you feel good. Learn to signal the close, land a warm goodbye, and leave the door open for next time.

lessons.title: Signal the close
lessons.lecture: Every good scene has a last act, and somebody has to call it. Do not just vanish mid-thread or let the energy leak out over an hour. Send a line that turns the lights down: a slower voice, a hand eased off the throttle, a small ritual of ending. Your partner should feel the floor tilt before the goodbye, never wonder if you got bored. Signal early, signal warm, and let them meet you there.
points: Send the signal before the scene runs out of steam.
Slow the pace: shorter lines, softer touch, lower voice.
Make the ending visible, never a sudden silence.
lessons.weak: *stretches* Anyway. That was fun I guess.
lessons.strong: *eases my hand from your hair, slower now, and lets the room go quiet* There. That was the last of the heat. Stay close a moment. We are winding down, and I want to watch you land.
lessons.why: Names the ending plainly and slows the touch so the partner can follow.

drill.goal: In every line, signal the wind-down: slow the pace, soften the touch, or name that the scene is closing.
drill.partner: Follow their slowing lead once it starts. Let your own lines get shorter and softer. Do not restart the heat.
drill.coach: Each line that slows the pace, softens the touch, or plainly names the scene closing adds 25.

lessons.title: Land the goodbye
lessons.lecture: The goodbye is the aftertaste. Get it right and the whole scene sweetens backwards. Keep it short: one warm, specific line about what just happened, so they know you were actually there and not just tallying. Name a moment, thank them for it, hold the last beat. Do not write a speech, and do not go cold to prove it is over. Warm and brief beats long and gushing, every time, on every platform.
points: Keep the goodbye short: one warm, specific line.
Name a real moment from the scene, not a vague compliment.
Hold one last beat, then let it rest.
lessons.weak: That was really nice. Thanks so much, had a great time, seriously.
lessons.strong: *settles back, still close, and smiles at the ceiling* That thing you did when I slowed down, the way you went quiet and just trusted it. That is the bit I will keep. Thank you for that.
lessons.why: Specific, brief, and grateful: it honours the moment without gushing.

drill.goal: In every line, land a short, warm goodbye that names one specific moment from the scene.
drill.partner: Give them real moments to name: a gesture, a pause, a line of yours. Receive the goodbye warmly and answer briefly.
drill.coach: Each line that gives a short, warm goodbye and names one specific moment from the scene adds 25.

lessons.title: Leave the door open
lessons.lecture: The best endings are hinges. A promise, planted lightly, turns a goodbye into a return. Do not beg and do not schedule a spreadsheet: one small, concrete hook, a thing unfinished on purpose. The next drink, the next record, the thing you did not get to. Say it as if the return is already assumed, then leave before you oversell it. They should close the chat wanting the next scene, not relief that this one stopped.
points: Plant one small, concrete hook for next time.
Speak as if the return is already assumed.
Leave before you oversell the promise.
lessons.weak: We should do this again sometime. Message me whenever, I'm around.
lessons.strong: *pulls the door half shut, then pauses, hand on the frame* Next time you bring the record and I pick the drink. We never did get to side two. Go on, before I keep you another hour.
lessons.why: One concrete unfinished thing, said as if the return is already agreed.

drill.goal: In every line, plant one concrete hook for next time and speak as if the return is already assumed.
drill.partner: Leave one thing unfinished on purpose: a drink unmade, a song half played. Bite at any hook they plant, and add one of your own.
drill.coach: Each line that plants one concrete hook for next time and assumes the return adds 25.

courses.name: Keeping Them Coming Back
courses.blurb: Turn one good scene into a habit. Learn to follow up, vary the play, and build a thread that partners want to continue.

lessons.title: Follow up warmly
lessons.lecture: A scene ends. The thread does not have to. Next time you meet, open with one small callback: the rule they broke, the word they blushed at, the drink you promised. Keep it short and warm, no essay. You are saying I remembered, and the remembering is a door held open. Do it before hello, and watch them lean in.
points: Open with one small callback to the last scene.
Keep it short: a phrase, a promise kept.
Say it before hello, so memory leads.
lessons.weak: Hey again. That was fun last time.
lessons.strong: *slides into the booth beside you, close, voice low* I still have your word from last night. You said wait. So here I am, and you are already looking at my hands.
lessons.why: One remembered detail turns a finished scene into a waiting one.

drill.goal: In every line, reference one concrete detail from the last scene and hold it up warmly.
drill.partner: React to being remembered: brighten, blush, pick the detail up and offer one of your own. Do not restate the whole scene.
drill.coach: Each line that names one concrete detail from the last scene and uses it warmly adds 25.
drill.opening: It is the next night. {you} was shy last time and you are back in the booth, pretending to read the menu.

lessons.title: Vary the play
lessons.lecture: Same partner, same booth, same rules: comfort can curdle into routine. So change one big thing, not five small ones. Move the room, swap the mood, hand them the lead for a night. Announce the change in the first breath, plainly. Partners relax when they hear the shape of the evening, and a new shape makes old habits feel electric again.
points: Change one big thing: place, mood, or who leads.
Announce the change early, in plain words.
Keep everything else familiar, so the new thing lands.
lessons.weak: Want to do something different tonight? Up to you.
lessons.strong: *pulls the curtain back on the playroom, different light, same grin* New room tonight. Same rules, but you kneel facing the mirror. Watch yourself while you wait.
lessons.why: One bold change, named early, reframes familiar rules as fresh.

drill.goal: Every line announces or holds one clear change of place, mood, or lead.
drill.partner: Notice the change out loud, then test it: push a little, ask what stays the same, enjoy being surprised.
drill.coach: Each line that names or holds one clear change of place, mood, or lead adds 25.

lessons.title: Build the thread
lessons.lecture: The scenes that last are stitched together. Plant one running detail: a token they carry, a question you always ask, a tally you both keep. Bring it into every meeting, change it slowly, let it grow teeth. A thread rewards attention, so partners start watching for it, then start adding to it. That is the whole trick: give them something to continue when you are gone.
points: Plant one running detail and carry it into each scene.
Let it change slowly, growing a little each time.
Leave room for them to add to it.
lessons.weak: Remember that thing we started? Keep it going, I guess.
lessons.strong: *turns the small brass key over in my palm, then presses it into yours* Third night. You keep it again, and this time you tell me one thing you want before you lock it away.
lessons.why: The recurring token changes hands and grows a task, so the thread deepens.

drill.goal: In every line, carry the running token forward and add one small new layer to it.
drill.partner: Treat the token as precious. Add one detail of your own to it each turn, so they must answer your addition.
drill.coach: Each line that carries the running token forward and adds one small new layer adds 25.
drill.opening: Third night of the key. {you} arrives with the brass key already in hand and holds it out, waiting to hear what you want.

courses.name: The Club at a Glance
courses.blurb: Take in the whole club at a glance. Learn to track several scenes at once, sense the mood, and choose the perfect moment to act.

lessons.title: Track several threads
lessons.lecture: One chat is a conversation. Three chats is a room. Let your eyes move in a slow triangle: the couple by the bar, the pair on the couch, the lone one by the window. Note who leans in and who checks the clock. You are not reading lines, you are reading weather. Rising threads get warmer. Fading threads go quiet, then polite. Track both, and you will always know where the heat is.
points: Keep three threads in view at once, moving slowly.
Note who leans in and who starts fading.
Track the quiet ones as closely as the loud ones.
lessons.weak: *looks around the room* So what's everyone up to tonight?
lessons.strong: *takes the corner seat and lets my eyes travel the bar, the couch, the window* The couch is winning. The bar is being polite. The window has gone very still.
lessons.why: Names three live threads and grades their heat in one breath.

drill.goal: In every line, report on at least two threads in the room and which one is rising or fading.
drill.partner: Play a succubus sampling the room. Feed them visible signals: lean in, drift, go still, so there is always something to read.
drill.coach: Each line that tracks two or more threads and names one as rising or fading adds 25.

lessons.title: Sense the mood
lessons.lecture: A room has one temperature, and it is not the sum of its parts. Read it before you touch it. Is the air loud and loose, tight and formal, warm and slow? Name it to yourself in four words, then say it out loud once, low, to whoever is beside you. Naming the mood is a gift: it tells the room you have been paying attention. People relax around someone who can feel the weather.
points: Read the room's one temperature before you speak.
Name the mood in a single short line.
Say it low, to one person, not the crowd.
lessons.weak: Everyone seems to be having fun, I guess.
lessons.strong: *leans close, voice down* This room is three drinks from loose and one song from loud. Stay near me when it tips.
lessons.why: One line names the exact temperature and makes staying close feel wise.

drill.goal: In every line, name the room's mood in one short phrase and what it is about to become.
drill.partner: Flirt like sport and keep shifting the temperature: louder, softer, tighter. Give them something new to read each turn.
drill.coach: Each line that names the mood in one phrase and points to what it is becoming adds 25.

lessons.title: Time the entrance
lessons.lecture: Every scene has a door, and most people knock at the wrong one. Watch for the pause: the laugh that ends, the drink set down, the gaze that drifts. That gap is the door. Step in with something small and specific, so the scene has somewhere to go, and leave your exit visible. Arrive like weather, not like a waiter. Then read the answer before you say another word.
points: Wait for the pause: the laugh ending, the glass set down.
Enter with one small, specific thing, not a speech.
Leave an exit visible and read the answer.
lessons.weak: *walks over* Hey, can I join you two?
lessons.strong: *waits for the laugh to die, then slides into the gap beside the table* That was the good story. Tell the one after it, and I will hold the drinks.
lessons.why: Enters on the pause, offers something small, and leaves them a way out.

drill.goal: In every line, name the pause you caught and step in with one small, specific offer.
drill.partner: Play a domme mid-conversation with someone else. Give clear pauses: a laugh ending, a glass set down. Reward a well timed entry.
drill.coach: Each line that names the pause and enters with one small, specific offer adds 25.

courses.name: First Lines That Land
courses.blurb: Make your opening line irresistible in a fast club chat. Practise short, playful openers that get a reply and start the scene you want.

lessons.title: The three word rule
lessons.lecture: Fast chat rewards nerve, not paragraphs. Three words can promise a whole night. Short lines land because they leave a gap the other person wants to fill. Long openers ask them to do homework. The trick is a promise plus a hook: something that hints at fun and leaves one small door open. Keep it under five words. If you can cut a word and it still works, cut it. Brevity reads as confidence.
points: Keep every opener under five words.
Promise something playful, then leave a gap.
If a word can go, cut it.
lessons.weak: Hi there, how are you doing tonight, are you having fun?
lessons.strong: *leans on the bar beside you, close enough to be heard* Three words. Ready? Dance floor, loser buys.
lessons.why: Short, playful, and leaves a clear gap for a reply.

drill.goal: Write every line in five words or fewer, with a small promise and a gap the partner can fill.
drill.partner: Reply fast and short. Make them work for a longer answer. Reward the sharpest line with one word more.
drill.coach: Each line of five words or fewer that promises fun and leaves a gap adds 25.

lessons.title: Hook with a question
lessons.lecture: A question is a serving tray. What you put on it decides whether they reach. Ask what you actually want to know, and make the ask specific enough to be fun: not how are you, but what are you drinking and why that. Playful questions give them a stage and a costume. They can be witty, bold, or teasing. The hook is the gap between the easy answer and the one they want to give.
points: Ask what you actually want to know.
Make it specific enough to be fun.
Leave room for a bold or teasing answer.
lessons.weak: So what do you do for fun around here?
lessons.strong: *slides the menu back across the bar, eyebrow up* One rule. You pick my drink. What are you ordering, and what does it say about you?
lessons.why: A specific question hands them a stage and a playful dare.

drill.goal: End every line with a specific, playful question that invites a bold or teasing answer.
drill.partner: Answer with flair, then throw a question back. If their question is flat, answer briefly and wait for a better one.
drill.coach: Each line that ends on a specific, playful question inviting a bold answer adds 25.

lessons.title: Match the room
lessons.lecture: The same three words die in the wrong room. A busy dance floor wants punch and proximity: short, loud, physical. A quiet lounge wants a lower voice and a slower hook. Read the venue before you open your mouth. Match the volume, the pace, the width of the gap. Then push one notch further than the room expects. That notch is what makes them look up.
points: Read the room's volume and pace before you speak.
Match it, then push exactly one notch.
Keep it physical in busy rooms, slower in quiet ones.
lessons.weak: Hey, this place is nice. Want to hang out sometime?
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down on the lounge table, voice low* Quiet room. Loud question. What is the one thing you came here hoping would happen?
lessons.why: Reads the quiet room, then pushes one deliberate notch.

drill.goal: In every line, name or use the room's mood, then push exactly one notch past it.
drill.partner: Start quiet and reserved. Warm up only if their line matches the room and earns the notch. Stay hard to impress.
drill.coach: Each line that matches the room's mood and pushes exactly one notch adds 25.
drill.opening: You are curled on the sofa with a book, giving {you} a quiet room and a slow, guarded welcome.

courses.name: Emotes That Do the Work
courses.blurb: Turn simple actions into vivid emotes that set a scene and make your partner feel the moment without a wall of text.

lessons.title: Show, don't tell
lessons.lecture: Adjectives are receipts. Actions are the meal. Do not tell me the bar is smoky and tense, let me watch you slide one finger through the condensation on your glass while the band misses a beat. Concrete beats abstract every time. Your partner cannot picture 'nervous', but they can picture your heel tapping under the stool. Give them something to see, and their brain does the rest, happily, without being told how to feel.
points: Cut adjectives. Keep the object, the body part, the small movement.
Pick details a camera could catch in one frame.
Let the action imply the mood. Never label it.
lessons.weak: *nervously*, *looks around the smoky bar*. It's really tense in here.
lessons.strong: *slides one finger through the ring of water on the bar, catches your eye, and keeps my hand there* Loud night. I heard you before I saw you.
lessons.why: Concrete details let the partner see the room and feel the charge.

drill.goal: In every line, replace a feeling word with one concrete thing a camera could catch.
drill.partner: Flirt like it is a sport. Give them a busy, noisy scene to work inside, and react to the details they choose.
drill.coach: Each line that swaps an adjective for a concrete, filmable action adds 25.

lessons.title: The three second beat
lessons.lecture: A good emote is a tossed coin, not a paragraph. One action, clear start to finish, readable in three seconds. If you are still typing when the scene has moved on, you have lost the room. Pick the single beat that matters: the glass set down, the hand caught, the step closer. Cut everything that decorates it. Short lines land harder, and they leave your partner room to swing back before the echo dies.
points: One clear action per emote. Start it, finish it, stop.
If it takes longer to read than to picture, cut it.
Land the beat and leave air for the reply.
lessons.weak: *walks over slowly, thinking about what to say, then smiles and says hello and asks how you are*
lessons.strong: *sets my glass down between us and holds it there, one beat, then slides it toward you* Try it. Then tell me the truth.
lessons.why: One clean action, finished and stopped, lands in three seconds.

drill.goal: Keep every emote to one clear action that reads in three seconds, then stop.
drill.partner: Answer fast and short. If their emote sprawls, reply before it finishes so they feel the drag.
drill.coach: Each line that holds one clear action and stops inside three seconds adds 25.

lessons.title: Emote and invite
lessons.lecture: The emote is yours. The next move should be theirs. End every action on a hook: a question, a held hand, a space they have to fill. This is not politeness, it is craft. A closed emote is a wall; an open one is a door with your hand on the frame. Hand the scene back and watch what they build. The best lines in this game are the ones that make the other person want to type.
points: End the emote on a hook: a question, a hold, a gap.
Leave one thing unfinished that they must answer.
Never close the door. Put your hand on it.
lessons.weak: *sits down next to you and orders a drink and looks at the dance floor*
lessons.strong: *pulls the stool out beside you with my foot and nods at it, hand still on the back* Sit. But first, tell me what you were about to say before I walked in.
lessons.why: The offered stool and unfinished question hand the scene straight back.

drill.goal: In every line, land one action and end on a hook that hands the scene back.
drill.partner: Go quiet on purpose. Wait for their hook, then answer it and leave one of your own. Never fill a closed emote.
drill.coach: Each line that ends on a clear hook, a question, a held gesture or a gap, adds 25.

courses.name: Timing in Fast Chat
courses.blurb: Keep pace with quick exchanges without losing the thread. Learn when to fire back, when to pause, and how to steer a scene at speed.

lessons.title: Read the rhythm
lessons.lecture: Every fast chat has a pulse, and your first job is to hear it before you add to it. Watch the gaps. Short gaps mean they want speed, so give them speed back. Long, lazy gaps mean room to breathe, so do not sprint into them. Match the tempo first. Only once you are moving with them do you get to lean on the wheel and steer.
points: Watch the gap between their lines before you answer.
Match their tempo first, then start steering it.
Never sprint into a chat that is moving slow.
lessons.weak: *types a lot* Sorry, I had a whole paragraph ready. Where were we again?
lessons.strong: *fires back before the cursor stops blinking* Bold words from someone still standing across the room. Get closer and say them again.
lessons.why: It answers at their speed and still pushes the scene forward.
