drill.goal: In every line, answer at the tempo of their last line and add one small push forward.
drill.partner: Keep your lines short and quick, then slow right down now and then. Do not wait for them. Make them chase the tempo.
drill.coach: Each line that matches the pace of the last line and moves the scene on adds 25.
drill.opening: Open fast and flirty, two short lines, and make {you} work to keep up.

lessons.title: The one line reply
lessons.lecture: Speed kills paragraphs. When the chat is flying, a wall of text is a traffic jam. Your line should do one job and do it now: a question, a dare, a small action, a confession. One idea, one breath, sent before the moment cools. If you cannot say it in a line, you are explaining instead of playing. Cut the explanation. Keep the spark.
points: One idea per line: a question, a dare, an action.
Send before the moment cools, not after.
If it needs explaining, cut the explanation.
lessons.weak: *thinks for a while* Well, I suppose what I am trying to say is that I quite like you, actually, in a way.
lessons.strong: *leans on the bar beside you* One drink. Then you tell me the thing you keep almost saying.
lessons.why: One clean idea, sent fast, that leaves them something to answer.

drill.goal: In every line, deliver exactly one idea: a question, a dare, an action or a confession, nothing more.
drill.partner: Reply fast with one idea of your own. If they send a paragraph, tease them for it. Keep the ball moving.
drill.coach: Each line that carries exactly one idea and sends it fast adds 25.

lessons.title: Pause with purpose
lessons.lecture: Fast is not the same as frantic. The master move is the held beat: you let the chat race, then you stop it dead with one short line and let the silence do the work. A pause after a dare, a pause before an answer, a pause where they can hear you deciding. Do not pause to think. Pause so they have to. Then land the line that pays it off.
points: Let the chat race, then stop it with one short line.
Pause after a dare or before a big answer.
Never pause to think. Pause so they have to.
lessons.weak: *long gap* okay so, um, give me a second, I am deciding something, hold on.
lessons.strong: *lets the chat run, then one line, no more* Come here. *nothing else, no explanation*
lessons.why: The held beat turns speed into tension they have to answer.

drill.goal: In every line, either hold a deliberate beat with a short line or pay off a beat they held.
drill.partner: Push the pace hard, then go silent and wait for them to fill it. Make the quiet feel expensive, not empty.
drill.coach: Each line that holds a deliberate beat or pays one off with a short, sharp line adds 25.

courses.name: Approaching in Clubs
courses.blurb: Walk into a busy club and start something with confidence. Learn to read the floor, pick your moment, and open without crashing the vibe.

lessons.title: Scan the floor
lessons.lecture: A busy club is a room full of doors, and most of them are already shut. Stand still, drink in hand, and watch for a full minute. Who is mid-scene and glowing? Leave them. Who is dancing with their own glass, glancing around? That is an open door. Aim at the open ones. Reading first is not hesitation. It is how you walk in like you belong.
points: Watch a full minute before you move.
Skip anyone deep in a scene or a kiss.
Aim at the ones glancing around, glass in hand.
lessons.weak: Hey everyone, anyone want to talk?
lessons.strong: *leans against the bar, slow sip, eyes moving across the floor* Not them, they're deep in it. Not them either. *settles on you, alone with your drink* You. You keep looking up.
lessons.why: It reads the room first, then picks one open door out loud.

drill.goal: In every line, name who you are skipping and who you are choosing, and why, from something visible.
drill.partner: Stay by the bar with a drink, glancing around. Let them spot you. Look pleased when they pick you out.
drill.coach: Each line that reads the floor visibly, naming who is closed and who is open, adds 25.

lessons.title: The side step
lessons.lecture: Groups are circles, and circles have gaps. Do not stand at the edge waving. Listen for the half second where a story lands and laughter fills it, then slide one short line into that gap. Something about what they just said, never about yourself. The circle closes around you or it does not. Either way you did not crash it. You slipped in like you were always coming.
points: Listen for the gap where a story lands.
Slide in one short line about what they said.
Never introduce yourself into the middle of a joke.
lessons.weak: Hi, I'm new here, can I join you all?
lessons.strong: *steps into the pause after the punchline, grin easy* Wait, she actually said that to his face? *lifts my glass* I need the rest of this story.
lessons.why: It lands in the laugh, asks about their story, not itself.

drill.goal: In every line, enter on something they just said: a question, a callback, or a shared laugh.
drill.partner: Be mid-story with friends, loud and laughing. Leave a real gap after each punchline and let them find it.
drill.coach: Each line that enters on something just said, in a natural gap, without crashing, adds 25.

lessons.title: The confident close
lessons.lecture: The opener is public. The close is private, and it takes three clean lines: what you noticed, what you want, where. No hedging, no maybe if you're free. Notice something only close attention would catch. Say the want plainly. Name the spot. Then stop talking and let them answer. Three lines, one breath, and the whole club goes quiet around the two of you.
points: Notice something only close attention would catch.
Say what you want plainly, no hedging.
Name the place. Then stop and let them answer.
lessons.weak: So, um, do you maybe want to get out of here sometime?
lessons.strong: *close enough that the music drops to background* You've been humming the same song for an hour. I want the version only you sing. Rooftop, ten minutes, my bottle. *waits*
lessons.why: Notices, wants, names the place, then stops and waits.

drill.goal: In every line, deliver one of the three moves: notice, want, or place. Then stop.
drill.partner: Blush at the notice. Do not fill silences. Answer only when the three moves are done, and make them wait.
drill.coach: Each line that cleanly delivers notice, want, or place, then stops without hedging, adds 25.

courses.name: Dressing the Scene
courses.blurb: Describe outfits and bodies so they feel touchable. Learn to build a look with words that flatter, tease, and invite a reply.

lessons.title: Two detail rule
lessons.lecture: You cannot describe everything, so do not try. Pick two details and let the rest of the outfit live in your partner's head, where it will burn brighter than anything you write. A collar, a cuff, the strap that slipped. Two concrete things, placed where their eye would land if they were really standing in front of you. More than two and you are cataloguing. Two and you are looking.
points: Choose exactly two concrete details, not five.
Place them where their eye would naturally fall.
Let the rest of the outfit stay imagined.
lessons.weak: You look nice. Nice dress, nice shoes, nice hair, nice everything really.
lessons.strong: *leans back in the booth and lets my eyes land, once, on the silver clasp at your throat, then on the strap that has slipped off your shoulder* That clasp. That strap. The rest I can guess at.
lessons.why: Two precise details give their imagination room to finish the picture.

drill.goal: In every line, name exactly two concrete details of what they wear or how it sits, and nothing more.
drill.partner: Dress up for the booth, a little daring. Shift so details catch the light, and let them look. Do not describe yourself first.
drill.coach: Each line that picks out exactly two concrete visible details, without cataloguing more, adds 25.

lessons.title: Fabric and feel
lessons.lecture: A look is not a photograph, it is a sensation. Silk says one thing, denim says another, and both are wasted if you only name them. Describe how the fabric moves, how it fits, where it clings and where it gives. Your partner wants to feel the outfit on their skin before you ever touch it. Write the cloth as if your hand already knows it, and theirs will believe you.
points: Name the fabric and how it moves or fits.
Write the feel as if your hand knows it.
Let cling and give do the teasing.
lessons.weak: That shirt looks soft. It fits you well, I think.
lessons.strong: *fingers hover at the loose cuff of your linen shirt, close enough to feel the weave breathe* Linen in this heat. It creases where you move, and it gives at the shoulder when you lean.
lessons.why: Specific fabric and movement let them feel the cloth on their skin.

drill.goal: In every line, describe one fabric and how it moves, fits, clings or gives, as if by touch.
drill.partner: Wear something soft and light for the heat. Lean close, let the fabric shift, and react to how it feels when they name it.
drill.coach: Each line that names a fabric and its movement, fit, cling or give, felt by touch, adds 25.

lessons.title: Undress with words
lessons.lecture: Undressing with words is a strip tease for the mind, and it keeps its clothes on far longer than the body does. Go in order, slowly, one fastening, one layer, one shift at a time. Let each detail land before the next. Say what is revealed and what it does to you, not just what it is. The tension comes from the pause between one piece and the next. Rush it and you are just listing laundry.
points: Take it in order, one fastening or layer at a time.
Let each detail land before you move on.
Say what the reveal does to you, not just what it is.
lessons.weak: So I undo your dress and it falls down and you are standing there in your underwear.
lessons.strong: *finds the zip at your back and draws it down an inch, then stops, palm flat on the bare line of skin it opens* First this. The dress loosens at the shoulder. I am not in a hurry, and you can hear that.
lessons.why: One slow fastening, then a pause, lets the reveal build its own pull.

drill.goal: In every line, reveal one layer, fastening or detail in order, and pause before the next.
drill.partner: Wear something with real fastenings, buttons or a zip. Hold still and let them work slowly. Do not finish undressing for them.
drill.coach: Each line that reveals one fastening, layer or detail in order, and holds a pause, adds 25.

courses.name: Poses and Presence
courses.blurb: Use posture and position to say something before you speak. Learn poses that project mood, invite approach, and anchor a scene.

lessons.title: Pose with intent
lessons.lecture: In chat, your pose arrives before your words and sets the temperature. So pick one mood and build the body to match it: back to the bar, chin down, drink held loose, or hip against the doorframe and arms folded. One mood, held cleanly, no shuffling. Your partner reads it in a glance and knows what kind of night this is. Split moods read as nerves.
points: Choose one mood before you type a single word.
Build the whole body to match it, head to feet.
Hold it cleanly. No fidgeting, no half poses.
lessons.weak: *stands there, kind of leaning, maybe smiling* Hi. So, um, here I am.
lessons.strong: *sets my back to the bar, elbows behind me, chin lowered, and lets the glass hang from two fingers* Took your time. I was starting to enjoy the waiting.
lessons.why: One relaxed, cocky mood, built from head to hands, before a word lands.

drill.goal: In every line, hold one clear mood in the body: same posture, same energy, no drifting.
drill.partner: Answer the pose in your reply and show what it does to you. If the mood slips, let your warmth cool a little. Reward a mood that holds by warming to it.
drill.coach: Each line that holds one clear mood in visible posture, carried from the last line, adds 25.

lessons.title: The open invitation
lessons.lecture: A closed pose is a wall. A great pose is a door left ajar. Make the gap obvious: a hand held out palm up, a chair nudged out with a foot, a shoulder turned so the space beside you is bare. The gap says step here, and it gives your partner something to do in their first line. Pose the invitation, then wait. Do not fill your own gap.
points: Leave one obvious gap: a hand, a chair, a bare shoulder.
Pose the invitation, then stop and let them move.
Never fill the gap yourself. That is their line.
lessons.weak: *pats the seat next to me* Come sit down if you want, I guess.
lessons.strong: *slides the stool out with my heel, turns my shoulder so the space stays bare, and rests one open palm on my knee* This seat is yours. I have not decided about the hand yet.
lessons.why: A bare seat and open palm give a clear door, then a hook.

drill.goal: Every line leaves one visible gap: an open hand, a made space, a turned shoulder waiting.
drill.partner: Step into the gap, but slowly. Hover once before you take it, so they must hold the offer and wait.
drill.coach: Each line that visibly offers a gap, hand, space or shoulder, and then waits without filling it adds 25.

lessons.title: Shift the frame
lessons.lecture: Poses are not statues. The master changes the frame and the room turns with it: from lounging to upright, from far to close, from open to folded, all in one clean move. Do not announce the shift, just make it, and let your next words carry the new weather. Change the body and the mood changes with it. Stillness is for the start. Command is in the move.
points: Change the pose in one clean, deliberate move.
Let the new words land after the shift, never before.
Shift to steer the mood, not to fill a silence.
lessons.weak: *moves around a bit* Okay, now I am being serious, I think, look at me.
lessons.strong: *pushes off the wall, crosses the room in four steps, and stops close enough that you have to look up* Enough lounging. Now we do this properly.
lessons.why: One decisive move changes the weather, and the words follow the body.

drill.goal: In every line, shift the pose visibly, then let the words carry the new mood the move created.
drill.partner: Match each shift with your own, and push back once by shifting first so they must answer it. Make them earn every change.
drill.coach: Each line that makes one visible pose change and lands words in the new mood, not the old, adds 25.
drill.opening: Lounge against the window, half turned away from {you}, and make them come to you first.

courses.name: Rooms That Set the Mood
courses.blurb: Use the game's spaces as props. Learn to pick a room, describe it in one line, and let the setting do half the seduction for you.

lessons.title: Choose the room
lessons.lecture: Every room in this game is a mood with walls. A hot tub says slow and skin and steam. A private gym says effort, sweat, a spotter's hands. Before you type a word, decide what you want them to feel, then walk them into the room that already feels it. Pick wrong and you fight the furniture all night. Pick right and the space flirts for you.
points: Decide the mood before you send a single line.
Pick the room that already feels like that mood.
Never fight a space that says the wrong thing.
lessons.weak: Want to hang out somewhere? Anywhere is fine, you pick.
lessons.strong: *pushes the hot tub gate open and steam rolls out past my shoulders* Get in. The water is already warm, and the pool lights are low.
lessons.why: The room is chosen for its mood before a single word of seduction.

drill.goal: In every line, name the room or a feature of it that matches the mood you are building.
drill.partner: Follow them into the space. React to the mood the room creates, and if the room fights the moment, let your character feel it and hesitate.
drill.coach: Each line that names the room or a feature matching the mood adds 25.

lessons.title: One line setting
lessons.lecture: A room lands in one line or not at all. Do not write a paragraph of decor. Choose the one detail that does the work: the candle already lit, the rain on the window, the rope coiled on the sheets. Name it and keep moving. One sharp detail lets your partner's imagination finish the room, and imagination always builds something better than your description.
points: Choose one detail, not a full tour.
Name it in a short line and move on.
Let their imagination finish the room for you.
lessons.weak: *describes the room* There is a bed, a lamp, some chairs, a window, and it is raining outside.
lessons.strong: *locks the door behind us, rain running down the glass, one lamp already low* The city can watch. You, come here.
lessons.why: Two details, rain and low light, then straight into the moment.

drill.goal: In every line, include one concrete room detail: a light, a sound, a surface, in a short phrase.
drill.partner: Pick up the details they give you and add your own. If they list the whole room, ask them to choose one thing.
drill.coach: Each line that carries one concrete room detail in a short phrase adds 25.

lessons.title: Let the space play
lessons.lecture: Now the room becomes a partner. Furniture is not scenery, it is something to use: press them against the door, lift them onto the counter, make them wait on the cold tiles. Lighting is a dial you turn. Move them through the space and let each surface ask something of them. The room does half the seduction, and you look like you planned it, because you did.
points: Use furniture as something to move them onto or against.
Turn the lighting like a dial as the mood shifts.
Let each surface ask something of your partner.
lessons.weak: *stands in the room* There is a couch over there if you want to sit down.
lessons.strong: *walks you back until the counter edge meets your hips, then lifts you onto it, one hand flat on the cold marble* Stay up there. The overhead light stays on until I say otherwise.
lessons.why: The counter and the light become active props that move the scene.

drill.goal: In every line, put a piece of furniture or a light to work: move them onto it, against it, or dim it.
drill.partner: Let the furniture move you. React to every surface they use, lean into it, and shift the lighting with them.
drill.coach: Each line that uses furniture or lighting as an active prop the partner can answer adds 25.

courses.name: Chatting on the Move
courses.blurb: Keep a scene alive while you hop rooms, change outfits, or dance. Learn to carry the thread and return without losing a beat.

lessons.title: Bridge the gap
lessons.lecture: A room change is a dead air you can fill. Most people drop the thread the second they walk, and the scene cools on the floor. You will not. Before you step, send one short line that keeps the promise alive: where you are going, what waits there, why they should follow. Two seconds of text carries the whole scene across the threshold. Keep it moving, keep it warm, and never let the gap go quiet.
points: Send one short line before you leave the room.
Name where you are going and what waits there.
Carry the mood with you, not just the fact.
lessons.weak: *walks off* Going to the other room, brb.
lessons.strong: *backs toward the archway, still watching you* Bar is too loud. I am taking my drink somewhere quieter, and I am taking my time. Come find me when the song ends.
lessons.why: Names the move, keeps the pull, and gives them a reason to follow.

drill.goal: In every line, carry the scene over a move: say where you are going and what stays alive there.
drill.partner: Notice the bridge and answer it from the old room. Follow only when the line gives you a reason to.
drill.coach: Each line that names the move and keeps the thread or mood alive across it adds 25.
drill.opening: You are dancing near {you} at the beach bar. Pull them into the set, then give them somewhere to follow.

lessons.title: Return with a hook
lessons.lecture: Coming back is a craft of its own. A plain hello drops like a wet towel on a good scene. So do not say hello. Re enter with the thread already in your hand: the drink you promised, the thing you saw, the dare you left hanging. One line, and it points forward, not back. They should feel the scene never paused, only stepped out for air and come back hungrier.
points: Re enter with the thread already in your hand.
Point the line forward, never just announce yourself.
Bring the thing you promised, or a better dare.
lessons.weak: *comes back* Hey, I'm back. Miss me?
lessons.strong: *slides the cold glass into your hand and leans on the rail beside you* Told you I would bring it. Now tell me what you did with the song while I was gone.
lessons.why: Returns the promise, resumes the touch, and asks a question that pushes on.

drill.goal: In every line, re enter with something carried over: a promise kept, a dare, or a detail from before.
drill.partner: Go quiet for a beat when they leave, then answer their return only if it hooks you forward. Reward a real hook.
drill.coach: Each line that re enters with a carried promise, dare, or detail and pushes forward adds 25.

lessons.title: Move with purpose
lessons.lecture: Now the master's cut. Anyone can hop rooms. You relocate because the story needs it: too many eyes, a song ending, a door you want them behind. Time it. Say it in the same breath as the touch, so the move is part of the heat, not a break from it. The room is not scenery. It is a lever. Choose the moment, make the move mean something, and let it pull them after you.
points: Relocate because the story needs it, not to fill time.
Time the move to a beat: a touch, a song ending.
Make the move itself part of the heat.
lessons.weak: *stands up* Want to go somewhere else now?
lessons.strong: *catches your wrist as the bass drops out, mouth close to your ear* Too many people. Stairs, now, before the next track starts and I change my mind about sharing you.
lessons.why: The move lands on the music and reads as want, not admin.

drill.goal: In every line, let a room or spot change land on a beat and pull the story forward, never just announce it.
drill.partner: Give them live beats to work with: a song ending, a crowd pressing in, a door. Follow a move that earns it, resist a flat one.
drill.coach: Each line that makes a timed, motivated relocation part of the story's heat adds 25.
drill.opening: The beach set is peaking and the crowd is tight around {you}. Give them a beat they can move on.

courses.name: Lag and AFK Grace
courses.blurb: Handle freezes and real life interruptions without killing the scene. Learn to signal, stall, and slide back in so nobody feels dropped.

lessons.title: Signal the stall
lessons.lecture: Real life does not wait for a good moment. The kettle boils, the door goes, the game stutters. The beginner goes silent and hopes. You will not. The instant you feel the pull away, fire one short line: a hand on their shoulder in text form. *one sec, don't move* does more than a paragraph an hour later. It tells them the scene is still lit and you are still in it. Signal first, explain never.
points: Send the signal the moment you feel the pull away.
Keep it short: a gesture, not an essay.
Say the scene holds, so they know to wait.
lessons.weak: sorry back soon
lessons.strong: *presses my hand flat to your chest and holds it there* Stay exactly like this. One minute, maybe two. Do not move a muscle till I am back.
lessons.why: One gesture freezes them in place, so the pause becomes part of the play.

drill.goal: In every line, send a short signal that you are still present and the scene is still holding.
drill.partner: Play Zara mid-scene at the club. When they signal, hold your position and stay warm. React with a little impatience, never hurt.
drill.coach: Each line that signals the stall in a short gesture and tells them the scene holds adds 25.

lessons.title: Hold the thread
lessons.lecture: A signal buys seconds. A hook buys minutes. When you know the freeze is coming, do not just say wait: leave something in their hands. A task, a question, an instruction they can chew on while you are gone. *Count the ice in my glass* beats *brb* every time, because they come back to you already busy with you. The scene keeps breathing on its own. You return to a partner mid-motion, not a blank screen.
points: Leave a small task or question they can hold.
Make the hook about the scene, not your excuse.
Give enough that they are busy when you return.
lessons.weak: *pauses* hang on a minute, something came up
lessons.strong: *lifts your chin with one finger, then lets go* Count to thirty, slowly, out loud. When I come back you tell me the number, and you do not stop at twenty-nine.
lessons.why: A counted task keeps them working inside the scene while you are gone.

drill.goal: In every line, leave one concrete hook, a task or question, that keeps the scene warm without you.
drill.partner: Play Yuki, imaginative and eager. Take every hook seriously and do it visibly. If the hook is vague, drift and look lost.
drill.coach: Each line that leaves one concrete task or question tied to the scene adds 25.

lessons.title: Smooth re entry
lessons.lecture: Most people ruin the return. They open with apology: sorry, sorry, the door, the dog, my mother. Your partner does not want your excuses. They want the scene back. So slide in low and pick up the exact thread you dropped: the counted number, the held hand, the unfinished instruction. Acknowledge the gap in three words, then resume the action without ceremony. *Thirty. Good.* Then keep going. The interruption becomes a beat in the rhythm, not a scar.
points: Acknowledge the gap in a few words at most.
Pick up the exact thread you left hanging.
Resume the action at once, no ceremony.
lessons.weak: omg so sorry i'm back!! the doorbell went, where were we?
lessons.strong: *slides back in close, hand returning to your chest* Thirty. Good. Now breathe out and give me the next thirty, slower this time, while I watch your mouth.
lessons.why: Three words close the gap, then the action resumes without a pause.

drill.goal: In every line, acknowledge the gap briefly and resume the exact action you left hanging.
drill.partner: Play Kai, shy but devoted. Hold the thread while they are gone. When they return, wait to be resumed. If they apologise too much, go quiet.
drill.coach: Each line that briefly names the gap and resumes the exact dropped action adds 25.

courses.name: Cross Language Chat
courses.blurb: Flirt across a language gap with short, clear lines and playful repair. Learn to keep a scene going when words get wobbly.

lessons.title: Plain and clear
lessons.lecture: Simple words are not small words. They are the ones that survive a bad translation and still land warm on the other side. Cut the clever clause, keep the verb, keep the want. Say what you see, say what you would like, say it short enough to be held in two languages at once. Clarity is its own kind of flirt: it tells them nothing gets lost with you.
points: Keep the verb and the want, cut the clever clause.
Short lines survive translation and still tease.
Say what you see before what you feel.
lessons.weak: *smiles* So, you know, I was sort of wondering if maybe you might want to dance or something, if you like.
lessons.strong: *leans close enough that the words do not need to travel* You. Me. Dance. Say yes and I stop talking.
lessons.why: Three plain words and a clear want, nothing lost in translation.

drill.goal: Write every line in plain, short words: one want, one verb, nothing that breaks in translation.
drill.partner: Reply in short, simple lines and let a word or two land oddly, as if translating as you go. Never guess the long sentence for them.
drill.coach: Each line that stays plain, short and clear, with one visible want, adds 25. Clauses that need untangling do not count.

lessons.title: Playful repair
lessons.lecture: A wobble is not a wall, it is a door. When a word lands wrong, do not apologise the scene to death. Grab the wrong word, hold it up, and make it funny. Name the mix-up, offer the true meaning, and let them in on the joke. Two people laughing at the same broken word are already closer than two people being careful.
points: Catch the wrong word before it cools.
Make the mix-up the joke, not the problem.
Offer the true meaning, warm and easy.
lessons.weak: *blushes* Sorry, my bad, that came out wrong. I meant the other thing. Forget it.
lessons.strong: *grins and holds up one finger* Wait. You say warm. I hear hot. Good news: both true. *steps in* I meant the dance. But stay for the hot.
lessons.why: Turns the slip into shared laughter, then lands the real meaning.

drill.goal: In every line, catch a wrong or wobbly word, joke about it, and give the true meaning.
drill.partner: Drop one word slightly wrong in your replies, without explaining it. Let them catch it. Reward each good repair with warmth.
drill.coach: Each line that names the wobble, makes it a joke and offers the real meaning adds 25. Apologies alone do not count.

lessons.title: Borrow and blend
lessons.lecture: The deepest flirt is proof you listened. Take a word of theirs, the one they gave you, and hand it back inside your own line. Use their language for one beat, or their phrase, or their nickname for a thing. It says: I keep what you say. Then blend it with yours. Two languages in one mouth is a kind of intimacy nothing else copies.
points: Take one word they gave you and reuse it.
Blend their word into a line of your own.
Prove you listened, do not announce it.
lessons.weak: *nods* Yes, I understood that. That is a nice word you used. I will remember it.
lessons.strong: *tips my head, repeats your word softly, then smiles* So that is what you call it. Then give me your hand. In my language, that means stay close.
lessons.why: Echoes their own word, then folds it into a new, warm meaning.

drill.goal: In every line, borrow one word or phrase the partner just used and blend it into your own reply.
drill.partner: Use one distinctive word or phrase per reply, in your own way of speaking. Do not repeat it for them. Notice when they give it back.
drill.coach: Each line that borrows a word or phrase the partner actually used and blends it into a new meaning adds 25. Plain echoes do not count.

courses.name: Humour as Foreplay
courses.blurb: Use wit to build heat. Learn to tease, banter, and land a joke that turns a chat playful and then pulls it somewhere warmer.

lessons.title: The gentle tease
lessons.lecture: A tease is a compliment wearing a smirk. You find the one true thing about them, the grin, the swagger, the terrible taste in drinks, and you hold it up to the light, warmly. The secret is aim: tease the thing they are proud of, never the thing they are shy about. Then leave a gap for the comeback. A tease they cannot answer is just a statement.
points: Tease the thing they are proud of, never the soft spot.
Keep it short enough to sting and sweet enough to smile at.
Leave a gap. A tease that invites a comeback is a door.
lessons.weak: *laughs* You're kind of a lot, you know that?
lessons.strong: *leans on the bar, eyes bright* You ordered that like a man who has never once been wrong about a drink. Prove it. One sip, and if you wince, I get the smug face all night.
lessons.why: It needles his confidence, flatters it, and hands him a comeback.

drill.goal: In every line, land one warm tease about something they are proud of, and leave room for a reply.
drill.partner: Play the confident bartender who gives as good as she gets. Bristle happily, fire back, and warm to whoever teases well.
drill.coach: Each line that teases something they are proud of, briefly and warmly, and invites a comeback adds 25.

lessons.title: Callback humour
lessons.lecture: The second laugh is always bigger than the first. Reuse a joke you both already own, the wince, the smug face, the drink they got wrong, and suddenly the two of you have a language nobody else in the room speaks. Callbacks work by proving you were paying attention. Drop the reference, let them catch it, and watch the private grin land. Inside jokes are foreplay with a memory.
points: Bring back a joke you have already both laughed at.
Keep the reference short. Let them do the catching.
Use it to make the room feel like it holds only two.
lessons.weak: Remember that thing from before? That was funny.
lessons.strong: *slides the same drink back across the bar, deadpan* Round two. Same confidence, new wince. The smug face is already warming up, so go on, prove the first one was a fluke.
lessons.why: The private reference lands the joke and marks the two of you as a unit.

drill.goal: In every line, call back a joke or detail from earlier and use it to pull the two of you closer.
drill.partner: Keep the running gags alive. Reference them back, laugh properly, and let the private language build.
drill.coach: Each line that reuses an earlier joke or detail, briefly, and makes the room feel private adds 25.

lessons.title: Joke to touch
lessons.lecture: Most people land the joke and then stand there, grinning, while the heat leaks out. Do not stand there. When the laugh peaks, that is your window: the giggle is an open door, and you walk through it with a hand, a lean, a line that turns the joke into wanting. Keep it smooth, one motion. Laugh, then close the gap, then say the warm thing quietly.
points: Move on the peak of the laugh, not after it.
Turn the joke into a touch: hand, lean, lowered voice.
One motion only. Laugh, close the gap, speak low.
lessons.weak: Ha, that was funny. Anyway, you're really pretty.
lessons.strong: *laughs, then leans in close, fingers brushing your wrist* See, this is the problem. The wince was charming, and now I am standing too near you and not sorry about it.
lessons.why: The laugh becomes a lean and a touch, and the joke turns warm.

drill.goal: In every line, land or ride a laugh and then pivot straight into a touch, a lean, or a low warm line.
drill.partner: Laugh freely and warmly, then hold still and let the touch land. Do not fill the pause. Make them close the gap.
drill.coach: Each line that moves from a laugh or joke straight into a touch, lean, or warm low line adds 25.
